1:1.t: What were the dimensions, then, of the temple of Solomon? Its length was sixty cubits, and its breadth twenty. And it was not turned to the east, that the worshippers might not worship the rising sun, but the Lord of the sun. And let no one marvel if, when the Scripture gives the length at forty cubits, I have said sixty. For a little after it mentions the other twenty, in describing the holy of holies, which it also names Dabir. Thus the holy place was forty cubits, and the holy of holies other twenty. And Josephus says that the temple had two storeys, and that the whole height was one hundred and twenty cubits. For so also the book of Chronicles indicates, saying, "And Solomon began to build the house of God. In length its first measure was sixty cubits, and its breadth twenty cubits, and its height one hundred and twenty; and he overlaid it within with pure gold."

The Prophet Jeremiah, for whom this prologue is written, was seen among the Hebrews to be certainly more rustic in style than Isaiah and Hosea and certain other prophets, but equal in meanings, which the same Spirit obviously prophesied. Furthermore, his simplicity of speech happened from the place in which he was born. For he was from Anathoth, which is up to today a village three miles distant from Jerusalem, a priest from priests and sanctified in his mother's womb, dedicating with her virginity a man of the Gospel to the Church of Christ. This boy began to prophesy the captivity of the city and Judea both not only by the Spirit, but also with eyes of flesh. The Assyrians had already transferred the ten tribes of Israel, and now colonies of gentiles had taken possession of their lands. For this reason he prophesied only in Judah and Benjamin, and he lamented the ruins of his city in a fourfold alphabet, which we have presented in the measure of the meter and in verses. […]

After the explanations of the twelve prophets, of Isaiah, of Daniel and of Ezekiel, I at last set my hand to Jeremiah, brother Eusebius, dedicating to you my short commentaries on him, so that you may join the man of the Gospel to Matthew the evangelist, whom I expounded many years ago, at your urging, in a compressed sense. And because the volume is very long and in most places is woven of a plain history, I advise your prudence of this: do not look in this work for a broad explanation, especially on those things which have already been said in the other prophets as well and which are clear to the understanding of themselves. And so I shall try to write by the hand of secretaries in such a way that nothing is lacking in the sense, though much is lacking in the words. I shall prepare for you the warp and the weft and the leashes; you yourself must make the most beautiful garment, so that you may be able not only to listen to us but also to teach others. […]

The words of Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah, of the priests who were in Anathoth, in the land of Benjamin. Which word of the Lord came to him in the days of Josiah, the son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign. And it came in the days of Jehoiakim, the son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, the son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the exile of Jerusalem in the fifth month. The other prophets, such as Isaiah, Hosea, Joel, were before the captivity of the ten tribes of Israel or of the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin; others after the captivity, such as Daniel, Haggai and Zechariah; but Jeremiah and Ezekiel wove their prophecy when the captivity was imminent, but one of them in the land of Judah, the other in Babylon. […]

1:2.t: God is ready at hand to do good, but slow to punish those who deserve punishment. Indeed, though He is able to bring punishment upon those condemned by Him in silence, without giving warning beforehand, He by no means does this; but even when He condemns, He speaks, since His purpose in speaking is that the one about to be condemned may turn back from the condemnation. Of these things one can take many examples from the Scriptures, but a few of those that fall to hand in the present suffice, so that we may also come to the aim of the passages set before us. For the Ninevites had become sinners and were condemned by God: "Yet three days, and Nineveh was about to be overthrown." God did not wish to condemn her in silence, but, giving them a place for repentance and conversion, He sent a Hebrew prophet, so that, when he had said, "Yet three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown," those who had been condemned might not be condemned, but, having repented, might obtain the mercy of God. […]

Jeremiah, like Isaiah, is one of the major prophets, not of the minor, like the others from whose writings I have just given extracts. He prophesied when Josiah reigned in Jerusalem and Ancus Martius at Rome, when the captivity of the Jews was already at hand; and he continued to prophesy down to the fifth month of the captivity, as we find from his writings. Zephaniah, one of the minor prophets, is put along with him, because he himself says that he prophesied in the days of Josiah; but he does not say till when. Jeremiah thus prophesied not only in the times of Ancus Martius but also in those of Tarquinius Priscus, whom the Romans had for their fifth king. For he had already begun to reign when that captivity took place.

1:5.t: Now, that the Word of God forms us in the womb, He says to Jeremiah, "Before I formed thee in the womb, I knew thee; and before thou wentest forth from the belly, I sanctified thee, and appointed thee a prophet among the nations." And Paul, too, says in like manner, "But when it pleased God, who separated me from my mother's womb, that I might declare Him among the nations." As, therefore, we are by the Word formed in the womb, this very same Word formed the visual power in him who had been blind from his birth; showing openly who it is that fashions us in secret, since the Word Himself had been made manifest to men: and declaring the original formation of Adam, and the manner in which he was created, and by what hand he was fashioned, indicating the whole from a part. For the Lord who formed the visual powers is He who made the whole man, carrying out the will of the Father.

The embryo therefore becomes a human being in the womb from the moment that its form is completed. The law of Moses, indeed, punishes with due penalties the one who shall cause an abortion, inasmuch as there exists already the rudiment of a human being that has imputed to it even now the condition of life and death, since it is already liable to the issues of both, although, by living still in the mother, it for the most part shares its own state with the mother.

Now after the prologue it is written that "the word of the Lord came to him," clearly to Jeremiah. And what does the word of the Lord say to him? Something exceptional beyond what was said to the rest of the prophets. For this we have found said to none of the prophets. Abraham was declared a prophet in the words, "he is a prophet and will pray for you," and yet God did not say to him: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb I sanctified you." But Abraham was sanctified at some later point, when he came forth from his land and from his kindred and from his father's house; from the promise Isaac was born, and we have not found even to him this saying spoken. And what need have I to enumerate what follows? Jeremiah obtained an exceptional gift, that of "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb I sanctified you."

Now whether it is said to Jeremiah or to the Savior: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you"—when you have read Genesis and observed the things said concerning the creation of the world, you will find that Scripture, most precisely in its terms, did not say "Before I made you in the womb I knew you." For when the one "according to the image" was created, "God said: Let us make man according to our image and likeness," He did not say: Let us form. But when He took "dust from the earth," He did not make the man, but "He formed the man," and "He set in paradise the man whom He had formed, to work it and to guard it." See the difference between making and forming, that the Lord, whether to Jeremiah or to the Savior, did not say: "Before I made you in the womb I knew you"; for that which is made does not come to be in a womb, but that which is formed from the dust of the earth, this is created in a womb.

"Before I formed you in the womb I knew you." […]

For unless he had grown old, he would not be a prophet. For it belongs to the aged to prophesy. Even if you should sometimes see a youth prophesying, do not hesitate to say of him that according to the inner man he has grown old, and therefore he is a prophet: in fine, Jeremiah, when he had heard: "Before I formed thee in the womb I knew thee, and before thou camest forth from the womb I sanctified thee, and made thee a prophet among the nations", answered: "I am a youth, and I know not how to speak". But He who granted him the grace that he should not be a boy, but should be an elder according to the inner man, said to him: "Say not, I am a youth". Otherwise, unless these things be so understood, what reason would there be that it should be said to a boy, whose age is youthful and untrained, "Say not, I am a youth"? — that is to say, do not say what is true. […]

We are not ignorant that some refer these things, as being too great for Jeremiah, to our Savior and Lord; and one must know that most of them are in accord with Him and can be referred to the Savior, which I will set forth; but a few of the things said to Jeremiah press hard upon the argument, being unable, as they can with respect to the many, to be fitted to the Savior. What, then, are the things that fit the Savior? "To all to whom I shall send you, you shall go, and according to all that I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid before their face, for I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord." These would not yet seem to be referred to the Savior; but what follows—"and the Lord stretched out His hand to me and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me: Behold, I have given my words into your mouth. Behold, I have set you this day over nations and kingdoms, to root out and to pull down"—presses hard upon the interpretation concerning Jeremiah. […]

Concerning Jeremiah, God says, "Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you." … If such terms are used in Scripture of things created, but the term ever is used of the Word, then it follows, O enemies of God, that the Son did not come out of nothing, nor is he to be numbered at all among created things, but he is the Father's image and eternal word, never having not existed, but never existing as the eternal radiance.

He is not ashamed to assume flesh, who is the creator of those very parts. Who tells us this? The Lord said to Jeremiah: "Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came forth out of the womb, I made you holy." If, then, in making humanity he was not ashamed of the contact, was he ashamed in making for his own sake the holy flesh, the veil of his Godhead? It is God who even now creates children in the womb, as it is written in Job, "Didn't you pour me out as milk and curdled me like cheese? You have clothed me with skin and flesh and have knit me together with bones and sinews." There is nothing polluted in the human frame unless a person defiles it with fornication and adultery. God, who made Adam, also made Eve. Both male and female were formed by God's hands. None of the parts of the body as formed from the beginning are polluted.

Just as the spiritual bosom of the Father is understood as a certain inner secret of paternal love and nature, in which the Son is always present, so also the spiritual bosom of the Father is the womb, the secret of the innermost mystery, from which the Son has proceeded as though from a generative womb. Finally, we read in diverse ways, sometimes the womb of the Father, sometimes his heart from which he uttered a word, sometimes his mouth from which justice proceeded, from which wisdom came forth, as he himself says: 'From the mouth of the Most High, I came forth.' (Sirach 24:5) Thus, just as we understand that generation from the Father, let us also understand the generation of Mary, the mother, when the womb of the mother is blessed, certainly the virginal womb of Mary, who gave birth to the Lord Jesus for us. Concerning which the Father says through the prophet Jeremiah: Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you (Jer. I, 5). […]
1:5.s: On the Blessings of the Patriarchs 11.51

1:5.t: To show them, however, the weakness and transparency of their objection, though it has no real relation to any truth, divine or human, I will prove to them that people have existed before they were born. Let them show that Jacob had not been appointed and ordained, even before he was born. While yet hidden in the secret chamber of his mother's womb, he supplanted his brother. Let them show that Jeremiah had not likewise been so, before his birth, "Before I formed you in your mother's womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the belly, I sanctified you, and appointed you for a prophet amongst the nations." … What do you [Arians] mean by your principle that "before he was begotten he did not exist"? Was the Father engaged for some time in conception, so that certain epochs passed away before the Son was begotten?

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you, I gave you as a prophet to the nations. Not that Jeremiah existed before his conception, as heresy surmises, but that the Lord foreknew that he would be, the Lord to whom things not yet made are already made, according to that which the Apostle says: who called the things which were not as if they were. And that he is sanctified in the womb we must take according to that saying of the Apostle: but when it pleased him, who set me apart from my mother's womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the nations. John the Baptist too is sanctified in the womb, and receives the Holy Spirit, and is moved in the womb, and speaks through his mother's mouth. […]

1:6.t: Someone of those who hear will say to me: Exercise the other argument as well, and try to present all the things written as fitting the Savior. Concerning the second matters, do not be anxious; for it is evident that the Savior rooted out the kingdoms of the devil and pulled down the nations, having destroyed the heathen life. Here, in what seems ill-omened as regards the Savior, exercise the argument somehow, how the Savior can say: "I do not know how to speak, for I am young," and what follows. Do you see that the argument is hard pressed? We know the Savior as Lord. We seek, according to the worth of the passage and according to the truth, to refer these things to the Savior. We must take the Scriptures as witnesses; for our undertakings are without witnesses, and expositions without witnesses are untrustworthy. […]

"And I said: O You who are, Master, Lord, behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am young. And the Lord said to me: Do not say that I am young, for to all to whom I shall send you, you shall go." We have often said that it is possible to be a child according to the inner man, even though one be in the aged stage of the body; and it is possible sometimes to be a child according to the outer man, but according to the inner a man. Such was Jeremiah, already having the grace from God while still being in the childhood stage as regards the body. Therefore the Lord says to him: "Do not say that I am young." And a sign that he is not young, but "a perfect man," is the "to all to whom I shall send you, you shall go, and according to all that I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid before their face." The Word of God knows that those who serve as ambassadors of the Word are in danger among their hearers; for, being convicted, men hate them, being rebuked, they persecute them. […]
Both Moses and Jeremiah, chosen by the Lord to declare the words of God to the people, avoided through modesty that which through grace they could do.
1:6.s: On the Duties of the Clergy 1.17.66

1:6.t: Therefore, you see, they had power either to speak or to refrain from speaking. For they were not bound by necessity, but were honored with a privilege. For this cause Jonah fled; for this cause Ezekiel delayed; for this cause Jeremiah excused himself. And God thrusts them not on by compulsion, but advising, exhorting, threatening; not darkening their mind; for to cause distraction and madness and great darkness, is the proper work of a demon: but it is God's work to illuminate and with consideration to teach things needful.

And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a boy. LXX: and I said, O Lord God, I do not know how to speak, for I am young. He shrinks from an office which, because of his age, he cannot sustain, with the same modesty with which Moses too says that he is of a thin and slender voice. But Moses is rebuked as one of great and robust age; to this one pardon is granted for his boyhood, which is adorned with modesty and shame.

1:7.t: But our present question may, perhaps, be solved in this way, that as every man is a man of God, simply because God created him, but not every man is called a man of God, but only he who has devoted himself to God, such as Elijah and those who are called men of God in the Scriptures, thus every man might be said in ordinary language to be sent from God, but in the absolute sense no one is to be spoken of in this way who has not entered this life for a divine ministry and in the service of the salvation of mankind. We do not find it said of any one but the saints that he is sent by God. It is said of Isaiah as we showed before; it is also said of Jeremiah, "To whomsoever I shall send thee thou shalt go"; and it is said of Ezekiel, "I send thee to nations that are rebellious and have not believed in Me." The examples, however, do not expressly speak of a mission from the region outside life into life, and as it is a mission into life that we are enquiring about, they may seem to have little bearing on our subject. […]
1:7.s: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 2:184

1:7.t: And the Lord said to me: Do not say: I am a boy, for to all that I shall send you to, you shall go, and all things whatsoever I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of their face, for I am with you to rescue you, says the Lord. 'Do not consider your age,' he says, '— for you have learned from another prophet who says: the gray hairs of a man are his wisdom —, let it only be of your will that you go forward; you will have me as companion, and with my help you will accomplish all things: open your mouth, and I will fill it. And do not consider the multitude of those to whom and against whom you are to speak, but me, who am with you to rescue you, says the Lord'. But the Lord delivers, not in the sense that the prophet is free of persecutions and distresses, since we read that he suffered many things, but so that by enduring he may overcome all things and not yield to distress.

1:9.t: The Scripture narrative goes on to explain in a popular manner that "they did not understand that he spoke to them about the Father," although they ought certainly to have known that the Father's words were uttered in the Son because they read in Jeremiah, "And the Lord said to me, 'Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.' "

We pray that words may be given us, as it is written in the book of Jeremiah that the Lord said to the prophet: "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth as fire. See, I have set you this day over the nations, and over the kingdoms, to root out and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, and to build and to plant."

"For I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord. And the Lord stretched out his hand toward me, and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me." Observe the differences between Jeremiah and Isaiah. Isaiah says, "Having unclean lips, in the midst of a people having unclean lips I dwell, and I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth." And since he confessed that he had no unclean deeds, but only trifling words (for up to that point he was a sinner), the Lord did not "stretch out his hand," but "one of the Seraphim touched his lips with his hand, and said: Behold, I have taken away your iniquities." But since this man was sanctified "from the womb," neither are tongs sent to him, nor a coal "from the altar" (he had nothing worthy of the fire), but the very hand of the Lord touched him. Therefore he says: "The Lord stretched out his hand toward me and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. Behold, I have set you this day over nations and kingdoms, to root up."

Surely these things were said for their sakes, that they might have no pretense of excuse. Since if this were not the case, what shall He have more than Isaiah? for he too saith the very same thing, "The Lord God giveth me the tongue of the learned, that I should know when I ought to speak a word." What more than Jeremiah? for he too when he was sent was inspired. What then Ezekiel? for he too, after eating the roll, so spake.
1:9.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 69

1:9.t: And the Lord put forth his hand and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me: Behold, I have given my words in your mouth. It is to be noted that here the hand of God is put forth to touch the mouth of the prophet, and it is said to him: behold, I have given my words in your mouth, whereas in Isaiah it is written: and one of the seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he had a coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar, and he touched my mouth and said: behold, this has touched your lips, and it will take away your iniquities and cleanse your sins. For there, because he was of firm and mature age, and he himself simply confesses that he has unclean lips and dwells in the midst of a people having unclean lips, one of the seraphim is sent, to touch his mouth not with a hand but with tongs and a coal, and to take away his iniquities and cleanse his sins. […]

1:10.t: Everyone who has received words from God and has the grace of the heavenly words has received them for the purpose of "rooting out and pulling down nations and kingdoms." But if it is said that everyone who has received words from God "roots out" "nations and kingdoms," do not understand the nations and the kingdoms in a bodily sense for me, but, having observed that human souls are ruled over by sin according to what is said by the apostle—"Let not sin therefore reign in our mortal body"—and seeing also the many kinds of sins, interpret figuratively the nations and the kingdoms as well, that is, the evil things that are in the souls of human beings, which are rooted out and pulled down by the words of God given whether to Jeremiah or to anyone whatever. And one can fit both the first things, those that press hard as regards the Savior, to Jeremiah, and the second things to Jeremiah, who knew how to interpret figuratively.

Who is so blessed as to root up, by the words given by God, the kingdoms which are many, which "the devil displays," being kingdoms of adverse powers, kingdoms corresponding to the sins? For it is written: "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. Behold, I have set you this day over nations and kingdoms, to root up." And just as there are kingdoms, so also there are nations; nor can anything be called a kingdom unless it be one having nations under it. For example, there is a kingdom of fornication, and the nations of fornication are each individual fornication. One kingdom is the generic sin itself of covetousness and defrauding, and there are many kingdoms among those who have many species of sins. Then, in the case of each of the sinners, understand for me the nations under the kingdom, so as to say that so-and-so has many nations of the kingdom according to fornication, so-and-so has many nations of the kingdom according to defrauding, according to slander, according to anger. […]

They refused to yield to the sentence of fifty bishops passed against them. They declined to resign the government of their Churches although the number of bishops assenting to the decree for their deposition was so many, on the alleged ground that they were not partakers of the Holy Ghost, and were not governing their Churches by the grace of God, but had clutched their dignity by the aid of human power, and through lust of vain glory. Now they are for receiving the men consecrated by these same persons as bishops. I should like you to ask them in my stead, (although they despise all mankind, as bereft of eyes, ears, and common sense), to perceive the inconsistency of their conduct, what sentiments they do really entertain in their own hearts. How can there be two bishops, one deposed by Euippius, and the other consecrated by him? Both are the actions of the same man. […]

And in the beginning of Jeremiah too something of the kind is written: Behold, I have put my words into your mouth; behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to root up and to undermine, and to destroy, and to build, and to plant. A very bad building is destroyed so that afterwards a good building may be put up; a wicked planting is rooted up so that a planting may be set in its place.

Behold, I have set you today over the nations and over the kingdoms, to pluck up and to destroy and to ruin and to scatter and to build and to plant. This, which we have added from the Hebrew, 'scatter' or 'put down', is not found in the LXX. And it must be considered that two joyful things follow four sad ones. For good things could not be built unless evil things had been destroyed, nor the best things planted unless the worst were rooted out. For every planting which the heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted out, and the building which does not have its foundation upon the rock but has been raised upon the sand is undermined and destroyed by the word of God. And that which Jesus will consume with the spirit of his mouth and will destroy by the coming of his presence, namely every sacrilegious and perverse doctrine, he will ruin forever. […]

In such wise Thou sayest, I build, as not to destroy: for some Thou destroyest and buildest not; and some whom Thou destroyest Thou dost rebuild. For unless there were some who were destroyed to be rebuilt, Jeremiah would not have written, “See, I have this day set thee to throw down and to build.” And indeed all who formerly worshipped images and stones could not be built up in Christ, without being destroyed as to their old error. While, unless some were destroyed not to be built up, it would not be written, “He shall destroy them, and not build them up.”

But you should know that we must make an effort with a twofold purpose in our exertion; both for the expulsion of vice, and for the attainment of virtue. And this we do not gather from our own conjecture, but are taught by the words of Him who alone knows the strength and method of His work: "Behold," He says: "I have set thee this day over the nations and over kingdoms, to root up, and to pull down, and to waste, and to destroy, and to build and to plant." He points out that for getting rid of noxious things four things are requisite; viz., to root up, to pull down, to waste, and to destroy: but for the performance of what is good, and the acquisition of what pertains to righteousness only to build and to plant. Whence it is perfectly evident that it is a harder thing to tear up and eradicate the inveterate passions of body and soul than to introduce and plant spiritual virtues.
1:10.s: The First Conference of Abbot Nesteros, Chapter 3

1:11.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: What do you see, Jeremiah? And I said: I see a watching rod, and the Lord said to me: You have seen well, for I will watch over my word, to perform it. For 'watching rod' the LXX translated 'staff of nut-wood'. We must therefore take pains that the Latin reader may briefly understand the Hebrew etymologian [etymology]. 'Saced' is said for 'nut', while 'watch' or 'watchful' or 'to watch' is called 'soced'. Hence also in later passages the watching leopard is set down under this name. So from the word for 'nut', because of the likeness of the word, the name has played upon the sense of 'watchful'. This indeed is written also in Daniel according to Theodotion, where from the trees schinu and prinu, namely the holm oak and the mastic, cutting asunder and sawing asunder is decreed for the adulterous elders. Besides, at the beginning of Genesis too, from 'man', which is called 'is', woman is called 'issa', as it were a kind of virago, because she was taken from man. […]

So too at the beginning of Jeremiah the word soced, if the accent is varied, signifies both nut (nux) and watchings (uigiliae). And it is said to him: What do you see, Jeremiah? And he answered: A nut. And the Lord said to him: You have seen well, for I will watch over my word, to perform it. Or rather this: it also has the etymology of the nut, in that God is going to watch and to repay the people what it deserves; this is the occasion of the saying.

In the mystery of prophetical revelation, Christ is symbolized especially by means of sight. The prophet saw "a branch of the watching-tree." Christ is symbolized through prophetical visions, and this in different ways: for one saw Christ as "a branch of the watching-tree," another saw Him "seated on a high and lofty throne," while yet another saw Him "dressed."

1:13.t: But let it set this candlestick of lamps in the south, that it may look toward the north. For, the light being kindled, that is, with a watchful heart, it ought always to look toward the north and to observe "him who is from the north"; just as the prophet also says that he sees "a kindled cauldron, or pot, and its face from the face of the north"; for "from the north are kindled the evils of all the earth". Let it therefore, watchful and solicitous and burning, ever behold the cunning devices of the devil and ever look from what quarter temptation is about to come, from what quarter the enemy rushes in, from what quarter the foe creeps up. For the Apostle Peter also says that "your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour".

And the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying: What do you see? And I said: I see a pot set on fire, and its face is from the face of the north. And the Lord said to me: From the north evils shall be opened — or shall blaze up — upon all the inhabitants of the earth. By certain degrees torments are assigned to sinners, so that they may come little by little to salvation: those who will not be amended when the rod strikes are sent into the bronze pot set on fire, of which Ezekiel writes more fully, which is kindled from the face of the north, signifying the Babylonian king and the city of Jerusalem.
In the mystery of prophetical revelation, Christ is symbolized especially by means of sight: the prophet saw "a boiling cauldron" and other things also.

1:14.t: And beautifully it is added: from the north evils shall blaze up upon all the inhabitants of the earth — either of the land of Judea or surely of the whole earth —, of whom it is written in Revelation too: woe upon all the inhabitants of the earth. For the saints are not inhabitants of the earth but strangers and sojourners, of whom one says: I am a stranger upon the earth and a sojourner, as all my fathers were, and another: few and very evil are my days, in which I sojourn on the earth. Hence Peter too writes his catholic epistle to the strangers and sojourners of Pontus, Galatia and Cappadocia. And according to the mystical senses Solomon says: the north wind is a harsh wind, but by name it is called right-handed, that is, by those who have grown stiff with its cold and have lost the warmth of faith.

1:15.t: For behold, I will call together all the families of the kingdoms of the north, says the Lord, and they shall come, and each one shall set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, and upon all its walls round about, and upon all the cities of Judah. And I will speak my judgments with them concerning all the wickedness of those who have forsaken me and have poured libations to foreign gods and have worshiped the work of their own hands. No one doubts that many nations, and the kings of the several nations, were subject to the Babylonian king; who, when Jerusalem was besieged, set round about, and especially at the outlets of the gates, their throne and tents, so that none of those who were shut in could break out; and that not only Jerusalem but all the cities of Judea were hemmed in by a like siege.

1:16.t: 'And when', he says, 'the city has been taken, then I will speak to them, that my judgments were right and that each one received what he deserved, not for the other vices to which the human condition is subject, but above all for idolatry, through which, forsaking me, they worshiped the works of their own hands'. Some take this place in a good sense, namely that those who have been boiled in the bronze pot through torments and purged will afterward be princes of Jerusalem, and that, after the Lord has had mercy on them, he will then reproach them because, having forsaken him, they venerated images. But this is a forced and perverse interpretation; let not an unlearned expounder raise a false charge.

1:17.t: You therefore gird up your loins, and arise, and speak to them all things which I command you. Job too is commanded to gird up his loins, and the apostles, with loins girded — which Elijah and John the Baptist mortified with girdles of skin —, to hold lamps in their hands, namely those of the preaching of the Gospel. Whoever therefore is to speak the words of God ought to gird up his loins, knowing that all the strength of the devil is in the loins, and that the righteous man says in the psalms: my loins are filled with illusions. And when he has girded his loins, let him hear that which is written: arise, you who sleep, and be lifted up, and Christ will enlighten you, so that, always watching and rising up from sleep, he may speak the things which God has commanded him.

Do not be afraid of their face; for I will not make you fear their countenance, or, as the Seventy and the other translators have: lest perhaps I make you fear. And the sense according to our translation is: 'do not be afraid of their face; for with me as your helper you will not be able to fear them'; according to the Seventy: 'do not be afraid of their face, have confidence in my command; for if you do not offer what you have, so as to cease to fear, I will forsake you and hand you over to fear, and I shall in a manner seem to make you fear, while I leave you to dread'. And this signifies that truth is always bitter, and that the multitude of men is not to be feared, who, when rebuked, do not bear correction but lay snares for him by whom they are corrected. And what follows according to the Seventy: for I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord, is not found in the Hebrew. […]

1:18.t: For I have given you today — or behold, I have set you on this day — as a fortified city, as an iron pillar and as a bronze wall over all the land: to the kings of Judah, to its princes and to the priests and to the people of the land. And they shall fight against you and shall not prevail, for I am with you, says the Lord, to deliver you. The divine word describes why the prophet ought not to fear. I, he says, have set or have given you today — that is, in the present life, while it is called today — as a very strong city, not as a single house, nor a tower or some walls, but as a whole city, which, set upon a mountain, cannot be hid, of which it is written: glorious things are spoken of you, city of God, and: I am a strong city, a city which is besieged. And as a pillar, he says, of iron, of which the Apostle writes: the pillar and ground of the truth. Hence Peter and John, who were reputed pillars of the Church, gave to Paul and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship. […]

2:1.t: The prophets say, "And the Word of the Lord came to me." … All these messages proscribe in every light the Arian heresy and signify the eternity of the Word, and that he is not foreign but proper to the Father's essence.

2:2.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, saying. This is not found in the Seventy, but was added under asterisks from the edition of Theodotion, who translated the Hebrew word 'carath', for which we said 'cry' or 'preach', as 'read'. For by its ambiguity it signifies reading and crying out and preaching. But the ears of Jerusalem we ought to take as the ears of its inhabitants.

Thus says the Lord: I have remembered you, pitying your youth and the love of your betrothal, when you followed me in the wilderness, in a land that is not sown. LXX: thus says the Lord: I have remembered the mercy of your youth and the love of your perfection. This is said more fully in Ezekiel, when the Lord joins Jerusalem to himself in marriage and, under the person of a wife, unites her to his embraces, or, to show a more ardent affection, calls her a girl and a young maiden and betrothed; for what we have not yet obtained, we desire the more to obtain. 'When', he says, 'you followed me in the solitude, and in the manner of betrothal gifts and a dowry I distributed to you the ornaments of the law and the necklaces of words'. And all this he refers not to her merit but to his own mercy, through which love too followed. This also, which we have set down: in the wilderness, in a land that is not sown, is not found in the Seventy.

2:3.t: Israel is holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his crops; all who devour him shall transgress; evils shall come upon them, says the Lord. When he calls Israel the firstfruits of the Lord's crops, he shows that the people gathered from the nations comes after the firstfruits, according to that which is written in another place: Remember your congregation, which you have possessed from the beginning. But firstfruits are owed to the priests and not to enemies. What follows: all who devour him shall transgress; evils shall come upon them, says the Lord, has this sense: just as those who devour the firstfruits, being in no way of priestly stock, are guilty of a crime, so those who defile Israel will be subjected to evils, according to that which the holy man says in Psalm 26 (27): While the harmful draw near against me to eat my flesh, those who trouble me, my enemies themselves have become weak and have fallen. […]

2:4.t: Hear the word of the Lord, house of Jacob and all the families of the house of Israel. Thus says the Lord: What iniquity did your fathers find in me, that they went far from me and walked after vanity and became vain? Another prophet too testifies to this sense: My people, what have I done to you, and how have I been troublesome to you? Answer me; for I brought you out of the land of Egypt and freed you from the house of servants. Now both names — Israel too — are set down, not according to the two and ten tribes, but for the whole people, since Jacob himself too was afterwards called Israel. And he traces the offense from the fathers, not so that the sins of the fathers are imputed to the sons, but so that the sons too, having the likeness of their fathers, are punished both for their own crime and for their parents'. We often read that God has mercy on sons for the sake of holy fathers. […]

2:5.t: And elsewhere again, "What transgression have your fathers found in me?" And again, "O my people, what have I done unto thee? and wherein have I grieved thee?" showing their thankless disposition, and that when in the enjoyment of all things, they requited it by the contraries; but here He expresses it with yet greater force. For He doth not plead, Himself, saying, "What ought I to have done that I have not done?" but brings in themselves to judge, that nothing hath been wanting, and to condemn themselves.
2:5.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 68:2

2:6.t: And they did not say: Where is the Lord, who made us go up from the land of Egypt, who led us across through the wilderness, through a land uninhabitable and pathless, through a land of thirst and the image of death, through a land in which no man walked nor did a human being dwell? For 'human being' the Seventy translated 'son of man', and for 'image of death' 'shadow of death' was added from Theodotion. Since this is plain according to the history, this must be considered according to anagōgēn [the higher, spiritual sense]: that as long as we are in this world and are being led out of Egypt, we go up little by little, and first we cross deserts and a land uninhabitable, which the holy man ought not to inhabit, and pathless, to show the difficulty of the journey; […]

2:7.t: And I brought you into the land of Carmel, that you might eat its fruit and its good things, and having entered you defiled my land and made my inheritance an abomination. 'For the toil of a very hard journey I gave you an abundance of all things'; for this is what 'Carmelus' signifies, which in Hebrew is called 'Chermel' and in our language sounds as 'knowledge of circumcision'. And as that people polluted and violated with idolatry the holy land, fertile in all things, so we, receiving the knowledge of the true circumcision, eat its fruit and, if negligence creeps in, defile the land of God and make his inheritance abominable.

2:8.t: The priests did not say: Where is the Lord? And those who held the law did not know me, and the shepherds transgressed against me, and the prophets prophesied by Baal and followed idols. After such great benefits they turned the privileges of their dignity into contempt, so that the priests did not seek the Lord, the teachers of the law, who ought to have taught others, did not know him, and the shepherds became transgressors through negligence, and the prophets, who discourse among the peoples, speak not for God but for an idol, and venerate their own fabrications. These words must be used against the teachers of our own order, who devour the people of God like bread for food and by their evil works do not call upon the Lord.

2:9.t: Therefore I will still contend with you in judgment, says the Lord, and with your sons I will dispute. Lest he seem to strike through power, he contends by reason as with equals, according to that which David sings and the Apostle adopts: that you may be justified in your words and may prevail when you are judged. And in setting down 'still', he testifies that he has often done so; and in adding 'with your sons', he shows a like obstinacy also in the sons of the wicked. And covertly he signifies that their sons too, at the coming of the Lord, followed the ancient denial of God.

2:10.t: But they forsook Him, and worshipped idols, as Jeremiah said concerning them:—Go to the distant isles, and send to Kedar, and consider well and see, whether there has been (anything) like this, whether the nations change their gods, those that are no gods. But My people has changed My honour for that which is not profitable. Be astonished, ye heavens, at this; and quake and fear greatly, saith the Lord; because My people have done two wickednesses; they have abandoned Me, the fountain of the water of life, and they have gone and dug for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns which cannot hold water. For the broken cisterns are the fear of images and idols. And He calls the heavens to astonishment, because they worshipped the hosts of the heavens. And the heavens shall receive as a penalty, that they shall be rolled up as a scroll, and all the host of them shall fall down.

Even that last horror has come to pass which I shrink from saying, and yet cannot leave unsaid, for it is as a burning and blazing fire in my bones, and I am undone and cannot endure. You have taken the members of Christ and made them the members of a harlot. This is an evil with which no other can be matched. This outrage in life is new. “For pass over the Isles of Chittim and see; and send unto Chedar and consider diligently, and see if there be such a thing. Hath a nation changed their gods which are yet no gods.” But the virgin has changed her glory, and her glory is in her shame. The heavens are astonished at this, and the earth is horribly afraid, saith the Lord, for the virgin has committed two evils; she has forsaken Me, the true and holy Bridegroom of holy souls, and has betaken herself to an impious and lawless destroyer of body and soul alike. She has revolted from God, her Saviour, and yielded her members servants to uncleanness and to iniquity. […]

Pass over to the islands of Kittim and see, and send to Kedar and consider earnestly, and see whether such a thing has been done: if a nation has changed gods — or its gods — ; and surely they are not gods. But my people has changed its glory into an idol or, for that from which nothing will profit it. He makes a comparison of a thing that is incomparable, and sets the true God beside lying ones. 'Go', he says, 'to the islands of Kittim', which we ought to take as those either of Italy or of the western regions, from the fact that the island of Cyprus, in which a city is called by this name, is near the land of Judea; from it too came Zeno, the chief of the Stoics. Kedar, however, is a region of the wilderness and of the Ishmaelites, whom they now call Saracens, against which a prophecy of this very prophet is woven in his final parts, and which David mentions, saying: I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner. […]

2:11.t: For since you are not persuaded out of the Scriptures, I am compelled to shame you by them that are without. This God also did unto the Jews, when He said, "Go ye forth unto the Isles of Chittim, and send unto Kedar, and know if nations will change their gods; which yet are no gods." And to the brutes likewise He sends us oftentimes, saying on this wise, "Go to the ant, thou sluggard, and emulate her ways:" and "go forth to the bee."
2:11.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 17:6

2:11.t: And what wonder? for He permitted opinions erroneous, and unworthy of Himself, to prevail, as that He was a body formerly, and that He was visible. In opposition to which He says, "God is a Spirit." Again, that He delighted in sacrifices, which is far from His nature. And He utters words at variance with His declarations of Himself, and many such things. For He nowhere considers His own dignity, but always what will be profitable to us. And if a father considers not his own dignity, but talks lispingly with his children, and calls their meat and drink not by their Greek names, but by some childish and barbarous words, much more doth God. Even in reproving He condescends, as when He speaks by the prophet, "Hath a nation changed their gods?", and in every part of Scripture there are instances of His condescension both in words and actions.

2:12.t: Let us further inquire whether the Lord took any care to foreshadow the water [of baptism] and the cross. Concerning the water, indeed, it is written, in reference to the Israelites, that they should not receive that baptism which leads to the remission of sins, but should procure another for themselves. The prophet therefore declares, "Be astonished, O heaven, and let the earth tremble at this, because this people hath committed two great evils: they have forsaken Me, a living fountain, and have hewn out for themselves broken cisterns. Is my holy hill Zion a desolate rock? For ye shall be as the fledglings of a bird, which fly away when the nest is removed."
2:12.s: The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter XI

2:12.t: For where the Church is, there is the Spirit of God; and where the Spirit of God is, there is the Church, and every kind of grace; but the Spirit is truth. Those, therefore, who do not partake of Him, are neither nourished into life from the mother's breasts, nor do they enjoy that most limpid fountain which issues from the body of Christ; but they dig for themselves broken cisterns out of earthly trenches, and drink putrid water out of the mire, fleeing from the faith of the Church lest they be convicted; and rejecting the Spirit, that they may not be instructed.

Reproof is the bringing forward of sin, laying it before one. This form of instruction God employs as necessary in the highest degree by reason of the feebleness of the faith of many. For he says by Isaiah, "You have forsaken the Lord and have provoked the holy One of Israel to anger." He says also by Jeremiah: "Heaven was astonished at this, and the earth shuddered exceedingly. My people have committed two evils. They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and have hewn out for themselves broken cisterns that will not be able to hold water."

Who that witnessed these things, or that has merely heard of them, will not be greatly amazed, and cry aloud unto the Lord, saying, 'Wilt Thou make a full end of Israel?' Who that is acquainted with these proceedings, will not with good reason cry out and say, 'A wonderful and horrible thing is done in the land;' and, 'The heavens are astonished at this, and the earth is even more horribly afraid.' The fathers of the people and the teachers of the faith are taken away, and the impious are brought into the Churches? Who that saw when Liberius, Bishop of Rome, was banished, and when the great Hosius, the father of the Bishops, suffered these things, or who that saw so many Bishops banished out of Spain and the other parts, could fail to perceive, however little sense he might possess, that the charges against Athanasius also and the rest were false, and altogether mere calumny? […]

Be astonished, O heavens, at this, and, its gates, be utterly desolate, says the Lord; for my people has done two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns, which cannot hold waters. LXX: the heaven was astonished at this and shuddered beyond measure and exceedingly, the rest likewise. The heaven, to which it was said: Give heed, O heaven, and I will speak and: Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, seeing the precepts of God trampled underfoot, shudders and cannot hide its astonishment. For every creature groans together and grieves together over the sins of men. Now the people of God has done two contrary things: first, that they forsook God, who is the fountain of life and gave the precept, saying: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt; second, what is written in the same place: You shall have no gods in my sight; […]

2:13.t: And our hearts are thus circumcised from evil, so that we are happy to die for the name of the good Rock, which causes living water to burst forth for the hearts of those who by Him have loved the Father of all, and which gives those who are willing to drink of the water of life. But you do not comprehend me when I speak these things; for you have not understood what it has been prophesied that Christ would do, and you do not believe us who draw your attention to what has been written. For Jeremiah thus cries: "Woe unto you! because you have forsaken the living fountain, and have digged for yourselves broken cisterns that can hold no water. Shall there be a wilderness where Mount Zion is, because I gave Jerusalem a bill of divorce in your sight?"

Hence also Jacob, as I remarked before, being himself a type of Christ, had married the two handmaids of his two free wives, and of them begat sons, for the purpose of indicating beforehand that Christ would receive even all those who amongst Japheth's race are descendants of Canaan, equally with the free, and would have the children fellow-heirs. And we are such; but you cannot comprehend this, because you cannot drink of the living fountain of God, but of broken cisterns which can hold no water, as the Scripture says. But they are cisterns broken, and holding no water, which your own teachers have digged, as the Scripture also expressly asserts, "teaching for doctrines the commandments of men."

Nor do we receive that useless baptism of cisterns, for it has nothing to do with this baptism of life. Wherefore also God has announced that you have forsaken Him, the living fountain, and digged for yourselves broken cisterns which can hold no water.

By reason, therefore, of this laver of repentance and knowledge of God, which has been ordained on account of the transgression of God's people, as Isaiah cries, we have believed, and testify that that very baptism which he announced is alone able to purify those who have repented; and this is the water of life. But the cisterns which you have dug for yourselves are broken and profitless to you. For what is the use of that baptism which cleanses the flesh and body alone? Baptize the soul from wrath and from covetousness, from envy, and from hatred; and, lo! the body is pure.

When we were together in council, dearest brethren, we read your letter which you wrote to us concerning those who seem to be baptized by heretics and schismatics, (asking) whether, when the), come to the Catholic Church, which is one,4 they ought to be baptized. On which matter, although you yourselves hold thereupon the truth and certainty of the Catholic rule, yet since you have thought that of our mutual love we ought to be consulted, we put forward our opinion, not as a new one,5 but we join with you in equal agreement, in an opinion long since decreed by our predecessors, and observed by us,-judging, namely, and holding it for certain that no one can be baptized abroad outside the Church, since there is one baptism appointed in the holy Church. And it is written in the words of the Lord, "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out broken cisterns, which can hold no water."

Friends godly and well beloved, do, I implore you, beware of the shepherds of the Philistines; let them not choke your wills unawares; let them not befoul the purity of your knowledge of the faith. This is ever their object, not to teach simple souls lessons drawn from Holy Scripture, but to mar the harmony of the truth by heathen philosophy. Is not he an open Philistine who is introducing the terms “unbegotten” and “begotten” into our faith, and asserts that there was once a time when the Everlasting was not; that He who is by nature and eternally a Father became a Father; that the Holy Ghost is not eternal? He bewitches our Patriarch’s sheep that they may not drink “of the well of water springing up into everlasting life,” but may rather bring upon themselves the words of the prophet, “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water;” […]

‘He hath opened a pit and dug it.’ We do not find the name of ‘pit’ (lákkos) ever assigned in the divine Scriptures in the case of something good, nor a ‘well’ of water (phréar) in the case of something bad. That into which Joseph was thrown by his brothers is a pit (lákkos). And there is a slaughter ‘From the firstborn of Pharao unto the firstborn of the captive woman that was in the prison (lákkon).’ And in the psalms: ‘I am counted among them that go down to the pit (lákkon).’ And in Jeremia it is said: ‘They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have digged to themselves cisterns (lákkous), broken cisterns, that can hold no water.’ Moreover, in Daniel the lions’ den (lákkos), into which Daniel was thrown, is described. On the other hand, Abraham digs a well (phréar); so do the sons of Isaac; and Moses, coming to a well (phréar), rested. We also receive the order from Solomon to drink water from our own cisterns (angeíōn) and from the streams of our wells (phreátōn). […]

Yea, rather with us is the living water, the very water which springeth from Christ; but thou, separated from the everlasting Fountain, whence receivest thou thy birth? Nor hath the Holy Spirit departed from the chief mother; whence then came He to thee? Unless perchance He hath followed one that is in strife, and abandoning so many priests, nor pleased to abide in His consecrated dwelling-place, hath preferred the broken cisterns of an adulterated fountain? Whence have your people the Spirit, not having been sealed by an anointed priest? Whence the water, being separated from its mother's womb? Whence renewal, who have lost the cradle of Bridal Peace?
2:13.s: Letter 3: Against the Treatise of the Novatians

2:13.t: So she went down to the fountain of wisdom, whether the Church or the soul, to fill her entire vessel and to draw from the pure disciplines of wisdom that the Jews refused to draw from the flowing fountain. Who is this fountain, listen to the one saying: "They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water." To this fountain ran the thirsting soul of the prophets, as David also says: "My soul thirsts for the living God"; so that it could quench its thirst with the richness of divine knowledge and wash away the blood of foolishness with the flow of spiritual waters.

So when the whole world was parched with the drought of Gentile superstition, then came that dew of the heavenly visits on the fleece. But after that the lost sheep of the house of Israel (whom I think that the figure of the Jewish fleece shadowed forth), after that those sheep, I say, "had refused the fountain of living water," the dew of moistening faith dried up in the breasts of the Jews, and that divine Fountain turned away its course to the hearts of the Gentiles. Whence it has come to pass that now the whole world is moistened with the dew of faith, but the Jews have lost their prophets and counsellors.

Between a well and a pit, that is, a cistern, there is this difference: a well has perpetual waters, flowing from a living spring; a cistern, which keeps water cool, holds waters that are external and brought in from outside. Hence God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves cisterns which cannot hold water.

Iniquity lies to itself either by corrupting the nature you have made and ordained or by perverting it. It lies to itself when it practices an immoderate use of things permitted or when it burns for things forbidden to that use which is against nature. It lies to itself when convicted, raging with heart and voice against you as it kicks against the goads, or when—breaking through the pale of human society—they audaciously rejoice in private cliques or divisions on the basis of whether they have been pleased or offended. These things happen whenever you are abandoned and whenever, from a self-willed pride, they choose to align themselves instead with something false that they cherish instead of you, O Fountain of life, the one, true Creator and Ruler of the universe.

The arrogance of pride, the pleasure of lust and the poison of curiosity are the motions of a dead soul. It is not that it is dead in such a way as to lack all movement; rather, it dies by "abandoning the fountain of life" and thus is taken up by the transitory world and is conformed to it.

2:14.t: Is Israel a slave, or one born in the house? I think it was from this passage that the Jews, puffed up with pride, said to the Savior: We are the seed of Abraham and have never been slaves to anyone; how do you say: You shall be free?, not knowing that everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin, and that each one serves him by whom he is overcome. Born, then, of Abraham, the friend of God, by their own vice they became as it were sons of Ham, to whom it was said: Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a slave to his brothers.

Why then has he become a prey? Lions have roared over him and given their voice; they have made his land a wilderness, and his cities have been burned, and there is none who dwells in them. The divine word asks so that it may itself reply. And by lions he means the princes of Babylon, who made his land a wilderness and destroyed his cities by fire. Or at any rate, according to anagōgēn, let us understand the lions as the adverse powers or the leaders of the heretics, who, desolating the land of the Church, have laid waste all its cities with heretical fire, and with that fire of which it is written: All committing adultery, their hearts are like an oven. For they truly give their voice, and in this same prophet, under the person of the partridge, they cry out and gather what they did not bring forth, and they make riches not with judgment. But for this reason its cities have been laid waste and destroyed, because they do not have God as their inhabitant, as Scripture says: and there is none who inhabits them.

2:16.t: The sons also of Memphis and Tahpanhes have debauched you even to the crown of the head. Has not this been done to you because you forsook the Lord your God at the time when he was leading you along the way? This, which we said: at the time when he was leading you along the way, is not found in the Seventy. Now he names two very great cities of Egypt, Memphis and Tahpanhes, and says that their sons debauched Israel even to the crown of the head, in that sense in which Isaiah set it down: From the sole of the foot even to the crown of the head there is no soundness in him. And so great was the lust of the Egyptians, who are great of flesh, that they spared no member but debauched everything. According to the letter, refer it to the idols of the Egyptians; according to the spiritual understanding, to the teachers of perverse doctrine, who pollute the purity of the Church with their own filthiness. […]

2:18.t: Woe to you, devil, or Antichrist, or perverse doctrine of the heretics, who with your teachings and your turbid potion make drunk the peoples of the deceived, and overturn their former faith, giving them a potion not from Siloam, not from the Jordan, not from the springs of Israel, but from the brook Kidron, and from the river of Egypt, of which Jeremiah says: What have you to do with the way of Egypt, that you should drink the water of Gihon? For this in the Hebrew is written sior, that is, turbid and muddy; for although the rivers of Egypt are believed to go out from the paradise of the Scriptures, yet because they are trampled by the feet of Pharaoh, they have lost their splendor, and, defiled by the Egyptian mud, have been turned into torrents, at having escaped which the holy one rejoices, saying: Our soul has passed through the torrent.

And now what do you want on the way of Egypt, to drink the water of Sior? And what have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the water of the river? For 'Sior' we translated 'turbid', which is what the Hebrew word signifies; for it the common edition has 'Geon'. Since, then, he had set down above the sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes, who debauched Israel even to the crown of the head, he now names Egypt itself more plainly. And no one doubts that the Nile has turbid waters, and that by the river of the Assyrians he signifies the Euphrates, as Scripture says that the land of promise extends from the torrent of Egypt even to the great river Euphrates. […]

But if thou remainest in the desert, thou wilt not be tested. For thou seest no woman in the desert nor anything that does harm to thy behaviour, nor [doest thou hear] evil sounds. What hast thou to do with the ways of Egypt and with drinking water from the Nile? Understand what I say.

It is fitting first to take in Scripture, then to chew it, and finally to assimilate it. What does it serve a man to drink dirty water? "And now what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the troubled water?" Drink instead healthy water, that is, wisdom.

2:19.t: The Lord has therefore endured all these things on our behalf, in order that we, having been instructed by means of them all, may be in all respects circumspect for the time to come, and that, having been rationally taught to love God, we may continue in His perfect love: for God has displayed long-suffering in the case of man's apostasy; while man has been instructed by means of it, as also the prophet says, "Thine own apostasy shall heal thee;" God thus determining all things beforehand for the bringing of man to perfection, for his edification, and for the revelation of His dispensations, that goodness may both be made apparent, and righteousness perfected, and that the Church may be fashioned after the image of His Son, and that man may finally be brought to maturity at some future time, becoming ripe through such privileges to see and comprehend God.

Your malice shall reprove you — or your transgression shall instruct you — and your turning away shall rebuke you. Know and see that it is an evil and bitter thing that you have forsaken the Lord your God and that the fear of me is not with you, says the Lord God of hosts. It must be noted that malice too, or transgression, after it has glutted the transgressor and, like the quails, has come to the point of nausea, instructs the one who does repentance; and he is commanded to see what he has forsaken, what he has followed, and how, spurning good and sweet things, he has chosen evil and bitter ones. And all this happened because he forsook the Lord his God, and the fear of him is not with him. For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; and because he did not have it, he is handed over to evil and bitterness.

"Know and see that it is evil and bitter that you have forsaken the Lord your God, and that the fear of me is not in you." If you do not fear God, you have lost grace, you have lost justice, and you have lost true wisdom. "See" therefore "how evil and bitter it is that you have forsaken the Lord your God." Where there is no fear, there is neither wisdom nor justice nor grace.

2:20.t: From of old you have broken my yoke — or your —, you have burst my bonds — or your — and said: I will not serve. For on every lofty hill and under every leafy tree you lay prostrate as a harlot or there you poured yourself out in fornication. He speaks to Israel as to a harlot, because she broke the marriage covenant and said: I will not serve — 'the Lord' or 'the husband' is understood —, but on every lofty hill and under every leafy tree lay prostrate to idolatry; for pleasant and lofty places are always dedicated to idols. This can also be said to him who, a Christian from the beginning and in part instructed in the sacred letters, afterwards, through desire for secular literature, which is signified in the hills, and for the pleasant things of eloquence, which are shown in the leafy trees, prostrates himself to demons, who, under the pretext of learning and lofty knowledge, pollute the souls of believers and make them spread their feet for every passer-by.

2:21.t: "God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living; for he created all things that they might exist, and the generative forces of the world are salutary, and in them there is no poison of destruction, nor is the kingdom of Hades upon the earth." Then, passing over a little of the text, I will say whence death entered: "but by the envy of the devil death entered into the world." If, then, God has made everything that is best concerning us, while we ourselves have created for ourselves wickedness and sins — for this reason here too the beginning of the reading in the prophet says, as it were in a manner of raising a difficulty, to those who have acquired in their soul a bitterness contrary to the sweetness which God fashioned for it: "How were you turned to bitterness, O alien vine?" As if it said: God did not make lameness, but made all men sound of foot; what, then, has become the cause of those who are lamed? […]

Just as Paul too glories that the observances of the law, and all the glory of the Jewish institution, were to him only as dung, that he might be found in Christ not having his own righteousness which is of the law, but the righteousness which is of God. As Paul, therefore, having received the faith of Christ, did not keep his own vineyard — namely, the observances of the Jewish tradition; and perhaps he did not keep it because, when the true vine had been planted by God, it was turned into the bitterness of a strange vine, and their vineyard was already the vine of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah, and the cluster of bitterness in them, and their wine the fury of dragons, and the incurable fury of asps.
2:21.s: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 2

2:21.t: Let us try, therefore, to discuss the third exposition also, according to the moral topic. If there is anyone who, while evils increase and vices overflow, is able to turn himself away from fluid and perishing and falling things and to hear the word of God and the heavenly precepts, this one builds within his heart an ark of salvation and consecrates within himself, so to speak, a library of the divine word, and places in it length and breadth and height — faith, charity, and hope. He stretches the faith of the Trinity to the length of life and immortality, he founds the breadth of charity by the affection of pardon and kindness, he raises the height of hope to the heavenly and lofty things; for, walking upon the earth, he has his "conversation in the heavens." But the sum of his acts he brings back to one. For he knows that "all indeed run, but one receives the prize" — namely, the one who has not been manifold through the variety of thoughts and the instability of mind. […]

Sin is a terrible thing, and the most grievous disease of the soul is iniquity, which corrupts the fiber of the soul and makes it liable to eternal fire. It is an evil freely chosen, the product of the will. The prophet clearly declares that we sin of our own free will: "I had planted you, a choice vine of fully tested stock; how could you turn into bitterness, a spurious vine?" The planting was good, but the fruit coming from the will is evil. So the planter is blameless, but the vine will burn with fire since it was planted for good and bore evil fruit of its own will.

Learn this also, that before the soul comes into the world, it has committed no sin. But though we came into the world sinless, we now of our own choice commit sin.… Remember also how God again accuses them and says, "I have planted you a choice vine, wholly of pure seed; how then have you turned degenerate and become a wild vine?"

Yet if the husband's power allures you, pray tell me who it was that spoke in the prophet, saying, "O Lord, make it known to me that I may know. Then I saw their thoughts. I was led as a harmless lamb to the slaughter and knew it not. They took counsel together against me, saying, Come, let us throw wood into his bread." For if the Son here spoke of the mystery of his coming incarnation—because it was blasphemous to suppose that the words are spoken concerning the Father—then surely it is the Son who speaks in an earlier passage: "I have planted you as a fruitful vine—how did you become bitter, and a wild vine?"

And they gave him wine mixed with gall to drink, and when he had tasted it he would not drink. God speaks to Jerusalem: I planted you a true vine; how have you turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine? A bitter vine makes bitter wine, which it gives the Lord Jesus to drink, so that what is written might be fulfilled: They gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. But what is said: when he had tasted it he would not drink, indicates that he tasted indeed the bitterness of death for us, but on the third day he rose again.

But I planted you a choice vineyard, wholly a true seed; how have you been turned for me into what is crooked, a strange vineyard? LXX: But I planted you a fruitful vineyard, wholly true; how have you been turned into bitterness, a strange vine? For the 'choice' or 'fruitful' vineyard the Hebrew has 'sorec', which is set down in the song of Isaiah. Now it is a kind of the finest vine, with which slip the Lord says he planted Israel too, and he marvels how the true seed and choice vineyard has been turned into bitterness and has therefore become a strange vineyard. And let no one be secure, if both the planting of the Lord and the true seed and the vineyard sorec is so changed by its own vice that through bitterness it withdraws from the Lord and becomes a strange vine. […]

All they that refuse Christ for King become strangers. Wherefore strangers are they made? Because even that vine, though by Him planted, when it had become sour what heard it? “Wherefore hast thou been turned into sourness, O alien vine?” It hath not been said, My vine: because if Mine, sweet; if sour, not Mine; if not Mine, surely alien.

2:22.t: After this let us look at the words: "though you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soapwort for yourself, you are stained in your iniquities before me, says the Lord." Did some sinful soul suppose that, by taking nitre and washing herself with perceptible nitre, she would cease from the stain and cease from sin? And did someone imagine that, by taking this soapwort which springs up from the earth, and washing and scrubbing himself with it, his soul would be cleansed — since here the word says to her who was turned to bitterness and became an alien vine: "though you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soapwort for yourself, you are stained in your iniquities before me, says the Lord"? But one must know that the word has every power; and just as it has the power of every writing, so the word has the power of every medicine, and it is the power of everything that cleanses, and is most effective for scouring: "for the word of God is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword." […]

If you wash yourself with nitre and multiply for yourself the herb borith, you are stained with your iniquity before me, says the Lord God. For 'herb borith', which we have rendered as it is set down in the Hebrew, the Seventy translated poan, to signify the fullers' herb, which, after the manner of the province of Palestine, grows in green and moist places and has the same power for washing away dirt as nitre does; but our 'nitre' and 'fullers' herb' is repentance. The preaching of the Church too, which reproves and rebukes and corrects the offender, has the likeness of a more biting nitre. He who is stained with the light dirt of sins is cleansed by lighter admonitions. But grave sins, which drag to death, can be washed away neither by nitre nor by the herb borith, but need heavier torments. For each one's work, of what sort it is, the fire will test, and in fire it will be revealed. […]

2:23.t: How do you say: I am not defiled, I have not gone after the Baals? See your ways in the vale or valley, which in Hebrew is called 'ge' and by the Seventy is translated polyandrion, which in our language can be called 'the tomb of a multitude'. 'In vain', he says, 'are you unwilling to confess your crimes, and do you boast of cleanness, you who are polluted with the filth of idolatry, and shamelessly deny that you worshiped the idol of the Baals. Look back at the vale of the sons of Hinnom, which is watered by the springs of Siloam, and there you will see the shrine of Baal, whom you venerated, having forsaken God'. And what is added: know what you have done, opens the closed eyes of her who denies, so that she may see what she blushes to look upon. According to tropology, let us refute by their works the shameless brow of those who will not confess their vices. […]

A light runner unfolding her ways, a wild ass accustomed to the wilderness, in the desire of her soul has drawn in the wind of her love; none shall turn her away. All who seek her shall not fail; in her monthly courses they shall find her. LXX: toward evening her voice howled, she widened her ways over the waters of the wilderness, in the desire of her soul she was borne by the spirit, she was handed over. Who will turn her back? All who seek her shall not toil; in her humiliation they will find her. In this passage the Seventy's edition disagrees greatly with the Hebrew truth; yet each has its own sense. Because above she said: I am not defiled, and he was speaking as if to a woman who had behaved shamefully, he describes her fornication. […]

2:25.t: Restrain your foot from nakedness and your throat from thirst. And you said: I have despaired, by no means will I do it; for I have loved strangers, and after them I will walk. LXX: turn back your foot from the rough way and your throat from thirst. She said: I will act manfully, because she loved strangers and walked after them. Those who are about to keep the Passover are commanded to have shoes on their feet. And the Apostle proclaims shod the feet of those who are prepared by the Gospel, lest, while they walk through the wilderness of this world, they lie open to venomous creatures, which ought to be trampled and crushed by the Gospel foot. We restrain the throat from thirst when we receive the precepts of the Savior, who says: Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink. She, out of despair of better things, denied that she would do what the Lord commanded, and set out the reason, saying: I have loved strangers, and I will follow them, thinking by a shameless confession to escape her crimes. […]

2:26.t: As a thief is confounded when he is caught, so are the house of Israel confounded, they and their kings, princes and priests and their prophets. Although the face of thieves is shameless and bold, yet it blushes when it has been caught in theft. And so Israel too, saying to wood: You are my father, and to stone: You have begotten me, so as to call those his parents whom he himself had fashioned, is confounded when he has been caught in his idolatry. And lest we think that he says this of the common people, he sets down kings and princes and priests and their prophets. Let us use this testimony if ever our princes, and those who are reckoned leaders in the Church, are caught in shameful sins.

2:27.t: It is adultery, if you abandon the ecclesiastical and true knowledge and the opinion about God, and consent to false and incompatible opinion, either by deifying any created object or by making an idol of anything that does not exist, so as to overstep, or rather step away from, knowledge.… For this reason, the noble apostle calls one of the kinds of fornication, idolatry. In following the prophet says, "My people have committed fornication with wood and stone. They have said to the wood, 'you are my father' and to the stone, 'you have begotten me.' "

With unspeakable mercy, God deigned to be called the Father of humankind. He is in heaven, they on earth. He is the eternal Maker. They are made in time. He holds the earth in the hollow of his hand. They are like grasshoppers on the earth. Yet people forsook their heavenly Father and said to wood, "you are my father, and to the stone, you have begotten me." And for this reason, I think, the psalmist says to humankind, "Forget your own people as well, and your father's house."
