How is a person wise who looks not for his Maker but says to a stone, "You are my father"? Who says to the devil as the Manichaean does, "You are the author of my being"? How is Arius wise, who prefers an imperfect and inferior creator to one who is a true and perfect one? How can Marcion or Eunomius be wise, who prefer to have an evil rather than a good God? And how can one be wise who does not fear his God? For "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom."
2:27.s: On the Duties of the Clergy 1.25.117

2:27.t: They have turned to me the back and not the face. Those who cast the words of God behind them themselves turn their back against him and not their face. For when a master gives instruction, it is a sign of one who obeys if he listens with his head bowed before him; but if he turns his back, it is a sign of one who despises, as it is written in another place: and they turned to me a withdrawing shoulder. 'So far', says God, 'have they despised my precepts that they would not even hear, but showed the swelling of their mind by the gesture of their body'.
And in the time of their affliction they will say: Arise and deliver us. Those who did not perceive God through benefits, let them perceive him through torments.

2:28.t: Where are your gods, which you made for yourself? Let them arise and deliver you in the time of your affliction. It is a shameless request, in time of need and distress, to seek help from him whom they despised in peace. And it is to be read with the feeling of one rebuking: 'Let your gods, which you made for yourself, deliver you; so that, since God is the creator of men but man has made a god, necessity may prove what they can do whom you formerly worshiped when you were secure.'

According to the number of your cities were your gods, O Judah. The several cities worshiped either the same gods or single and different ones, so that they did not seem to have agreement even in impiety, but a superstition fighting against itself followed diverse error. And what follows: and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem they sacrificed to Baal, was added by the Seventy.

2:29.t: Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment? You have all forsaken me, says the Lord. Human perversity is prone to excuse itself, so that whatever men suffer deservedly they appear to suffer unjustly, and they refer their own fault to the judgment of God. 'In vain', therefore, he says, 'do you put forward complaints and plead that the judge is unjust, since what you suffer comes from your impiety.' And what follows: and you have all acted unjustly against me, was likewise added by the Seventy.

2:30.t: In vain have I struck your sons; they did not receive discipline, for which the Seventy set down: you did not receive. And the sense in the Hebrew is: 'They themselves, who were struck, were unwilling to receive discipline,' but in the Seventy: 'I struck your sons for this reason, that by their death you might be instructed. And lest perhaps you should say: You were unwilling to correct us when we sinned, learn from the blows dealt your sons that I desired to cure you with a harsher remedy.'

Your sword has devoured your prophets. 'Not my prophets but yours, and by no means my sword but yours, has devoured them, the sword which you suffered for your sins'. But the Seventy do not have 'your', but translated simply: the sword has devoured your prophets, 'so that it may be shown to be either the enemy's sword or my sword, by which I have pierced your sins.'

Like a ravaging lion is your generation. LXX: like a ravaging lion, and you did not fear. 'The sword', he says, 'which devoured your prophets' — there is no doubt that he means the soothsayers of Baal and of the idols —, 'has laid everything waste like a lion, and yet your generation, which ought to have been amended by the slaying of a few, has persevered entire in crime'. But according to the Seventy this is the sense: 'Thus the sword of the Lord, which has displayed the sword of the adversaries, has devoured and torn your false prophets like a lion, which most greedily tears the prey it has found, and yet not even by the punishment of your prophets could you be turned to better things.'

2:31.t: At the beginning of what has been read, the Lord says concerning Israel that he did not become a "wilderness" to him, nor "a parched land." Who then, coming to this passage, would not inquire, examining the intention of what is written? Grant that God did not become a wilderness in Israel, that he did not become in Israel a parched land: has the Lord then become a wilderness to Israel today, or is he now to him a parched land? And what of this: when to Israel he was neither a wilderness nor a parched land, was he to the nations a wilderness and a parched land? For if to all he is always not a wilderness, and to all he is always not a parched land, what need was there for it to be said to Israel in particular and by way of exception, "Have I become a wilderness to the house of Israel, or a parched land?" But it is possible to come first to the universal benefactions of God, and then, after his universal benefactions, to the particular ones. […]

See the word of the Lord: Have I become a wilderness to Israel, or a late-yielding land? Why then has my people said: We have withdrawn, we will come to you no more? LXX: hear the word of the Lord: thus says the Lord: Have I become a wilderness to Israel, or a land full of thorns, because my people said: We will not serve, nor will we come to you? Moses too saw the voice of God, and John the apostle says that he saw and handled the word of God. And he marvels how the people of Israel held God as a wilderness, while it followed idols as though they were the throng of cities. A late-yielding land is one that does not receive the rains of doctrines nor the discipline of the Gospel; and full of thorns, because it had not been cultivated. The people, then, that was once God's is the more wicked in this, that it withdrew from the Lord and is unwilling to return again to its God. It is a great offense to be unwilling to appease him whom you have offended.

2:32.t: It is the virgin Mary of whom God by the mouth of Jeremiah speaks, saying, "Can a maid forget her ornaments or a bride her attire?" Concerning her we read of a great miracle in the same prophecy—that a woman should compass a man and that the Father of all things should be contained in a virgin's womb.

The band covers the breast, and holds that place in women which the Rational holds in the High Priests. Of this breast-band Jeremiah too spoke in mystical speech: If a bride can forget her adornment, or a virgin her breast-band, I too will forget you, says the Lord (Jer 2:32). The virgin, such as the Apostle desires to present us to Christ (2 Cor 11), so long as she is not corrupted in Egypt and her breasts, which are bound with the breast-band, are not broken, is joined to the bridegroom; and though daily she bears sons of the virtues, she by no means ceases to be a virgin. But if at some time she has spread her feet to every passer-by and followed her lovers, and, according to the prophecy of Hosea, the Lord has hedged in her ways and shut off her paths, she will return to her former husband and will hear: Put off the garments of mourning, and put on the garments of your glory (Hos 2).

Will a virgin forget her ornament, a bride the band of her breast? But my people has forgotten me days without number. Through these words we learn that Christ is the bridegroom of the virgin Church, which has no spot or wrinkle. And if he himself is the bridegroom, the words are his, of whom John the Baptist also speaks: He who has the bride is the bridegroom. He, therefore, loses his ornament who withdraws from the Lord, and he loses the understanding of doctrines, which is signified in the breast. Hence also John the Evangelist reclines upon the breast of the Lord, and for the priests, among other things, the breast of the victims is set apart. But the greater the number of the times in which we forget God, the greater the penalty of the sin, because it could not be tamed even by the length of ages.

2:33.t: Why do you strive to show your way good, to seek love? You who moreover have also taught your wickednesses, your ways, and on your wings — or in your hands — has been found the blood of the souls of the poor and innocent. Not in pits did I find them, but in all these or under every oak. 'In vain', he says, 'do you desire to defend yourself by the art of words and to show your works as good, so as to merit love, you who besides have also taught others your ways and been an example of evil works to all. And on your wings indeed — or in your hands — has been found the blood of the innocent, whom you sacrificed to idols, or whose souls you destroyed by the likeness of sacrifices'. 'The poor' we set down from the Hebrew; they are not found in the Seventy. […]

2:35.t: And you said: I am without sin and innocent, and therefore let your fury be turned away from me. Behold, I will contend with you in judgment, because you said: I have not sinned. How exceedingly vile you have become — or since you have greatly despised — repeating your ways! These words must be used against those who will not acknowledge their sins, but in the time of affliction and distress say that they suffer unjustly what they suffer, and provoke the wrath of God the more, since it is another and greater sin not to mourn what they have done, but to put forward vain excuses for their sins. In judgment, he says, I will contend with you because you said: I have not sinned, as though it were something greater than this sin to hold one thing in the conscience and to utter another in speech. Let the new heresy sprung from the old hear that it is the very greatest wrath of God to be unwilling to confess sin humbly, and instead to boast shamelessly of righteousness.

And besides this we say, that it makes God angry for us to imagine that we are free from all impurity: for He is even found saying to one of those who led polluted lives, "Behold I have a lawsuit with you because you say I have not sinned, in that you have acted very contemptuously in repeating your ways." For the repetition of the way to sin is for us, when we are overtaken by offences, to refuse to believe that we are guilty of the defilement which arises from them.
2:35.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

2:36.t: And you shall be confounded by Egypt, as you were confounded by Assyria; for from this one too you shall go out, and your hands shall be upon your head, since the Lord has crushed your confidence — or hope — and you shall have nothing prosperous in it. To avoid the onset of the Egyptians they fled for refuge to the Assyrians, whose protection was vain; for we read that they were conquered by the Egyptians. Again, to escape the wrath of the Assyrian they relied on the help of the Egyptians, who, as history relates, were overcome by the Assyrians. They are rebuked, therefore, because, abandoning hope in God, they rely on the help of men, which has all been crushed and so overthrown that they can find nothing of use in it. Hence he says: and from this one you shall go out, that is, from Egypt, as you went out from the Assyrians, and your hands shall be upon your head, and you will mourn that you vainly expected protection from the Egyptians. […]

2:37.t:
Moreover, the experience of the Vandals was not dissimilar: when our people went against them in Spain and had as much confidence in a complete victory as they had recently against the Goths, the same overweening pride engulfed them in the same disastrous ruin. Then the words of the prophet were fulfilled for our army: "The Lord shall reject thy confidence and thou shalt not prosper in it."

For we trusted in our own wisdom and strength against the command of the Lord, who said: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither the mighty man in his might, but let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the Lord."

So we have not been conquered undeservedly, for the enemy sought better aid than we did. While we prided ourselves on arms and auxiliaries, on the side of the enemy the Book of the Divine Law opposed us. […]
2:37.s: On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapter 11

3:1.t: since indeed Scripture designates the sons of adulterers as imperfect. For such a soul, which, having deserted the conjunction of the spirit, prostrates itself wholly to the sense of the flesh and to bodily desires, as though turned away from God will impudently hear that "you have made yourself the face of a harlot, you have become without shame toward all." Therefore as a harlot she will be punished, and her sons are commanded to be prepared for slaughter.

Again He took up a parable against them and reminded them of that which is written in the law, and He wished that the law might speak falsely for the sake of their repentance. For He said: "When a man takes a wife and she shall go forth from him and shall be unto another man, and if the other man who took her shall die or shall dismiss her, and she shall return unto her first husband, it will not be possible for her first husband to take her again after she has been polluted; and if he shall take her, behold that land will surely be polluted. And now also I have taken thee, Jerusalem, to Myself, and thou hast become Mine, and thou hast gone from Me, and thou hast departed, and thou hast committed fornication with stones and trees. Now return unto Me, and I will receive thee, and in thy repentance I will loose the law" (Jere. 3: 1 sqq., and Dt. 24: 13 sqq., both loosely).

If a man living with a wife is not satisfied with his marriage and falls into fornication, I account him a fornicator, and prolong his period of punishment. Nevertheless, we have no canon subjecting him to the charge of adultery, if the sin be committed against an unmarried woman. For the adulteress, it is said, “being polluted shall be polluted,” and she shall not return to her husband: and “He that keepeth an adulteress is a fool and impious.” He, however, who has committed fornication is not to be cut off from the society of his own wife. So the wife will receive the husband on his return from fornication, but the husband will expel the polluted woman from his house. The argument here is not easy, but the custom has so obtained.

For this end he hath mentioned Ruth also and Rahab, the one an alien, the other an harlot, that thou mayest learn that He came to do away with all our ills. For He hath come as a Physician, not as a Judge. Therefore in like manner as those of old took harlots for wives, even so God too espoused unto Himself the nature which had played the harlot: and this also prophets from the beginning declare to have taken place with respect to the Synagogue. But that spouse was ungrateful towards Him who had been an husband to her, whereas, the Church, when once delivered from the evils received from our fathers, continued to embrace the Bridegroom.
3:1.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 3:5

3:1.t: And you will find the prophets filled with examples of this kind, when they address Jerusalem; for she fell into fornication, and a novel form of it, even as Ezekiel says: "To all harlots wages are given, but thou hast given wages to thy lovers, and there hath been perversion in thee beyond all other women," and again another saith "Thou didst sit waiting for them like a deserted bird." This one then who hath committed fornication in this fashion God calls back again. For the captivity which took place was not so much by way of vengeance as for the purpose of conversion and amendment since if God had wished to punish them out-right He would not again have brought them back to their home. He would not have established their city and their temple in greater splendour than before: "For the final glory of this house" He said "shall exceed the former." Now if God did not exclude from repentance her who had many times committed fornication, much more will He embrace my soul, which has now fallen for the first time. […]

It is commonly said — for which the Seventy translated only it is said — : if a man dismisses his wife, and she, departing from him, marries another man, will he return to her any more? Will she not be polluted and defiled, that woman — or that land — ? And you have committed fornication with many lovers or shepherds. For the word 'rehim', which is written with four letters, 'res, ain, ioth, mem', signifies both 'lovers' and 'shepherds'; and if we read 'rehim', it means 'lovers', if 'rohim', 'shepherds'.

Yet return to me, says the Lord or and you used to return to me, says the Lord. In the Hebrew he even receives her as a penitent after her fornication and exhorts her to return to him; but in the Seventy he does not call her to repentance, but rebukes the shamelessness of the harlot, in that after adultery she dares to return to her husband. And as to what he says: and that woman will be defiled, for which in the Hebrew we read 'land', he leaves the example and speaks more plainly of the land of Israel, which is compared to an adulterous woman. Let us use this testimony against those who, abandoning faith in the Lord and entangled in the errors of the heretics, after many fornications and the deception of souls, pretend to return to the former truth, not in order to lay aside the poisons of their breast, but in order to instill them into others.

Hence again under the figure of Judea it is said to every sinful soul: "If a man puts away his wife, and she departs and marries another man, will he return to her again? Will not that woman be polluted and contaminated? But you have fornicated with many lovers; nevertheless return to me, says the Lord." Behold, he gave the example of a shameful woman. He showed that after such shame she cannot be received back. But he overcomes by mercy this very example that he set forth, when he says that a fornicating woman can by no means be received back, and yet he himself waits to receive the fornicating soul. Consider, brothers, the weight of such great tenderness. He says what cannot be done, and demonstrates that he himself can do this even against custom. Behold, he calls, and those whom he declares to be defiled, he also seeks to embrace, those by whom he complains he has been abandoned.

Those who have experienced the sins of the flesh are to be admonished to observe vigilantly with how great a benevolence God opens the bosom of his pity to us, if after transgressions we return to him. He says through the prophet, "If a man puts away his wife, and she goes from him and becomes another man's, shall he return to her again? Shall not that woman be polluted and contaminated? But you have played the harlot with many lovers. Yet return again to me, says the Lord." So, concerning the wife who has played the harlot and has deserted, the argument of justice is put forward. Yet to us, returning after the fall, not justice but pity is displayed. Where we are surely meant to gather, how great is our wickedness if we return not, even after transgression, seeing that, when transgressing, we are spared with so great pity. Or what pardon for the wicked will there be from him who, after our sin, ceases not to call us.

3:2.t: Lift up your eyes straight ahead and see where you have not been prostrated; you sat in the ways waiting for them like a robber in the wilderness or like a deserted crow. In place of 'robber' and 'crow' in the Hebrew 'arabe' is written, which can also signify 'Arabs', a nation given to brigandage, which to this day raids the borders of Palestine and besets the roads for those going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, a thing the Lord too recalls in the Gospel. 'Lift up, therefore, your eyes, O Jerusalem, and look around this way and that, and see where you have not been by fornication prostrated. For just as robbers are accustomed, toward evening and in deserted places, to lay ambushes for travelers, so you, like the harlot of Proverbs, sat in the ways toward evening, to kill by your intercourse the souls of those who commit fornication; on account of which the whole land is polluted with your fornications'. […]

And you have polluted — or killed — the land with your fornications and in your evils. Therefore the drops of the rains have been withheld, and there was no late rain or and you had many shepherds for your stumbling. The land was killed or polluted on account of the killing of those who perished by the fornication of idolatry; hence the blessing of all things was taken away, so that they suffered a drought of the word of God. Or she had shepherds through whom she offended God, so that those who ought to have been teachers, to keep others from error, became the authors of impiety.

3:3.t: Accusation is censure of wrongdoers.… Of this help the divine Instructor made use by Jeremiah, saying, "You have a prostitute's forehead. You were shameless toward all. You did not call me to the house, I who am your father, and Lord of your virginity." "And a fair and graceful harlot skilled in enchanted potions." With consummate art, after applying to the virgin the disgraceful name of whoredom, he at once calls her back to an honorable life by filling her with shame.

No, a widow must take every precaution not to overstep by an inch the bounds of chastity. For if she once oversteps them and breaks through the modesty that becomes a matron, she will soon riot in every kind of excess. So much so that the prophet's words shall be true of her, "You have a whore's forehead, you refuse to be ashamed."

When they go out, they do their best to attract notice and with nods and winks encourage troops of young fellows to follow them. Of each and all of these the prophet's words are true, "You have a whore's forehead. You refuse to be ashamed." Their robes have but a narrow purple stripe, it is true. And their headdress is somewhat loose, so as to leave the hair free.

The brow of a harlot woman has become yours, you were unwilling to blush. LXX: the face of a harlot has become yours, you have become without blushing toward all. Because he had said above: I have not sinned, and she had sinned the more by denying her crimes, therefore he now rebukes her as a brazen woman of excessive shamelessness, so that she is not borne with brazen face to one man and another only, but blushes before none. Let us use this word against the conventicle of the heretics, who glory in their errors.

For their own misery has taught them, which happiness had made negligent, alas, what an evil thing it is to fornicate against the Lord by presuming upon themselves; oh how good it is to cling to the Lord, always thinking humbly. For withdrawing from that simple and singular good into the multitudes of pleasures, and into the love of the world and corruptions of the earth, this is to fornicate against the Lord. To this one it is called out: "A harlot's face has been made for you, and you have become shameless in your entirety."

3:4.t: Therefore at least from now on call me: My father, you are the guide of my virginity; will you be angry forever, or will you persevere to the end? Let the heretics blush, who are unwilling to be turned to better things or to go back to the Father, their creator, and let them hear: at least from now on call me: my father, you are the guide of my virginity. He himself has betrothed your soul to his embraces and teaches how it ought to pray and to do repentance. But the more merciful he is who shows the way of salvation after fornication, the more wretched is the harlot who is unwilling to receive healing after her wounds.

3:5.t: Behold, you have spoken and done evil things, and you were able. 'In place of words of repentance you have blasphemed with words of pride, and you have fulfilled your evil thought and shown your strength against your husband, so that you can do what you handled in speech.'

3:6.t: If, then, he says that first I sent away Israel because of its sins and sent it into deportation, but Judah, hearing what had happened to Israel, did not turn back, he speaks concerning our own sins. Since the things that befell Israel are read, and the transgressions concerning that people, we ought to fear, and: "if he did not spare the natural branches, how much more will he not spare us either; if that One who is both kind and at the same time loving to mankind, God, did not spare but cut off those who boasted to be a 'cultivated olive tree,' those rooted in 'the root' of the patriarchs Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, how much more will he not spare us." For he is not kind and yet not severe, nor severe and yet not kind. For if he were only kind but not severe, we would to a greater degree despise "his kindness." If he were severe but not kind, perhaps we would even despair over our sins. […]

The very wording of the passage that has been read has something obscure in it, which must first be understood; and after this, if God grants it, we shall come to know his mystical intent. Now he wants us to know this: that, as is written in the books of Kingdoms, the people were divided in the times of Rehoboam into the kingdom of the ten tribes under Jeroboam and into that of the two tribes under Rehoboam; and those under Jeroboam were called Israel, but those under Rehoboam Judah. And this division of the people has remained, so far as concerns the historical record, down to the present; for we know of no historical account that has gathered Israel and Judah together into one. Now Israel sinned first and more grievously — the people under Jeroboam and his successors — and sinned so much beyond Judah that they were condemned by Providence to become captives "into Assyria," as the Scripture says, "unto this day." […]

And the Lord said to me in the days of King Josiah: Have you seen what averse Israel has done? She went off by herself upon every high mountain and under every leafy tree, and committed fornication there. And I said, when she had done all these things: Turn to me; and she did not return. And her sister, Judah the transgressor, saw that, because averse Israel had committed adultery, I had dismissed her and given her a bill of divorce; and the transgressor Judah, her sister, did not fear, but went and committed fornication, she too, and by the facility of her fornication she defiled the land and committed adultery with stone and wood. And in all these things her sister, Judah the transgressor, did not return to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood, says the Lord. The torments of some are the remedies of others; and when a murderer is punished, he himself indeed receives what he has done, but others are deterred from the crime. […]

3:7.t: For this is a new kind of his goodness, that even after adultery he receives the soul, provided she returns and repents from the heart; as he himself also says through the prophet: "if a woman go out from her husband and sleep with another man, shall she return again to her husband? Shall she not be defiled with defilement? But you have fornicated with many shepherds, and yet you were returning to me". Likewise elsewhere he says: "and after you had fornicated in all these things, I said: return to me; and not even so did you return, says the Lord".

"And she played the harlot there. And I said, after she had committed all this fornication: Turn back to me; and she did not turn back, and the faithless Judah saw her faithlessness." We too have been reproached — I mean those of us who sin and do not keep the covenants of God, nor look to the fact that those others destroyed the covenant though they were nobly born, being of Abraham, having received the promise. We ought, then, to reckon that, since those others fell out of the blessings and the promises and it profited them nothing to be from the fathers, how much more shall we, when we sin, be forsaken. "If you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham," the Savior says to them. And again John: "Do not begin to say among yourselves, We have Abraham as father; for I tell you that God is able out of these stones to raise up children to Abraham" — hinting by "stones" at us who have the stony heart and are hardened against the truth. […]

Then He directs His speech unto the city, in this way too being minded to correct His hearers, and saith, "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem!" What meaneth the repetition? this is the manner of one pitying her, and bemoaning her, and greatly loving her. For, like as unto a woman beloved, herself indeed ever loved, but who had despised Him that loved her, and therefore on the point of being punished, He pleads, being now about to inflict the punishment. Which He doth in the prophets also, using these words, "I said, Turn thou unto me, and she returned not."
3:7.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 74:3

3:7.t: For these two indeed are chief sins, engendered of violent lust, the one of sexual desire, the other of the desire of money.… Let no man then of them that live in vice despair; let no man who lives in virtue slumber. Let neither this last be confident, for often the harlot will pass him by; nor let the other despair, for it is possible for him to pass by even the first. Hear what God saith unto Jerusalem, "I said, after she had committed all these whoredoms, Turn thou unto me, and she returned not." When we have come back unto the earnest love of God, He remembers not the former things. God is not as man, for He reproaches us not with the past, neither doth He say, Why wast thou absent so long a time? when we repent; only let us approach Him as we ought. Let us cleave to Him earnestly, and rivet our hearts to His fear.… How many other such changes wouldest thou see, both to have taken place of old, and now taking place every day? […]
3:7.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 67:3-4

3:7.t: Have we provoked Him severely, so as no other man ever did? this is just the reason why we ought specially to abstain from our present deeds and to repent for the past, and exhibit a great change. For the evils we have once perpetrated cannot provoke Him so much as our being unwilling to make any change in the future. For to sin may be a merely human failing, but to continue in the same sin ceases to be human, and becomes altogether devilish. For observe how God by the mouth of His prophet blames this more than the other. "For," we read, "I said unto her after she had done all these deeds of fornication, return unto me, and yet she returned not."… Hear at least what He says by the mouth of the prophet: "Declare thou first thy iniquities that thou mayest be justified." Now this He demands from us in order to intensify our love towards Him.

3:8.t:
"Go," therefore, "and read these words toward the north."

If the wording has been understood, let us see what it means to make plain in these things. The calling of the Gentiles took its beginning from the transgression of Israel, and the apostles, when they preached to the synagogues of the Jews, say: "To you the word of salvation was sent; but since you judge yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles." And the apostle, knowing what he knows about these matters, says: "By their transgression salvation has come to the Gentiles, to provoke them to jealousy." So then the many sins of that people brought about that they were forsaken and that we came to the hope of life — we who were strangers to the covenants, aliens to the promises. […]

"And the faithless Judah did not fear, and she went and played the harlot herself also." Israel having played the harlot first, Judah too played the harlot afterward. "And her fornication became as nothing, and she committed adultery with wood and stone." Whenever we sin, we do nothing else than, becoming stony-hearted, commit adultery with "the stone." Whenever we sin and play the harlot "beneath every leafy tree," we too commit adultery with "the wood." "And the faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood." If we turned to God, but deficiently, we are charged as not having turned "with the whole heart." Therefore "the faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart." He did not say: and the faithless Judah turned, and stood firm, but: "and the faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood" she turned. […]

3:9.t: Let us now proceed to consider the mode of his loving discipline, with the aid of the prophetic testimony. Admonition, then, is loving care's censure and produces understanding. Such is Christ the Educator in his admonitions, as when he says in the Gospel, "How often would I have gathered your children, as a bird gathers her young ones under her wings, and you did not allow it!" And again, the Scripture admonishes, saying, "And they committed adultery with wood and stone and burned incense to Baal." For it is a very great proof of his love, that, though knowing well the shamelessness of the people who had kicked and bounded away, he notwithstanding exhorts them to repentance and says by Ezekiel, "Son of man, you live in the midst of scorpions; nevertheless, speak to them, if perhaps they will hear."

Admonition, then, is loving care's censure and produces understanding. Such is Christ the Educator in his admonitions, as when he says in the Gospel, "How often would I have gathered your children, as a bird gathers her young ones under her wings, and you would not!" And again, the Scripture admonishes, saying, "And they committed adultery with stock and stone and burned incense to Baal." For it is a very great proof of God's love that, though knowing well the shamelessness of the people who had kicked and bounded away, he nevertheless exhorts them to repentance. He says by Ezekiel, "Son of man, you dwell in the midst of scorpions. Nevertheless, speak to them, if by chance they will hear." Further, to Moses he says, "Go and tell Pharaoh to send my people forth, but I know that he will not send them forth."

3:10.t: "And yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah has not returned to me with her whole heart, but feignedly." It is a smaller sin to follow evil that you think is good than not to venture to defend what you know for certain is good. If we cannot endure threats, injustice and poverty, how shall we overcome the flames of Babylon? Let us not lose by hollow peace what we have preserved by war. I should be sorry to allow my fears to teach me faithlessness when Christ has put the true faith in the power of my choice.

3:11.t: And the Lord said to me: Averse Israel has justified her soul in comparison with the transgressor Judah. 'More righteous,' he says, 'is Israel in comparison with Judah, because the former perished at once, at the beginning, while the latter could have been corrected by the torments of the former'. Let the new heresy sprung from the old take note that Israel is said to be justified in comparison with a worse one. Nor is this surprising of sisters of one nation, since Sodom too, in comparison with Jerusalem, receives the name of righteousness, as the Lord says through Ezekiel: 'Sodom has been justified by you', and the publican becomes righteous in comparison with the Pharisee.

And Scripture keeps up this comparison on the other side also, i.e., in weighing the merits of sinners, so that in comparison with the wicked it justifies those who have sinned less, saying: "Sodom is justified above thee;" and again: "For what hath thy sister Sodom sinned?" and: "The rebellious Israel hath justified her soul in comparison of the treacherous Judah."
3:11.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Theonas, Chapter 4

3:12.t: AGAINST NOVATIAN. — His disciples say to Jesus, “Lord, do you want us to say that fire should come down from heaven and consume them, as Elijah did?” And the Lord answered them, saying, “You do not know of what spirit you are. For the Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them” (Luke 9:54–56). Although it was certainly fitting to take revenge on the Samaritans who did not receive him, nevertheless the Lord, who came to grant mercy, removed the sentence, so that those who were corrected afterwards might be changed. And the prophet Elisha, angered at the boys who insulted him, took vengeance on them with God as judge, so that in that place they were eaten by bears, where there is said to be no forest (2 Kings 2:23–24); but the Lord spared the prostitute who was brought before him, namely the one whom the leaders of the Jews said they had caught in adultery (Jn. 8:11), so that, since a loving declaration had begun, he might teach that she was not to be condemned, but pardoned. […]
3:12.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 102: AGAINST NOVATIAN

3:12.t: Go and cry — or read — these words toward the north, and you shall say: Return, averse Israel, says the Lord, and I will not turn away — or I will fix — my face from you — or upon you —, for holy — or merciful — am I, says the Lord, and I will not be angry forever. Yet know your iniquity, that you have transgressed against the Lord God — or you have acted impiously — and you have scattered — or poured out — your ways to strangers under every leafy tree, and you have not heard my voice, says the Lord. The Hebrew word 'carath' is understood both as 'call' or 'cry' and as 'read'; hence Aquila and Symmachus translated 'keep crying', the Seventy and Theodotion 'read'. Now the word is directed to the north and against Babylon and the Assyrians, to the ten and to the two tribes, and their return is proclaimed. 'And I will not turn away', he says, 'my face from you, or I will not fix my face against you, so that I may receive you not with the severity of a judge but with a countenance of mercy. […]

3:14.t: Brethren and especially priests, if God rebukes whom he loves, and rebukes him for the very purpose of amending him, do not hate, but love those whom you rebuke, that you may amend them. God also before predicted by Jeremiah and pointed to our times, when he said, "And I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they shall feed you with the food of discipline." But if in Holy Scripture discipline is frequently and everywhere prescribed, and the whole foundation of religion and of faith proceeds from obedience and fear, what is more fitting for us urgently to desire? What is there more to wish for and to hold fast than to stand with roots strongly fixed and with our houses based with solid mass on the rock, which is unshaken by the storms and whirlwinds of the world, so that we may come by the divine precepts to the rewards of God?
3:14.s: Treatise II. On the Dress of Virgins 1-2

3:14.t:
[Passage quoted Jer. iii. 14-16.]

Here again he prophesies that the conversion of Israel will be at the coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ, in which He will choose one from a city, and two from a family, very few and small in number, to be shepherds of the nations that have believed on Him and of the nations that have been increased upon the earth through their destined call by them. No more, he says, will they say "the ark of the covenant of the Lord"—for they will no longer run after the more external worship, having received a new covenant.
3:14.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

3:14.t: Be converted, returning sons — or wandering and departing —, says the Lord, for I am your husband — or I will be lord over you —, and I will take you, one from a city and two from a kindred, and I will bring you into Zion, and I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you with knowledge and doctrine. And when you have been multiplied and have increased in the land in those days, says the Lord, they will no longer say: the ark of the covenant — or testament — of the Lord; nor will it come up upon the heart, nor will they remember it, nor will it be visited, nor will it be made any more. The Jews think that this was fulfilled after the return from Babylon under Cyrus, king of the Persians, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, even though not all returned; that this is what is signified by: I will take one from a city and two from a kindred. […]

3:15.t: The Lord does not say: I will appoint other good shepherds, to do these things, but I, He says, will do; I will commit my sheep to no one. Be secure, Brothers; you sheep, be secure. ...Here I find all good shepherds in one shepherd. For truly good shepherds are not lacking, but they are in one. There are many who are divided. This one is proclaimed, because unity is commended. Nor indeed are the shepherds now silent, and it is said "shepherd," because the Lord has not found one to whom He might entrust His sheep. But then He commended, because He found Peter. Moreover, even in Peter himself, He commended unity. There were many Apostles, and it is said to one: Feed my sheep. Let it not be that good shepherds are now lacking, let it not be that they are missing from us, let it not be that by His mercy, He does not beget and establish them. Surely, if there are good sheep, there are also good shepherds, for from good sheep come good shepherds. But all good shepherds are in one, they are one. They feed, Christ feeds. […]

3:17.t: At that time they will call Jerusalem the throne of the Lord, and all the nations will be gathered to it in the name of the Lord in Jerusalem, and they will not walk after the depravity of their most wicked heart. The Lord will by no means sit upon the ark of the testament and the cherubim, to whom that people formerly used to say: you who sit upon the cherubim, show yourself, but all who believe with a perfect mind will be the throne of God. Or certainly the whole is better understood of the Church, when all the nations are gathered in the name of the Lord into 'Hierusalem', in which is the 'vision of peace', and by no means walk after the depravity of their most wicked heart, so as to do what they desire, nor follow their own errors, but say with the prophet: my soul has clung after you, your right hand has upheld me.

3:18.t: In those days the house of Judah will go to the house of Israel, and they will come together from the land of the north to the land which I gave to your fathers. This is properly fulfilled at the coming of Christ, when out of the twelve tribes together they believed the Gospel, and, leaving the land of the north and of the harshest cold and withdrawing from the dominion of the devil, then received the land of promise which he had promised to their fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. I recently published a small book on the land of promise.

3:19.t: But I said: how or I will set you among sons and give you a desirable land, a glorious inheritance of the hosts of the nations! And I said: You will call me father, and you will not cease to walk after me. In place of 'a glorious inheritance of the hosts of the nations', which the Seventy translated: a named inheritance of God almighty of the nations, Theodotion translated more significantly: a renowned inheritance of the strength of the mightiest one of the nations, signifying Christ, who is the leader and lord of all the nations that believe in his name and passion. He himself said to Israel: you will call me father, and: he who believes in me believes in the Father. He himself promised: 'I will set you among sons, that is, in the number of my sons who have believed in me from the people of the nations and to whom I have given a desirable land'. For as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God.

And hence it comes that for the most part when instead of good things we ask for the opposite, our prayer is either heard but tardily or not at all; and again the Lord vouchsafes to bring upon us even against our will, like some most beneficent physician, for our good what we think is opposed to it, and sometimes He delays and hinders our injurious purposes and deadly attempts from having their horrible effects, and, while we are rushing headlong towards death, draws us back to salvation, and rescues us without our knowing it from the jaws of hell.

And this care of His and providence with regard to us the Divine word has finely described by the prophet Hosea under the figure of Jerusalem as an harlot, and inclining with disgraceful eagerness to the worship of idols, where when she says: "I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread, and my water, and my wool, and my flax, and my oil, and my drink;" […]
3:19.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapters 7-8

3:20.t: But as if a woman should despise her lover, so has the house of Israel despised me, says the Lord. It is the voice of Christ toward the people of the Jews, to whom he had said: I will set you among sons and give you a desirable land, and you will call me father and will not cease to walk after me. 'As,' he says, 'a woman despises not a husband but a lover, once she has been joined with him, when she sees him serving her lust and the law of nature reversed in her regard, by which she had once been subject to a husband, as the Lord says: and toward you shall be her turning, so the house of Israel, that is, the people of the Jews, has despised the Lord, the Savior, to its own ruin.'

3:21.t: A voice in the ways — or on the lips — was heard, the weeping and wailing of the sons of Israel, because they have made their way wicked, they have forgotten the Lord their God. Be converted, returning sons, and I will heal your aversions — or bruises — , for which Symmachus translated conversions. God gladly receives the penitent, and runs to meet the son worn out with want and squalor, and at once clothes him in his former garments and restores glory to the one returning, provided only that he returns with weeping and wailing. For by his own fault he has made his way wicked and has forgotten the Lord, his God and Father; to such the prophetic word now speaks: be converted, returning sons. 'Whom I call sons for this reason, because, having understood your sins, you return with weeping and wailing to your parent. And when you', he says, 'have returned to the Lord, he will heal all your bruises or aversions, by which you had withdrawn from the Lord, or certainly your conversions'. […]

3:22.t: It is clearly written in the Acts of the apostles that the apostles first went into the synagogue of the Jews, proclaiming to them, as to kinsmen through Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, the things written concerning the coming of Jesus Christ. But when, since those men would not receive what was said, it was necessary that there should be other hearers of what was spoken, then, having defended their cause to them, they left them behind; for it is written: "It was necessary that the word of God should be proclaimed to you; but since you judge yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the nations." And this thing, though it is clearly stated in the Acts of the apostles, is in effect said in many places also by the prophets. For the Holy Spirit first speaks through the prophets to those of that people, but if ever, after it has said much, it is not heard, it prophesies the word that is proclaimed to the nations. […]

Behold, we come to you; for you are the Lord our God. Truly the hills were liars, and the multitude — or strength — of the mountains; truly in the Lord our God is the salvation of Israel. Let the penitent say this, leaving behind all pride and the multitude or height of the mountains and hills through which he grew proud against God, and, prostrate in humility, let him speak: truly in the Lord our God is the salvation of Israel.

3:23.t: Then, having condemned our former evils — when we thought the idols great and lofty things, and worshipped and regarded as wonderful the things we served; but now have condemned them, judging that all those things were false and were nothing — we say, turning back: "Truly the hills were for a lie," we too having condemned our former lofty things and our former wonders. And perhaps, if we exercise some skill, we shall find the difference between the hills and the mountains among the nations, which, having forsaken, those who said "Behold, here we are, we will be yours, for you are the Lord our God" accuse them as false, both the hills and the mountains. What, then, is the difference between the mountains and the hills among the nations, which, having condemned, we say: "Truly the hills were for a lie, and the power of the mountains"? This we say, having condemned our former things. Of the objects of worship among the nations, some are worshipped as gods, and some as heroes. […]

3:24.t: Therefore we who are of the nations say, concerning ourselves, repenting over the false things which we thought to be true: "Truly the hills were for a lie, and the power of the mountains"; and concerning Israel who shall be saved after us: "yet through the Lord our God is the salvation of the house of Israel." Then, confessing concerning the sins in which both our fathers came to be and we ourselves, worshipping idols, we say: "But shame has consumed the toils of our fathers from their youth, their sheep and their oxen, their sons and their daughters." "Shame has consumed the toils of our fathers," and the rest of what is said. If, then, the wretched toil and the false work of the fathers is to be consumed, shame must come about; for before shame the toil of the fathers is not consumed, and the things brought in after. On this account let us consider the differences of those who sin. There are those who sin and are not ashamed nor feel any shame over their sins, nor blush. […]

Confusion has devoured the labor of our fathers from our youth, their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters. All the labors of the heretics, of which it is written: they have failed, searching with searching, from the youth of those whom they had deceived, their sons and their daughters, who had advanced in heresy or were held only by luxury, our confusion has overwhelmed. Hence they add:

3:25.t: After these things, these who make confession say: "We have lain down in our shame"; and after this they say: "and our dishonor has covered us over." Concerning the veil that lies upon the face of those who do not turn back to the Lord it has often been said by us. Because of this veil, "if Moses is read," the sinner does not understand him; for "a veil lies upon his heart." Because of this veil, if the old covenant is read, the hearer will not understand. Because of this veil the Gospel too is veiled to those who are perishing. We were saying, then, concerning the veil, that the shame is the veil. For insofar as we have "the works of shame," it is clear that we have the veil, according to what is said somewhere in the forty-third Psalm: "and the shame of my face has covered me." I set forth that he who does not have works of shame does not have a veil; such was Paul, saying: "But we all, with unveiled face, behold as in a mirror the glory of the Lord." Paul, then, has an unveiled face; […]

We will sleep in our confusion, and our shame will cover us, because we have sinned against our God, we and our fathers, from our youth up to this day, and we have not heard the voice of the Lord our God. Let Israel say this, who did not hear his Lord; let every heretic say this who repents; and yet it is a part of salvation to confess and to know one's sins. 'Tell,' he says, 'your iniquities first, that you may be justified'. For truly Israel forsook Christ, the Lord his God, and sinned against him not only at the time when he was seen in the flesh, but also before his coming. Hence they say: 'we and our fathers, from our youth up to this day, and we have not heard the voice of our God, who spoke to our fathers: if you believed Moses, you would believe me also; for he wrote of me'.

4:1.t: Upon these things God says concerning Israel: "If Israel turns back to me, says the Lord, then he shall be turned back"; that is, if he turns completely, then he shall be turned back with a turning — not if he as it were begins to turn. Then he says: "and if he removes his abominations out of his mouth, and stands in awe before my face, and swears, 'The Lord lives,' in truth and in judgment and in righteousness, then the nations shall be blessed in him." If they do these things, "the nations shall be blessed in him." But what are these things they are to do, so that the nations may be blessed in him? "If he removes his abominations out of his mouth." And what is it to remove the abominations out of the mouth? Whatever we speak badly are abominations in our mouth. Let us therefore remove the abominations out of our mouth, taking away slanders, vain words, idle words that are going to cause us to be accused "in the day of judgment; for by your words you shall be justified, and by your words you shall be condemned." […]

If you return, Israel, says the Lord, to me, turn back, for which the Seventy translated: if Israel is turned, says the Lord, to me, he shall be turned. And the sense is: 'if he has returned to me, he will return from captivity', or otherwise: 'when he has offered what he has'. For to him who has, it shall be given; but from him who has not, even that which he seems to have shall be taken away. But according to the Hebrew the sense is this: 'if you return to me, Israel, and once for all desire salvation, and say that you have sinned and have not listened to the voice of your Lord, turn back fully; believe in him whom you denied, and then there will be full conversion'.

If you take away your stumbling blocks from before my face, you shall not be moved. When, therefore, we are moved and say: but my feet were almost moved, we do not suffer this through the weakness of nature, but because we set up stumbling blocks and our idols against the Lord.

4:2.t: But if the old law had belonged to the devil, it would not have led people away from idolatry, but rather would have drawn them on and cast them into it; for this did the devil desire. But now we see the opposite effect produced by the old law. And indeed this very thing, the oath, was ordained of old for this cause, that they might not swear by the idols. For "ye shall swear," saith He, "by the true God." They were then no small advantages which the law effected, but rather very great. For that they came unto the "strong meat," was the work of its care.
4:2.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 17:5

4:2.t: And you shall swear: the Lord lives, in truth and in judgment and in righteousness, and the nations shall bless him and shall praise him. And how is it that the Gospel forbids us to swear? But here 'you shall swear' is said for confession and for the condemnation of the idols by which Israel used to swear. Accordingly the stumbling blocks are taken away and he swears by the Lord. And as for what is said: the Lord lives, in the Old Testament it is an oath for the condemnation of the dead, by whom all idolatry swears. At the same time it must be noted that an oath has these companions: truth, judgment and righteousness; if these are lacking, it will by no means be an oath, but perjury. 'And when,' he says, 'Israel has done this too, and through the apostles has become the teacher of the nations, then all the nations shall bless, or be blessed, in him, and shall praise him, because salvation has gone forth from Israel'.

In the Old Testament it is said that he who swears in the name of God should swear and not perjure himself. For to perjure is the same as to forswear, and this is to take the name of God in vain.

Jeremiah says: "And you shall swear: the Lord lives, in truth and in judgment and in justice;" and the Gloss says there that "an oath ought to have three companions: truth, judgment, and justice."

First, an oath ought to be made with truth; that is, without falsehood. Truth is present in an assertory oath when a man does not deny what is true, nor affirm what is false, nor knowingly assert what is doubtful; for speech is indicative of those things which are in the heart. But do you know what it means when a man testifies to something false by the witness of divine truth? It is to say that he lies and that divine truth lies along with him.

Second, an assertory oath must be made with justice. […]

4:3.t:
He adds: "And the nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him they shall give praise to God in Jerusalem. For thus says the Lord to the men of Judah and to those who dwell in Jerusalem." He has spoken to those from the nations, he has spoken also to those from Israel, and he now speaks to those from Judah. I remember the figurative interpretations spoken earlier concerning Judah and those who dwell in Jerusalem. For we too dwell in Jerusalem, if God grants it. Since "where the treasure is, there also is the heart," if we lay up treasure in heaven, we also have our heart in the Jerusalem above, concerning which the apostle says: "But the Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother, as it is written," and what follows.

"Thus," then, "says the Lord to the men of Judah and to those who dwell in Jerusalem: Break up for yourselves fresh ground, and do not sow among thorns." […]

There is, moreover, the apostolic injunction, that the grace given us should not be unprofitable; for those things which he wrote particularly to his disciple, he enforces on us through him, saying, ‘Neglect not the gift that is in thee. For he who tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread; but the paths of the slothful are strewn with thorns;’ so that the Spirit forewarns a man not to fall into them, saying, ‘Break up your fallow ground, sow not among thorns.’ For when a man despises the grace given him; and forthwith falls into the cares of the world, he delivers himself over to his lusts; and thus in the time of persecution he is offended, and becomes altogether unfruitful.

For thus says the Lord to the man of Judah and Jerusalem: break up fallow ground for yourselves, and do not sow upon thorns; be circumcised to the Lord and take away the foreskins of your hearts, men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem, lest my indignation go forth like fire and be kindled, and there be none to quench it, because of the wickedness of the thoughts — or devices — of yours. For what we said: be circumcised to the Lord and take away the foreskin of your hearts, Symmachus put: be purified to the Lord and take away the wickednesses of your hearts, understanding circumcision as cleansing and foreskins as vice. And this is commanded to the men of Judah and Jerusalem who follow the true faith and dwell in the Church: that they should not sow upon thorns, which the word of the Gospel signifies, thorns that choke the seed of God, but should first make fallow ground, dig up all the brambles and take away the briars, so that clean fields may receive clean seeds. […]

Lastly, why should we any longer linger over those things which we have sufficiently discovered and proved by experience? We have often seen those who were cold and carnal, i.e., worldly men and heathen, attain spiritual warmth: but lukewarm and "natural" men never. And these too we read in the prophet are hated of the Lord, so that a charge is given to spiritual and learned men to desist from warning and teaching them, and not to sow the seed of the life-giving word in ground that is barren and unfruitful and choked by noxious thorns; but that they should scorn this, and rather cultivate fallow ground, i.e., that they should transfer all their care and teaching, and their zeal in the life-giving word to pagans and worldly men: as we thus read: "Thus saith the Lord to the men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem: break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns."

4:4.t: He speaks moreover concerning our ears, how He hath circumcised both them and our heart. The Lord saith in the prophet, "In the hearing of the ear they obeyed me." And again He saith, "By hearing, those shall hear who are afar off; they shall know what I have done." And, "Be ye circumcised in your hearts, saith the Lord." And again He says, "Hear, O Israel, for these things saith the Lord thy God." And once more the Spirit of the Lord proclaims, "Who is he that wishes to live for ever? By hearing let him hear the voice of my servant." And again He saith, "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for God hath spoken." These are in proof. And again He saith, "Hear the word of the Lord, ye rulers of this people." And again He saith, "Hear, ye children, the voice of one crying in the wilderness." Therefore He hath circumcised our ears, that we might hear His word and believe, for the circumcision in which they trusted is abolished. […]
4:4.s: The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter IX

4:4.t: Paul mentioned "certain false brethren as having crept in secretly," who wished to turn the Galatians to another gospel. He shows that that adulteration of the gospel was not meant to transfer them to the faith of another god and christ, but rather to perpetuate the teaching of the law. He blames them for maintaining circumcision and observing times, and days, and months and years, according to those Jewish ceremonies that they ought to have known were now abolished, according to the new dispensation willed by the Creator, who foretold in ancient times this very thing by his prophets. Thus he says by Isaiah: "Old things have passed away. Behold, I will do a new thing." And in another passage: "I will make a new covenant, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt." In the same he said by Jeremiah: Make to yourselves a new covenant, "circumcise yourselves to the Lord, and take away the foreskins of your heart." […]

And next to this it is said: "Be circumcised to your God, circumcise the foreskin of your heart." "Be circumcised to your God"—of necessity is added "to your God." You will understand this from the perceptible example: they are circumcised, I mean according to the perceptible sense, not only those of the circumcision according to the law of Moses, but also many others. Among the Egyptians the priests of the idols are circumcised, but that circumcision is a circumcision to idols and is not a circumcision made to God; whereas that of the Jews was perhaps, but at all events then, made to God. If, then, the word says, "Be circumcised to your God," having understood the literal sense, pass over also to the figurative interpretation, so that you may find how, among those circumcised figuratively (so that perhaps some of them might say, "We are the circumcision"), some are circumcised to God, while others are indeed circumcised, but not to God. […]

The first circumcision of the flesh is made void, and the second circumcision of the spirit is promised instead. In Jeremiah, "Thus says the Lord to the men of Judah, and to them who inhabit Jerusalem, 'Renew newness among you, and do not sow among thorns. Circumcise the foreskin of your heart lest my anger go forth like fire, and burn you up, and there be none to extinguish it.' "
4:4.s: Treatise XII. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews 1:8

4:4.t: How could it be shown from the testimony of the prophets, already received among the Gentiles in the New Testament, that the promise which God made to Abraham has been fulfilled through the coming of Christ? — It is written in the prophet Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Isa. 56:7). But perhaps the Jews will say: The house of God, that is, the synagogue, is open to all. Nor do we object; yet in such a way that, as always, the circumcised join themselves to the Law. For their Law is that by which they were commanded, after the manner of Abraham, to be circumcised. Therefore, nothing new can seem to be signified by this example of the prophet; since anyone coming from any nation has never been forbidden from the beginning of Judaism to join himself to the Law. Nothing new spoken by the prophet can be thought, indeed it would be unessential, if the Gentiles have always been admitted to serve the God of Abraham and are never found to have been forbidden. […]
4:4.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 44: HOW THE PROMISE TO ABRAHAM WAS FULFILLED IN CHRIST

4:4.t: Let us see, then, how Abraham is the father of many nations. We confess that he is the father of Jews, through descent according to the flesh. But if we hold to the descent according to the flesh, we are forced to say that the prophecy was false. For he is no longer father of us all according to the flesh. Yet the example of his faith makes us all children of Abraham. How and in what manner? With people it is unbelievable that one should rise from the dead. In the same way, it is also unbelievable that there should be offspring from aged persons as good as dead. Yet when Christ is preached as having been crucified on the tree, as having died and risen again, we believe it. By the likeness of our faith, therefore, we become the adopted children of Abraham. […]

4:5.t:
"Declare it in Judah, and let it be heard in Jerusalem; say, declare, signal with a trumpet upon the earth, and cry aloud." These things, he says, which are announced, say in Judah, to those from the tribe of Judah of Christ; "for it is evident that our Savior arose out of Judah."

"Signal with a trumpet upon the earth." The lofty word, which rouses the hearer, which prepares him for the war against the passions, for the war against the workings of the adversaries, which prepares him for the heavenly feasts—for it is spoken with reference to both of these—is taken as a trumpet. In Numbers such a word is a trumpet; for instance, the word commands me, and if it is given to anyone else (it is given to the one who wishes and who has sought the meaning of the Scriptures), it commands to make "trumpets of hammered silver." Thus the word says: "Signal with a trumpet upon the earth, and cry aloud; say: Gather together and let us enter into the walled cities." […]

Declare in Judah and make it heard in Jerusalem; speak, sound the trumpet in the land, cry aloud, say: gather together, and let us enter the fortified cities. Let 'Iudas' hear this, let 'Hierusalem' hear this, in which is the 'confession' of faith, and in which the 'peace' of Christ dwells, and to which it was said through Isaiah: go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; lift up your voice, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem; let it cry aloud and give command thus: 'let us enter the fortified cities — the wars of the heretics are rising: let the fortifications of Christ hold us — ; raise the standard of the cross on the watchtower and on the height of the Church; be strong, you who fear, do not stand still, but run to the help of Christ; for evil,' he says, 'I bring from the north, and great destruction, the true Nebuchadnezzar, who is permitted by me to exist in this world for this very reason, that your strength and victory may be proved'.

4:6.t: "Take up your baggage and flee to Zion"; as many of you as are outside Zion, "take up your baggage and flee to Zion; hasten, do not stand still," you who are in progress hasten to the Watchtower, "for I bring evils from the north and great destruction"—of the evils brought "from the north," from the north of the adversary, as has often been said; and whoever is found not to have hastened, nor to have entered "into the walled cities," not having come to be in "the churches of God," but standing outside, he himself, being seized by the enemies, will be destroyed. And who is the enemy? Let us see from what follows in what manner it is said: "A lion has gone up from his lair, destroying he has cut off nations." This is the enemy, whom we must flee. A lion pursues us. Who is this? Peter teaches us, saying: "Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, walks about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, firm in the faith." […]

4:7.t: "A lion has gone up," then, "from his lair." Where? When? He is fallen below, he has gone down into the lowest parts of the earth. "A lion has gone up from his lair." You are a man, you are higher than the devil; for you are stronger than he, whatever sort you may be; he, because of his wickedness, is below. "A lion has gone up," then, "from his lair, destroying he has cut off nations"; having gone up "from his lair," from the place proper to his own punishment, "destroying he has cut off nations; he has gone forth from his place to make your land a desolation." He wishes to enter into your land, concerning which we were speaking a little while ago. He wishes to feed upon each of us. He comes, then, "to make your land a" desolation, that the lion may trample down the seeds, that he may make your land desolate. "And your cities shall be pulled down so that they are not inhabited. For these things gird yourselves with sackcloth." […]

The lion has come up from his lair, and the plunderer of the nations has raised himself up; he has gone forth from his place to make your land a desolation; your cities will be laid waste, remaining without inhabitant. This is, as we have said, the true Nebuchadnezzar, of whom Peter also speaks: our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion. And he comes up, it may be, from the abysses, into which he is to be bound again, and he begs not to be sent there, and the plunderer — or the devastator — of the nations has raised himself up, of whom it was said: he shall rule over all his enemies, and who boasts in the sight of the Lord: I have gone around the whole earth and trodden it down. For who is there whom the poisons of the devil do not touch, except him alone who can say: behold, the prince of this world comes and finds nothing in me? […]

4:8.t: For this gird yourselves with sackcloth, lament and howl, for the wrath of the fury of the Lord has not turned away from us or, as the Seventy translated, from you. In no other way can we escape the lion and most savage beast unless we do repentance and turn to the Lord, not only in mind but also in deed. For as long as he lays waste the Church and the land of Judah, and ravages Jerusalem as well, the wrath of God is manifest.

4:9.t: And it shall be in that day, says the Lord: the heart of the king shall perish, and the heart of the princes, and the priests shall be astounded, and the prophets shall be dismayed. While the plunderer lays waste the Church of the Lord and the wrath of the Lord remains against us, all help will be useless. The heart of the king shall perish, whose heart ought to be in the hand of God, and the heart of the princes, who were thought to be wise; for God has made foolish the wisdom of the world, because through it they did not know God. The priests themselves too, who ought to teach the law of the Lord and to defend the peoples subject to them from the fury of the lion, made senseless by a kind of stupor, shall be turned to madness — for so the Seventy translated, expressing 'ecstasy of mind' for 'stupor' — and the prophets shall be dismayed, or, as Aquila translated the Hebrew word 'iethmau', they shall be out of their minds. […]

4:10.t: And I said: alas, alas, alas, Lord God — for which the Seventy translated: O Lord God —, have you then deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying: you shall have peace? And behold, the sword has reached even to the soul. Because he had said above: at that time they shall call Jerusalem the throne of God, and all the nations shall be gathered to it in the name of the Lord in Jerusalem, and now he says: the heart of the king shall perish, and the heart of the princes, and the priests shall be astounded, and the prophets shall be dismayed, the prophet is troubled and thinks that God has lied to him, and does not understand that the former was promised for long ages after, while this would come about in the near time, in accordance with which the Apostle too says: has God rejected his people? Far from it. And the sword reaches even to the soul when nothing living is left in the soul. […]

4:11.t: At that time it shall be said to this people and to Jerusalem: a burning wind — or of error — in the ways that are in the desert, the ways of the daughter of my people, not for winnowing and cleansing. A full spirit shall come to me from these. When the sword has reached even to the soul and the threshing floor has been finished, then the burning wind will come from the desert, which will not cleanse and winnow it, so that, with the chaff scattered here and there, the grain may be laid up in the granaries; but a full spirit will come, not to the people at all, but to me, so that my wheat may be scattered. 'Wind' and 'spirit' are called among the Hebrews by the same name, 'ruha', and according to the nature of each passage we should take it either as 'wind' or as 'spirit'. […]

4:12.t: And now I — but I will speak my judgments with them. Aposiōpēsis [breaking off], after that line of Vergil: whom I — but it is better to calm the troubled waves. Being about to speak of good fortune, then, he restrains himself and joins sorrows to sorrows; for these are the judgments which God speaks with his people of old, so that they may know that they justly suffer what they suffer.

4:13.t: Behold, he shall come up like a cloud, and like a tempest his chariots; his horses are swifter than eagles. Woe to us, for we are laid waste! He sees things to come as present and describes the Babylonian army, the din of whose chariots and wheels is compared to a most savage tempest, and the swiftness of whose horses is likened to eagles. When the prophet had said this and had pointed out with his finger the enemies as though they were coming, the people groans and feels these things not as future but as already done, saying: woe to us, for we are laid waste! Refer this same thing to the Church: that daily the army of the true Nebuchadnezzar assails us, and the chariots of Pharaoh and all his cavalry outstrip the onrush of eagles. If the man of the Church understands this, believing that saying: 'when you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved', he will say: woe to us, for we are laid waste!

4:14.t: Then we wash our hands when we enter into church, but our hearts not so. Why, do our hands send forth a voice? It is the soul that utters the words: to that God looketh; cleanness of the body is of no use, while that is defiled. What profits it, if thou wipe clean thine outward hands, while thou hast those within impure? For the terrible thing and that which subverts all good is this, that while we are fearful about trifles, we care not for important matters. To pray with unwashed hands is a matter indifferent; but to do it with an unwashed mind, this is the extreme of all evils. Hear what was said to the Jews who busied themselves about such outward impurities. "Wash thine heart from wickedness, how long shall there be in thee thoughts of thy labors?" Let us also wash ourselves, not with mire, but with fair water, with alms-doing, not with covetousness.
4:14.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 73

4:14.t: Wash your heart from wickedness, Jerusalem, that you may be saved; how long shall harmful thoughts linger in you? To the people saying: woe to us, we are laid waste! the prophet answers, nay rather God through the prophet: wash your heart from wickedness, Jerusalem, with that water of which Isaiah too speaks: wash yourselves, be clean, the water of saving baptism, the water of repentance. And he speaks to the metropolis of the Jews, so that by the city the peoples may be understood: 'how long do you lie subject to wicked thoughts, which proceed from your heart?' And in the holy Scriptures we should take the heart for the soul and the understanding.

4:15.t: For the voice of one declaring from Dan, and of one making known an idol — or pain — from mount Ephraim. The divine word now speaks according to the lie of the land of Judea. For the tribe of Dan, near Mount Lebanon and the city which is now called Paneas, faces the north, from which Nebuchadnezzar is to come. And he describes an idol, whether Bel, or pain, or iniquity, as coming from mount Ephraim. For after the tribe of Dan comes the land of Ephraim, through which one comes to Jerusalem. 'Dan' means 'judgment', 'Ephraim' 'abundance'. The judgment of the Lord, therefore, will come upon the land that sins against the Lord, with all the abundance of punishment.

4:16.t: Say to the nations: behold, it has been heard in Jerusalem that guards are coming from a distant land; and they have given their voice over the cities of Judah; like guards of fields they have become over her round about, because she has provoked me to anger, says the Lord. He wants all the nations round about to know the sentence of God, and all to receive correction from the scourging of Jerusalem. 'It is told,' he says, 'by common report in Jerusalem that adversaries are coming from a distant land, and that the roar of a howling army is rising against her, who besiege the city so diligently and shut in the city with siegeworks, that you would think them not so much adversaries as guards of fields and vineyards. But all this has come about not by the strength of the enemies, but by the fault of Jerusalem, because she provoked God to anger'. For if the adverse powers have no power over swine, how much more is this true of men, and of men once of the city of God!

4:18.t: Your ways and your thoughts have done these things to you; this is your wickedness, because it is bitter, it has touched your heart. He makes an apostrophe to the city of Jerusalem: that her ways and thoughts, by which she sinned both in deed and in word, have made all that came upon her come, and that her wickedness, which is bitter in itself, has touched her heart and pierced the inmost parts of her soul. Whatever, therefore, befalls us befalls us through our own fault, who turn the sweet God into bitterness and force him to rage against his will.

4:19.t: "My belly! my belly aches!" — cried Jeremiah. What belly of his aches? That belly aches which we too have, and which aches when it brings people into the world. But the feelings cause pain of a different order: they are the pain of my heart.

My belly, my belly, I am in pain; the senses of my heart are troubled. I will not keep silent, for my soul has heard the sound of the trumpet, the clamor of battle. Destruction upon destruction has been called, and all the land is laid waste; suddenly my tents are laid waste, in a moment my skins. Where we, following Symmachus, have put 'are troubled', and in the Hebrew is written 'homae', the Seventy and Theodotion put maimassei, a word whose meaning I do not know to this day. Aquila, however, put ochlazei, which itself also means 'tumult'. Let this be said about the word, over which I know there is a great dispute among very many. And the voice is introduced of the prophet, and through the prophet of God speaking, that he grieves over the destruction of his people and his inner bowels are torn as a man's are, just as the Savior too grieved over the death of Lazarus and lamented Jerusalem, so as not to hide his grief in silence; […]

4:21.t: How long shall I see those fleeing, shall I hear the sound of the trumpet? Either those fleeing the Babylonian king, or those fleeing me and withdrawing from my service.

4:22.t: In the beginning, God commanded that you do these things because of your wickedness. In the same way, because of your determination to remain wicked, or rather, because you are increasingly prone to do it, he uses the same precepts to call you to remember it or come to know it.
