But you are a people hard-hearted and without understanding, both blind and lame, children without faith, as he himself says, honoring him only with your lips, far from him in your hearts, teaching doctrines that are your own and not his.

And therefore the scribes and Pharisees, too, who from the times of the law had begun to despise God, did not receive His Word, that is, they did not believe on Christ. Of these Esaias says: "Thy princes are rebellious, companions of thieves, loving gifts, following after rewards, not judging the fatherless, and negligent of the cause of the widows." And Jeremiah, in like manner: "They," he says, "who rule my people did not know me; they are senseless and imprudent children; they are wise to do evil, but to do well they have no knowledge."

And the Lord himself through the prophet: The leaders of my people have not known me; they are foolish sons, and without understanding; they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have not known. They were indeed called my leaders, he says, and leaders of my people, but because they did not know me, and destroyed the name by their deeds, therefore they are foolish sons and without understanding; they have prudence only to this end, that they may subject the simple flock to themselves and trample it under their feet; but to do good and to rule the people they have not known.

For my foolish people has not known me. They are unwise sons and senseless; they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have not known. The cause of the destruction, the devastation, the flight, the trumpet: that the people has become foolish, not by nature but by the bent of its will. And this very folly is proved from this, that they did not know God; and instead of wise sons they have become foolish sons and senseless. For what greater folly can there be than that, while the ox knows its owner and the ass its master's crib, Israel should not know the Lord and should despise him when present, whom it always desired to see? And as for what is added: they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have not known, here wisdom is to be taken for wickedness, in accordance with which the sons of this age too are wiser than the sons of light, and the steward of iniquity is said to have done certain things wisely, and the serpent in paradise is read to have been more prudent than all the beasts. […]

4:23.t: I looked at the earth, and behold, it was empty and nothing, and at the heavens, and there was no light in them. I saw the mountains, and behold, they were moving, and all the hills were troubled. I gazed, and there was no man, and the bird of the sky had departed. I looked, and behold, Carmel was deserted, and all its cities were destroyed before the face of the Lord and before the face of the wrath of his fury. The prophet sees in the spirit the things that are to come, so that the people, hearing, may be terrified and, having done repentance, may by no means suffer what it dreads. The earth is empty, its inhabitant destroyed; the heavens have no light, since the people does not see for the greatness of its terror; the mountains themselves and the hills have unsafe hiding places, and by hyperbolēn [hyperbole] they seem to move and be troubled.

4:25.t: He gazed and looked around here and there, and not even a bird could be found; for even the mute elements feel the wrath of God, and the irrational animals dread it. That this is true the whole world now shows, in that, a multitude of men having been slain, the birds too, which are wont to follow the inhabitants, have gone away and perished.

4:26.t: Carmel itself too, which overhangs the great sea, planted with olives and thick with shrubs and vines, will come to such desolation that it will have the waste of a wilderness; all the cities too will become deserted. And the cause of all these evils is this: that through the fault of the sinning people the wrath of the Lord has been roused. Whatever we have said according to the history of Jerusalem and Judea, let us refer to the Church of God when it has offended God and has been laid waste either by vices or by persecution, so that where once there was a choir of virtues and joy, there a multitude of sins and sorrows dwells.

4:27.t: For thus says the Lord: all the land shall be deserted, but yet I will not make a full end; the earth shall mourn and the heavens above shall grieve, because I have spoken, I have purposed, and I have not repented, nor have I turned back from it. God's mercy being mixed with wrath, all the land is deserted, but a full end is not made, so that there may be those who understand his clemency.

4:28.t: The heaven too will look sad above, and the earth itself will mourn, because the sentence of the Lord has come right to its end, and he has not repented of the things he purposed and spoke. But repentance is ascribed to God when a sentence foretold is withdrawn and raging wrath does not come right to its end. He threatened through Jonah, and the multitude of tears and groans overcame the impending sword.

4:29.t: At the sound of the horseman and of the one shooting the arrow — or bending the bow — every city has fled — or region — ; they have gone into the heights and climbed the rocks — and what follows: and they have gone into the thickets or caves, was added by the Seventy —, all the cities are abandoned, and no man dwells in them. The divine word describes the army of the raging Babylonian: that for fear of it the whole people abandoned the city and climbed every height, and yet could not escape the wrath of the Lord. But whatever, as we said above, is understood in the history against Jerusalem, refer to the Church when it has offended God and has been handed over to adversaries, either in a time of persecution or, at any rate, through vices and sins.

4:30.t: And if Plutus is blind, are not those women who are crazy about him and have an attraction with him blind too? Having, then, no limit to their lust, they push on to shamelessness. For the theater, and pageants, and many spectators, and strolling in the temples and loitering in the streets, that they may be seen conspicuously by all, are necessary to them. For those who glory in their looks, not in heart, dress to please others. For as the brand shows the slave, so do gaudy colors the adulteress. "For though you clothe yourself in scarlet, and deck yourself with ornaments of gold and anoint your eyes with paint, in vain is your beauty," says the Word by Jeremiah. Is it not monstrous that while horses, birds and the rest of the animals spring and bound from the grass and meadows, rejoicing in ornament that is their own, in mane and natural color and varied plumage, woman, as if inferior to the brute creation, should think herself so unlovely as to need foreign, bought and painted beauty?

But you, laid waste, what will you do? For 'laid waste', which in Hebrew is said 'sadud', which Aquila alone translated so, the others translated 'wretched' and 'pitiable', through her own fault, because she has offended the merciful God. Accordingly it follows:

When you clothe yourself in scarlet and are adorned with a golden necklace and paint your eyes with antimony, in vain will you adorn yourself; your lovers have despised you, they will seek your soul. He speaks under the figure of an adulterous woman: 'once you have offended God and, as it were, left your husband, the Creator, in vain do you seek out ornaments; the demons, your lovers, have despised you, and they will seek not at all the uncleanness of debauchery, but the destruction of your soul'. This same thing is to be understood spiritually against those who have lost conjugal affection and the chastity of the true faith. […]

4:31.t: For I have heard a voice as of a woman in labor, anguish — or groans — as of a woman in childbirth; the voice of the daughter of Zion, swooning and spreading out her hands: woe to me, for my soul has fainted because of the slain! He describes the city of Jerusalem wailing and crying out after the likeness of a woman in childbirth, that is, one who is bearing her first offspring. For as a woman giving birth, who has not yet experienced the pain of childbearing, swoons — she suffers anguish, she can scarcely breathe, and with her hands spread out she collapses —, so too the daughter of Zion, when she sees her children slain, bursts out into these words and says: woe to me, for my soul has fainted because of the slain! Two examples are compared in one passage: of a woman bearing children and of a woman mourning, so that whatever a woman suffers in childbirth or in the deaths of her children, Jerusalem may suffer in her peoples.

5:1.t: Go about the ways of Jerusalem, and look, and consider, and seek in its squares, whether you may find a man who does judgment and seeks faith, and I will be merciful to it. But if they even say: The Lord lives, this too they will swear falsely. Great is the love of righteousness: not that God should deliver the city for ten righteous men, as in Abraham's question and God's answer, but that if he finds a single one in Jerusalem, now on the very point of perishing, who does judgment and seeks faith — or, as Symmachus translated, truth —, God would nonetheless have mercy on Jerusalem.

5:2.t: Disasters occur either to discipline the obstinate people or punish evil people. The same God declares in the Holy Scriptures, "I have struck your children in vain. They have not received correction." The prophet devoted and dedicated to God answers these words in the same way and says, "You struck them, but they have not grieved. You scourged them, but they have refused to receive correction." See, God inflicts stripes, and there is no fear of God.
5:2.s: Treatise V. An Address to Demetrianus 7

5:2.t: And because it could happen that some would be found among the people who feigned the worship of God and swore by the Lord, he forestalls this: that God is in no way delighted by empty words, but by the truth of faith; and he says: 'I do not love them because they swear by me, and they swear in falsehood; but those whose hearts and lips agree'.

5:3.t: "Lord," he says, "your eyes are toward faithfulness," just as "the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous," for he turns them away from the unrighteous; so too the eyes of the Lord are toward faithfulness, for he turns them away from faithlessness. Therefore it is well said, by one who understands what he is saying in his prayer, "Lord, your eyes are toward faithfulness." Now what is written here is "Lord, your eyes are toward faithfulness." But since "if a man of understanding hears a wise word, he will praise it and add to it," see how many things it is possible to make out of the words "Lord, your eyes are toward faithfulness." Paul says, "But now these three abide: faith, hope, love; and the greatest of these is love." Just as the eyes of the Lord are toward faithfulness, so the eyes of the Lord are toward hope, the eyes of the Lord are toward love. […]

Then let us look at what is said concerning sinners: "You scourged them, and they felt no pain." These perceptible scourges, when applied to living bodies, produce pain in them whether those scourged wish it or not; but the scourges of God are of such a kind that some of those scourged feel pain, while some of those scourged do not feel pain. Let us see whether we can explain what it is to feel pain from God's scourges and what it is not to feel pain, and that those who feel no pain from God's scourges are wretched, whereas those who do feel pain from God's scourges are blessed. For Wisdom says, "Who will set scourges over my thought, and over my lips a seal of prudence, that they may not spare me in my ignorances, and my sins may not destroy me?" Give heed to the "Who will set scourges over my thought?" So then there are scourges that scourge the thought. The scourges of God scourge the thought; […]

"You consumed them, and they refused to receive instruction." When God, who exercises providence over all things, performs the purifying works for the salvation of a soul, then as far as it depends on him he has consumed it. And you will understand the words "You consumed them, and they refused to receive instruction" from the example of the one who hands on knowledge and the one who is unwilling to receive the knowledge from the one who hands it on. For let the teacher do everything that is in his power and bring everything to completion for the handing on of knowledge, while the other does not accept what is said; I would say concerning such a one to the teacher, "You consumed this man, and he was unwilling to receive instruction." […]

"They made their faces harder than rock." This too you will understand from things more bodily. Of those who sin, some, hearing words of rebuke over their sin, blush and shrink back and give way, when the rebuking word touches them; but others are of such a kind that they are shameless, feeling no shame over the things for which they are rebuked, for the things in which they have sinned. You might therefore say concerning these who feel no shame, "They made their faces harder than rock." If you have understood this in bodily terms, pass over with me in thought to the soul, understanding the "face" concerning which it is said, "but then face to face." And behold a hardened soul, such as was the hardened heart of Pharaoh, so that it stands unyielding against the things announced to it and, as it were, casts off what is said, not being molded according to the things announced. For there you will find that the words fit, "They made their faces harder than rock, and they refused to turn back. […]

Lord, your eyes look upon faith. You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to receive discipline; they hardened their faces beyond rock, and they would not return. After the words of the Lord, by which he had given command, saying: Go about the ways of Jerusalem and the rest, the prophet speaks to the Lord: Lord, your eyes look upon faith, which in Hebrew is called 'emuna': not the works of the Jews, in which they exulted according to the ceremonies of the law, but the faith of Christians, through which we have been saved by grace. From this passage we learn that punishments are inflicted for this reason: that vices may be corrected. Accordingly he says: You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to receive discipline. For Jerusalem is corrected through every torment and scourge; […]

The fewness of those who were present has of itself shown, dearly-beloved, that the religious devotion wherewith, in commemoration of the day of our chastisement and release, the whole body of the faithful used to flock together in order to give God thanks, has on this last occasion been almost entirely neglected: and this has caused me much sadness of heart and great fear. For there is much danger of men becoming ungrateful to God, and through forgetfulness of His benefits not feeling sorrow for the chastisement, nor joy for the liberation. Accordingly I fear, dearly-beloved, lest that utterance of the Prophet be addressed in rebuke to such men, which says, “thou hast scourged them and they have not grieved: thou hast chastised them, and they have refused to receive correction.” For what amendment is shown by them in whom such aversion to God’s service is found? […]

We are judged by the ever-present judgment of God, and thus a most slothful race has been aroused to accomplish our destruction and shame. They go from place to place, from city to city, and destroy everything. First they poured out from their native land into Germany, which lay nearest them, a country called barbarous, but under Roman control. After its destruction, the country of the Belgae burst into flames, then the rich estates of the luxurious Aquitanians, and after these the whole body of the Gallic provinces. This ruin spread gradually, however, in order that while one part was being visited with destruction, another might be reformed by its example. But when has there been any amendment among us, or what part of the Roman world, whatever its affliction, is corrected by it? As we read: "They are all gone out of the way, they are altogether become useless." And in like manner the prophet cried out to the Lord, saying: "Thou hast stricken them but they have not grieved; […]
5:3.s: On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapter 12

5:4.t: In my own case this is now the third year of my silence, and my boast has become like that of the Psalmist, “I was as a man that heareth not and in whose mouth are no reproofs.” Thus I shut up in the bottom of my heart the pangs which I suffered on account of the calumnies directed against me, for calumny humbles a man, and calumny makes a poor man giddy. If, therefore, the mischief of calumny is so great as to cast down even the perfect man from his height, for this is what Scripture indicates by the word man, and by the poor man is meant he who lacks the great doctrines, as is the view also of the prophet when he says, “These are poor, therefore they shall not hear;…I will get me unto the great men,” he means by poor those who are lacking in understanding; and here, too, he plainly means those who are not yet furnished in the inner man, and have not even come to the full measure of their age; it is these who are said by the proverb to be made giddy and tossed about.

But I said: Perhaps they are poor and foolish — or they could not — not knowing the way of the Lord, the judgment of their God. I will go therefore to the nobles and will speak to them; for they have known the way of the Lord, the judgment of their God. He speaks here of the poor and the nobles not in terms of want and riches; rather, he compares the people with the princes. And the sense is: 'Seeing the obstinacy of the unbelieving people, and that with hardened face it would not receive discipline, I was reasoning this out with myself: perhaps the ignoble common crowd cannot know the teaching of God and is therefore excusable, because through inexperience it is not able to know the commandments of God. I will go therefore to the priests and to those who preside over the people, and will speak to them; for they have known the will of the Lord and know the judgment of their God'. He says this in the language of one who doubts, according to that saying of the Gospel: I will send my son; […]

5:5.t: "I will go to the great ones and speak to them." Those who are great in soul are spoken of in praise. For among the Greeks too "greatness" (to hadron) is continually used to name the grandeur of the rational soul. For whenever someone undertakes great matters and has purposes worthy of account and always considers what is fitting — how he may live according to right reason, wishing and looking upon nothing lowly and small — such a one has the greatness and grandeur in his soul. These men, then, since they were poor — the former ones whom the word blamed — did not listen, says the prophet. For this reason they did not listen, because they are poor. "I will go to the great ones and speak to them." And if it is a blessed thing to speak "into the ears of those who hear," it is a blessed thing if one meets with a great and mighty hearer. […]

And behold, these all the more together have broken the yoke, have burst the bonds. Therefore a lion from the forest struck them, a wolf at evening laid them waste, a leopard watching over their cities. Everyone who goes out from them will be taken, because their transgressions are multiplied, their turnings-away are strengthened. 'Those whom I thought to be teachers were found to be worse than the disciples; and the greater the authority among the rich, the greater the insolence of their sins'. For they broke the yoke of the law, as the Apostle says: Now therefore why do you tempt God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we are saved, in the same way as they also; and they burst the bonds of the precepts of God, and not of the Pharisees, of whom it is said in the second Psalm: Let us burst their bonds asunder, and cast away their yoke from us.

And the prophet of God reproacheth severely those who have broken the yoke, and cut the bands of the fear of God. Now Israel became rebels because there was no fear [in them]; and they trod under foot the commandments because they were not mindful of what was threatened; and they despised the law because they remembered not the penalty of Him that ordained it. For He Who ordained the law because He knew to whom He was giving the law, against [the breaking of] His commandments multiplied His threats in His wisdom, so that although freewill might hold the law in contempt, the fear which followed thereafter might incite [Israel] to the keeping thereof. And because he that received the law became a rebellious slave, He made him to labour in bondage in the fear of tribulation. Before his face He displayed all the various forms of punishment, so that as long as he looked thereupon he might take heed to the commandments, and keep the law.
5:5.s: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 6 -- First Discourse on the Fear of God

5:6.t:
[Passage quoted, Jer. v. 6-10.]

Here once more the charge against their whole race is shewn, and the siege that came on them, and the remnant again, which he names "the foundation" as belonging to the Lord. Because being inspired and strengthened by their faith in the Christ of God, they did not undergo such sufferings as the rest of their race.
5:6.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

5:6.t: Jeremiah also speaks of sinners: A lion from the forest struck them, and a wolf destroyed them even to their houses; and a leopard kept watch over their cities. All who go out from them will be taken. In this, note that no one is taken except one who has gone out from the cities of God.

Because, then, they did these things, a lion from the forest struck them, namely the Babylonian kingdom; a wolf at evening laid them waste, signifying the Medes and Persians, in place of which in the vision of Daniel a 'bear' is set down, in whose mouth there were three rows; a leopard watching over their cities, prefiguring the onslaught of Alexander and his swift course from the west all the way to India. He calls him a leopard on account of his variegation, and because he fought against the Medes and Persians with very many nations subject to him. And there were, he says, four heads on the beast, and power was given to it. And because he is not prophesying of the future, but is weaving the history of the past or of things now on the very point of coming, for that reason he is silent about the Roman empire, of which perhaps it is said: Everyone who goes out from them will be taken. […]

5:7.t: On what ground shall I be able to be merciful to you? Your sons have forsaken me and swear by those who are not gods. I filled them, and they committed adultery, and in the house of the harlot they ran riot. They have become to me horses, lovers toward the females, and stallions; each one neighed after the wife of his neighbor. Shall I not visit for these things? says the Lord, and on such a nation shall not my soul take vengeance? A Katalogos [a catalogue] of the sins of Jerusalem, while God says that he does not know on what ground he could have mercy on her. 'The sons', he says, 'of yours have forsaken me: by no means mine, but yours, because they swear by those who are not gods. I filled them, and they committed adultery'. Let those hear this who, brooding over the riches they have received from the Lord, are slaves to luxury.

5:8.t: Those who do indeed reject the Spirit's counsel, and are the slaves of fleshly lusts, and lead lives contrary to reason, and who, without restraint, plunge headlong into their own desires, having no longing after the Divine Spirit, do live after the manner of swine and of dogs; these men does the apostle very properly term "carnal," because they have no thought of anything else except carnal things. For the same reason, too, do the prophets compare them to irrational animals, on account of the irrationality of their conduct, saying, "They have become as horses raging for the females; each one of them neighing after his neighbour's wife." And again, "Man, when he was in honour, was made like unto cattle." This denotes that, for his own fault, he is likened to cattle, by rivalling their irrational life. And we also, as the custom is, do designate men of this stamp as cattle and irrational beasts.

At another time, he speaks of us under the figure of a colt. He means by that that we are unyoked to evil, unsubdued by wickedness, unaffected and high-spirited only with him our Father. We are colts, not stallions "who whinny lustfully for their neighbor's wife," beasts of burden unrestrained in their lust. Rather, we are free and newly born, joyous in our faith, and hold fast to the course of truth. We are swift in seeking salvation, and we spurn and trample on worldliness.

Rebuking censures what is base and highlights what is noble. This is shown by Jeremiah: "They were horses mad for females. Each one neighed for his neighbor's wife. Shall I not visit them for these things? says the Lord. Should not I avenge my soul against such a nation as this?" He everywhere interweaves fear, because "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of reason."
The neighing horse depicts the recklessness of young men.

Yet for all this some are so cold and senseless, as to be always seeking only the things that are here, and uttering those absurd sayings, "Let me enjoy all things present for a time, and then I will consider about things out of sight: I will gratify my belly, I will be a slave to pleasures, I will make full use of the present life; give me to-day, and take tomorrow." Oh excess of folly! Why, wherein do they who talk so differ from goats and swine? For if the prophet permits not them to be accounted men, that "neigh after their neighbors wife," who shall blame us for esteeming these to be goats and swine, and more insensible than asses, by whom those things are held uncertain, which are more evident than what we see?
5:8.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 13:7

5:8.t: They have become horses, lovers toward the females. For 'stallions' in the Hebrew is written 'mosechim', which all with one accord translated helkontes, that is, 'drawing', so that the size of the genitals may be shown, according to that saying of Ezekiel: like the flesh of asses is their flesh. This is what is written in another place: they were likened to senseless beasts and became like them. And at the same time he shows so great a madness of lust that he calls it not the appetite of pleasure but chremetismon, that is, 'neighing', and keeps the metaphoran [metaphor] of horses raging for lust.

Perhaps I am doing an injustice in reckoning the actions of the rich as sins, for when they kill their poor slaves they consider it an act of justice, not a crime. Nor is this all; they also abuse their privilege in their vile breaches of chastity. What rich man keeps his marriage vows, who among them does not plunge headlong into passionate lust, who does not use his household slaves as harlots and pursue his madness against any one on whom the heat of his evil desires may light? They illustrate well the words of the Holy Scriptures about such men as they: "They are become as horses rushing madly on the mares." Is it not a proof of what I just said, that the average man wishes to make his own by physical union whatever his eyes have beheld with desire?
5:8.s: On the Government of God, Book 4, Chapter 5

5:8.t: When the master of the house acts as husband of the maidservants, the mistress is not far removed from the mean position of the slave. Who among the rich men of Aquitania did not so act? Who among them has not been considered by his shameless maids, and with good, reason, as either adulterer or husband? For, as the prophet said: ''They were as fed horses in the morning; everyone neighed after his neighbor's wife." Those of whom he spoke sinned perhaps less grievously, and, I think, with less intention of wrong than did our men. The Aquitanians more truly resembled the post horses: they whinnied not after a few women merely, but after all their household maids — that is, after their own herds — and, like those; beasts called the stallions of the herd, they waxed wanton with the heat of their intoxicating passion, and attacked whatever woman was first exposed to the onslaught of their shameless lust.
5:8.s: On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapter 4

5:9.t: 'When you have done these things', he says, 'are you not deserving of a fitting visitation?' And note that here 'visitation' is put for penalty and punishments, according to what is written: I will visit their iniquities with the rod. And on such a nation shall not my soul take vengeance? After she has been bound by sins, she is no longer called the people of God, but a nation, from which the soul of God has withdrawn, according to what is written: your new moons and sabbaths and feast days my soul hates. But what in the Old Testament is said by way of affection, in the New is written as truth, as the Savior says: I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up.

5:10.t: Go up upon her walls — or bulwarks — and destroy, but do not make a full end! Take away her shoots — or props —, because they are not the Lord's! For with transgression the house of Israel and the house of Judah has transgressed against me, says the Lord. He commands the nations of which he had said above: a lion from the forest struck them, a wolf laid them waste, and a leopard in their cities, to go up upon the walls of Jerusalem, or its bulwarks, and destroy it, but not to make a full end, so that the remnant may be saved and there may be one to announce the glory of God among the nations; and he mingles clemency with severity. And as for what he added: take away her shoots or props, he orders all the aids to be removed which she lost by her own fault, because the house of Israel and the house of Judah transgressed against God, signifying the ten tribes and the two. […]

5:11.t: Accusation is the censure of wrongdoers. This mode of instruction God employs by David, when he says, "The people whom I did not know served me, and when their ears heard they obeyed me. Sons of strangers came to me, and halted from their ways." And by Jeremiah: "And I gave her a divorce decree, but covenant-breaking Judah did not fear." And again: "And the house of Israel disregarded me. The house of Judah lied to the Lord."

5:12.t: They have denied the Lord and said: He is not — or these things are not — nor will evil come upon us; sword and famine we shall not see. The prophets have come to wind, and an answer — or a word — was not in them. These things therefore will come upon them. Because they have denied the Lord — or they have lied to the Lord — and said: 'He is not, by whose judgment all things come to pass, but all these things have happened by chance; and the things which the voices of the prophets threaten us with will not come, nor shall we see the sword, nor shall we endure the famine of a siege; and whatever the prophets spoke, they spoke to the wind, and all things have passed away void, nor did they have an answer, that is, an oracle, or the word of God was not in them', therefore they will endure what the following discourse describes. Let the Church hear this, when it is negligent and rejects the providence of God: that it will endure both sword and famine, unless it believes that the things which are spoken will come.

5:14.t: Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Because you have spoken this word, behold, I give my words in your mouth into fire, and this people into wood, and it will devour them. 'You said: The prophets have come to wind, and the things they threaten will not come; therefore, O prophet, I give my words in your mouth, which are to have the power of fire, and which are to turn this people into wood, so that the unbelieving may be burned up together by your discourse and prophecy.' So God is called a consuming fire, that he may consume in us whatever, upon the foundation of Christ, we have built of hay, wood, stubble.

5:15.t: Behold, I will bring upon you a nation from afar, O house of Israel, says the Lord, a strong nation, an ancient nation, a nation whose language you will not know, nor will you understand what it says. Its quiver is like an open sepulchre; all are mighty. And it will eat your crops and your bread, it will devour your sons and your daughters, it will eat your flock and your herds, it will eat your vine and your fig tree, and it will crush with the sword your fortified cities, in which you have confidence. Nevertheless in those days, he says, I will not make you into utter destruction. 'Not after a long time, nor, as you falsely believe, will the prophets speak to you into the wind; but even now I will bring upon you a nation of the Babylonians, which will come from afar, a strong nation' — for which in the Hebrew is written 'etham' —, 'an ancient nation' — over which Nimrod the giant once held dominion —, 'whose language you will not know or' — as is written in the Hebrew — 'nor will you understand what it says; […]

5:16.t: And what follows: its quiver is like an open sepulchre, which is not said in the edition of the Seventy, signifies the Babylonian armament. Nor is there any doubt that the kingdom of the Assyrians, the Babylonians, the Medes and the Persians is most skilled in archery.

5:17.t: And at the same time he describes the devastation of the land of Judea and the slaughter of many, the driving off of cattle, the overthrow of cities and of walls: that all things are taken by the hostile sword, and that yet amid such great evils he does not destroy them to extermination, but keeps a remnant safe, either of those who were led into Babylon and released for the cultivation of the fields of the land of Judea, or of those who, after the heat of persecution, kept the faith of the Lord either by flight or by confession.

5:18.t: God, who judges "little by little," gives to those being chastised room for repentance, and does not, in punishing at the very moment of sin, bring the full completion of the punishment upon the one who has sinned. For this reason, "judging little by little," he chastises. And an example of this is in Leviticus; for in the curses against those who transgress the Law it is written, after the earlier punishments: "And it shall be, if after these things you do not turn back, says the Lord, I too will add to you seven plagues." And again he recounts another punishment: "And it shall be, if after these things you do not turn back, but walk toward me crookedly, I too will walk with you in crooked wrath." And you will find God measuring out punishments with sparing restraint, since he wishes to lead the one who has sinned to conversion, and does not repay them all at once. Such things, then, so far as the letter goes, had come about concerning the people; […]

5:19.t: "And it shall be, when you say, 'For what reason has the Lord our God done to us all these evils?' — and you shall say to them, 'Because you forsook me and served other gods in your land, so shall you serve in a land not your own.'" Let the letter be understood, and it suffices for the present to set forth the reminder from the letter for those able to hear. So then, the sons of Israel had the holy land, the temple, the house of prayer. They ought to have served God. But transgressing the divine commandments, they both practiced idolatry and took up the idols of Damascus, as it is written in the books of Kingdoms, and they took up other idols of the nations into the holy land. Through the idols of the nations which they took up, they made themselves worthy to be cast down into the land of the idols, to end up there where they worshiped the idols. So the word says to them according to the letter: "Because you forsook me and served foreign gods in your land, so shall you serve foreign gods in a land not your own." […]

But if you say: Why has the Lord our God done all these things to us? you shall say to them: As you have forsaken me and served a foreign god — or foreign gods — in your land, so you shall serve foreigners in a land not yours. Great is the folly of not knowing why they have suffered, when they have sinned so greatly; and brief is the answer to those who are in doubt: as you have served a foreign god — that is, Baal — or foreign gods of all the nations in the land of Judea, so you shall serve foreign gods in a land not yours, no doubt the Babylonians and Chaldea. 'For if a strange religion delights you, what need is there to take up an error from afar? Dwell with such people; nay rather, serve those whose gods you worship.' This can also be taken of heretics, of whom it is written: they went out from us, but they were not of us; […]

5:20.t: Declare this to the house of Jacob and make it heard in Judah, saying: Hear, O foolish people, who have no heart, who having eyes do not see, and ears and do not hear! In many ways he draws sinners back to salvation, and he calls foolish the people that has abandoned the author of wisdom, and he compares them to the images of which it is written: They have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear. Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them. Properly, however, he speaks to Judah and to the house of Jacob — for Israel had already for a long time been in exile among the Assyrians — and at the same time he gives us to understand that even without a precept we ought to understand by natural sense the things that are right.

5:21.t: And with the same meaning the Lord rebukes by the prophet the unnatural but freely chosen blindness of the Jews, which they by their obstinacy brought upon themselves, saying: "Hear ye deaf, and ye blind, behold that you may see. Who is deaf but My servant? and blind, but he to whom I have sent My messengers?" And that no one might ascribe this blindness of theirs to nature instead of to their own will, elsewhere He says: "Bring forth the people that are blind and have eyes: that are deaf and have ears;" and again: "having eyes, but ye see not; and ears, but ye hear not." The Lord also says in the gospel: "Because seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not neither do they understand." And in them is fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah which says: "Hearing ye shall hear and shall not understand: and seeing ye shall see and shall not see. […]
5:21.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapter 12

5:21.t: That it is the height of folly not to fear, the Lord says in Jeremiah: "Hear, O foolish people, who have no heart: who having eyes, see not, and ears, and hear not. Will you then not fear me, and will you not be grieved at my presence? I who have set the sand as the boundary of the sea, an everlasting decree, which it shall not pass beyond." Do you not fear me?

5:22.t: For ye are not ignorant that we, being exposed to all, as rocks running out in the sea, sustain the fury of the heretical waves, which, in that they break around us, do not cover the district behind. I say “we” in order to refer it, not to human power, but to the grace of God, Who, by the weakness of men shows His power, as says the prophet in the person of the Lord, ‘Will ye not fear Me, who have placed the sand as a boundary to the sea?’ for by the weakest and most contemptible of all things, the sand, the Mighty One has bounded the great and full sea.

For fear the water should spread beyond its bed, and in its successive invasions cover one by one all countries, and end by flooding the whole earth, it received the order to gather unto one place. Thus we often see the furious sea raising mighty waves to the heaven, and, when once it has touched the shore, break its impetuosity in foam and retire. “Fear ye not me, saith the Lord.…which have placed the sand for the bound of the sea.” A grain of sand, the weakest thing possible, curbs the violence of the ocean. For what would prevent the Red Sea from invading the whole of Egypt, which lies lower, and uniting itself to the other sea which bathes its shores, were it not fettered by the fiat of the Creator? And if I say that Egypt is lower than the Red Sea, it is because experience has convinced us of it every time that an attempt has been made to join the sea of Egypt to the Indian Ocean, of which the Red Sea is a part. […]
5:22.s: The Hexaemeron, Homily 4: Upon the Gathering Together of the Waters

5:22.t: Let them recognize the fact, therefore, that this is the result of divine precept and of celestial operation, for the Lord addresses Job from the clouds, saying, among other things, this, also, about the barrier of the sea: ‘I set my bounds around it and made it bars and doors, and I said: “hitherto thou come and shalt go no further, but on thyself shall be broken thine own waves.”’ Do we not ourselves often see the sea billowing so that its waves rise up ‘like a sheer mountain of water,’ when it breaks its force in foam against the shore, beaten back by what might be called the barriers of the low-lying sandy beach, according to what the Scripture says: ‘Will you not then fear me, saith the Lord, who has set the sand a bound for the sea?’ Thus the violent onslaught of the sea is held in check by the most unstable of all things, ordinary coarse sand of the seashore. The waves recoil and are guided to their prescribed bounds by a command from heaven, and the violent movement of the water is broken by meeting itself. […]

Will you not then fear me, says the Lord, and will you not grieve before my face — or fear — ? I who set the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting precept, which it will not pass. And they will be moved and will not be able — or it will be troubled and will not be able — and its waves will swell — or will sound — and will not pass over it. But to this people there has come to be an unbelieving and provoking heart, and they have withdrawn and gone away, and they have not said in their heart: Let us fear the Lord our God, who gives us the early and the late rain in its season, keeping for us the fullness of the yearly harvest! He recounts his benefits in order to convict the ungrateful. 'Me,' he says, 'you will not fear, I who have bestowed such great things on you? […]

And again God demanded from the Jews the fear of Himself by the hand of Jeremiah, and reproached them by the testimony of the dumb things in nature, which, though silent, trembled at the fear of Him, while the Jews despised His commandments. "Fear ye not Me? saith the Lord: will ye not tremble at My presence? For I have placed the sand for the bound of the sea, [by] an everlasting law, and it shall not pass over it." And here again the Creator demanded fear and trembling from created things, and because they forsook His fear they were reproached through the dumb things of nature, which feared and trembled at the Majesty of the Creator, while His commandments were despised by the children of men. And God in all places shewed the majesty of His nature by the hand of the Prophet, that He might cast the fear thereof into those who listened. For to those who would have despised His meekness—if it had been shewn unto them—He revealed the majesty of His nature that they might tremble thereat; […]
5:22.s: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 7 -- Second Discourse on the Fear of God

5:23.t: Things that have no sense of hearing hear me and perceive me; and the people once mine, made foolish by its own fault, not only despises but even provokes its sweet God. They have withdrawn,' he says, 'from me, and turned their backs on me, and gone away with hurried step, nor did a silent conscience draw them back, so that they should say in their hearts: Let us fear him who gives us the early and the late rain! — through all of which I have shown good things, the fullness of the yearly harvest', for which Aquila's first edition and Symmachus translated 'weeks'; for in the Hebrew is written 'sabaoth', which, owing to the ambiguity of the word, signifies both 'weeks' and 'fullness'.

5:25.t: Our iniquities have turned these things aside, and our sins have withheld good from us. Therefore, if at any time the sea both oversteps its boundaries and the rain is held back, by no means has the hand of the Lord been shortened, so as not to do these things; but our sins have turned aside these things as they were coming to us, so that they went on to others who had not sinned. 'And they have withheld,' he says, 'the good that was already coming to us, according to that which is written according to the letter: I will command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it'. But we can take the early and the late rain as the law and the Gospel, and as the various callings from the first hour to the eleventh, in which one reward of eternal life is promised to the laborers of the vineyard.

5:26.t: For among my people there have been found ungodly men lying in wait like fowlers, setting snares and traps to catch men! As a trap full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit. That the early and the late rain might turn aside from them and all good things might not come, the causes are added: because there have been found among his people 'ungodly men'. He did not say 'unjust' and 'sinners', as the new heresy would have it, but 'ungodly'. Ungodliness openly denies God; iniquity and sin, if it confesses its error, easily bends God to mercy. And for what we have said, lying in wait like fowlers, which is not found in the Seventy, Aquila and Symmachus translated the word 'iasir' as like the net of a fowler, because even he who among them seems good and upright lays snares like a fowler, while they hunt one another to death and fill their own houses with the losses and costs of others, so that that saying of the philosophers is fulfilled: Every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man. […]

5:27.t: Therefore they have been magnified and enriched. They have grown fat and sleek, and they have passed over my words most wickedly. They have not judged the cause, the cause — or judgment — of the orphan they have not directed, and the judgment of the poor — or of the widow — they have not judged. Shall I not visit for these things? says the Lord, or shall my soul not take vengeance on a nation such as this? If I should wish to note one by one the things that have been left out in the edition of the Seventy, it will become long. 'Those who lay snares,' he says, 'and rejoice in the nakedness of others, therefore they have been magnified and enriched.' Because they did the things above, they have grown fat and sleek, according to that which is written: He grew fat and sleek, and the beloved kicked. And they have passed over my words, because in the consciousness of their riches they said that saying from the Gospel: Soul, you have many goods laid up for very many years; rest, eat, drink, feast! […]

5:30.t: Astonishment and wonders have come to pass in the land: the prophets prophesied a lie — or wicked things — and the priests clapped with their hands, and my people loved such things! What then will you do at the last — or after these things — ? Above he had said: I will go to the chief men and will speak to them; perhaps they have known the way of the Lord. And behold, these rather have together broken the yoke, they have burst the bonds; now he describes who the chief men are, namely the prophets and the priests, some of whom foretell things to come, while others determine from the law the things to be done. 'And behold,' he says, 'while those men prophesied a lie, the priests clapped with their hands.' And so that it may be shown that the people too is not without fault, which lets itself be led away by such men, it is written: and my people loved such things: once mine, but after it loved them, it ceased to be mine. What then will they do when the last time of judgment has come, or the necessity of captivity? […]

6:1.t: Be strengthened, sons of Benjamin, in the midst of Jerusalem, and in Tekoa sound the trumpet, and over Beth-haccherem raise a signal — or a standard —, for evil has been seen — or has appeared — from the north, and great destruction! No one is unaware that Jerusalem is situated in the tribe of Benjamin. That Tekoa too is a small village situated on a mountain, twelve miles distant from Jerusalem, we see daily with our own eyes. Between these is another village, which in the Syriac and Hebrew tongue is named Bethacarma, and it too is set on a mountain. What he says, therefore, is this: 'Since from the north Nebuchadnezzar is now on the very point of coming and captivity is near and threatening, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, seize your arms and sound the trumpet in Tekoa and in Beth-haccherem raise the standard', he says, 'so that you may be able to resist your enemies!' Beniamin means 'son of the right hand', Thecua 'trumpet', Bethaccarem 'estate of the vineyard'. […]

6:2.t: I have likened the daughter of Zion to a beautiful and delicate woman. To her shepherds will come with their flocks; they have pitched — or they will pitch — their tents against her round about; each one will pasture those who are under his hand. Sanctify — or Prepare — war against her; arise, and let us go up at noon! The beauty of Jerusalem is described, which is Zion itself, so that the one name denotes the whole city, the other the citadel of the city. For Sion means 'citadel', that is, watchtower, and she is compared to a beautiful woman; and as lovers come together to the one, so shepherds are said to come together to the other. […]

6:4.t: These princes or shepherds will say to their flocks: 'Sanctify against Jerusalem war, for it is the command of the Lord. Arise, and let us go up at noon: let us fight not by night and by ambush, but in full daylight; for no one can resist us'.

Woe to us, for the day has declined, for longer have grown — or have failed — the shadows of evening. Arise, and let us go up by night, and let us destroy the houses — or foundations — of her! Those say: 'Arise, and let us go up at noon, and let us fight in clear daylight'; these reply: woe to us, for the shadows of evening have grown longer, according to that saying of Vergil: and now far off the rooftops of the farmhouses smoke, and greater shadows fall from the high mountains. And the sense is: 'If we suffer these things by day, what shall we suffer by night?'

6:5.t: And again those who had said above: 'Sanctify war against her and arise', now rouse themselves to battle, saying: 'Arise, and let us go up by night, so that our adversaries may know that the victory belongs not to the time of day but to strength, and let us destroy the houses, which are fenced in vain by the firmness of their walls'.

6:6.t: For thus says the Lord of hosts: Cut down her tree — or her trees —, pour out — or heap up — a mound around Jerusalem! 'Therefore', they say, 'we are secure of victory, because it is the command of the Lord, who orders the Chaldeans: cut down the trees and heap up a mound for the siegeworks to come!' By these words it is shown, before it comes to pass, that the city was not to be taken at once by an encircling ring of troops, but by a long siege, as we read afterwards.

This is the city of visitation — or the lying city —, all false accusation — or oppression — is in her midst. As a cistern makes cold — or a pit — its water, so she has made her wickedness cold. The Lord commands that the trees be cut down, that mounds be cast up round about, because the time of her visitation has come, that she may receive the due for her sins, the greatest of which is sykophantia, that she oppresses the innocent by false accusation.

6:7.t: As, therefore, a cistern or pit makes its water cold, so in the midst of Jerusalem the wickedness that is in her has lost all the warmth of life. And this is to be noted, that the saints are called fervent in spirit, whereas evils are cold; whence that also is written, that in the last days, when iniquity has been multiplied, the love of many will grow cold. I think that this too means the same: I have been likened to those who go down into the pit. And let the Latin reader understand this, so that it may suffice to have said it once: that 'lacus' [pit] does not mean 'pool' according to the Greeks, but 'cistern', which in the Syriac and Hebrew tongue is called 'gubba'. In the present passage, however, for 'lacus', which all translated alike, in the Hebrew it is 'bor'.

Iniquity and devastation will be heard in her; before me continually are sickness and wound. Be instructed, Jerusalem, lest perhaps my soul depart from you, lest perhaps I make you a desert, an uninhabitable land! LXX: Ungodliness and misery will be heard in her before her face. Through every pain and scourge you will be instructed, Jerusalem, lest perhaps my soul depart from you, lest I make you a trackless land, which is not inhabited. Through these words we learn that the Lord scourges every son whom he receives; and for that reason Jerusalem is instructed by blows and torments, that she may be corrected, and that the soul of God may not depart from her and she be reduced to a wilderness. If ever, therefore, we lie under frequent distresses, let us recall for our consolation this little verse: through every pain and scourge you will be instructed, Jerusalem.

6:8.t: See the mercy and the loving-kindness of the good God. When he wishes to have mercy, he says that he is indignant and angry, as through Jeremiah he says: "with grief and with scourge you shall be chastised, Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from you". If you understand these things, it is the voice of a God who has mercy, where he is angry, where he is jealous, where he applies griefs and scourges. "For he scourges every son whom he receives".

6:9.t: And another prophet, Jeremiah, says, "Turn to the Lord your God, as a grape gatherer to his basket, and you shall find mercy." The sayings in the Holy Scriptures regarding repentance are many, yes, countless. God always desires that the human race turn from all its sins.
6:9.s: Theophilus to Autolycus, Book III, Chapter XI

6:9.t: God invites us to knowledge also, when he says by Jeremiah, "If you had walked in the way of God, you would have dwelled forever in peace." … God grants pardon to those who have erred. He says, "Turn, turn, as a grape gatherer returns to his basket." Do you see the goodness of justice in that it advises us to repent?

Thus says the Lord of hosts: Even to the last cluster they will glean, as in a vineyard, the remnant of Israel; turn back your hand like a grape-gatherer to the basket! LXX: For thus says the Lord of powers: Glean, glean as in a vineyard the remnant of Israel; return like a grape-gatherer to his basket! Some take these words in a good sense, others in a bad. In the good sense: 'When Jerusalem has been laid waste, let the remnant be saved'. In the bad, thus: 'Let not even one cluster and small bunch of grapes remain in the vineyard; let everything be gathered; and whatever you find, throw into the basket like a grape-gatherer, so that, as he drags the clusters to the winepress, so you may drag the captives to Babylon'.

6:10.t: To whom shall I speak, and whom shall I solemnly warn, that he may hear? Behold, their ears — or your ears — are uncircumcised, and they cannot hear! Behold, the word of the Lord has become to them a reproach, and they will not receive it! They cannot hear because they were unwilling to circumcise their ears; yet the inability is not free of punishment, since it comes down from contempt and unbelief. If anyone, therefore, does not receive the words of God and has no understanding of his precepts, he is of uncircumcised ears. And at the same time it is to be noted that circumcision in the Scriptures is spoken of in three kinds: in the foreskin, in the heart, and in the ears; whence the Lord too says: He who has ears to hear, let him hear. It is by our own will, therefore, that we do not receive the word of God; and for that reason it becomes to us a reproach, so that what had been given for salvation is turned by our own fault into punishment.

6:11.t: Therefore I am full of the fury of the Lord; I have toiled in holding it in. LXX: And I have filled up my fury and held it in, and I did not consume it. According to the Hebrew it is said in the person of the prophet, that he foresees the wrath of God that is coming, and is full of the fury and anger of the Lord, and can hold it in no longer, nor dares to entreat the Lord for sinners. According to the Seventy, however, a new sense is set down: that the Lord himself speaks and says: I have completed my fury, by striking the sinful people, and yet that he restrained it and did not pour it all out, so that a remnant might be saved. This seems to me to be self-contradictory; for if he completed his fury, how did he hold it in so as not to complete it?

Pour out — or He poured out — upon the little child outside and upon the council of young men together; for man with wife will be taken, the old man with him who is full of days. And their houses will pass to others, their fields and wives alike. Either the prophet in the spirit commands the coming Chaldean to pour out the fury of the Lord upon the little children and to spare not even their innocent age, or else he relates what has been done upon the council of young men together, who had seized their arms to fight back. For man with wife will be taken: names most sweet to one another will alike feel captivity, the old man with him who is full of days. Therefore old age is not the last age, but that of those who are 'full of days', whom in our own speech we call 'depositos' [given up for dead] or 'decrepitos' [decrepit].

6:12.t: There follows: and their houses will pass to others through the evil of captivity, their fields and wives together, so that both wife and possession pass to the enemy. Whatever we understand according to the letter of Jerusalem, let us refer according to the spiritual understanding to the Church, if she has offended God.

For I will stretch out my hand over those who inhabit the earth, says the Lord. For from the least even to the greatest, all are devoted to avarice, and from prophet even to priest all practice deceit. And they were healing the breach of the daughter of my people with disgrace, saying: Peace, peace! And there was no peace. What in the Hebrew is said: I will stretch out my hand over sinners or the inhabitants of the earth, among the Seventy is always written 'I will lift up'; and each is the posture of one who strikes, according to what is written: and still the hand of the Lord is stretched out or lifted high. The inhabitants of the earth, moreover, are always in vice; whence in Revelation too it is said quite frequently: Woe to the inhabitants of the earth!

6:13.t: From the least even to the greatest, all are devoted to avarice, according to that saying of the Apostle: the root of all evils is avarice. And from prophet even to priest all practice deceit: the one by prophesying a lie, the other by perversely interpreting the law of God; for the prophet also says in another place: Seek the law from the priests.

6:14.t: Idol temples had fallen before the standard of the cross and the severity of the gospel. Now, on the contrary, lust and gluttony endeavor to overthrow the solid structure of the cross. And so God says by Isaiah, "O my people, they who bless you cause you to wander and trouble the paths of your feet." Also by Jeremiah, "Flee out of the midst of Babylon, and save everyone his life, and believe not the false prophets who say, 'Peace, peace,' and there is no peace." Who are always repeating, "The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord." "Your prophets have seen for you false and foolish things. They have not laid bare your iniquity that they might call you to repentance. They devour God's people like bread. They have not called on God." Jeremiah announced the captivity and was stoned by the people. Hananiah, the son of Azzur, broke the bars of wood for the present but was preparing bars of iron for the future. False prophets always promise pleasant things and please for a time.

'And though', he says, 'they were doing such things, they kept announcing prosperity of every kind to my people, and as it were desired to heal the wound and the disgrace of my daughter, saying: Peace, peace, when there was no peace at all'. This is properly to be understood of the priests and teachers who promise prosperity to the rich and to those whom they see set in the highest honor, and proclaim God to be merciful, rather preparing them for punishment and wrath.

6:15.t: Were they confounded because they committed abomination? Nay rather, they were not confounded with confusion, and they knew not how to blush. This is to be read more closely according to the Hebrew. 'And though', he says, 'they have done such things, were they at all confounded? Did they at all blush in their crimes? Nay rather, they increased their contempt, and they knew not how to blush' — and he put 'knew not' here for 'would not' — 'or else, through excessive contempt and the vice of an ingrained evil, they could not even understand'.

Therefore they will fall among those who fall; in the time of their visitation they will collapse, says the Lord. 'Since', he says, 'they knew not how to blush, and had not only not the deed but not even the knowledge and the sense of repentance, therefore those who formerly stood will fall among them; they will collapse through their own vices and, when the time of their visitation and punishment has come, they will be joined to all who fall'. And it is a great ungodliness not only not to guard against sins but not even to be willing to understand them, and to make no distinction between good and evil works.

6:16.t: Since the soul became too enfeebled for the apprehension of realities, we needed a divine teacher. The Savior is sent down—a teacher and leader in the acquisition of the good, as the secret and sacred token of the great Providence. "Where, then, is the scribe? Where is the searcher of this world? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?" it is said. And again, "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent," speaks plainly of those who are wise in their own eyes and contentious. Excellently, therefore, Jeremiah says, "Thus says the Lord, 'Stand in the ways, and ask for the eternal paths, what is the good way, and walk in it, and you shall find expiation for your souls.' "

And through Jeremiah, he provides further enlightenment in the truth for those who have erred: "Thus says the Lord, stand in the roads, and look. Ask for the eternal paths of the Lord. Look for the good path, and walk in it, and you shall find purification for your souls." He leads us to repentance in order to promote our salvation.

But what sprinklings shall we now employ, while we celebrate the feast? Who will be our guide, as we haste to this festival? None can do this, my beloved, but Him Whom you will name with me, even our Lord Jesus Christ Who said, ‘I am the Way.’ For it is He Who, according to the blessed John, ‘taketh away the sin of the world.’ He purifies our souls, as Jeremiah the prophet says in a certain place, ‘Stand in the ways and see, and enquire, and look which is the good path, and ye shall find in it cleansing for your souls.’ Of old time, the blood of he-goats and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled upon those who were unclean, were fit only to purify the flesh; but now, through the grace of God the Word, every man is thoroughly cleansed.

Thus says the Lord: Stand upon the ways and see, and ask about the ancient paths, which is the good way, and walk in it! And you will find refreshment — or purification — for your souls. And they said: We will not walk — or We will not go —. And I set watchmen over you: hear the voice of the trumpet! And they said: We will not hear. Therefore hear — or they heard —, O nations, and know, O congregation — or you who pasture flocks, or according to Symmachus: and know the testimony that is in them —, how great things I will do to them! Hear, O earth! The parable of the Gospel, if it is understood, will furnish the understanding of this passage; in it the good merchant is said to sell all his pearls, so that with their price he may buy the one most precious pearl: namely, that through the patriarchs and prophets we come to him who says: I am the way. […]

There are many ways, and many ways lead to one way. Indeed, it is also said in Jeremiah: 'Stand in the ways of the Lord, and ask for the eternal paths of the Lord, and you will find the way, and you will walk in it.' See what it says, Stand in the ways, and ask for the eternal paths of the Lord, and you will find the one way, and walk in it. See how through many ways we come to one way. This is also said in the gospel in other words, under another meaning of the parable, concerning that merchant who had many pearls, who sold them, and bought one most precious pearl. What it says is this: Stand in the ways, that is, have very many pearls. Stand in the ways, and ask for the eternal paths of the Lord. Beautifully it says eternal, lest we should think that at the coming of Christ the law and the prophets were brought to an end. But see what it says. Stand in the ways, in the law and the prophets. Stand in the ways; do not so believe in the one way that you abandon the many ways; […]

6:17.t: And at once he adds: 'And I set watchmen over you' — no doubt the choir of the apostles is indicated, according to Ezekiel: Son of man, I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel —, 'and I commanded that you hear the voice of the trumpet, either the commands of the Gospel or the teaching of the apostles, according to that saying of Isaiah: Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; lift up your voice like a trumpet, you who announce to Jerusalem'.

6:18.t: They said: We will not hear, and when invited to the supper they would not come; therefore it is said: Hear, O nations! This the apostles too followed when they speak in Lycaonia: It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you; but since you thrust it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. And know, O congregation: by no means the Jewish one, but that of all nations; or, you who pasture flocks: the bishops and presbyters and the whole order of the Church; or, know the testimony that is in them; for the testimony of God is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones. To them the Lord also speaks: Fear not, little flock, and: Behold, I and my children, whom God has given me. 'Know, therefore, how great things I will do to the people that does not believe.'

6:19.t: And in what is added: Hear, O earth, the whole world is called to hear, as we also read at the beginning of Isaiah: Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth: that is, what the Lord is going to do to the people of the Jews.

Behold, I will bring evils upon this people, the fruit of their thoughts — or of their turning away —, because they have not heard my words and have cast away my law. He calls 'evils' the punishments and penalties of those who suffer, not upon the Gentiles, who are called to the truth of the Gospel, but upon the people that answered: We will not hear. And it is going to receive the fruit of its thoughts or of its turning away, as David says: You shall eat the labors of your hands. And the cause is plain: because they did not hear the words of the Lord and cast off his law.

6:20.t: For it was not because He was angry, like a man, as many venture to say, that He rejected their sacrifices; but out of compassion to their blindness, and with the view of suggesting to them the true sacrifice, by offering which they shall appease God, that they may receive life from Him. As He elsewhere declares: "The sacrifice to God is an afflicted heart: a sweet savour to God is a heart glorifying Him who formed it." For if, when angry, He had repudiated these sacrifices of theirs, as if they were persons unworthy to obtain His compassion, He would not certainly have urged these same things upon them as those by which they might be saved. But inasmuch as God is merciful, He did not cut them off from good counsel. For after He had said by Jeremiah, "To what purpose bring ye Me incense from Saba, and cinnamon from a far country? Your whole burnt-offerings and sacrifices are not acceptable to Me;" He proceeds: "Hear the word of the Lord, all Judah. […]

To what purpose do you bring me frankincense from Sheba, and sweet-smelling calamus from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not accepted, and your victims have not pleased me. That frankincense comes from Sheba no one doubts; whence also that line of Vergil: and a hundred altars glow with Sabaean incense. And that 'calamus', which in Hebrew is called 'cane', for which the Seventy and Theodotion translated 'cinnamon', comes from a distant land, the prophetic word shows, so that we may understand India, from which many spices come by way of the Red Sea. This kind of spice physicians call kassian syringos [pipe cassia]. And the sense is: 'In vain do you bring me spices of sweetest odor for compounding the ointments that are prescribed in the law, and kindle burnt offerings, you who do not do my will in the law', according to what was said above: they have not heard my words and have cast away my law. […]

6:21.t: Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will put ruins into this people, and they will fall in them — or weakness, and they will be weakened in it —, fathers and sons together, neighbor and kinsman, and they will perish. We see fulfilled all the things with which the Lord threatened that people; for daily they fall in their blasphemies, and they have nothing strong in them, but all is weakness among them. The sons follow the blasphemies of their fathers, and daily receive that imprecation: His blood be upon us and upon our children; and not only they themselves, but also their neighbors and kinsmen, all who follow the law and the prophets according to the letter that kills and not according to the spirit that gives life; and all alike will perish, because alike they have sinned.

6:22.t: Thus says the Lord: Behold, a people comes from the land of the north, and a great nation will rise from the ends of the earth. It will seize arrow and shield — or zibynnam [spear] —; it is cruel — or shameless — and will not have mercy; its voice will sound like the sea, and they will mount upon horses, prepared like a man for battle against you, daughter of Zion. This is properly prophesied of the Babylonians, who are to come against the people of Jerusalem; and the whole array of their armor and the onset of the combatants is described, so that, shaken by the terror of the voice, they may do repentance and appease a most merciful God. Finally, he gives occasion for entreaty when he says: against you, daughter of Zion. We may apply this testimony, in a transferred sense, to a time of persecution, when the whole rage of the devil is stirred up against us, and there is no mercy, and like the waves of a most violent sea they overwhelm those who resist.

6:24.t: We have heard the report of it; our hands have grown feeble; tribulation has seized us, pains as of a woman in labor. The people answers, whom the prophet, nay rather the Lord through the prophet, has threatened with the Babylonians: that before they come they have been overcome by fear, and cannot lift up their hands, and anguish has seized them as pain seizes a woman in labor; than which pain those women who have felt it affirm that nothing is more grievous.

6:25.t: Do not go out into the fields, and do not walk on the road, for the sword of the enemy, terror is all around! The Gospel teaches that one must not go out into the field nor come down from the height of the housetops, but must heed that word: Save yourself on the mountain, to which in Isaiah and Micah we are commanded to run and climb. According to the letter, however, it is commanded that they not go outside, that they not desert the walls, but that they protect themselves with strong fortifications.

6:26.t: Daughter of my people, gird yourself with sackcloth and sprinkle yourself with ashes; make for yourself the mourning for an only-begotten — or a beloved —, a bitter lament — or a pitiable one —, for suddenly the destroyer will come — or misery — upon us — or upon you — ! Since he had said above: Do not go out into the fields, and do not walk on the road, for the sword of the enemy, terror is all around, and had forbidden flight as well, he teaches what they ought to do: namely, that they be converted to repentance and have this as their firmest and safest armor. Where we have said: make for yourself the mourning for an only-begotten, for 'only-begotten' in the Hebrew is written 'iaid', which means 'solitary' rather than 'only-begotten'. For if it were 'beloved' or 'lovable', as the Seventy translated, 'ididia' would be set down, which is also the name God gave to Solomon. And nothing is more grievous than to lose one son, or an only son. […]

6:27.t: I have given you as a strong assayer among my people, and you will know and test their way. All these are princes turning aside — or disobedient —, walking deceitfully — or perversely —, bronze and iron; all of them are corrupted. The bellows has failed in the fire — which the Greeks more expressively call physētēra —, the lead is consumed, in vain has the smelter smelted — or the silversmith —; for their wickednesses have not been consumed. Call them reprobate silver, for the Lord has cast them away! The prophet is given to the unbelieving people as a 'strong' assayer, which in Hebrew is called 'mabsar', which means either 'fortified', according to Aquila, or 'shut in' and 'surrounded', according to Symmachus and the Seventy, like a most strongly fortified city, so that he may fear no ambushes of the people: 'so that, when you have tested', he says, 'and known the way of the transgressing people, you may then understand that silver mixed with bronze can by no means be purified'.

6:28.t: For as lead is mixed with metals that are adulterated and debased, so that the foreign matter may be separated, and, if perhaps it has not been purified, all the lead is consumed and reduced to nothing, so all the eloquence of teaching and the prophetic word perishes in those who scorn to hear. Let us speak also of those who, like deaf asps, stop their ears so as not to hear the voices of the charmers. For in vain has the silversmith smelted or the smelter; for their wickednesses have not been consumed. Hence they are called not 'silver' but 'reprobate silver', for the Lord has cast them off. And the princes are those who withdraw from the Lord, or the disobedient, who walk perversely and deceitfully.

6:29.t: And the prophet seeing that all the remedies of this life will have been applied in vain for their healing, and already as it were despairing of their life, declares: "The bellows have failed in the fire, the founder hath melted in vain: for their wicked deeds are not consumed. Call them reprobate silver, for the Lord hath rejected them." And the Lord thus laments that to no purpose has He applied this salutary cleansing by fire to those who are hardened in their sins, in the person of Jerusalem crusted all over with the rust of her sins, when He says: "set it empty upon burning coals, that it may be hot, and the brass thereof may be melted; and let the filth of it be melted in the midst thereof. Great pains have been taken, and the great rust thereof is not gone out, no not even by fire. Thy uncleanness is execrable: because I desired to cleanse thee, and thou art not cleansed from thy filthiness." […]

6:30.t: And again in like manner does Jeremiah speak: "I set watchmen over you; hearken to the sound of the trumpet; and they said, We will not hearken. Therefore have the Gentiles heard, and they who feed the flocks in them." It is therefore one and the same Father who planted the vineyard, who led forth the people, who sent the prophets, who sent His own Son, and who gave the vineyard to those other husbandmen that render the fruits in their season.

7:1.t: And thus did He send prophets prior to the transmigration to Babylon, and after that event others again in greater number than the former, to seek the fruits, saying thus to them (the Jews): "Thus saith the Lord, Cleanse your ways and your doings, execute just judgment, and look each one with pity and compassion on his brother: oppress not the widow nor the orphan, the proselyte nor the poor, and let none of you treasure up evil against his brother in your hearts, and love not false swearing. Wash you, make you clean, put away evil from your hearts, learn to do well, seek judgment, protect the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow; and come, let us reason together, saith the Lord." And again: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips that they speak no guile; depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it." In preaching these things, the prophets sought the fruits of righteousness.

7:2.t: The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Stand in the gate of the house of the Lord and proclaim — or read — there this word, and say: Hear the word of the Lord, all Judah, you who enter by these gates to worship the Lord! This is not found in the edition of the Seventy, but has been added from Theodotion out of the Hebrew. Now the prophet is commanded to stand in the gate of the Lord, through which the multitude of the people enters to pray to the Lord, so that on this occasion they may be able to hear what the Lord commands. By this we understand the hardness of the people of the Jews, in that they held the prophets as liars and madmen, since it is through the occasion and the throng of the place that they are compelled to hear the words of the Lord, and not because they are the words of the Lord.

7:3.t: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Make good — or direct — your ways and your pursuits — or your devices — and I will dwell with you in this place or I will make you dwell in this place. The most merciful physician desires to heal the wounded with every remedy. But when he says: make good or correct your ways, he shows that they are perverse and have nothing good in them. And because it is natural that each person loves his native soil and holds nothing sweeter than his fatherland, he promises rewards to the obedient. 'I will dwell,' he says, 'with you, so that I may make you secure about your dwelling, or I will found you yourselves' — according to Symmachus — 'with a firm dwelling', who says: and I will establish you in this place.

7:4.t: And now hear concerning faith that is based upon the Stone, and concerning the structure that is reared up upon the Stone. For first a man believes, and when he believes, he loves. When he loves, he hopes. When he hopes, he is justified. When he is justified, he is perfected. When he is perfected, he is consummated.
