But if we received, why do we glory as if we had not received? Therefore, as "he that glorieth must glory in the Lord," it comes from His mercy, not their merit, that God wills to impart this to some, but from His truth that He wills not to impart it to others. For to sinners punishment is justly due.
9:24.s: ON THE MERITS AND FORGIVENESS OF SINS, AND ON THE BAPTISM OF INFANTS 2:31

9:24.t: For as many of this race as are delivered by God's grace are certainly delivered from the condemnation in which they are already held bound. Whence, even if none should be delivered, no one could justly blame the judgment of God. That, therefore, in comparison of those that perish few, but in their absolute number many, are delivered, is effected by grace, is effected freely: thanks must be given, because it is effected, so that no one may be lifted up as of his own deservings, but that every mouth may be stopped, and he that glorieth may glory in the Lord.

9:25.t: Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will visit upon everyone who have the foreskin circumcised, upon Egypt and upon Judah and upon Edom and upon the sons of Ammon and upon Moab and upon all who are shorn about the hair, dwelling in the desert; for all the nations have the foreskin, but all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart. In part, the peoples of many nations, and especially of those that border on Judea and Palestine, are circumcised to this day, and above all the Egyptians and the Edomites, the Ammonites and the Moabites, and the whole region of the Saracens, which dwells in the wilderness and of whom it is said: upon all who are shorn about the hair, dwelling in the desert. Judah, therefore, who is mingled with the nations written above, ought not to glory because he does not have the foreskin but is circumcised by the law of God, since others too do these things who do not keep the commandments of the law and do not know the God of Israel. […]

9:26.t: But perhaps the novelty of the saying may deter not only the Jews but also some of our brethren. For Paul seems to presume impossible things, in that he introduces "circumcision of the heart." For how can it come about that a member be circumcised which, hidden by the inner organs, lies concealed even from the very sight of men? Let us return, then, to the prophetic utterances, so that, while you pray, these matters about which we inquire may from there become clear. The prophet Ezekiel says: "Every stranger uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh shall not enter into my sanctuary." And likewise elsewhere the prophet, reproaching them no less, says: "all the strangers are uncircumcised in flesh, but the sons of Israel are uncircumcised in heart." It is signified, therefore, that unless one has been circumcised in heart and circumcised in flesh, "he shall not enter into the sanctuary" of God.

10:2.t: Hear the word which the Lord has spoken concerning you, house of Israel! Thus says the Lord: Do not learn according to the ways of the nations, and do not be afraid of the signs of heaven, which the nations fear, for the laws of the peoples are vain! He speaks properly against those who venerate the heavenly bodies and suppose that the human race is ruled by those which have been set as signs of years, seasons, months and days, and that earthly things are governed by the causes of heavenly ones. And in saying: the laws or the statutes of the peoples are vain, he shows that all human wisdom is futile and has no usefulness in itself.

10:3.t: For he has cut wood from the forest, the work of the craftsman's hands with the adze; with silver and gold he has adorned it, with nails and hammers he has fastened it, that it may not come apart — or may not be moved —. They are fashioned after the likeness of a palm tree and will not speak; carried, they will be lifted, because they cannot walk. Do not therefore fear them, for they can do neither evil nor good. A description of the idols which the nations venerate. He has cut wood, he says, from the forest — the material of idols, then, is cheap and perishable — the work of the craftsman's hands — since the craftsman is mortal, mortal therefore are those things too which he fashions —; with silver and gold he has adorned it, so that by the gleam of both materials he may deceive the simple. And this error has passed down even to us, so that we think religion lies in riches. With nails and hammers he has fastened it, that it may not come apart or that it may not be moved. […]

10:6.t: Therefore we ought to believe that God is good, eternal, perfect, almighty and true, such as we find him in the Law and the Prophets and the rest of the Holy Scriptures, for otherwise there is no God. For he who is God must be good, seeing that fullness of goodness is of the nature of God. God, who made time, cannot be in time. Again, God cannot be imperfect, for a lesser being is plainly imperfect, seeing that it lacks somewhat whereby it could be made equal to a greater. This, then, is the teaching of our faith—that God is not evil, that with God nothing is impossible, that God does not exist in time, that God is beneath no being. If I am in error, let my adversaries prove it.

These tokens so declare the nature of the Son, that by them you may know both that the Father is eternal, and that the Son is not diverse from Him; for the source of generation is He Who is, and as begotten of the Eternal, He is God; coming forth from the Father, He is the Son; from God, He is the Word; He is the radiance of the Father's glory, the expression of His substance, the counterpart of God, the image of His majesty; the Bounty of Him Who is bountiful, the Wisdom of Him Who is wise, the Power of the Mighty One, the Truth of Him Who is true, the Life of the Living One.

There is none like you, O Lord; great are you, and great is your name in might. Who will not fear you, O king of the nations? For yours is the beauty; among all the wise of the nations and in all their kingdoms there is none like you. The wise and the foolish alike shall be proved; the teaching of their vanity is wood; silver wrapped — or drawn out — is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz, the work of the craftsman and of the hand of the coppersmith; blue and purple are their clothing; the work of craftsmen — or of the wise — are all these things. But the Lord is the true God; this is the living God and the everlasting king. At his indignation the earth will be shaken, and the nations will not endure his threatening. These words are not found in the Seventy, but in most copies they have been added from Theodotion's edition, and although according to the letter they seem clear, according to the anagōgēn [the higher, spiritual sense] they hold great difficulty. […]

The fear of God arises in us from the consideration of divine power. Whence in Jeremiah: "There is none like unto thee, O Lord; thou art great, and thy name is great in might: who would not fear thee, O king of nations?" He sets forth first the magnitude of divine power, when he says: "There is none like unto thee, O Lord"; whence in the book of Wisdom: "As a drop of morning dew, so is the whole world before thee." Therefore who would not fear thee, unless he be impious and foolish?

10:7.t: The fear of God arises in us from the consideration of divine power. "Who would not fear thee, O king of nations? For thine is the glory: among all the wise men of the nations and in all their kingdoms, who is like unto thee?" Therefore who would not fear thee, unless he be impious and foolish? If a man is impious, he is in need of punishment; if he is foolish, he is in need of understanding.

10:8.t: They are at once wise and foolish; their teaching, according to the quality of their talent, is either cheap and is compared to wood, or is like silver because of the charm of its eloquence; it is brought from Tarshish — either it is a region of India, as Josephus would have it, or else the whole sea is called Tarshish and has a likeness to the sky — and yet it is wrapped in the artifice of words; for if it were laid open, it could not deceive. And gold from Uphaz. Gold is called by seven names among the Hebrews, of which one is called 'ophaz', which we can call 'obryzum' [refined gold], so that it may gleam on the surface of the idols, which within is wood and of cheap material. They are covered with blue and purple, so that by their surface they may deceive the eyes, while they promise themselves the color of the heavens and the heavenly kingdoms; and yet all these things are works of the wise, who are thought wise in the world, but before God are foolish.

10:10.t: But the Lord our God is the true God — all those, therefore, are lies — and he himself is the living God — so those which are fashioned are dead — and the everlasting king — the shadows of the heretics prevail for a time, but in the long run they decay —; at his indignation the earth will be shaken — those who have earthly works and fashion earthly images — and the nations will not endure: by no means the people of the Lord, but the multitude of the nations, which cannot bear God's threatening.

10:11.t: But if heretics deny that either the heavens or the earth were made by you, O Lord, let them take heed of the abyss into which they are hurling themselves by their own madness. The prophet writes, "Perish the gods that have not made heaven and earth." Shall he then perish, O Arian, who had found and saved that which had perished?

Next, he adduces what indeed is the greatest token of divinity; "of Whom are all things." For this implies also that those others are not gods. For it is said, "Let the gods who made not the heaven and the earth perish." Then he subjoins what is not less than this, "and we unto Him." For when he saith, "of Whom are all things," he means the creation and the bringing of things out of nothing into existence. But when he saith, "and we unto Him," he speaks of the word of faith and mutual appropriation, as also he said before, "but of Him are ye also in Christ Jesus."

Thus therefore you shall say to them: The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth, let them perish from the earth and from those things which are under heaven! These words are to be said to the false gods and to those which have been put together by artifice — for they made neither the heavens nor the earth —, words which the fellow workers of Christ, who are called God's and the Lord's, for the most part frame through the Church's teaching.

In reading what is said in this Psalm of Christ and of the Church, he would find that what is there foretold is fulfilled in the present state of the world. He would see the idols of the nations perishing from off the earth, and he would find that this is predicted by the prophets, as in Jeremiah, "Then shall ye say unto them, The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth, and from under heaven;" and again, "O Lord, my strength, and my fortress, and my refuge in the day of affliction, the Gentiles shall come unto Thee from the ends of the earth, and shall say, Surely our fathers have inherited lies, vanity, and things wherein there is no profit. Shall a man make gods unto himself, and they are no gods? Therefore, behold, I will at that time cause them to know, I will cause them to know mine hand and my might; and they shall know that I am the Lord." Hearing these prophecies, and seeing their actual fulfillment, I need not say that he would be affected; […]

Ye heard when Jeremiah was being read before the reading of the Apostle, if ye listened; ye saw therein the times in which we now live. He said, “The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth, let them perish from the earth, and from under the heaven.” He said not, The gods that have not made the heavens and earth, let them perish from the heaven and from the earth; because they never were in heaven: but what did he say? “Let them perish from the earth, and from under the heaven.” As if, while the word earth was repeated, the repetition of the word heaven were wanting (because they never were in heaven): he repeateth the earth twice, since it is under heaven. “Let them perish from the earth, and from under the heaven,” from their temples. Consider if this be not now taking place; if in a great measure it hath not already happened: for what, or how much, hath remained? The idols remained rather in the hearts of the pagans, than in the niches of the temples.

10:12.t: The prophet of God, having taken up as it were three excellences of His—His strength, His wisdom, and His understanding—assigns to each of them a work proper to it: to the strength the earth, to the wisdom the inhabited world, and to the understanding the heaven. For listen to the passage as it says: "The Lord who made the earth in His strength, who set upright the inhabited world in His wisdom, and in His understanding stretched out the heaven." And we too, as regards our earth (for it was said to Adam, "Earth you are, and to earth you shall depart"), have need of the strength of God, and apart from the power of God we are not able to accomplish these things, all that is not according to "the mind-set of the flesh." And when "the members that are upon the earth" have been put to death, then there will be what is according to the will of the Spirit, since "by the Spirit the deeds of the flesh," according to the apostle, are put to death. "The Lord," then, "who made the earth in His strength." […]

The Lord, who makes — or made — the earth by his might, prepares the world by his wisdom, and by his prudence stretches out the heavens. At his voice he gives a multitude of waters in the heaven, and lifts up — or brings out — the mists from the ends of the earth; he has made lightnings into rain, and brings out the wind — or the winds — from his treasuries. Every man has become foolish from knowledge; every craftsman is confounded in his carved image, for what he has cast is false, and there is no spirit in them. They are vain and works worthy of laughter; in the time of their visitation they will perish. Not like these is the portion of Jacob; for he who formed all things, he it is, and Israel is the rod of his inheritance; the Lord of hosts is his name. He who makes the earth by his might is God the Father. And he makes it by his might, that is, by the Lord the Savior; for Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. He himself is also the prudence in which he stretches out the heaven. […]

10:13.t: "And He brought up clouds from the end of the earth." This saying fell to us recently also in the psalm, and we were saying how God "brought up clouds from the end of the earth." Which things it is necessary to take up again—for those who know, for the clarification and reminder of what has been said, but for those who have forgotten or were not present, for the plain understanding of this, whether it be revealed and made manifest or however it may be understood. And we were saying that the saints are clouds. For the phrase "your truth is unto the clouds" cannot be referred to the lifeless clouds; but the truth of God is unto the clouds, which hear the commandment of God and know where they should send forth rain and from what places they should withhold it. For, as of clouds which exist, to which God gives command not to rain or to rain, it is written, "I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it." […]

At his voice he gives a multitude of waters in the heaven. For all the teaching of the Lord flows from heavenly things, as David says: A willing rain you will set apart, O God, for your inheritance, and it was weakened; but you have perfected it. And he lifts up — or brings out — the mists from the ends of the earth. The mists or clouds, which the Lord commanded not to rain a shower upon Israel, are brought out from the extremities of the earth; one of these mists said: For I think that God has displayed us apostles as last, as men destined to death, because we have been made a spectacle to this world, both to angels and to men. He has made lightnings into rain. For when the shower of teachings has come from heaven and has sated the parched hearts of men, then you will find flashes and the bright lightnings of wisdom. And he brings out the winds from his treasuries, in which are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

10:14.t: "Every man was made foolish from knowledge." If every man was made foolish from knowledge, and Paul too is a man, Paul was made foolish from knowledge; for "knowing in part and prophesying in part," he was made foolish from knowledge; "seeing through a mirror," seeing in an enigma, seeing and grasping a small fraction, and, if one may say so, an infinitesimal fraction of things. But you will understand from the contrary "every man was made foolish from knowledge." There are sins of Jerusalem, and sins also of Sodom, but by comparison with the worse sins of Jerusalem, the sins of Sodom are righteousness; for it says, "Sodom was justified from you." As, then, the sins of Sodom are not righteousness but injustice, yet as compared with the greater injustice it is righteousness, so, from the contrary, knowledge—the knowledge that belongs to Paul—as compared with that knowledge which is in the heavens, as compared with the perfect knowledge, is foolishness. On this account "every man was made foolish from knowledge." […]

The psalmist writes, "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me. It is high; I cannot attain unto it." In another: "When I thought how I might know this, it was too painful for me until I went into the sanctuary of God and considered their latter end." And later in the same psalm, "I was as a beast before you; nevertheless I am continually with you." And Jeremiah says, "Every person is become brutish and without knowledge."

Every man has become foolish from knowledge. Though it be Paul, though Peter, though Moses and Abraham, in comparison with God all their wisdom will be counted as nothing; whence also the foolishness of God is wiser than men. Every craftsman is confounded in his carved image, he who has fashioned images out of his own heart, and what he has cast is false. But if every man is foolish from knowledge, everything that he has made is foolish and false. And there is no spirit in them. It should be noted that in this passage too 'wind' and 'spirit' are called by one name among the Hebrews, 'ruha'; but he means the spirit of sanctification, which cannot be found in the minds of heretics.

In the second word: You shall not make a graven image, all false and superstitious inventions of errors are prohibited. Every error is nothing other than a fiction of the mind. For imagination produces error by clouding reason and making what is not appear to be. All false and superstitious inventions of errors arise either from the wicked audacity of philosophical investigation, or from a perverse understanding of Sacred Scripture, or from a disordered affection of human carnality. Concerning such men, however, who devise, or defend, or imitate these or similar errors, Jeremiah says: Every man has become foolish by his own knowledge, that is, by his own investigation and excessive philosophy; every craftsman has been confounded by his graven image: their works are vain and worthy of ridicule, and in the time of their visitation they shall perish. We must therefore stand upon what the lights of faith dictate, and whatever is opposed to this, we ought to abominate entirely as a graven image.

The first brightness, namely that of philosophical knowledge, is great according to the opinion of worldly men: but it is easily eclipsed, unless a man guards himself from the head and tail of the dragon. If anything is interposed between him and the sun of justice, he suffers an eclipse of foolishness. "Every man is made foolish by his knowledge," namely occasioned by it, not caused by it. He who trusts in philosophical knowledge and esteems himself on account of this and believes himself to be better, has been made foolish—namely, when through this knowledge without any further light he believes himself to apprehend the Creator: just as if a man should wish to see the heavens or the body of the sun by candlelight.

10:15.t: They are vain and a work worthy of laughter. For who would not laugh when he has looked closely at the images of the heretics? For either what they say is rustic, and it is wood; or it is composed in fine speech, and it is found to be silver; or else it is feigned out of their own mind, and in vain they promise the image of gold. In the time of their visitation they will perish. Heresy prevails for a time, so that all the elect may become manifest and be proved; but when the visitation of God has come and his eye has looked upon foolish things, all things fall silent.

10:16.t: Not like these is the portion of Jacob, that is, of those who supplanted the Jews and daily destroy the heretics. But the portion of the saints is God, of whom the prophet says: The Lord is my portion. For he who formed all things, he it is, who made and molded all things, both in mind and in body, and Israel is the rod of his inheritance. Everyone who is 'upright in God' or 'discerns God with the mind' is the scepter of his inheritance, whose name is 'the Lord almighty' or 'of powers'; for this is what 'the Lord of hosts' means, which in the Hebrew is written 'the Lord sabaoth'.

10:17.t: Gather out of the land your confusion, you who dwell under siege, for thus says the Lord: Behold, I will cast far away the inhabitants of the land at this turn, and I will afflict them, that they may be found. LXX: She has gathered from outside her substance, she who dwells in a stronghold, for thus says the Lord: Behold, I will supplant the inhabitants of this land and afflict them, that they may be found. Jerusalem is commanded to gather whatever substance she has outside into the most strongly fortified city and to prepare provisions for a long siege; for he is threatening no longer, as before, about a future and distant time, but now about the captivity close at hand, which is about to come at any moment. 'Gather,' he says, 'both from outside and from the land, that is, from the fields, your substance into confusion. For whatever you have is worthy of confusion; […]

10:19.t: Woe is me over my crushing, my most grievous wound! LXX: Woe over your crushing, your most grievous wound! According to the Hebrew, Jerusalem herself speaks, because she is grievously afflicted and bears an incurable wound; but according to the Seventy, the prophet speaks to Jerusalem and laments her over her crushing and her own wound.

But I said: Truly this is my infirmity — or my wound — and I will bear it or it has seized me. Jerusalem herself speaks: 'Whatever I suffer, I suffer through my own fault; I understand my wound, which has seized me, or I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him'.

10:20.t: My tabernacle is established, all my cords are broken — or all my skins are torn apart —, my sons have gone out from me — or my sheep — and they are not; there is no one to stretch out my tent any more — or there is no more place for my tabernacle — and to raise up my skins. Jerusalem laments the overthrow of her city as so easy that you would think it not the razing of the walls and all the fortifications to the ground, but the taking down of a tabernacle and a tent. 'My tabernacle,' she says, 'that is, my dwelling, has suddenly been taken away. All my cords are broken — she keeps the metaphoran [metaphor] of the tabernacle — or all my skins are torn apart. My sons have gone out from me or my cattle'; this, added by the Seventy, does not stand according to the history; for in a long siege how could sheep and cattle have been carried off from Jerusalem, when, even if there had been any, famine had consumed them? 'And they do not', she says, 'subsist or they are not'; […]

10:21.t: For the shepherds have acted foolishly and have not sought the Lord; therefore they have not understood, and all their flock has been scattered. Through the metaphor of shepherds and sheep the guilt of the princes and the scattering of the people are described. For because the princes acted foolishly and did not seek the Lord, whom they ought to have sought with their whole heart, therefore they did not see the evils that were coming, or did not understand the Lord, and the whole multitude of Jerusalem has been scattered hither and thither.

10:22.t: A voice of hearing, behold, comes, and a great commotion from the land of the north, to make the cities of Judah a desolation and a dwelling of dragons — or a lair of ostriches and, as Symmachus translated, of sirens —; for this in the Hebrew 'thannim' is set down. The words of the prophet: 'Behold,' he says, 'the sound and roaring of the Babylonian as he comes is heard, and a great commotion, or earthquake, from the land of the north, to reduce all the cities of Judea to desolation, their inhabitants slain, and to make dragons and all venomous creatures dwell in place of men, or ostriches'; this animal too is at home in desolation, and is born and nourished in deserts; or else we can understand sirens, certain monsters and phantoms of demons. All these things, which both the past and the present discourse have described, let us refer to the times of the Church's persecution, when the tabernacles of the Lord are overthrown and every dwelling of the Church is reduced to desolation. […]

10:23.t: "All are governed by their own free choice." What Christian can bear to hear this? For if not one, or a few or many, but all of us are governed by our own free choice, what becomes of the help of God? How do you explain the proverb that "A person's goings are ordered by the Lord?" Or "A person's way is not in himself"? Or "No one can receive anything, unless it be given him from above"? And elsewhere, "What do you have that you did not receive?"

I know, O Lord, that his way is not man's, nor is it a man's to walk and to direct his steps. Let the new preachers blush, who say that each one is ruled by his own will, when this prophet too says: his way is not man's, and David sings in a lyric song: By the Lord shall a man's steps be directed, and he will greatly desire his way. Or else this is the sense: 'What we suffer from the Babylonians comes not from dread of them, but from our desert and from your indignation'.

This the general of our forces learned when he entered as a captive the same city of the enemy that he had boasted he would enter that same day as victor. He proved indeed the words of the prophet: "For a man's way is not his own, nor is it in his own power to walk and direct his steps.'' Since he thought his actions were under his own control, he could neither direct his steps nor find the way of safety. So we read: "He poureth contempt upon the prince and causeth him to wander in the wilderness where there is no way. . . . He has been brought to nothing, even as the waters which run continually." In him, indeed, in addition to his actual misfortune, the present judgment of God was clearly shown. He has endured all the sufferings that he had boasted he would inflict on others. Because he trusted that the enemy could be taken without God's aid and consent, he has himself been captured; he claimed foreknowledge and wisdom and has met with disgrace for his presumption; […]
10:23.s: On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapter 10

10:24.t: Chasten me, O Lord, but yet in judgment and not in your fury, lest perhaps you bring me to nothing! Pour out your indignation upon the nations which have not known you, and upon the provinces — or generations — which have not called upon your name, for they have devoured Jacob and consumed his place, and his beauty — or pastures — they have scattered or reduced to desolation. We read this passage in the Psalm: O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, nor chasten me in your wrath! And the sense is: 'We deserve indeed all that we endure, and we deserve much greater things than we suffer; yet this I beseech, that you chasten me as a father, not as an adversary, that you amend me as a son and do not punish me as an enemy; for you chastise every son whom you receive, and through every pain and scourge you amend Jerusalem. But the enemies, who have not known you, and the provinces or regions, which have not called upon your name, ought by no means to feel your judgment, but your indignation. […]

11:1.t: According to the recorded coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, His sojourn came about bodily in a certain universal way, shining upon the whole world, when "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." For "there was the true Light which enlightens every man coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through Him, and the world knew Him not. He came unto His own, and His own received Him not." Yet one must know that even earlier He sojourned, though not bodily, in each of the saints, and that after this His visible coming He sojourns among us again. And if you wish to receive a demonstration of these things, attend to the passage: "The word which came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Hear," and what follows. For what is "the word which came from the Lord," whether to Jeremiah or to Isaiah or to Ezekiel or to whomever, other than He who was in the beginning with God? […]

The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Hear the words of this pact — or covenant — and speak to the men of Judah and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel. It is not, indeed, set down in the heading at what time, or under which king and in which year of his, this prophecy was made; but we understand either that it is to be joined to the former prophecy and its time, or certainly that this word of the Lord came to the prophet some interval of time after the former prophecy. It is to be noted, moreover, that the word 'berith' Aquila and Symmachus always translated 'pact', the Seventy and Theodotion 'covenant'. Properly, however, the word is now directed to Jerusalem and to the men of the tribe of Judah.

11:2.t: What then are we also to hear? "Hear the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem." We are men of Judah because of Christ; for it is plain that our Lord "has arisen out of Judah," and if I establish, according to Scripture, that the name of Judah refers to Christ, then the men of Judah will not be the Jews who disbelieve in Christ, but ourselves, as many as believe in Christ. "Judah, may your brothers praise you. Your hands are upon the back of your enemies"—"may they praise you." His brothers did not praise that Judah, the son of Jacob. But this Judah his brothers will praise, since this Judah says, "I will declare your name to my brothers, in the midst of the church I will hymn you." It is not said with reference to that Judah. "Your hands are upon the back of your enemies": where is that Judah found laying his hands upon the back of his enemies? The narrative has recorded nothing of the sort concerning him. […]

11:3.t: "Hear," then, "the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Cursed is the man who will not hear the words of the covenant which I commanded your fathers." Who most of all hears "the words of the covenant which God commanded the fathers"? Is it those who believe in Him, or those who are shown not even to believe Moses by the very fact that they have not believed in the Lord? For the Savior says to those men: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote concerning me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?" Therefore those men have not believed in Moses, but we who believe in Christ believe the covenant given through Moses, and it is spoken to us, that we may not become accursed: "Cursed is the man who will not hear the words of the covenant which I commanded the fathers." Those men, then, have this—to be accursed. […]

11:4.t:
"In the day," He says, "when I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace." Us too God has led out "of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace," especially according to him who has understood what is written in the Revelation of John, that the place "where their Lord was crucified is called spiritually Sodom and Egypt." For if it "is called spiritually Egypt," and this Egypt is not that Egypt which is spiritually called Egypt, for this one is perceptible to the senses, it is clear that if you understand the Egypt which is spiritually so called and go out from it, you are the one who has gone out "of the land of Egypt and out of the iron furnace," and it is said to you: "Hear my voice and do according to all" these things.

Then there is a promise of God to those who hear, if they do what He has commanded, saying: "And you shall be to me a people, and I will be to you a God." Not everyone who says he is the people of God is the people of God; […]

Cursed be the man who will not hear the words of this pact, which I commanded your fathers in the day in which I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace, saying: Hear my voice and do all that I command you, and you shall be my people and I will be your Lord. Not because of the privileges of race, not because of the injury of circumcision and the idleness of the sabbath, but because of obedience does God become the God of the people of Israel, and Israel his people. And here, indeed, he speaks as to servants, that they may please God; but in the Gospel the Lord says to the disciples: You, he says, are my friends, if you do what I command you. No longer do I call you servants, because the servant does not know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, because all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. And when they have become friends, from friends they pass over into sons; for as many as received him, to them he gave power to become sons of God. […]

11:5.t: What then does God promise me? "You shall be to me a people, and I will be to you a God." He is not the God of all, but only of those to whom He grants Himself, just as He granted Himself to that patriarch to whom He said, "I am your God," and again to another, "I will be your God," and concerning others, "I will be their God." When, then, do we attain—I speak of each individual—to God being our God? But if you wish to learn whose God He is and to whom He grants the invocation of Himself, "I," He says, "am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob." And the Savior, expounding this very thing, says: "God is not the God of the dead but of the living." Who is the dead? The sinner, who does not have the One who said, "I am the Life," the one who has dead works, the one who has not yet repented from dead works, concerning which the apostle says: "Not again laying a foundation of repentance from dead works." […]

Then to what was said beforehand by the Lord the prophet answers—to the words "Cursed is the man who will not hear the words of this covenant"—and he says: "And I answered and said, So be it, Lord." What is "So be it, Lord"? Cursed is he who will not abide in the words of this covenant.

This was the reason why He sent not Jeremiah only into Egypt, but also Ezekiel into Babylon, and they did not refuse to go. For when they found their Master love the people exceedingly, they continued themselves to do so likewise. Much as if a right-minded servant were to take compassion upon an intractable son when he saw his father grieving and lamenting about him. And what was there that they did not suffer for them? They were sawn asunder, they were driven out, they were reproached, they were stoned, they underwent numberless grievances. And after all this they would run back to them.… And for the people of the Jews, Jeremiah has composed Lamentations in writing. And when the general of the Persians had given him liberty to dwell securely, and with perfect freedom, wherever he pleased, he preferred above dwelling at home the affliction of the people, and their hard durance in a strange land.

That I may raise up the oath which I swore to your fathers, that I would give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as it is this day. The fathers are seen to receive when the sons receive, and the promise to Abraham is fulfilled in his posterity. A land moreover streaming with milk and honey we ought to take hyperbolically, for an abundance of all things, as in that line: let honey flow for them, and let the rough bramble bear amomum, and again: and he held back the wine running everywhere in streams; or else, tropologically, let us understand the land streaming with milk and honey as the Church of Christ, in which, as little ones and sucklings, we are brought up through faith, so that we may be able to take solid food.

And I answered and said: Amen, O Lord, for which LXX: So be it, O Lord — for this is what 'amen' signifies — is what they translated. The Lord had said: I swore to your fathers that I would give them a land streaming with milk and honey, as is proved today by the facts themselves. The prophet, loving his people, takes up the voice of the Lord and longs that what has been given may be true and may endure forever. Hence he says: 'Truly, O Lord, you have fulfilled what you promised; or So be it, O Lord, that is: may what you have given remain always!'

11:6.t: "And the Lord said to me: Read these words in the cities of Judah and outside Jerusalem." And to those outside we read the words of God, calling them to salvation. "Hear the words of this covenant and do them."

And the Lord said to me: Cry out — or read — all these words in the cities of Judah and outside Jerusalem, saying: Hear the words of this pact and do them! The most merciful God frequently foretells what is to come, so that the mind that is hard to believe may at last be softened. And he foretells it both in the city of Jerusalem and outside in the countryside, so that those whose peril is common may have the same penitence.

11:7.t: For, testifying, I testified to your fathers in the day in which I brought them out of the land of Egypt, even to this day; rising early I testified and said: Hear my voice! And they did not hear nor incline their ear, but each one went away in the perversity of his evil heart; and I brought upon them all the words of this pact, which I commanded them to do. Up to this point it is not found in the LXX, and what follows: and they did not do it, was placed by them and joined to the end of the preceding passage, in which it is written: Hear the words of this pact and do them! And they did not do it. But what it means to rise early and frequently press the words of God upon them through the prophets, and to bring them out of Egypt, and often to admonish them and to say: Hear my voice, and that they went away after the perversity of their heart, and that afterwards he renders to them what they deserve to receive, we have already said before.

11:9.t: "And they did not do them. And the Lord said to me: A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem." Are we going to repent over the sins spoken of concerning the men of Judah, knowing that we are men of Judah because of Christ who was prophesied and spoken of? For perhaps, since there are among us certain sinners who act contrary to right reason, for this reason the prophet says: "A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem." For when there is found, in certain persons who bear the name of the church, a bond of injustice and a bond of sins, so that to them may be applied what is said of the sinner, "and each one is bound tight by the cords of his own sins," God would say: "A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah." But let no conspiracy be found among us. And how is a conspiracy not found among us, even if until now there is a conspiracy in certain persons? […]

And the Lord said to me: A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem. They have turned back to the former iniquities of their fathers, who would not hear my words; and these, therefore, have gone after foreign gods to serve them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have made void my pact, which I made with their fathers. For 'conspiracy', which we have translated following Symmachus, Aquila and the Seventy and Theodotion translated syndesmon, which we can call 'a binding-together'. Hence also Athaliah, when she discovered that a plot was being prepared against her in the temple, spoke with the same word: Conspiracy, conspiracy. Properly, however, Scripture employs this word when one strives toward wrongdoing not by a sudden and chance sin but by prepared plots and conspiracy, and when with like mind and one zeal they act so as to despise the commandments of God.

11:10.t: "A conspiracy," then, "has been found among the men of Judah and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem. They have turned back to the injustices of their fathers of former times." "They have turned back to the injustices"—of whom? He does not say simply "of the fathers." What is the addition? "They have turned back to the injustices of their fathers of former times." We were saying that these things are spoken to us and to those among us who sin. How then have those among us who sin turned back not "to the injustices of the fathers," but "of their fathers of former times"? Perhaps, then, our fathers are twofold, and there is among us the worse kind of fathers; for before we believed we were sons, so to speak, of the devil, as the evangelic word shows, saying: "You are of your father the devil," but when we believed, we became sons of God. When, therefore, we sin, we turn back to the injustices not simply of the fathers, but of the former fathers. […]

And he says that both fathers and sons, with one mind and an equal resolve, neglecting God, worshiped idols, namely both Israel and the house of Judah, that is, both the ten tribes and the two, whose rule was in Jerusalem, so that those who had one zeal in contempt of God may have an equal punishment in enduring captivity.

11:11.t: Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will bring upon them evils from which they will not be able to go out; and they will cry to me and I will not hear them. And the cities of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will go and cry to the gods to whom they pour libations; and these will not save them in the time of their affliction. God does not hear in the time of need and distress, because they too would not hear the voice of the Lord. This Saul also suffered; for when, dreading the ranks of the Philistines, he had not deserved to receive the word of the Lord, he turned to the pythoness, so as to learn from idols what he ought to have wrung from the Lord by the insistence of prayer and of tears. Through these things we learn that, even if the Lord does not hear, we must by no means cease, nor flee for refuge to demons. They cannot help their worshipers; but we must flee to the help of the Lord, who, though angered, is quickly turned and changes his sentence, if those too with whom he has been angry are changed. […]

Theodore: Sometimes holy Scripture is wont by an improper use of terms to use "evils "for "affliction;" not that these are properly and in their nature evils, but because they are imagined to be evils by those on whom they are brought for their good. For when divine judgment is reasoning with men it must speak with the language and feelings of men. For when a doctor for the sake of health with good reason either cuts or cauterizes those who are suffering from the inflammation of ulcers, it is considered an evil by those who have to bear it. Nor are the spur and the whip pleasant to a restive horse. Moreover all chastisement seems at the moment to be a bitter thing to those who are chastised, as the Apostle says: "Now all chastisement for the present indeed seemeth not to bring with it joy but sorrow; […]

11:13.t: For according to the number of your cities were your gods, O Judah, and according to the number of the ways of Jerusalem you have set up altars of confusion for pouring libations to the Baals. Let us read the books of Kings and of Chronicles, and we shall find that Judah and Jerusalem did far worse things than Israel, so that as many cities as they had, so many kinds of idols they also had, and as many as were the streets and street-corners in the city of Jerusalem, so many altars they had, to their own confusion, on which they sacrificed victims to the idols of the Baals.

11:14.t: Or having sins unrepented they ask mercy, which thing it is impossible to receive, not only if themselves ask it, but although others having much confidence towards God entreat for them, like as even Jeremiah praying for the Jews did hear, "Pray not thou for this people, because I will not hear thee." But if all things are there, and thou ask things expedient, and contribute all thine own part, and exhibit an apostolical life, and have concord and love towards thy neighbor, thou wilt obtain on thy entreaty; for the Lord is loving towards man.
11:14.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 60:2

11:14.t: "How then do they not obtain all things?" Because many are causes of their failing. For either they often ask things inexpedient. And why marvellest thou, if this is the case with some others, whereas it was so even with Paul, when he heard, "My grace is sufficient for thee; for my strength is perfected in weakness." Or they are unworthy to be reckoned with them that heard these words, and contribute not their own part, but He seeks for such as are like them; therefore He saith "of you," of the virtuous, of them that show forth an angelic rule of life. Or they pray against them that have aggrieved them, seeking for redress and vengeance; and this kind of thing is forbidden, for, "Pray," saith He, "for your enemies." Or having sins unrepented they ask mercy, which thing it is impossible to receive, not only if themselves ask it, but although others having much confidence towards God entreat for them, like as even Jeremiah praying for the Jews did hear, "Pray not thou for this people, because I will not hear thee."
11:14.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 60:2

11:14.t: You, therefore, do not pray for this people, and do not take up praise and prayer for them, for I will not hear in the time of their crying to me, in the time of their affliction! Jeremiah is commanded not to wish to entreat the Lord for those against whom the sentence has already been completed, lest his prayer should seem weak and should not be heard because of their own crimes. 'Do not', he says, 'pray for them, nor take up praise, striving, by recounting the clemency of the ancient history with which I have always had mercy on him, and by praising me, to change my sentence! For even if you do this, I will not hear those who are forced to ask me in the time of necessity'. From which we learn that it is in vain for anyone to ask on behalf of another, when the one for whom God is asked does not deserve to receive.

11:15.t: And the other half shall be split toward the west and the sea, with a very great chasm: this is the people of the circumcision, to whom God speaks through the prophet: Why has my beloved done abomination in my house? Shall vows and holy flesh take away your wickedness from you, or will you escape by these? This beloved did abomination in the house of God, so that she crucified the Son of God and heard: The Lord called your name a shady olive tree and a wooded beauty; and your branches became useless, which were broken off from the good root, so that we might be grafted in their place.

What is it that my beloved has done many crimes in my house? Will holy flesh take away from you your wickednesses, in which you have gloried? A rich olive, beautiful, fruitful, comely, the Lord called your name; at the sound of a great speech a fire blazed up in it, and its thickets were burned up. He calls beloved and most dear the people of Judah, which set up idols in his temple and worshiped them, and thinks that in it it appeases the wrath of God if it sacrifices many offerings, and glories in the multitude of sacrifices, which cannot take away the wickednesses of sins. He compares Jerusalem, or the whole people of the Jews, to a beautiful and fruitful olive, which, exalted through pride, by no means acted humbly nor understood its creator and ruler, but, lifted up through pride and having spoken grandly, was set on fire by the fire of the Lord, so that its branches or thickets were burned up and reduced to nothing, that is, the whole people was destroyed by the sword of the adversaries. […]

11:17.t: And the Lord of hosts, who planted you, has spoken evil against you for the evils of the house of Israel and of the house of Judah, which they did to themselves to provoke me, pouring libations to the Baals. 'A rich olive,' he says, 'beautiful, fruitful, your Lord called you, and he planted you; but because at the sound of the great speech of God a flame came down upon you and consumed all your branches, therefore he who had planted you has now spoken evil against you, not out of the injustice of his sentence nor out of a sudden perversity of speech, but for the evils which the house of Israel and the house of Judah did to themselves and zealously carried out, pouring libations to the Baals, so as to provoke me to anger'. And although God can do what he wills, he gives his reasons, lest he should seem to act unjustly, according to that which is written: that you may be justified in your words and may overcome when you are judged.

11:18.t: If there are oracles of God in the Law and the Prophets, in the Gospels and the Apostles, then whoever is being made a disciple by the oracles of God will need to inscribe God as his teacher; for "he who teaches man knowledge" is God, as it is also written in the Psalms. And the Savior too testifies that no one should be inscribed as a teacher upon the earth, saying, "And do not call anyone teacher upon the earth; for one is your teacher, the Father who is in the heavens." But "the Father who is in the heavens" teaches either by himself, or through Christ, or in the Holy Spirit, or through Paul, let us say, or through Peter, or through some other of the saints — only let the Spirit of God and the Word of God be present and teach. And for what purpose have I said these things? Because the prophet says, "Make it known to me, Lord, and I will know"; for I will not know unless you make it known to me; […]
That the Jews would fasten Christ to the cross.… Also in Jeremiah: "Come, let us cast the tree into his bread, and let us blot out his life from the earth."
11:18.s: Treatise XII. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews 2:20

11:18.t: Listen to Jeremiah and be convinced: "I was as a meek lamb that is carried to be a victim. Did I not know it?" (Read it thus as a question, as I have put it. For he who said, "You know that after two days the Passover shall be here, and the Son of man will be delivered up to be crucified," did he not know?) "I was a meek lamb that is carried to be a victim. Did I not know it?" (What sort of lamb? Let John the Baptist interpret, when he says, "Behold the lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world!") "They devised a wicked counsel against me, saying (Was it that he who knew the counsels did not know their result? And what did they say?): "Come, and let us put wood on his bread." (If the Lord shall count you worthy, hereafter you shall learn that his body, according to the Gospel, bore the figure of bread.) "Come, and let us put wood on his bread, and cut him off from the land of the living (Life is not cut off. Why do you toil to no purpose?) And let his name be remembered no more."

But you, O Lord, have shown me and I have known; then you showed me their pursuits. And I was like a gentle lamb that is carried to be a victim, and I did not know that they had devised counsels against me: Let us put wood into his bread and crush him from the land of the living, and let his name be remembered no more! But you, O Lord of Sabaoth, who judge justly and test the reins and the heart, let me see your vengeance on them! For to you I have revealed my cause. This is the consensus of all the churches, that they understand these words to be spoken by Christ under the person of Jeremiah: that the Father showed him how he ought to speak, and showed him the pursuits of the Jews, and that he himself, like a lamb led to be a victim, did not open his mouth and did not know — 'sin' is understood, according to what is said by the Apostle: who, though he had not known sin, was made sin for us —, and that they said: Let us put wood into his bread — namely the cross into the body of the Savior; […]

11:19.t: The careful student of the sacred books, moreover, may gather not a few similar passages from the prophets, as where He calls Himself a chosen shaft, and a servant of God, and a light of the Gentiles. Isaiah also says, "From my mother's womb hath He called me by my name, and He made my mouth as a sharp sword, and under the shadow of His hand did He hide me, and He said to me, Thou art My servant, O Israel, and in thee will I be glorified." And a little farther on: "And my God shall be my strength, and He said to me, This is a great thing for thee to be called My servant, to set up the tribes of Jacob and to turn again the diaspora of Israel. Behold I have set thee for a light of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation to the end of the earth." And in Jeremiah too He likens Himself to a lamb, as thus: "I was as a gentle lamb that is led to the slaughter." These and other similar sayings He applies to Himself. […]
11:19.s: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 1:23

11:19.t: These are the prophet's words. Then let us see what the Savior says in the prophet: "I, like an innocent lamb led to be sacrificed, did not know. Against me they devised a device, saying, Come and let us cast wood into his bread, and let us wipe him out from the land of the living, and his name shall no more be remembered." As the prophet Isaiah also says, Christ "was led as a sheep to slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth." There, then, Isaiah speaks about him, but here Christ says about himself, "I, like an innocent lamb led to slaughter to be sacrificed, did not know." He did not say what he did not know. For he has not said, "I did not know evils"; he has not said, "I did not know good things"; nor has he said, "I did not know sin"; but simply, "I did not know." To you, then, he has left it to examine what he did not know. And learn what he did not know from this: "the one who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf"; […]

While then the better, the great and worthy and divine sacrifice was not yet available for men, it was necessary for them by the offering of animals to pay a ransom for their own life, and this was fitly a life that represented their own nature. Thus did the holy men of old, anticipating by the Holy Spirit that a holy victim, dear to God and great, would one day come for men, as the offering for the sins of the world, believing that as prophets they must perform in symbol his sacrifice, and shew forth in type what was yet to be. But when that which was perfect was come, in accordance with the predictions of the prophets, the former sacrifices ceased at once because of the better and true Sacrifice.

This Sacrifice was the Christ of God, from far distant times foretold as coming to men, to be sacrificed like a sheep for the whole human race. As Isaiah the prophet says of him:

"As a sheep he was led to slaughter, and as a lamb dumb before her shearers."

And he adds:

"4. He bears our sins and is pained for us; […]
11:19.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 10

11:19.t: And hearken unto the prophet who also proclaimed our Lord with his simple teaching, and who likened Him unto a lamb and a sheep, the most innocent of all animals: "Like a lamb was He led to the slaughter, and like a sheep before the shearer He was silent." The lion and the wolf and bear are crafty, together with the other wild beasts, because craftiness was mingled with their evil nature when they were made; but sheep and lambs and ewes are simple and innocent in their ways and movements, and to them was our Lord likened, and by their name are believers called. Our Lord did not liken Himself unto a lion, which bringeth suffering and death, and He did not call His flocks by the names of wild animals, which by the nature in which they were created are cunning in respect of evil things, but He was called "lamb" and "sheep", and being meek like unto them He was led to suffering and to death, for "like a sheep before his shearer He was silent", and thus He in His humility opened not His mouth.
11:19.s: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 5 -- Second Discourse on Simplicity

11:20.t: "Lord of the powers, who judge righteous things, who test the reins and hearts, may I see the vengeance from you upon them." Prophetically he prays these things, to see the vengeance from God upon them; for "Jerusalem is encircled by armies, and its desolation has drawn near," and it has been said to her, "Behold, your house is left to you." "May I see," then, "the vengeance from you upon them, because to you I have revealed my case."

Hence they rightly believed and confessed that as God he knew all things and that as the Son of God He had come from God. It is a clear indication of divinity to know the secret things of another's thoughts, as Solomon affirmed when he said in supplication to God, "For you alone know the hearts of all the children of human beings." Hence, Jeremiah too said, "You, O Lord of Sabaoth, are the one who judges righteously and probes the loins and hearts of human beings."

11:21.t: "Therefore thus says the Lord against the men of Anathoth who seek my life, who say: You shall not prophesy in the name of the Lord, and if you do, you shall die in our hands. Behold, I will visit upon them: their young men shall die by the sword, and their sons and their daughters shall perish by famine. And there shall be no remnant of them, for I will bring evils upon the inhabitants of Anathoth in the year of their visitation." For the sake of a figure the name of Anathoth is here taken up. And the whole Jewish mystery is spoken in it figuratively; for Anathoth is interpreted "Hearkening." Since, then, a hearkening of God was in that people, as also the kingdom of God, and it came to pass concerning the kingdom that "the kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits," according to this it also came to pass that "the men of Anathoth," those who are in the Hearkening, "seek the life" — not of Jeremiah (for neither does the history say that men of Anathoth sought the life of […]

Therefore thus says the Lord to the men of Anathoth, who seek your life and say: You shall not prophesy in the name of the Lord, and you shall not die in our hands. Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will visit upon them; the young men shall die by the sword, their sons and their daughters shall die by famine, and there shall be no remnant of them; for I will bring evil upon the men of Anathoth, the year of their visitation. This seems to run counter to the former view, by which we wish to prove that the things that were said were said in the person of Christ, and not in that of Jeremiah, who properly dwelt in the little village of Anathoth, which is three miles distant from Jerusalem. […]

12:1.t: "You are righteous, Lord, that I shall make my defense before you. Yet I will speak judgments to you. Why is it that the way of the ungodly prospers? All those who deal treacherously in treacheries have flourished." We still inquire whether God, who has given the Law and the Prophets, is good, seeing that "the way of the ungodly prospers" and he does not punish the ungodly. "All those who deal treacherously in treacheries have flourished." Those very ones who speak against the Creator, who blaspheme him, "have flourished, they have been planted and rooted, they have begotten children and have produced fruit." How much fruit has Marcion produced by begetting children, how much Basilides, how much Valentinus? For this is what is prophesied concerning the ungodly and said in the words "they have begotten children and produced fruit." "You are near to their mouth, but far from their reins": they name the name of Jesus, but they do not have Jesus; for they do not confess him as they ought.

Righteous indeed are you, O Lord, if I dispute with you — or for I will satisfy you — ; yet I will speak judgments to you: Why is it that the way of the wicked prospers, and it is well with all who transgress and act wickedly? You planted them and they have put forth root; they prosper — or they have begotten sons — and they bear fruit; you are near to their mouth and far from their reins. This disputation is indeed against all who act wickedly, and the meaning of Psalm 72 (73) is briefly summed up in it, in which the prophet says: How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright of heart! But my feet were almost moved, my steps had almost been poured out, because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners, and so on. […]

Jeremiah also, when conversing with God on this prosperity of sinners, although he never professes to doubt about the justice of God, as he says "for Thou art just, O Lord, if I dispute with Thee," yet in his inquiry as to the reasons of this inequality, proceeds to say: "But yet I will speak what is just to Thee. Why doth the way of the wicked prosper? Why is it well with all them that transgress and do wickedly? Thou hast planted them and they have taken root: they prosper and bring forth fruit. Thou art near in their mouth and far from their reins."
12:1.s: First Conference of Abbot Serenus, Chapter 31

12:3.t: "And you, Lord, know me, you have seen me, you have tested my heart before you; purify them for the day of their slaughter." What shall I do, that I may make these things clear? He calls the punishments a purification of those being punished; for "purify them," he says, "for the day of their slaughter." Through their being slaughtered, purify them; for "whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives."

And you, O Lord, have known me, you have seen me and have tested my heart with you. Gather them like a flock to be victims, and sanctify them in the day of slaughter! 'It is no stumbling-block', he says, 'that the wicked, or all the heretics, flourish for a time; for you, O Lord, have known me and have seen me and have tested my heart with you'. Whom does God the Father know as he knows his Son? For no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him. 'Although', he says, 'the heretics prosper, although they beget sons and bear fruit, and you are near to their mouth and far from their reins, that is, from their conscience, yet it is no small consolation that like cattle they are being fattened to be victims. You gather them into the city of Jerusalem, or into their own conventicles, so that like victims they may be slaughtered unto death, and may then be sanctified when they have been slain by the sword of the Church; […]

12:4.t: "How long shall the land mourn and the grass of the field be dried up from the wickedness of those who dwell in it?" As though of a land that has a soul, here too the prophet discourses, saying that the land mourns because of the wickedness of those who tread upon it. In the case of each one of us, then, the land either mourns or rejoices; for it either mourns "from the wickedness of those who dwell in it," or it rejoices from the virtue of those who dwell in it. In the case of each one of us, then, the very element either rejoices or mourns. And if the land, then perhaps the remaining elements too. I will say likewise both the water and the angel appointed over the water, that I may explain also the land that mourns or does not mourn; for it is not this body, "the land," that mourns "from those who dwell in it," but understand for me that, in addition to the ordering of the whole, a certain angel is appointed over the land, and another appointed over the waters, and another over the air, and a fourth over the fire. […]

How long will the land mourn, and the grass of every region wither, because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it? Beast and bird are consumed, because they said: He will not see our last end or God will not see our ways. Whatever happens in the world, whether of good or of evil, does not happen without providence and by fortuitous chance, but by the judgment of God. The land is now barren, the grass withers: do you wish to know the reason? The wickednesses of its inhabitants bring this about, so that both the animals upon the earth and the birds of the sky are consumed, since all these things were created for the uses of men. They rose up to such blasphemy as to say that God is ignorant of their ways and does not know what each one is going to suffer. And when he says 'how long', he signifies that the wrath of God remains, because the mind of those who sin is not changed.

12:5.t: If, running with footmen, you have grown weary, how will you be able to contend with horses? If in a land of peace you have been confident, what will you do in the pride — or roaring — of the Jordan? 'If', he says, 'the frequent captivity inflicted by the neighboring nations has worn you out, by the Moabites and Ammonites, the Philistines and Edomites, what will you do in the face of the long captivity which is to lead you all the way to Chaldea?' And he compares footmen with horsemen, because in truth and according to the history all Persia and all Chaldea and the army of those regions delight in cavalry. But these nations which I have mentioned above, because of the difficulty of their terrain, are suited not so much to battle as to brigandage. And he keeps the metaphoran [metaphor] and says: 'If, running with footmen, you have failed from weariness, what will you do if you wish to match your running to horses? […]

12:6.t: For even your brothers and the house of your father, they too have fought against you and have cried out after you with full voice; do not believe them when they speak good things to you! 'So far', he says, 'will you be covered by the most grievous floods of the Jordan, and so far will the multitude of horsemen coming against you from afar lay you waste, that your brothers too, the Edomites, and the house of your father, who were begotten of the stock of Lot, Moab and Ammon, will themselves, in the time of necessity and distress, fight against you and insult you. Therefore beware of being willing to believe them and of placing hope in kinship, on account of which they rage against you with greater hatred than enemies do'. This can also be taken of the Savior, that his brothers and the house of his father fought against him and cried out with full voice, saying: Crucify, crucify him; we have no king but Caesar.

12:7.t: "I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my inheritance, I have given my beloved soul into the hands of its enemies." Behold for me the one who exists "in the form of God," being in the heavens; behold his house, above the heavens. And if you wish to see something yet higher (that he is "in the Father"), behold that his house is God. He leaves "the father and the mother," the "Jerusalem above," and comes to the earthly place and says, "I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my inheritance." For that was his inheritance, the regions with the angels, the rank with the holy powers. "I have given my beloved soul into the hands of its enemies." He delivered his soul into the hands of the enemies of the soul, into the hands of the Jews who killed him, into the hands of the rulers gathered together against him, into the hands of kings, when "the kings of the earth stood by and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ."

And although the Apostle himself told the Hebrews that a testament is of no force, until the death of the testator happen, that is to say, a testament is of no strength while the testator liveth, but is established by his death, yet as in Jeremiah the Lord, speaking of the Jews, has said, Mine heritage is unto Me as a lion, he would not deny that they were heirs. But there are heirs without possessions, there are heirs also with them; and while the testator lives those whose names are written in the will are called heirs, though without possessions... As then young children, so the Jews also, are under a schoolmaster. The Law is our schoolmaster, the schoolmaster brings us to our Master; and our One Master is Christ: Neither be ye called masters, for one is your Master, even Christ.

I have left my house, I have abandoned my inheritance, I have given my beloved soul into the hand of its enemies. My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; it has given forth its voice against me, therefore I have hated it. He who said in the Gospel: Rise, let us go hence, and again: your house shall be left to you deserted, here too, in the prophet, threatens the same things, and says that he has done what he is going to do. For the inheritance of the Lord is Israel, and the cord of his inheritance. And what he says: I have given my beloved soul into the hand of its enemies, is this: I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again.

Behold, your house will be left to you deserted. He had said this very thing long before, in the person of Jeremiah: I have left my house, I have abandoned my inheritance; my inheritance has become to me like the cave of a hyena. We prove that the house of the Jews, that is, that temple which before shone more majestically to the eyes, is deserted, because it lost Christ its inhabitant and, eager to snatch the inheritance, killed the heir.

"For they cried out, it says, saying, Crucify Him, crucify Him." And this their unholy cry the Lord blamed, saying, by the voice of Jeremiah, "I have left My house, I have abandoned My inheritance: I have given My dearly beloved, My soul, into the hand of her enemies. My inheritance has become to Me like a lion in a thicket: it has uttered its voice against Me; therefore I have hated it." It was hated therefore because as a lion it sprang upon Christ, and uttered a cruel and pitiless cry against Him: but we praise Christ, Who for our sakes and in our stead suffered in the flesh: by Whom and with Whom to God the Father be praise and dominion, with the Holy Spirit, for ever and over. Amen.
12:7.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

12:8.t: "My inheritance became to me as a lion in a thicket." This inheritance of his upon the earth, which he had received as inheritance, turned savage against him, and the inheritance — the Jews — became wild against him "as a lion in a thicket." It is no wonder if then his inheritance became "as a lion in a thicket"; even now there are still lions in the thicket wishing to curse Jesus and blaspheming him and plotting against those who believe in him. "My inheritance," then, "became to me as a lion in a thicket. It uttered its voice against me; therefore I hated it."

And the inheritance that was once the Lord's, the people of the Jews, became like a lion in the forest against him, when in the passion it cried out against him with one voice. And because it gave forth its voice against him, therefore he held it in hatred and cast it off, and she who was once beloved and most dear is now called hateful.

12:9.t: "Is my inheritance to me a hyena's den?" He prophesies concerning this inheritance: has my inheritance perhaps become a hyena's den, a hyena's den — of the most savage beast, the corpse-eater, the one about the tombs, the one that eats the dead bodies? "Is my inheritance to me a hyena's den? Or a cave round about it on every side? Go." Since they have become such, I command you, the angels, to go and gather the beasts and deliver them to the beasts. "Go and gather all the beasts of the field, and let them come to devour it." The beasts of the field have come; they devour that people. See their hearts being devoured by the opposing powers. If Jesus did not spare those, but said, "Go, gather the beasts," how much more will he not spare us? If we do not do the Law of God, the word of the Gospel, he will say again: Go, gather the beasts and deliver it up. But we have boldness to say in our prayers: "Do not deliver to the beasts a soul that confesses to you." […]

Is my inheritance to me a bird of many colors? Is it a bird dyed all over? Come, gather together, all you beasts of the earth, hasten to devour! LXX: Is my inheritance to me a hyena's cave? Or a cave round about it, upon it? Go, gather all the beasts of the field, and let them come to eat it! By the bird of many colors and dyed all over he means, according to the letter, the peacock. 'Such beauty', he says, 'did Israel have, and with such virtues was Jerusalem adorned, that there was nothing good that was not seen in her. Because, therefore, what was once my inheritance, that is, the people of Israel, has become to me like a lion in the forest and has given forth its voice against me, and I have detested it with all hatred, therefore come and gather together against it, all you beasts of the earth, the multitude of diverse nations, and devour her who has not known her Lord!' […]

12:10.t: For in reality, as the Scripture says, the shepherds became brutish, and many shepherds destroyed My vineyard, and defiled my pleasant portion, I mean the Church of God, which has been gathered together by the sweat and blood of many toilers and victims both before and after Christ, aye, even the great sufferings of God for us.

Many shepherds have demolished — or have corrupted — my vineyard, they have trampled — or have polluted — my part, they have made my desirable portion a desert of solitude — or pathless —. They have made it — or it has been made — a ruin, and it has mourned over me or has perished. Let those hear these things who desire to be princes of the peoples, and who are to render account in the day of judgment not only for themselves but also for the flocks entrusted to them; for because of them the part of the Lord is trampled and polluted, so that where once was the lodging of God, there is the dwelling-place of beasts. Others, however, understand not the leaders of the people and the priests, but the princes of the enemies, who laid Jerusalem, that is, the vineyard of the Lord, in ruins.

12:11.t:
Who is it that says, "Because of me the whole earth has been laid utterly waste"? Christ says these things, before whose coming many sins had indeed been committed by the people, but not such sins as to cause them to be utterly forsaken and handed over into a captivity of long duration. But when they had filled up "the measure of their fathers" and had added, to the killing of the prophets and the persecuting of the righteous, the slaying of "the Christ of God," then came to pass the word, "Your house is left to you." And it is because of him that they have suffered these things, and "the whole earth has been laid utterly waste."

But if you wish also to hear in a loftier sense the words, "Because of me the whole earth has been laid utterly waste," look at the earth within you, in what manner it was laid waste when Jesus came; […]

And it has mourned over me; with desolation the whole land has been made desolate, because there is no one who considers in his heart. Upon all the ways of the desert the destroyers have come, because the sword of the Lord has devoured from the end of the earth to its end; there is no peace for all flesh. LXX: because of me with ruin the land has been ruined, and the rest. This, which we have set down: and it has mourned over me, is joined according to the Hebrew to the preceding verse, so that it reads: they have made it a ruin, that is, my inheritance, and it has mourned over me, bereft of my help. According to the Seventy, however, God says that because of him the land has been ruined and reduced to a solitude, because there is no one who considers in his heart, nor is there any peace for all flesh. For flesh cannot receive the peace of God; for the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, and those who are in the flesh cannot please God. […]

12:13.t: And it is said to those who have sinned, "You sow wheat and you reap thorns"; for even if they discourse in the oracles of God, those who do not discourse rightly in them, nor live in the way they ought, nor believe, are sowing wheat and reaping thorns. And these things are most of all to be understood with reference to the heterodox, who engage with the Scriptures and reap thorns not from the Scriptures but from their own inventions. "Their lots will not profit them." These things others also have expounded. And since we do not reject their exposition, we in good conscience bring it forward into the midst, not as though we had found it ourselves, but as having learned a good lesson. This word will profit both you and us, if we attend to what is written — we who seem to be certain persons appointed from the clergy and set over you, so that some desire to come to this clerical order. But know that the clerical order does not by any means save; […]

They have sown wheat and reaped thorns; they have received an inheritance, and it will not profit them. LXX: You have sown wheat and reaped thorns; their clergy will not profit them. 'They expected better things', he says, 'and the worst came; they hoped for prosperity and suffered adversity; they received from the Lord an abundance of all things, which will not profit them'. According to the Seventy, however, all the heretics sow as it were wheat and reap thorns, while the Lord waited for them to bear fruit; and they did not do judgment, but a cry. This is said also to churchmen, who ruin the words of the Lord and his teaching by their evil manner of life, concerning whom it is added: their clergy will not profit them; for what can the name of bishop and of presbyter, or the rest of the ecclesiastical order, help them, when they are rather weighed down by their dignities, and the mighty suffer torments mightily, and the more has been entrusted to them, the more is required of them?

Be confounded at the fruits — or at your boasting — because of the wrath of the fury of the Lord — or at the reproach in the sight of the Lord —. Thus says the Lord against all my most wicked neighbors, who touch the inheritance which I distributed to my people Israel: Behold, I will pluck them up from their land, and I will pluck up — or cast out — the house of Judah from the midst of them. And when I have plucked them up, I will turn — or return — and have mercy on them and bring them back — or make them dwell —, each man in his inheritance and each man in his land. It is said to those whom their clergy and the ecclesiastical order will not profit, that they should be confounded at their boasting and at the reproach before the Lord.
