What is our iniquity, and what is our sin that we have sinned against the Lord our God?, you shall say to them: Because your fathers forsook me, says the Lord, and went after strange gods and served them and worshiped them, and forsook me and did not keep my law. But you too have done worse than your fathers. When the Church has sinned, all joy and all gladness is taken away from her, of which the Apostle says: rejoice; again I say: rejoice; the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, of whom it is written: he who has the bride is the bridegroom.

16:10.t: 'But if', he says, 'the people asks you why it suffers these things, and seeks the causes of its miseries, you shall answer them: because your fathers forsook me, says the Lord, those who preside over you in the churches, and went after strange gods — whose god is the belly, and avarice and luxury, and their glory is in their shame — and served them — for by whatever one is overcome, of that he is also the slave — and worshiped them — for each one worships what he loves — and forsook me and did not keep my law'. It belongs properly to priests not only to teach the law but also to do it, so that they may teach the peoples subject to them and the flock entrusted to them not by words at all, but by examples.

16:12.t: And lest they should perhaps say: 'it is an unjust sentence that the fathers eat the sour grape and the children's teeth are set on edge', he adds: but you too have done worse than your fathers, so that just punishments may be brought upon those who have sinned worse than their fathers.

For behold, each one walks after the depravity of his evil heart, so as not to hear me. And I will cast you out of this land into a land which you do not know, you and your fathers, and there you shall serve strange gods day and night, who will not give you rest. Once forsaken by the Lord, they do the things that are not fitting, so as to go after the desires of their evil heart, out of which come the worst thoughts; and for this reason they are separated from the Church, so as to go into a far country, which neither they nor their fathers had known before they sinned, so that there they may serve strange gods, who are not gods, but are thought to be so by the error of those who worship them. But in adding 'day and night', he shows the perpetual perseverance of sinners in wickedness, since both in the days they serve shameful deeds and in the nights lust. Who will not give, he says, you rest; there is no doubt that he means the false gods, of whom he said: and there you shall serve strange gods. […]

16:14.t: Therefore, behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and it shall no longer be said: The Lord lives, who brought the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt, but: The Lord lives, who brought the sons of Israel out of the land of the north and out of all the lands to which I cast them; and I will bring them back into their land, which I gave to their fathers. Plainly the future restoration of the people of Israel is foretold, and mercy after the captivity, which according to the letter was in part fulfilled under Zerubbabel and Jeshua the high priest and Ezra, and according to the spiritual understanding is described as to be fulfilled more truly and more perfectly in Christ. 'The time will come', he says, 'when it will no longer be said that the people was brought back from Egypt through Moses and Aaron, but that it was brought back from the land of the north when Cyrus, king of the Persians, released the captives'. And out of all, he says, the lands; […]

16:16.t: It is recorded in the Gospel according to Matthew that our Savior came alongside the Sea of Galilee and saw "Simon and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen." Then the text says that the Savior, seeing them, said: "Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men. And they left their nets and followed him." And Jesus made them take up the work of fishing for men. And "he found two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with their father, mending their nets; and these too he called" to the same skill, and he made these also fishers of men. And if anyone has considered those who have from God the grace of a word woven together like nets and composed out of the sacred Scriptures like a casting-net, so that the mesh is thrown around the souls of the hearers, and has considered too that this is done skillfully according to the art, he will see in a certain manner that not only then but also now our Savior sends out fishers of men, having trained them, […]

God has made you a hunter, not a harrier, for He says: ‘Behold I will send you many hunters’—hunters, not of crime, but of absolution therefrom; hunters, certainly not of sin, but of grace. You are a fisher of Christ, for whom it is said: ‘Henceforth thou shalt make men live.’ Spread your nets, direct your eyes, and control your tongue in such a manner that you destroy no one, but bring rescue to those who struggle in the waters.

But our writers more rightly and better think that the prophet prophesied these things about the future. For since he had said above: I will bring them back into their land, which I gave to their fathers, he now shows how they are to be brought back: that first he sends the apostles, to whom the Savior said: come after me, and I will make you fishers of men, and afterwards hunters, whom we can take to be either churchmen or angels, who, once the time of the consummation has come, are to hunt all the saints from the mountains of lofty doctrines and from the hills of good works and from the caves of the rocks, the apostles and apostolic men. For not only is Christ the rock, but he also granted to the apostle Peter that he should be called rock; those who rest in his thoughts are rightly said to have been transferred from the rock.

Behold, I will send many fishers, says the Lord, and they shall fish them; and after this I will send them many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain and from every hill and from the caves of the rocks, for my eyes are upon all their ways. They are not hidden from my face, and their iniquity was not concealed from my eyes. And I will repay first their double iniquities and sins, with which they have defiled my land with the carcasses of their idols and have filled my inheritance with their abominations. The interpretation of this passage is diverse. For the Jews suppose that the Chaldeans are signified, who are described under the name of fishers, and afterwards the Romans, who are compared to hunters and who hunted the unhappy people from the mountains and hills and caves of the rocks. […]

And He saw two ships standing by the lake, but the fishermen were gone out of them, and, were washing their nets.

LET us admire the skilfulness of the method employed in making them a prey who were to make prey of the whole earth; even the holy Apostles, who, though themselves well skilled in fishing, yet fell into Christ's meshes, that they also, letting down the drag-net of the Apostolic preachings, might gather unto Him the inhabitants of the whole world. For verily He somewhere said by one of the holy prophets, "Behold I send many fishers, saith the Lord, and they shall catch them as fish: and afterwards I will send many hunters, and they shall hunt them as game." By the fishers He means the holy Apostles; and by the hunters, those who successively became the rulers and teachers of the holy churches. […]
16:16.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

16:17.t: For "my eyes," he says, "are upon all their ways." Upon such as these, who make their haunts in the mountains and in the hills and in the clefts of the rocks, upon all their ways God has his eyes. "And they were not hidden from my face," such as these; for the wicked are hidden from the face of God. Adam, after the transgression, heard "the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the evening" and hid himself; but the holy one is not hidden, but has a heart with boldness before God in accordance with the holy conduct of life. For "if our conscience does not condemn us, we have boldness before God, and whatever we ask we receive from him." Now Adam, even if he sinned, did not sin a sin exceeding in grievousness; on this account he hid himself "from the face of God." But Cain, more sinful than he and most impious, the fratricide, what did he do? "He went out from the face of God." So that, by comparison of evils, to be hidden from the face of God is the lesser; […]

And he shows that either the apostles or those who are afterwards to be hunted had sins and received their double iniquities. For the servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it shall be beaten much. And it must be known that in the Hebrew 'first' is set down, and in the edition of the Seventy it is omitted. But when he says: I will repay first their double iniquities and sins, he intimates that after they have received evils, they will receive good things too. And these who are afterwards to be transferred have defiled the land of the Lord with the carcasses of their idols and have filled his inheritance with their abominations, so that the whole world may become subject to God and be preserved not at all by its own merit, but by his mercy. What we have set down here from the Hebrew: they are not hidden from my face, is not found in the Seventy.

16:18.t: The following words are going to produce a struggle for us. For whether we understand them as consequent, we shall take careful thought concerning the recompense of sins; or whether they seem not to be consequent upon the things previously set forth concerning those fished up and hunted, in that way too they cast us into no ordinary struggle. For he says: "And I will first repay double their iniquities and their sins, whereby they profaned my land with the carcasses of their abominations and with their lawlessnesses, with which they filled my inheritance." Whether some, not understanding it, removed the word "first" from what was written, or whether the Seventy managed to remove it, God would know. […]

16:19.t: "Lord, my strength and my help and my refuge in the day of evils; to you the nations shall come from the end of the earth and shall say: As false things did our fathers acquire idols, and there is no profit in them." From the end of the earth the nations came to God, and the nations have said: "As false things did our fathers acquire idols, and there is no profit in them"? How "from the end of the earth"? There are some who are first of the earth and there are some who are last of the earth. Who are the first? "The wise of the world" are first of the earth, not simply first; "the wise of the world, the well-born," the rich, the men of rank. Who are the last? "The foolish things of the world God has chosen, the base things, the things despised, the things that are not." […]

[Passage quoted, Jer. xvi. 19-21.]

THE Lord prays to another Lord, clearly His Father and the God of the Universe, and says in the opening of His prayer, "O Lord, thou art my strength," and that which follows. And He clearly prophesies the conversion of the Gentiles from idolatrous error to godly religion. And this prophecy, moreover, has been shewn most clearly to have been fulfilled after the Coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ to men.
16:19.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 30

16:19.t: O Lord, my strength and my might and my refuge in the day of tribulation or of evils! All the strength of men without the power of God, which is Christ, is reckoned feeble and of no account; hence one must flee to God and say: Lord, you have become a refuge for us from generation to generation; and in another place: he who dwells in the help of the Most High shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven. And the day of tribulation or of evils is to be understood as that of which the Apostle also says: that he might rescue us from the present evil age, and: redeeming the time, because the days are evil.

To you the nations shall come from the ends of the earth and shall say: Truly our fathers possessed a lie, vanity, which did not profit them. LXX: to you the nations shall come from the ends of the earth and shall say: How false are the idols our fathers possessed, and there is no profit in them! After Israel has been cast out and carried away by the fishers and hunters, the multitude of the nations is accordingly called to faith and confesses that it, or its fathers, had been engaged in their former error. And those who say: 'how false are the idols our fathers possessed, in which there is no profit!' confess that the things to which they are passing over are true and supported by every protection.

Further, Jeremiah says of Christ, "Behold the days come, says the Lord, and I will raise up to David a just branch. A king shall reign and shall be wise. He shall execute justice and judgment in the earth. In those days shall Judah be saved, and Israel shall dwell confidently. This is the name that they shall call him: The Lord our just one." On the calling of the Gentiles that he foresaw and we today see as realized, the prophet had this to say: "O Lord, my might and my strength, and my refuge in the day of tribulation; to you the Gentiles shall come from the ends of the earth and shall say, 'Surely our ancestors have possessed lies, a vanity that has not profited them.' "

For truly what is thus effected by Christians is not a thing which belongs only to Christian times, but one which was predicted very long ago. Those very Jews who have remained enemies to the name of Christ, and regarding whose destined perfidy these prophetic writings have not been silent, do themselves possess and peruse the prophet who says: "O Lord my God, and my refuge in the day of evil, the Gentiles shall come unto Thee from the ends of the earth, and shall say, Surely our fathers have worshipped mendacious idols, and there is no profit in them." Behold, that is now being done; behold, now the Gentiles are coming from the ends of the earth to Christ, uttering things like these, and breaking their idols! […]
16:19.s: The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 1, Chapter 26

16:20.t: "Shall a man make gods for himself?" Not only from images do human beings make gods for themselves, but you will find human beings making gods for themselves also from fabrications; for as many as are able to fabricate another god and another cosmogony besides the one recorded by the Spirit, a dispensation of the world besides the true world, all these have made gods for themselves and have worshiped the works of their hands. For instance, conceive for me, whether among the Greeks those who begot doctrines, say, of this philosophy or of that, or among the heresies those who first begot doctrines, these have made for themselves idols and fabrications of the soul, and turning aside have worshiped the works of their own hands, having accepted their own fabrications as truth. Convicting, then, all those who make gods for themselves both perceptibly and intelligibly, the word says: "Shall a man make gods for himself, and are these not gods? […]

Shall a man make gods for himself, and they are not gods? This too the nations say, who have come to the Savior from the ends of the earth, rebuking the ignorance both of themselves and of their ancestors, by which they thought that gods are made by man, when it belongs to God to make men.

Hermes Trismegistus lamented these vain, deceptive, pernicious, sacrilegious things because he foresaw that the time was coming when they would be abolished. He was as impudent in his grief as imprudent in his prophecy, since the Holy Spirit had made no revelation to him as to the holy prophets who exultantly proclaimed their inspired visions: "Shall a person make gods to himself, and they are not gods?" And again: "And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord of hosts, that I will destroy the names of idols out of the earth, and they shall be remembered no more." It is relevant to recall that holy Isaiah uttered a particular prophecy concerning Egypt: "And the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt in the midst thereof" and the rest.

Although Hermes calls these idols gods, he nevertheless admits that they were made by people whose example we should not follow, and thus, willy-nilly, he proves that these idols should not be worshiped by people who are unlike the people who made them, that is, by wise, believing and religious people. Moreover, he implies that the fabricators brought on themselves the guilt of reckoning as gods things that are not gods. Very true is that prophecy: "Shall a person make gods to himself, and they are not gods?" This, then, is what Hermes means by fabricated gods. Such gods, made and adored by such people, are but evil spirits imprisoned by magic in idols and bound there by the chains of their own passions.

16:21.t: Therefore, behold, I will show them at this turn, I will show them my hand and my power, and they shall know that my name is the Lord. The hand of God, through which he has wrought all things, and the power, of which the Apostle said: 'Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God', is shown to the nations once the passion of the Son has been completed. And beautifully he said: 'I will show them at this turn; and I will show them plainly, and not as before in shadow and in image and in prophecy of things to come, so that, after they have come to know it, they may know my name and hear from the Son: Father, I have made your name manifest to men'.

17:1.t: Then there is another prophecy, which — I do not know how — we did not find among the Seventy, but we found in the remaining editions, clearly lying in the Hebrew, and it is filled with matters most necessary, able, if we attend, to turn our soul back. And the words are thus: "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, with an adamantine point engraved upon the breast of their heart." It is possible to give oneself over to the easier course and to say: these things are written concerning the Jews, that their sin "is written." But if you see, as we have often shown, Judah spoken of figuratively as Christ, perhaps "the sin of Judah" is ours who believe on Christ who is from the tribe of Judah. But if you are able to hear otherwise, in a more mystical way, perhaps he prophesies concerning Judas the betrayer, so that the prophecy is concerning him, saying: "The sin of Judas is written with a pen of iron, with an adamantine point engraved upon the breast of the heart"; […]

[Passage quoted, Jer. xvii. 1-4.]

THOUGH this passage is not found in the Septuagint, yet it is in the Hebrew and in the editions of the other translators, and is quoted with asterisks in the more accurate copies of the Septuagint. I have necessarily quoted it, because it gives the name of the traitor Judas, and teaches that the sin he committed can never be wiped out. For this I think is implied by the words, "The sin of Judas is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond." It could refer also to the whole Jewish nation, as a threat of the utter destruction that would overtake them in the immediate train of their indelible iniquity, an interpretation I have no time now to expound word by word,
17:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 5

17:1.t: The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with an adamantine nail, engraved upon the breadth of their heart — or on the breast of their heart — and on the horns of the altars — or altar-stones — of them. Concerning the nations which had been converted to the Lord, it was said above: behold, I will show them at this turn, I will show them my hand and my power; now he speaks of Israel, which has been cast off: the sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with an adamantine nail, and so on. Why this was passed over by the Seventy I do not know, unless perhaps they spared their own people, as it is evident that they did also in Isaiah: cease therefore from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, because he himself has been reckoned exalted; and many things of this kind, for which, if I wished to set them all out, there would be need, I will not say of a book, but of books. […]

17:2.t: When their sons remember their altar-stones and their groves and leafy trees on the high mountains, sacrificing in the field, I will give your strength and all your treasures for plunder, your high places on account of sins in all your borders. And you shall be left alone, bereft of your inheritance, which I gave you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land which you do not know, since you have kindled a fire in my fury; it will burn forever. These things too are not found in the Seventy, for the same reason, I think, that we stated above, namely, lest an eternal sentence should remain against them. You shall be left, he says, alone, bereft of your inheritance, which I gave you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land which you do not know, either under the Babylonians or, as is truer, under the Romans. For they themselves kindled the fire and provoked the most merciful Lord to fury, and this fire of his fury will burn forever. […]

17:5.t: Then, since many words have been gone through, there was indeed something to say about each of the things spoken, but time does not allow, as it presses upon us. Let us therefore speak on the passage read next: "Cursed is the man who has his hope on man." From this †, against those who suppose that the Son of God, the Savior, was but a man of God (for they dared, along with many of the evils of men, to say this also, that "the only-begotten," "the firstborn of all creation," is not God); for "cursed is he who has his hope on man." It is clear that they are cursed who have their hope on man. I would say that I do not have my hope on man, since, hoping on Christ Jesus, I do not know a man. Not only do I not know a man, but I know Wisdom, righteousness-itself, a man through whom "all things were created in the heavens and upon the earth, whether visible or invisible, whether principalities or authorities." "Cursed is the man who has his hope on man." […]

He who puts his trust in himself or in the man who has been entrusted with the charge of his needs, and considers his own work or that of his comrade a sufficient basis for his living, inasmuch as he has set his hope on man, is in danger of incurring the curse which says: “Cursed is the man that putteth his hope in man and will stablish the flesh of his arm, and his heart would depart from the Lord.” The Scripture by “who putteth his hope in man” forbids, that is, putting trust in another, and by “will stablish the arm of his flesh” forbids self-confidence. Each of these it calls apostasy from the Lord and it adds the doom of both that “He shall be as the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh.” So Scripture shows that to put trust in one’s self or any one else is to apostatise from the Lord.

Thus says the Lord: cursed is the man who trusts — or has hope — in man and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord. For he will be like a tamarisk in the desert, and he will not see when good comes, but he will dwell in dryness in the desert, in a land of saltness and uninhabitable. If every man who trusts in man is cursed, and Paul of Samosata and Photinus, although they proclaim the Savior holy and exalted above all in virtues, nevertheless confess him to be a man, then they will be cursed, having hope in a man. But if it is objected to us that we too believe in him who says: but now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you, which I heard from God; this Abraham did not do. You do the works of your father, we shall answer with that saying of the Apostle: even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him. […]

"For vain is the salvation of man." "Cursed is the man who has his hope in man." There is no need to interpret this: this saying is plain to all. Someone hoped in an emperor, hoped in a prince, in a father, or a mother: in the course of some affair the spirit of the one in whom he hoped was suddenly taken away, and his salvation vanished. He did not say, "vain is the salvation of that man in whom he hopes," but "the salvation of him who hopes in man."

But of these matters, all of which are true objects of faith, those only pertain to hope that are embraced in the Lord's Prayer. For "cursed is the one that trusts in humankind" is the testimony of Holy Scripture. Consequently, this curse attaches also to the person who trusts in himself. Therefore, we ought to ask for nothing that we either hope to do well or hope to obtain as a reward for our good works except from God the Lord.

Out of that confession of faith that is briefly contained in the creed and that, pondered according to the flesh, is the milk of babes but spiritually considered and studied is the food of the strong, arises the good hope of believers, which holy charity accompanies. But of all those things that are to be believed by faith, only those pertain to hope that are contained in the Lord's Prayer. For "cursed is everyone who puts hope in humankind," as the divine Scriptures testify; and, consequently, one who puts hope in himself is also ensnared in the chain of this curse. Therefore, we ought to make petition only of the Lord God, whatever it is that we hope to do well or to obtain as a reward for good works.

People who despise being in need before God, lest they receive true perseverance from him, glory in their own false endurance and seek to "confound the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his hope." Nor do they regard, seeing they are human and attribute so much to their own, that is, to the human will, that they run into that which is written, "Cursed is everyone who puts his hope in humankind."

But it is said, "It is by his own fault that any one deserts the faith, when he yields and consents to the temptation which is the cause of his desertion of the faith." Who denies it? But because of this, perseverance in the faith is not to be said not to be a gift of God. For it is this that a man daily asks for when he says, "Lead us not into temptation;" and if he is heard, it is this that he receives. And thus as he daily asks for perseverance, he assuredly places the hope of his perseverance not in himself, but in God. I, however, am loth to exaggerate the case with my words, but I rather leave it to them to consider, and see what it is of which they have persuaded themselves—to wit, "that by the preaching of predestination, more of despair than of exhortation is impressed upon the hearers." For this is to say that a man then despairs of his salvation when he has learned to place his hope not in himself, but in God, although the prophet cries, "Cursed is he who has his hope in man."

We must find out from what source true perseverance, worthy of the name, is to be had. There are those who attribute it to the powers of human will, not those that people have from divine assistance, but from their own free will. But that is an arrogant error. It is the error of the rich about whom the psalm speaks: "a reproach to the rich, and contempt to the proud." Glorying in their own false endurance, they wish "to confound the counsel of the poor person, but the Lord is his hope." Since they are people and attribute so much to themselves, that is, to their human will, they do not tend to apply to themselves the words of Scripture: "Cursed is everyone who trusts in humankind."

In order that we fall not away from the virtue of the soul, we ought to watch especially against those snares of the suggestions of the devil that we presume not of our own strength. For "cursed is everyone who places his hope in humankind." And who is he, but mortal? We cannot therefore truly say that the person who places his hope in humankind places it in himself. For this also is to "live after humankind," what is it but to "live after the flesh"? Whoever therefore is tempted by such a suggestion, let him hear, and if he has any Christian feeling, let him tremble. Let him hear, I say, "If you live after the flesh, you shall die."

It is, however, to be feared lest all these and similar testimonies of Holy Scripture (and undoubtedly there are a great many of them), in the maintenance of free will, be understood in such a way as to leave no room for God's assistance and grace in leading a godly life and a good conversation, to which the eternal reward is due; and lest poor wretched man, when he leads a good life and performs good works (or rather thinks that he leads a good life and performs good works), should dare to glory in himself and not in the Lord, and to put his hope of righteous living in himself alone; so as to be followed by the prophet Jeremiah's malediction when he says, "Cursed is the man who has hope in man, and maketh strong the flesh of his arm, and whose heart departeth from the Lord." Understand, my brethren, I pray you, this passage of the prophet. […]
17:5.s: On Grace and Free Will, Chapter 6

17:5.t: But if we were altogether deprived of the protection of our parents, the services of the princes of this world would not be wanting, as they would most thankfully rejoice to minister to our necessities with prompt liberality. And supported by their bounty, we should be free from the care of preparing food, were it not that this curse of the prophet terribly frightened us. For "Cursed," he says, "is the man that putteth his hope in man;" and: "Put not your trust in princes."

All things which are good, even those of which man is the agent, really come from God rather than man. "It is the spirit," we are told, "that gives life, the flesh has nothing to offer." Hence there is a curse on the man who puts his trust in man, for although our whole hope rightly depends on God made man, it is not because he is man but because he is God.
17:5.s: Sermons on the Song of Songs, Sermon 10

17:6.t: And he will be like a tamarisk — which in Hebrew is called 'aroher', or, as Symmachus translated, an unfruitful tree — in the wilderness, and he will not see when good things come, which the multitude of the nations is to see, but he will dwell in dryness in the desert. This is said of the people of the Jews, who dwell in the desert and bear no fruits and are in a land of saltness, which bears no fruits, and uninhabitable, which has neither God as its guest, nor the protection of angels, nor the grace of the Holy Spirit, nor the knowledge of teachers.

But let us see what kind of fruits a bad tree produces, and let us avoid bearing such fruits. The prophet Jeremiah says, "Cursed is the one who puts his trust in human beings and makes his flesh his support, and whose heart turns away from the Lord; such a person will be like a tamarisk in the desert."

17:7.t: Let no one deceive himself. Let none be misled. Only the Lord can grant mercy. Sins committed against him can be cancelled by him alone who bore our sins and suffered for us, by him whom God delivered up for our sins. People cannot be above God, nor can the servant by any indulgence of his own remit or condone the graver sort of crime committed against his Lord, for that would make the apostate liable to this further charge, he knows not the words of the prophet: "Cursed is the one who puts his hope in humankind." It is our Lord we must pray to, it is our Lord we must win over by our penitence. For he has said he will deny the person who denies him, and he alone has received all power of judgment from his Father.

Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his confidence — or hope — ; and he will be like a tree that has been transplanted — or fruitful — upon the waters, that sends out its roots toward moisture; and it will not fear when the heat comes, and its leaf will be green — or its twigs in leaf — and in the time — or year — of dryness it will not be anxious — or will not fear — nor will it ever cease to bear fruit. Let that be said of the Jews and of the heretics, who have hope in man, namely in their Christ, whom they think will come not as the Son of God but as a mere man. On the contrary, the man of the Church, who trusts in the Lord, hears this: and know that the Lord himself is God.

Nay, I say that either before the law, or in the time of the Old Testament, they were freed from sins,-not by their own power, because "cursed is every one that hath put his hope in man," and without any doubt those are under this curse whom also the sacred Psalm notifies, "who trust in their own strength;" nor by the old covenant which gendereth to bondage, although it was divinely given by the grace of a sure dispensation; nor by that law itself, holy and just and good as it was, where it is written, "Thou shalt not covet," since it was not given as being able to give life, but it was added for the sake of transgression until the seed should come to whom the promise was made; but I say that they were freed by the blood of the Redeemer Himself, who is the one Mediator of God and man, the man Christ Jesus. […]
17:7.s: A Treatise Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, Book 1

17:8.t: He trusts in the Lord and will be compared to that tree of which it is sung also in the first Psalm: and he will be like a tree that has been planted beside the courses of waters, which will give its fruit in its season; and its leaf will not fall off. Upon the waters, moreover: the grace of the Holy Spirit, its diverse gifts. That sends out its roots toward moisture: that it may receive fruitfulness from the Lord; but we can also say otherwise, that we have been transplanted from the Jewish dryness into the everlasting grace of baptism. And it will not, he says, fear when the heat comes — either the time of persecution or the day of judgment — ; and its leaf will be green — or there will be twigs in leaf on it —, so that it never fears dryness, but buds with the grace of all the virtues. And when the time or the year of dryness comes, it will not be afraid, when the Lord in anger commands the clouds not to rain a shower upon Israel. […]

17:9.t: For this reason [it is, said], "Who shall declare His generation?" since "He is a man, and who shall recognise Him?" But he to whom the Father which is in heaven has revealed Him, knows Him, so that he understands that He who "was not born either by the will of the flesh, or by the will of man," is the Son of man, this is Christ, the Son of the living God. For I have shown from the Scriptures, that no one of the sons of Adam is as to everything, and absolutely, called God, or named Lord. But that He is Himself in His own right, beyond all men who ever lived, God, and Lord, and King Eternal, and the Incarnate Word, proclaimed by all the prophets, the apostles, and by the Spirit Himself, may be seen by all who have attained to even a small portion of the truth. Now, the Scriptures would not have testified these things of Him, if, like others, He had been a mere man. […]

For it is of him that Isaiah writes: "A man of suffering and acquainted with the bearing of weakness." Jeremiah writes: "He is man, and who has known him?" And Daniel writes: "On the clouds he came as the son of man." The apostle Paul likewise says: "The man Christ Jesus is the one mediator between God and humankind."

The apostle says, "For God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin condemned sin in the flesh, that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us." He does not say "in the likeness of flesh," for Christ took on himself the reality, not the likeness, of flesh. Nor does he say in the likeness of sin, for he did not sin but was made sin for us. Yet he came "in the likeness of sinful flesh." That is, he took on him the likeness of sinful flesh, the likeness, because it is written, "He is man, and who shall know him?" He was man in the flesh, according to his human nature that he might be recognized, but in power he was above humanity, that he might not be recognized, so he has our flesh but has not the failings of this flesh.

The heart of all is depraved and inscrutable; who will know it? I the Lord search the heart and prove the reins, who give to each one according to his way and according to the fruit of his devices. LXX: the heart is deep above all things, and it is man; who will know him? and so on in the same way. The Hebrew word 'enos' is written with four letters, 'aleph' and 'nun' and 'uau' and 'sin'; if, then, it is read 'enos', it means 'man'; but if 'anus', 'inscrutable' or 'desperate', because no one is able to find out the heart of men. Symmachus, however, translated this passage thus: inscrutable is the heart of all; but who is the man that can find it out? […]

On hearing this curse pronounced in the figurative language of prophecy on him that trusts in man, and the blessing in similar style on him that trusts in God, the inquirer might have doubts about our doctrine, in which we teach not only that Christ is God, so that our trust is not in man, but also that He is man because He took our nature. So some err by denying Christ's humanity, while they allow His divinity. Others, again, assert His humanity, but deny His divinity, and so either become infidels or incur the guilt of trusting in man. The inquirer, then, might say that the prophet says only that Christ is God, without any reference to His human nature; whereas, in our apostolic doctrine, Christ is not only God in whom we may safely trust, but the Mediator between God and man—the man Jesus. The prophet explains this in the words in which he seems to check himself, and to supply the omission: "His heart," he says "is sorrowful throughout; and He is man, and who shall know Him?" […]

So also, notwithstanding the surpassing justice and wisdom of Christ, His manhood was much more plainly and readily recognized by strangers, who, indeed, were not wrong in believing Him to be man, but they did not understand His being God as well as man. Hence Jeremiah says: "He is both a man, and who shall know Him?" He is a man, for it is made manifest that He is a brother. And who shall know Him? for it is concealed that He is a husband. This must suffice as a defense of our father Abraham against Faustus' impudence and ignorance and malice.

17:10.t:
For such things as these serve for exercise and trial, so that, having approved ourselves zealous and chosen servants of Christ, we may be fellow-heirs with the saints. For thus Job: ‘The whole world is a place of trial to men upon the earth.’ Nevertheless, they are proved in this world by afflictions, labours, and sorrows, to the end that each one may receive of God such reward as is meet for him, as He saith by the prophet, ‘I am the Lord, Who trieth the hearts, and searcheth the reins, to give to every one according to his ways.’

Not that He first knows the things of a man on his being proved (for He knows them all before they come to pass), but because He is good and philanthropic, He distributes to each a due reward according to his actions, so that every man may exclaim, Righteous is the judgment of God! As the prophet says again, ‘The Lord trieth the just, and discerneth the reins.’

But that it belongs to God only to know men's secrets, hear what saith the prophet, "Thou most entirely alone knowest the hearts;" and again, "God trieth the hearts and reins;" and Jeremiah too saith, "The heart is deep above all things, and it is man, and who shall know him?" and, "Man shall look on the face, but God on the heart." And by many things one may see, that to know what is in the mind belongs to God alone.
17:10.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 29:2

17:11.t: On the notorious question we have come to see who the partridge is, concerning which Scripture now says: "The partridge cried out, it gathered what it did not bring forth, making its wealth not with judgment. In the midst of his days they shall forsake him, and at his end he shall be a fool." From the study of the nature of animals we must take up what has been recorded about the partridge, so that, knowing the facts about the animal, we may know whether the partridge now spoken of ought to be assigned to a better rank or to a worse one. It is said, then, to be a most malicious and crafty and cunning animal, one that wishes to deceive those who hunt it and that often rolls about the feet of the hunter, so as to draw him away, since the animal is nearby, in order that he may not come to the nest. And whenever it guesses that it has drawn the hunter off and that the chicks have fled, then it too flies away. […]

The partridge is cunning in that she steals the eggs of another partridge and fosters them with her own body. But she is unable to profit from this, because she loses the brood as soon as she has hatched it. When these hear the voice of the partridge who has laid the eggs, they leave their adopted nest and, following a natural instinct, go to her whom they recognize as their true and natural mother. In this way they indicate that the function of a nurse is totally different from that of a mother. Thus, she performs her own proper labors in vain and pays the penalty of her own deceit. Hence Jeremias says: ‘The partridge uttered a cry and gathered what she did not lay,’ that is, she gathered the eggs and gave forth a cry as if rejoicing at the effect of her own deceit. But she spends her labor in vain. Her prolonged period of brooding benefits another and not herself.

The Devil imitates this bird in his endeavor to lay claim to the generations of the eternal Creator. […]

The partridge has brooded — or has gathered —, what it did not bring forth — and, as the Seventy translated: the partridge cried out, it gathered what it did not bring forth —, he makes his riches not with judgment; in the half of his days he will leave them — or in the half of his days they will leave him — and at his end he will be a fool. The writers of natural history, of beasts and birds as well as of trees and plants, whose chief men among the Greeks are Aristotle and Theophrastus, and among us Pliny Secundus, say that this is the nature of the partridge: that it steals the eggs of another partridge, that is, eggs not its own, and sits on them and broods them, and that when the young have grown up, they fly away from it and leave their alien parent. […]

17:12.t: Now the beginning of the second chapter, which was read, is this: "A throne of glory exalted from the beginning is our place, our sanctification, our support, the support of Israel. O Lord, let all who have forsaken you be put to shame; departing, let them be written upon the earth, because they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of life." The blessed prophet Isaiah said, seeing the Lord and his kingdom: "I saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne lofty and lifted up." Jeremiah too saw how God reigns, on account of which, glorifying him, he says: "A throne of glory exalted from the beginning is our place, our sanctification." Whether you should wish to understand these words of Christ, you will not err, or of the Father, you will not think impiously: for the Savior is a lofty throne of glory and is from the beginning. "A throne of glory," because of which his kingdom is exalted; "our sanctification." [Our sanctification] is Christ; for "both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one."

A throne of glory of the height from the beginning, the place of our sanctification, the expectation of Israel, O Lord, all who leave you will be confounded! Let those who depart be written in the earth, since they have forsaken the vein — or fountain — of living waters, the Lord. The partridge being forsaken for its folly, the expectation of Israel, that is, of the people of God and of the one who believes in the Lord, is he himself who made all things, whose throne is glorious and exalted from the beginning, and who is the place of sanctification of all believers; so that the Lord is not in a place, but wherever he is, that place is sanctified. On the contrary, those who forsake the Lord will be confounded with perpetual confusion, and departing or turning aside from him they will be written in the earth, blotted out from the book of the living. […]

As if anticipating that the inquirer would ask next by what plain mark a young disciple, not yet able to distinguish the truth among so many errors, might find the true Church of Christ. Since the clear fulfillment of so many predictions compelled him to believe in Christ, the prophet answers this question in what follows, and teaches that the Church of Christ, which he describes prophetically, is conspicuously visible. His words are: "A glorious high throne is our sanctuary." This glorious throne is the Church of which the apostle says: "The temple of God is holy, which temple ye are." The Lord also, foreseeing the conspicuousness of the Church as a help to young disciples who might be misled, says, "A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid."

17:13.t:
"The endurance of Israel." Just as the Savior is righteousness-itself, truth-itself, sanctification-itself, so also he is endurance-itself. And it is not possible either to be righteous apart from Christ, or holy apart from him, or to endure without having Christ. For he himself is the endurance of Israel. And even if you refer it to God, not even so will you be committing impiety.

"O Lord, let all who forsake you be put to shame, having departed from you." Each one of us, whenever he sins, through the things by which he sins forsakes Christ, and having forsaken Christ he forsakes God. For in doing wrong he forsakes righteousness, and in becoming profane he forsakes sanctification, and in making war he forsakes peace, and in coming to be under the enemy he forsakes redemption, and in being outside the wisdom of God he forsakes wisdom. To all, then, who forsake God the prophet utters an imprecation, teaching us what will befall them, saying, "Let all who forsake you be put to shame." […]

[Daniel 7:10] "There were millions ministering unto Him, and a billion stood by His side." This was not intended to be a specific number for the servants of God, but only indicates a multitude too great for human computation. These are the thousands and tens of thousands of which we read in the Psalms: "The chariot of God is attended by ten thousands; thousands of them that rejoice. The Lord is among them" (Psalm 68:17). And in another place: "He who maketh His angels spirits, and His ministers a flaming fire" (Psalm 104:4). Now the duty of angels is twofold: the duty of one group is to bestow rewards upon just men; the duty of the other is to have charge over individual calamities.

"...The court was in session, and the books were opened." The consciences of men, and the deeds of individuals which partake of either character, whether good or bad, are disclosed to all. One of the books is the good book of which we often read, namely the book of the living. […]
17:13.s: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER SEVEN

17:13.t: Finally, when the Lord would for their speedy fall turn away His merciful countenance from the people, whom He had chosen out of all nations, the giver of the law interposes on their behalf and cries out: "I beseech Thee, O Lord, this people have sinned a great sin; they have made for themselves gods of gold; and now if Thou forgivest their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me out of Thy book which Thou hast written. To whom the Lord answered: If any man hath sinned before Me, I will blot him out of My book." David also, when complaining in prophetic spirit of Judas and the Lord's persecutors, says: "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living;" and because they did not deserve to come to saving penitence because of the guilt of their great sin, he subjoins: "And let them not be written among the righteous." […]
17:13.s: The Second Conference of Abbot Joseph, Chapter 25

17:14.t: Then again there is a prayer that runs thus: "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my boast. Behold, they say to me, 'Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.' But I have not grown weary in following after you, and I have not desired the day of man, you know it." To him alone who came for the sake of those who are sick, the physician who says, "Those who are strong have no need of a physician, but those who are sick," everyone who wishes to be cured of the sickness of his soul may confidently say, "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed." But if anyone else besides him professes the healing of souls, you would not be speaking truly if you said to that one, "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed." For that woman too who "had a flow of blood" spent "all that she had" on the physicians, and "was not able to be healed by any of them"; […]
He says to him who alone is the true physician, "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed. Save me, and I shall be saved. You are my praise and my hope."

Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, since you are my praise! Many physicians in the Gospel had treated the woman with the issue of blood, who had spent all her substance on them, and yet she could be cured by none except by him who is the true physician and in whose wings is healing. Hence now too the prophet, having suffered reproaches from the people and having been often beset by plots, desires to be healed and to be saved by him who is his true praise and his true medicine.

17:15.t: Behold, they say to me: where is the word of the Lord? Let it come! But I was not troubled, following you as shepherd — or I have not labored following you — and I have not desired the day of man; you know. What went out from my lips was right in your sight — or is before your face —. Do not be a terror to me, my hope in the day of affliction, or do not become a stranger to me, sparing me in the worst day! Those who do not think that what has been spoken will come say to the prophet: where is the word of the Lord? let it come!, judging the delay to be a setting aside of the sentence.

17:16.t: Further, also, it is written concerning the Sabbath in the Decalogue which [the Lord] spoke, face to face, to Moses on Mount Sinai, "And sanctify ye the Sabbath of the Lord with clean hands and a pure heart." And He says in another place, "If my sons keep the Sabbath, then will I cause my mercy to rest upon them." The Sabbath is mentioned at the beginning of the creation [thus]: "And God made in six days the works of His hands, and made an end on the seventh day, and rested on it, and sanctified it." Attend, my children, to the meaning of this expression, "He finished in six days." This implieth that the Lord will finish all things in six thousand years, for a day is with Him a thousand years. And He Himself testifieth, saying, "Behold, to-day will be as a thousand years." Therefore, my children, in six days, that is, in six thousand years, all things will be finished. "And He rested on the seventh day." […]
17:16.s: The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter XV

17:16.t: "Behold, they say to me, 'Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.' But I have not grown weary in following after you." Jesus says to you, "Take up your cross, and follow me," and "Leave all things, and follow me," and "Whoever will not forsake his father and his mother and follow after me is not worthy to be my disciple." If, then, you become such a one as to follow Jesus always, you will indeed follow, and however far you follow you will not grow weary; for "there shall be no toil in Jacob, nor shall trouble be seen in Israel." There is no weariness for the one who follows Jesus; the very act of following takes away the weariness. For this reason he himself says—so that we may toil no longer, having toiled before we began to follow him—"Come to me, all you who toil and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." If, then, though toiling we come to him and follow him, we shall say, "But I have not grown weary in following after you." […]

For I love those presbyters and deacons who when they have performed their mission will not allow themselves to remain absent any longer from their duties. For the prophet says, I have not been weary in following thee. And who can be weary in following Jesus, when He Himself says, Come unto Me all ye that labour, and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Let us therefore never cease from following Jesus, which if we do we shall never fail, for He gives strength to them that follow Him. The more nearly you approach to the Source of power the stronger you will be. Often, while we are thus following Him, the adversaries say to us, Where is the word of the Lord? let it come now. But let us not grow weary in following Him, let us not be turned aside by meeting with this crafty question. It was said to the prophet, when he was thrown into prison, when he was cast into the pit of mire, Where is the word of the Lord? let it come now. […]

But while they are saying these things, he says: 'I was not troubled, nor did I labor, following you as shepherd, or walking in your footsteps; nor was I content to stop there, but I have not desired the day of man, either a longer life or any of the prosperities of this world'. And he calls the same one as witness whom he calls as judge: you have known. There follows: what went out from my lips was right in your sight, meaning that he never lied, that he said nothing contrary to the will of the Lord.

Next we come to the passage where His brethren—that is to say, His relations according to the flesh—urge Him to go up to the feast-day, in order that He may have an opportunity of making Himself known to the multitude. And here, again, how supremely elevated is the tone of His reply! "My time is not yet come, but your time is alway ready. The world cannot hate you; but me it hateth, because I testify of it that the works thereof are evil." So it is the case, then, that "your time is alway ready," because ye desire that kind of day to which the prophet refers when he says, "But I have not laboured following Thee, O Lord; and the day of man I have not desired, Thou knowest:" that is to say, to soar to the light of the Word, and to desire that day which Abraham desired to see, and which he did see, and was glad.
17:16.s: The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 4, Chapter 10

17:16.t: For it is but little for a monk to have once made his renunciation, i.e., in the early days of his conversion to have disregarded the present world, unless he continues to renounce it daily. For to the very end of this life we must with the prophet say this: "And I have not desired the day of man, Thou knowest." Wherefore also the Lord says in the gospel: "If any man will come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me."

17:17.t: Do not, he says, be a terror to me, my hope in the day of affliction! This is clear according to the Hebrew; but according to what the Seventy translated, saying, do not become to me as a stranger, sparing me in the evil day, the sense is: 'do not spare me in the present world, which is evil, but render to me according to my sins, so that I may have everlasting rest! for I know that it is written: whom the Lord loves, he reproves; and he scourges every son whom he receives'. But the evil day is either the whole world or the day of judgment for those who are tormented on account of their sins.

17:18.t: Let those who persecute me be confounded, and let me not be confounded! Let them tremble, and let me not tremble! Bring upon them the day of affliction, and crush them with a double crushing! The prophet calls down imprecations against those who taunt him with the word of the Lord and say, where is the word of the Lord? let it come: that those who persecute him may be confounded, and may blush and return to salvation; that they, who lie, may tremble, and not he, who foretells true things; and that, when the day of vengeance has come, he may crush them with a double crushing, famine and sword.

But they certainly have to labour, and when they attack men, exert themselves in no lesser degree in order to secure from each one that victory which they want to obtain, and there is hurled back upon them the same confusion which was awaiting us had we been worsted by them; as it is said: "The head of their compassing me about, the labour of their own lips shall overwhelm them;" and: "His sorrow shall be turned on his own head;" and again: "Let the snare which he knoweth not come upon him, and let the net which he hath hidden catch him, and into that very snare let him fall;" viz., that which he contrived for the deception of men. […]
17:18.s: First Conference of Abbot Serenus, Chapter 21

17:19.t: Thus says the Lord to me: go and stand in the gate — or in the gates — of the sons of the people, through which [gate] — or through which [gates] — the kings of Judah go in and go out, in all the gates of Jerusalem, and you shall say to them: hear the word of the Lord, kings of Judah and all Judah — or Judea — and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, who go in through these gates! 'Since', he says, 'they scorn to hear your words and do not come to you to inquire what the sentence of God may be, go you to the most frequented place, either of the gates of the temple or of those of the city, through which the kings and all the common people go in and go out, so that they may be compelled by necessity to hear, and you may preach the word of God out of season and in season, and no excuse may remain to them that they did not do it because they did not hear'.

17:21.t: Thus says the Lord: guard your souls, and do not carry weights on the sabbath day, nor bring them in through the gates of Jerusalem! And do not cast out loads from your houses on the sabbath day, and you shall do no work, and sanctify the sabbath day, as I commanded your fathers! And they did not hear, nor did they incline their ear, and they hardened their neck — and what is not found in the Hebrew: above their fathers —, that they might not hear me and might not receive instruction. And it shall be, he says, if you hear me, says the Lord, so as not to bring in loads through the gates of this city on the sabbath day, and if you sanctify the sabbath day, so as not to do any work on it, there will enter through the gates of this city kings and princes sitting upon the throne of David and mounting in chariots and on horses, they and their princes, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and this city will be inhabited forever. […]

17:22.t: And do not, he says, cast out loads from your houses — for they are not to be carried, but utterly cast away — and do no work — either servile work or that of which it is written: food for the belly and the belly for foods; but God will destroy both it and them —, but that work is to be worked of which the Savior speaks: 'work the work that does not perish!' Sanctify, he says, the sabbath day, so that we may spend all the time of our life in sanctification, as our fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did.

17:23.t: And when God had commanded these things, they did not incline their ear — that of the mind, surely, not of the flesh —, but they hardened their neck, rejecting the yoke of the law and, by metaphoran [metaphor], bearing the likeness of untamed animals.

17:24.t: Let us see what is the reward of those who do not carry loads on the sabbath day and who sanctify it. There will enter, he says, through the gates of this city kings, whose heart is in the hand of God and who reign over their bodies, and princes sitting upon the throne of David, so that they imitate the example of Christ, and mounting in chariots and on horses, of which it is written: the chariot of God is ten thousandfold, manifold, thousands of those who rejoice; the Lord is among them in Sinai, in the holy place, and elsewhere: your riding is salvation: every man who 'confesses' God and who dwells in Jerusalem, of which it has been said: was made in Salem, that is, in peace, his place, and his dwelling in Zion; and the Church of God will be inhabited forever.

17:26.t: And they will come from the cities of Judah and from round about Jerusalem, of which we have already spoken, and from the land of Benjamin, who is the 'son' 'of power' and 'of the right hand', and from the plains, which in Hebrew is called 'sefela' and signifies the plain understanding of the history, and from the hill country, namely the lofty doctrines, and from the south, of which it is written, God will come from the south, whence comes heat and full light, and where all cold is driven out. Bringing, he says, burnt offerings — consecrating themselves to God — and a victim or incense, so that they may say: a sacrifice to the Lord is a troubled spirit, and: we are the good odor of Christ in every place, and elsewhere: let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight; and sacrifice, for which the Seventy put the Hebrew word itself, 'manaa', which by a very bad custom, nay rather by the carelessness of scribes, is read in our books as 'manna'; […]

17:27.t: 'But if', he says, 'you will not hear my precepts, and do the things which I commanded not to be done, I will kindle a fire in its gates' — that is, of Jerusalem: that fire of which it is said, all committing adultery, like an oven, their hearts —, 'which will devour the houses or streets of Jerusalem' — which the Seventy translated as amphoda, Aquila and Symmachus as bareis, that is, 'towered houses', and which are called in Hebrew 'armanoth' — 'and this burning will never be extinguished', as the Apostle says: the fire will test what sort each one's work is, and again: if anyone's work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire. […]

18:1.t: There are two visions of Jeremiah that have just been read, one following the other. The former of these contains what concerns the clay vessel in the potter's hand, which admits of restoration after being broken (for it is possible for it to be remolded); but the other vision contains what concerns the earthen jug, which, once shattered, admits of no cure. For when it was clay, if it was broken — even if it had already been given its shape — since it was clay, it was possible for it to become a second lump and to be fashioned a second time; but when, after being clay, it has already become earthenware and has been hardened by fire, then it was not possible, after the shattering of the earthenware, for any cure to come to it. What, then, these things intend, let us first consider by way of reflection, and then, if it be granted, let us examine them according to the letter. […]

18:2.t: The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Arise and go down into the potter's house, and there you shall hear my words! And I went down into the potter's house, and behold, he was doing a work upon the wheel — or stones —. And the vessel that he was making from clay with his hands was broken; and turning — or and again — he made it another vessel, as it had pleased in his eyes to make it. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Can I not do with you as this potter, O house of Israel? says the Lord; behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel! Suddenly — or in sum — I will speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to root it out — or to take it away — and to destroy and to ruin it. If that nation repents of its evil, which I have spoken against it, I too will repent of the evil which I thought to do to it. And suddenly — or in sum — I will speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build and to plant it. […]

18:3.t: The prophet, then, goes down to the house of the potter and recounts what he beheld, saying: "And behold, he was doing a work upon his hands, and the vessel which he was making of the clay fell apart in his hands; and again he made it into another vessel, as it pleased him to make it." But I do not know what the prophet saw when he came to the potter. For he saw the potter working; the vessel that had been made was of clay; the vessel fell apart. Why did he not say precisely: he let the vessel go out of his hand — nor did he lay the cause upon the potter? But since the word is about ensouled vessels, which fall apart of themselves, for this reason it is said: "the vessel fell apart from his hands." Take heed, then, to yourself as well, lest, while being in the potter's hand and still being molded, you fall apart from his hands by your own doing. For "no one snatches out of his hands," according to what is said in the Gospel according to John. […]

When, therefore, God speaks of an irremediable calamity, he does not say vessels of the potter, but an earthen vessel; when, for instance, he wished to teach the prophet and the Jews that he delivered up the city to an irremediable calamity, he bade him take an earthen wine-vessel, and crush it before all the people, and say, "Thus shall this city be destroyed, be broken in pieces." But when he wishes to hold out good hopes to them, he brings the prophet to a pottery, and does not show him an earthen vessel, but shows him a vessel of clay, which was in the hands of the potter, falling to the ground: and brings him to it saying, "If this potter has taken up and remodelled his vessel which has fallen, shall I not much rather be able to restore you when you have fallen?" […]

'And when,' he says, 'I had set out and had gone down into the potter's house, he was doing a work upon the wheel', which the Seventy, led astray by the ambiguity of the word, translated 'stones'; for 'abanim', according to the nature of the context and the difference of pronunciation, is used both for an 'instrument', that is, the potter's 'wheel', and for 'stones'.

18:4.t: 'And when,' he says, 'I saw a vessel being made from clay, it was suddenly broken', God's providence bringing this about, so that the craftsman's hand, without knowing it, should by its own mistake figure forth a parable. And again that potter, who had lost the vessel of clay as the wheel was running, made another for himself, as it seemed good to him.

18:5.t: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Shall I not be able to do to you as the potter, O house of Israel? says the Lord." Each one understands the things written according to his ability, the one more superficially, as though drawing his understanding from them from a surface spring, the other more deeply, as one drawing up from a well. And both can be helped, since the same thing is for one a spring and for the other a well. The Gospel bears witness, when it recounts the things concerning the Samaritan woman; for there the same thing is named "spring" and "well," and in turn it is sometimes called a spring and sometimes a well. Let him who is able take note, that he may know that the same thing in its substance is for the superficial one a spring, but for the deeper one a well. This is for me a preface to the account that is coming, concerning the clay vessel that fell apart from the potter's hand and was again molded. Some have viewed these things more simply and have understood them. […]

And at once the Lord says to the prophet: 'If a potter,' he says, 'has this power, that from the same clay he makes again what had been broken, shall I not be able to do this in you, who, as far as lies in you, seem to have perished?'

18:7.t: But let us hear the Lord himself recounting and saying: "Shall I not be able to do to you as the potter, O house of Israel? says the Lord. Behold, as the clay of the potter, so are you in my hands. At the end I will speak against a nation and a kingdom, to remove them and to destroy them; and that nation shall turn from their evils of which I spoke against it, and I will repent of the evils which I purposed to do to them. And at the end I will speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build it up and to plant it, and they shall do wicked things before me, so as not to hear my voice, and I will repent concerning the good things which I said I would do to them, says the Lord." This concerning the house of the potter we see to be referred not to any of the individuals, but to two nations; for, beginning, he says that he is going to speak about nations, that he may suggest something to those able to hear hidden mysteries: "At the end I will speak against a nation." […]

It was not as though it were unknown that He had promised in their behalf that things should be thus, and then the years were diminished and also were increased, but as known; for He knew the measure of that which was to come, and on account of His mercies He gave a time for repentance that men might be without excuse; and men despised the longsuffering of God, and when they heard that there was much time until the wrath which was promised should come, becoming bold they sinned before Him and said: "That which the prophets say is prophesied for a remote time." On account of this when there arose a disputing concerning these things in the days of Ezekiel the prophet and they said: "That which hath been prophesied is for a remote time," He said to Ezekiel: "As I live," saith the Lord of dominions, "there shall not again be a delay to My words, for the word which I shall speak I shall shortly accomplish." And He cut off that which He had foretold, to give to men a time for repentance, that perhaps they might repent; […]

[Daniel 4:27] "'Wherefore, O king, let my counsel meet with thy favor, and make up for thy sins by deeds of charity, and thine iniquities by showing mercy to the poor. Perhaps God will forgive thy transgressions.'" Since he had previously pronounced the sentence of God, which of course cannot be altered, how could he exhort the king to deeds of charity and acts of mercy towards the poor? This difficulty is easily solved by reference to the example of King Hezekiah, who Isaiah had said was going to die (Isaiah 38:1); and again, to the example of the Ninevites, to whom it was said: "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be destroyed" (Jonah 3:4). And yet the sentence of God was changed in response to the prayers of Hezekiah and the city of Nineveh, not by any means because of the ineffectualness of the judgment itself but because of the conversion of those who merited pardon. […]
18:7.s: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER FOUR

18:7.t: You may as well accuse God of falsehood because he said by the mouth of Jonah: "Yet three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown." But God will reply by the mouth of Jeremiah, "At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to break down and to destroy it; if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do to them. And at what instant I shall speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it; if it does evil in my sight, that it obeys not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them." Jonah, on a certain occasion, was indignant because, at God's command, he had spoken falsely; but his sorrow was proved to be ill founded, since he would rather speak truth and have a countless multitude perish than speak falsely and have them saved.

And though they promise themselves prosperity, they will afterwards endure evils; while, on the other side, the saints fear and do not sin, and therefore by no means die by the sword, because they said: Evils will draw near to us, and the punishments which our sins have deserved will come upon us; of which God speaks more fully in Jeremiah: I will take it up and speak against a nation and a kingdom, to take it away and destroy it; if that nation turns from its evils, I too will repent of the things that I had thought to do to it. God, therefore, is not changed, who is always immutable; but we change him by our conversion. He rages, he is angry, he threatens, and says that he will inflict punishments: If we repent, he too will repent of his sentence. Again, according to the same Jeremiah, he promises prosperity: If we grow slack through negligence, he too will repent of his pledge, and will change what he promised. […]

And to signify free will, he says that he announces both evils to this or that nation and kingdom and, again, good things; and yet that what he himself has foretold does not come about, but that the contrary happens, so that good things befall the evil, if they repent, and evils befall the good, if after the promises they have turned to sins. And we say this not because God does not know that this or that nation or kingdom will do this or that, but because he leaves man to his own will, so that he may receive either rewards or punishments by his own desert. Nor will what befalls be wholly man's at once, but belongs to the grace of him who has bestowed all things; for the freedom of the will must be preserved in such a way that the grace of the giver excels in all things, according to that prophetic word: Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain; unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it has watched in vain. […]

And that we may not fancy that the Lord granted this specially to the Ninevites, He continually affirms by Jeremiah that He will do the same in general towards all, and promises that without delay He will change His sentence in accordance with our deserts; saying: "I will suddenly speak against a nation and against a kingdom to root out and to pull down and to destroy it. If that nation repent of the evil, which I have spoken against it, I also will repent of the evil which I thought to do to them. And I will suddenly speak of a nation and a kingdom, to build up and to plant it. If it shall do evil in My sight, that it obey not My voice: I will repent of the good that I thought to do to it." To Ezekiel also: "Leave out nota word, if so be they will hearken and be converted every one from his evil way: that I may repent Me of the evil that I thought to do to them for the wickedness of their doings." […]
18:7.s: The Second Conference of Abbot Joseph, Chapter 25

18:10.t: "At the end I will speak against a nation or also against a kingdom." It will seem that "the end" is said simply. But it is said in this way. In the "I will speak against a nation or a kingdom," the "end" is of this sort: "I will raze" is said to the former nation as the "end"; to the second nation, "I will build you up." And again, "I will uproot" is said to the former ones, and "I will plant" to the second. Is it, then, that because the "end" has been spoken, the end must come to pass? God, though he does not repent, is said in Scripture to repent. And let us attend to the wording, that if we are able to give a defense of how these things are said, we may accept the account. "At the end I will speak," he says, "against a nation or against a kingdom, to remove them and to destroy them; and if that nation should turn from their evils of which I spoke against it, then I will repent concerning the evils which I purposed to do to them. […]

18:11.t: Next, after the discourse concerning the two nations — the former, to which the threat is given, and the second, to which the promise is given — he says (he said, that is, to the former ones): "And now I have spoken to the men of Judah and to those who dwell in Jerusalem; thus says the Lord: Behold, I am molding evils against you." Because these things which I am molding against you are in my hand, they can fall apart. Make these things fall apart from my hand, so that the evils which I am molding against you I may change and make into good things. You would not find, "Behold, I am molding good things against you," and the things said correspondingly after them, so that after this he might make manifest that the good things which he molds he releases from his hands, that he may make them evil. […]

"Let each one turn back, then, from his evil way, and make your practices better." Sometimes the more simple-minded say: blessed were the men of old, because they heard the Lord through the prophet saying, "and the Lord spoke to them." And to us now the Lord speaks through the things that are written: "Let each one turn back from his evil way"; the Lord himself converses with you, declaring, "and make your practices better." But those to whom the hortatory words concerning repentance were spoken made an answer, and let us see what they answered, so that we too may not answer in such a way. What, then, do they say in reply? "We will play the man, for we will go after our own backslidings, and each of us will do the pleasing things of his evil heart." […]

Now therefore say to the man of Judah and to the inhabitant of Jerusalem, saying: These things — or thus — says the Lord: Behold, I am fashioning evil against you and devising a device against you; let each one turn back from his evil way, and make straight your ways and your pursuits! And they said: We have despaired — or we will be strong —; for we will walk after our own thoughts, and each one of us will do the depravity — or what has pleased his evil heart —. Therefore thus says the Lord: Ask among the nations: who has heard such horrible things as the virgin of Israel has done exceedingly? The Lord fulfills the parable which he had taught both by sight and by words, and says: 'Behold, I am fashioning evil against you, as a potter fashions clay' — evil, however, in the sense of Isaiah, who says: making peace and creating evil, not that it is evil in itself, but that it seems to be evil to those who suffer it — 'and devising a device against you' — that is, to pass sentence according to desert —; […]

18:12.t: 'But they, on the contrary,' he says, 'said: We will be strong' — in their evil works, that is, or, according to Aquila, we have despaired, and according to Symmachus, we have failed, both of which offend God, that one should either think that he can by no means be saved, or should have failed in spirit for appeasing God — 'and after our own thoughts,' he says, 'we will walk.' Where, then, is the power of free will and the judgment of one's own will apart from the grace of God, when it is a grave offense against God to follow one's own thoughts and to do the will of a depraved heart?

18:13.t: Therefore he adds, saying: 'Ask among the nations and all the peoples round about, who has done, who has heard, while serving idols, what the virgin of Israel has done exceedingly.' And he calls her a virgin because she had served the one God, as the prophet says: God is known in Judea, his name is great in Israel.

18:14.t: "Shall the breasts fail from the rock, or the snow from Lebanon? Or shall water be turned aside that is borne violently by the wind? For my people have forgotten me; they have burned incense in vain, and they shall grow weak in their ways, the everlasting paths, so as to walk in tracks that have no way for journeying, so as to make their land a desolation and a perpetual hissing." He has here spoken of differences of waters: first in "shall the breasts fail from the rock?"; second in "or the snow from Lebanon?"; third in "or shall water be turned aside that is borne violently by the wind?" These three kinds of waters are the springs of the waters which the soul of the righteous, likened to the deer, longs for, so that each one may say: "As the deer longs for the springs of the waters, so my soul longs for you, O God."
