Who, then, has become a deer, an enemy to the race of serpents, suffering nothing from their venom, as is recounted concerning the deer? […]

Will the snow of Lebanon fail from the rock of the field? Or can the cold waters that burst forth and flow down be torn away? LXX: Will breasts fail from the rock, or snow from Lebanon? Or will water violently carried off by the wind turn aside? Something of the same kind that line of Vergil also sounds: Sooner, therefore, shall the nimble stags graze in the air, and the seas leave the fishes bare upon the shore, than his face shall slip from our heart; and in another place: While rivers run into the seas, while shadows move over the slopes of the mountains, while the sky feeds the stars, ever shall your honor, your name and your praises abide. 'Just as,' he says, 'the snow cannot fail from the summits of Lebanon, nor is it overcome by any heat of the sun so as to melt entirely, and the streams flowing down from the mountains are by no means dried up at their springs, so my name, which is in itself stable and everlasting, cannot be changed; […]

18:15.t: "For my people have forgotten me, they have burned incense in vain." Everyone who sins has forgotten God, but the righteous one says, "All these things have come upon us, and we have not forgotten you, nor have we done wrong" — and he burned incense in vain. But what "they have burned incense in vain" means must be considered. If we take up again the things said earlier upon the hundred and fortieth Psalm, we shall understand what "they have burned incense in vain" is. Now there was in the Psalm something of this sort said: "Let my prayer be set forth as incense before you." Therefore my prayer, being composed of a fine heart — when our heart is not made gross — being sent up, becomes as incense before God. If, then, the prayer of the righteous is incense before God, the prayer of the unrighteous is indeed incense, but such incense that it may be said concerning it and concerning the unrighteous who prays, "they have burned incense in vain"; as is written concerning Judas, "Let his prayer become sin." […]

For my people has forgotten me, making libations in vain and stumbling in their ways, in the paths of the age — or everlasting —, so that they walked in them on a road not trodden. He who forgets God and forsakes him who says: I am the way, and pours libations to strange gods, stumbles in his own ways — not God's at all, but his own — and forsakes the ancient and everlasting paths, which are trodden by the footprints of all the saints who worship God. These, however, have walked on a road not trodden and, having abandoned the worship of God, have venerated idols; on account of which the punishment that follows is brought upon them:

18:16.t: So that their land should become a desolation and an everlasting hissing; everyone who passes by it shall be astonished and shall shake his head. 'And because they have forsaken,' he says, 'the worship of God and have followed the depraved paths of idolatry, therefore their land has been reduced to a wilderness and to a wonder and a hissing to all, so that those who saw the land and city, once most flourishing, collapsed into a desert and ashes should marvel and be astonished and show the confusion of their soul by the gesture of their body'; for this is what it is to shake the head and to show the astonishment of the mind by hissing. And this we understand to have been fulfilled more fully and more correctly after the coming of the Lord, when none of the Jews is permitted by law to enter the land and the once holy city; but when they come to mourn, they marvel at and weep over the prophecies of the prophets fulfilled in deed.

18:17.t: Like a burning wind I will scatter them before the enemy — or the enemies —; the back and not the face will I show them in the day of their perdition. To this day the sentence of God remains upon the Jews; they have been scattered throughout the whole world before the enemy, the devil, or the enemies, the demons, and, though day and night in the synagogues of Satan they call upon the name of God, God shows them his back and not his face, so that they may understand that he is always withdrawing and never coming to them. Now the day of the perdition of the Jews is the whole time after the Savior's passion until the consummation of the age, so that, after the fullness of the nations has come in, then all Israel may be saved.

18:18.t: And they said: Come and let us devise devices against Jeremiah! For the law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet; come and let us strike him with the tongue, and let us not heed all his words! This was both then the thought of the Jews against Jeremiah, or against the Lord the Savior, and is today the thought of heretics against his servants: to contrive calumnies and to forestall holy men with accusation, and not to consider what truth those men speak, but what falsehood they themselves may contrive; for they boast that the law of God and counsel and utterance remain in their own priests and wise men and false prophets, though Scripture says: Into a perverse soul wisdom shall not enter.

18:19.t: Attend to me, O Lord, and hear the voice of my adversaries! Is evil repaid for good, that they have dug a pit for my soul? Remember that I stood in your sight to speak good for them and to turn away your indignation from them! Therefore give their children up to famine and lead them into the hands of the sword; let their wives be childless and widows, and let their husbands be put to death, let their young men be pierced by the sword in battle, let an outcry be heard from their houses! In the type of the Savior, indeed, Jeremiah suffers all these things from the people of the Jews, who were afterwards laid waste when the Babylonian came; but they are fulfilled more fully and more perfectly in Christ. And when the city was overthrown they were slaughtered by the Roman sword, not because of idolatry, which did not exist at that time, but because of the killing of the Son of God, when the whole people together cried out: Away, away with such a man; we have no king but Caesar! […]

18:22.t: For you will bring a robber upon them suddenly, because they have dug a pit to catch me and have hidden snares for my feet. But you, O Lord, know all their counsel against me unto death; do not be propitious to their iniquity, and let their sin not be blotted out from before your face; let them be falling — or stumbling — in your sight; in the time of your fury consume them or deal with them! If we understand it of Jeremiah, let us refer the sudden robber to Nebuchadnezzar; if of the Savior, which is truer and better, to the Roman army. And lest the sentence of God should seem unjust, he sets out what they did against Christ, the Son of God, and what they suffered.

18:23.t: But what he adds: do not be propitious to their iniquity, and let their sin not be blotted out from before your face, is by no means contrary to the earlier sentence, in which he entreats the Father for the people; but after the time given for repentance has passed and they persevere in their crime, they are punished not so much for themselves as for others, lest a sin left unpunished should harm the rest by its example. And what he adds: let them be stumbling — or falling — in your sight, is like that saying of Isaiah and of the apostle Peter: and you shall not stumble as on a stone of offense and a rock of scandal; which the prophet also mentions in the psalms: The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner; this was done by the Lord.

19:1.t: Thus says the Lord: Go and take a potter's earthen flask, and some of the elders of the people and of the elders of the priests, and go out to the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is by the entrance of the earthen gate — or Charsith —, and you shall preach — or you shall cry or you shall read — there the words which I shall speak to you, and you shall say: Hear the word of the Lord, O kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem! For 'potter's flask', which in Hebrew is called 'bocboc', the Seventy translated 'little jar', and for 'earthen gate' Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, 'Harsith', for which the Seventy, according to their custom, added the Greek 'chi' for the aspiration of the letter 'heth', so as to say 'Charsith' for 'Harsith', just as there is 'Chebron' for 'Hebron', and 'Hiericho' for 'Hieriho'. Now divine Scripture wishes the people to be taught not only by the ears but also by the eyes; […]

19:3.t: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will bring affliction — or evils — upon this place, so that the ears of everyone who hears of it — or of them — shall tingle, because they have forsaken me and have made this place strange and have poured libations in it to strange gods, whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah knew; and they have filled this place with the blood of the innocent and have built the high places of the Baals to burn their sons with fire as a burnt offering to the Baals, which I did not command — or think of — nor speak, nor did they come up into my heart. And some foolishly refer this place to the heavenly Jerusalem. So that I need not always give warning of this, let it suffice to have said this once: that an explanation of this kind, nay rather heresy, is to be avoided, which overturns what is plain and tries to bring certain conjuring tricks into the churches of Christ. […]

19:6.t: Therefore, behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and this place shall no longer be called Topheth and the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter. LXX: Therefore, behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and this place shall no longer be called ruin and polyandrion of the son of Hinnom, but polyandrion of slaughter. What the valley of the son of Hinnom is, which in Hebrew is called 'gehennom', whence they think 'gehennam' [Gehenna] too was named, we have said above. But I wonder what the Seventy meant by putting diaptōsin, that is, 'ruin', for 'Topheth', and polyandrion, which signifies 'a multitude of men', for 'valley', unless perhaps because there the people fell and a multitude of men was slain, either spiritually in the error of idolatry or, according to the letter, by the Babylonian army, as is read more plainly in what follows.

19:7.t: And I will scatter the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place, and I will overthrow them by the sword before their enemies and by the hand of those who seek their lives, and I will give their corpses as food to the birds of the heaven and to the beasts of the earth, and I will make this city an astonishment and a hissing; everyone who passes by it shall be astonished and shall hiss over all its wounds. And I will feed them with the flesh of their sons and with the flesh of their daughters, and each one shall eat the flesh of his friend in the siege and in the distress in which their enemies, and those who seek their lives, shall shut them in. […]

19:10.t: And you shall break the flask before the eyes of the men who will go — or will go out — with you, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: So will I break this people and this city, as a potter's vessel is broken, which cannot be restored any more. This is plainly said not of the Babylonian but of the Roman captivity; for after the Babylonians both the city was restored and the people was brought back into Judea and restored to its former abundance. But after the captivity which happened under Vespasian and Titus, and afterwards under Hadrian, the ruins of Jerusalem will remain until the consummation of the age, although the Jews think that a golden and jeweled Jerusalem is to be restored to them, and again victims and sacrifices and the marriages of the saints and the kingdom of the Lord the Savior on earth. […]

19:11.t:
And they shall be buried — or they shall bury — in Topheth, because there is no other place for burying. So will I do to this place, says the Lord, and to its inhabitants, that I will make this city like Topheth — or like ruin —. And the houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah shall be like the place Topheth or of ruin. But what is added in the Seventy: all the houses of the kings of Judah like the place Topheth, is not found in the Hebrew. And there follows:

Unclean are all the houses on whose housetops — or roofs — they have sacrificed to all the host of heaven and have poured out libations to strange gods. What he had said above: this place shall no longer be called Topheth and the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter, he now sets out more plainly: that so great a slaughter will take place in that very place that the people will be buried there in heaps and the place once of religion will become a tomb of the dead; […]

19:14.t: Then Jeremiah came from Topheth, where the Lord had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the court of the house of the Lord and said to all the people: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will bring upon this city and upon all its towns all the evils which I have spoken against it, because they have hardened their neck so as not to hear my words. After Jeremiah, in Topheth, in the presence of the elders of the people whom he had brought with him, broke the flask, or jar, and prophesied with the words of the Lord the breaking of the people and of the city of Jerusalem, he returns and stands in the court of the house of the Lord and speaks to the whole multitude, which had refused to go to the place Topheth, that the Lord is about to bring upon the city of Jerusalem and upon all its towns the evils which he has spoken against it. […]

20:1.t:
…of the mind of the Scripture, which comes to be present to an eye that has room for the clarity of the sacred writings. These things I have said by way of preface, rousing and awakening both myself and my hearers to attend to what has been read, so that we may ask Jesus to come and to appear to us and to teach us now the things written here.

"Jeremiah prophesied; and Paschor son of Emmer the priest heard the words of the prophecy." And although in all likelihood many, so far as the mere sequence of the prophecy goes, had heard Jeremiah, no other hearer is quickly recorded except Paschor. But the Scripture took care to say also whose son he was, that he was son of Emmer, and that he held the office of priest, and what rank he had among the people—that he had been appointed governor of the house of the Lord at the time when Jeremiah was prophesying these words. And it is recorded that, having heard the words of this prophecy, Paschor struck Jeremiah; […]

And Pashhur son of Immer, the priest, who had been appointed prince in the house of the Lord, heard Jeremiah prophesying these words. And Pashhur struck Jeremiah the prophet and put him in the stocks that were in the upper gate of Benjamin in the house of the Lord. For 'Phassur' the Seventy translated 'Phaschor', which means 'blackness of mouth'; and for the 'stocks' which we have given, the Seventy and Theodotion translated 'cataracten' [a trapdoor], Symmachus basanistērion or streblōtērion, both of which signify 'tortures'; we, however, said 'neruum' [stocks] according to common usage, a kind of torture that we also read of in the Acts of the Apostles, when the apostles Paul and Silas were given into the custody of the prison. Now this man was the high priest of the temple, and, the dignity of the priesthood having been given to him, he abuses it perversely, not to teach and to correct by word, but to terrify by torments. Hence both the Savior and the apostle Paul are beaten at the command of the high priest. […]

20:2.t: …The enchanters of the Egyptians also had rods, rods that wished to slander the rod of Moses and that of Aaron as though they were not from God. But those from God overturn those of the sophists and enchanters: "the rod of Aaron swallowed them up"; for this rod sufficed for this even without the rod of Moses. So Paschor "struck Jeremiah the prophet," and with emphasis: "and he struck Jeremiah the prophet." "The prophet" is added. Here, then, the one who struck struck Jeremiah the prophet. But it is recorded in the Acts that someone struck Paul, being ordered to do so by Ananias the high priest. Wherefore Paul said: "God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall." And even now the Ebionites, ordered by a transgressing high priest of the word, strike the apostle of Jesus Christ with blasphemous words. And Paul says to such a high priest of the word: "God is going to strike you." And such a high priest is on the surface fair and a whitewashed wall, but "within full of dead men's bones and all uncleanness." […]

20:3.t: "And it came to pass on the next day that Paschor brought Jeremiah out of the dungeon." O Lord Jesus, come again, make clear to me these things also, and to those who have come for the spiritual nourishment. How does he "on the next day" himself bring "Jeremiah out of the dungeon"? For as long as the present day stands (and today is all this present age), the sinner casts the prophet down into the dungeon; but if the present day cease and the morrow come, then, having repented, he brings him out of the dungeon. Then Jeremiah tells him what Paschor will suffer. What does he say to him? "The Lord did not call your name Paschor, but Exile. For thus says the Lord." This Paschor is going to be deported, according to the desert of his sins, to Babylon—not alone, but also with his friends. For he is handed over to Nabuchodonosor and departs into the Confusion (Sygchysis) and is punished for his sins, since "he cast the prophet into the dungeon." […]

And when it had dawned on the morrow, Pashhur brought Jeremiah out of the stocks, and Jeremiah said to him: Not Pashhur has the Lord called your name, but terror on every side. Here too all have likewise translated both the name of the high priest and the kind of torture as above. And the name of the high priest is changed so that from the name the punishment of things to come may be shown. 'By no means,' he says, 'will you have blackness of mouth and the rule of unjust power, but you will be led captive to Babylon — for this is what 'terror on every side' or 'round about' signifies —, 'so that, trembling and uncertain of your own safety, you may look around this way and that and dread the adversaries coming against you.' For 'terror', which in the Hebrew is written 'magur', the Seventy and Theodotion translated metoikon, that is 'migrant'; Aquila's second edition 'stranger', the first 'looking around'; Symmachus 'carried off' or 'gathered' and 'compelled'.

20:4.t: For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will give you into terror, and all your friends, and they shall fall by the sword of their enemies, and your eyes shall see it; and all Judah I will give into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall carry them over into Babylon and shall strike them with the sword. And I will give all the substance — or strength — of this city, and all its labor, and every price — or glory — and all the treasures of the kings of Judah I will give into the hand of their enemies, and they shall plunder them and take them and lead them into Babylon. But you, Pashhur, and all the inhabitants of your house shall go into captivity, and you shall come into Babylon, and there you shall die and there you shall be buried, and all your friends, to whom you prophesied a lie. […]

20:7.t: And indeed the one passage has been completed; but now let us begin the second also; for it too has matters, right from its first phrase, that are not trivial. And attending to the phrasing, let us again ask Jesus to come, and let us exhort him to come more manifestly and more brightly, so that coming he may teach us all whether the prophet spoke truthfully—as is fitting to think concerning a prophet—the things that follow, or falsely, which it is not lawful to say concerning a holy prophet. He says to God: "You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived; you prevailed and were mighty; I became a laughingstock, all the day long I continued being mocked; because with a bitter word of mine I will laugh, I will call upon faithlessness and misery; because the word of the Lord became to me a reproach and a derision all the day. And I said: I will not name the name of the Lord, and I will no longer speak upon his name. […]

All the things written about God, even if they seem inappropriate on their face, must be understood to be worthy of a good God. For who will not say that it is unfitting for such things to be referred to God — that He has anger, that He employs wrath, that He repents, and indeed even that He sleeps? Yet each of these, in the judgment of one who knows how to "hear dark sayings," will be found worthy of God. For His anger is not fruitless, but as His word instructs, so also His anger instructs; for those who are not instructed by the word He instructs by anger. And it is necessary for God to make use of what is called anger, just as He makes use of what is named "word"; for neither is His word such as is the word of all others. For no one's word is a "living being," no one's word is "God," no one's word "was in the beginning" with Him with whom the Word was, even if He alone † be from some beginning. So too the anger of God is called anger, but not as is the anger of just anyone. […]

Others, however, think that Isaiah offered himself for this reason, because he supposed that prosperous things were to be announced to the people: but because he heard: Go, say to this people: With your ears you shall hear and shall not understand, and seeing you shall see and shall not know (Isa 6:9), for that reason, in what follows, when the voice of the Lord says to him: Cry, he does not cry at once, but asks, what shall I cry? And Jeremiah, to whom it had been said: Take the cup, and you shall give drink to all the nations to whom I shall send you (Jer 25:15), gladly accepting the cup of punishments to pledge it to the hostile nations, that they might drink and vomit and fall, after he heard, go, and first you shall give drink to Jerusalem, answered: You have deceived me, Lord, and I have been deceived (Jer 20:7). This is an observation of the Hebrews. For our part, however, we say that it was not of rashness but of obedience that he offered himself to the Lord to be sent.

As for what is set down above, Why have you made us stray (Isa 63:17)?, in what sense it is to be taken Jeremiah teaches most fully: You have led me astray, O Lord, and I was led astray; you took hold of me, and you prevailed (Jer 20:7). For while you promise me mercy, and like a merciful father you conceal your severity, and like a skilful physician you hide the sharpest knife so as not to frighten the sick man before you heal him, you have made me careless.

You have seduced me, O Lord, and I was seduced — or you have deceived me, O Lord, and I was deceived —; you were stronger than I and you prevailed — or you held fast and you were able —; I have become a derision all the day, all mock me, for long since I speak crying out iniquity, and I keep proclaiming devastation or for with my bitter word I shall laugh, I shall call upon transgression and misery. The prophet says that he was deceived by the Lord because, hearing at the beginning: I have given you as a prophet to the nations, and again: behold, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot and to destroy and to ruin and to scatter and to build and to plant, he supposed that he would say nothing against the people of the Jews, but against the various nations round about, and therefore he willingly took up prophecy; and that the contrary came about, so that, preaching the captivity of Jerusalem, he endured persecutions and straits. […]

20:8.t: "Because with my bitter word I shall laugh." There is a certain laughter that is promise, of which promise the patriarch Isaac is the namesake; for he is interpreted "Laughter." And that laughter is promise is clear from the words "Blessed are those who weep now"; and the promise is "for they shall laugh." Just as it is a promise that "they shall be called sons of God," and "they shall see God," and "they shall inherit the earth," and "theirs is the kingdom of heaven," so laughter is a promise; to which promise the contrary is the weeping that is called blessed. And you will inquire whether, with this good laughter, according to one and another conception, the weeping that is called blessed sings in harmony, while there is opposed to it another weeping, laid up, over which those bewailed with the contrary woes lament. For "Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep"; for one is the weeping that is called blessed, another the weeping laid up for those who have lived badly. […]

And so far as the literal truth is concerned, it is useful to recount what things Jeremiah suffered among the people, with respect to which he said, "And I said, I will not speak, nor will I call on the name of the Lord." And again, elsewhere, "I was continually being mocked." And how great sufferings he endured from the then king of Israel are written in his prophecy. And it is also written that some of the people often came to stone Moses to death. His homeland was not the stones of any place but was instead the people who followed him, among whom also he was dishonored.
20:8.s: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 10:18

20:8.t: For not only did he bear those things nobly which happen to the body, the afflictions, and whatever he enumerated, but those also which touch the soul; for neither are these wont to disturb slightly. Jeremiah at least having borne many temptations, gave in upon these, and when he was reproached, said, "I will not prophesy, neither will I name the Name of the Lord." And David too many places complains of reproach. Isaiah also, after many things, exhorteth concerning this, saying, "Fear ye not the reproach of men, neither be ye overcome by their reviling." And again, Christ also to His disciples; "When they shall speak all manner of evil against you falsely, rejoice and be exceeding glad," He saith, "for great is your reward in heaven."

'And I cry out the Babylonian devastation and the iniquity of the enemies, by which my people is to be oppressed.' But if we follow the Seventy in what they said: for with my bitter word I shall laugh, I shall call upon transgression and misery, this is the sense: 'I know that the present sadness is to be exchanged for future joy, according to what is written: blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh; and therefore I willingly endure misery and iniquity and affliction, so that I even desire them and call upon them, and make up for the brevity of the injury with the eternity of happiness'.

For the word of the Lord has become to me a reproach and a derision all the day. And I said: I will not remember him — or I will not name the Lord — nor will I speak any more in his name. And there came to be in my heart as it were a burning fire, shut up in my bones, and I fainted — or I was dissolved — not enduring to bear it; for I heard the insults — or the reproach — of many, and terror round about — or of those gathered from every side —: Persecute, and let us persecute him! 'When I cried out and said that the Babylonian army was already coming and that the sword of the enemy would plunder everything, the word of the Lord was turned for me into a reproach and a derision, since they think the delay of the prophecy is a lie; for which reason I resolved in my mind that I would no longer speak words to the people of God nor name his name. […]

20:9.t: That people, then, was sick; manifold diseases were in the people that had been called the people of God. God sent them physicians, the prophets. One of the physicians was Jeremiah too; he reproved the sinners, wishing to turn back those who were doing evil. But they, when they ought to have listened to what was said, accused the prophet, and accused him before judges who were much like themselves. And the prophet was always in lawsuits at the hands of those who, so far as his prophecy was concerned, were being healed, but who, because of their own disobedience, were not being healed. Concerning these things he says at one point: "And I said, I will not speak, nor will I name the name of the Lord. And it became like a burning fire, blazing in my bones, and I am unstrung on every side and cannot bear it." And at another point he says, seeing himself always brought to trial, reviled, accused, borne false witness against: "Woe is me, mother, as what have you borne me?" […]

Then consider how the prophets are right-minded men, and do not hide their own sins as we also do, and speak not only concerning those then living, but concerning all the generations, if they have sinned. And I hesitate to confess my sins before these few here, since those who hear will be about to condemn me. But Jeremiah, having suffered something sinful, was not ashamed, but recorded his own sin; for it was a sin, what was brought in with the words, "And I said: I will not name the name of the Lord, and I will no longer speak in his name." You were taught "to do all things in the name of the Lord," to act in the name of God; and yet you say, "May I not name the name of the Lord"? But what sort of name are you about to name? "The name of other gods you shall not call to remembrance in your hearts," and you say, "I will not name the name of the Lord, and I will no longer speak in his name"? He speaks then having suffered something human, which we too are often in danger of having suffered. […]

Now a fire such as this laid hold of Jeremiah the prophet, when the word was in him as a fire, and he said, ‘I pass away from every place, and am not able to endure it.’ And our Lord Jesus Christ, being good and a lover of men, came that He might cast this upon earth, and said, ‘And what? would that it were already kindled!’ For He desired, as He testified in Ezekiel, the repentance of a man rather than his death; so that evil should be entirely consumed in all men, that the soul, being purified, might be able to bring forth fruit; for the word which is sown by Him will be productive, some thirty, some sixty, some an hundred. Thus, for instance, those who were with Cleopas, although infirm at first from lack of knowledge, yet afterwards were inflamed with the words of the Saviour, and brought forth the fruits of the knowledge of Him. The blessed Paul also, when seized by this fire, revealed it not to flesh and blood, but having experienced the grace, he became a preacher of the Word.

Or possibly there are some who advise you to hide, because you have given your word upon oath not to accept the office if elected. For I hear that they are buzzing in your ears to this effect, and consider that they are thus acting conscientiously. But if they were truly conscientious, they would above all have feared God, Who imposed this ministry upon you. Or if they had read the divine Scriptures, they would not have advised you contrary to them. For it is time for them to blame Jeremiah also, and to impeach the great Moses, in that they did not listen to their advice, but fearing God fulfilled their ministry, and prophesying were made perfect. For they also when they had received their mission and the grace of Prophecy, refused. But afterwards they feared, and did not set at nought Him that sent them. Whether then you be of stammering utterance, and slow of tongue, yet fear God that made you, or if you call yourself too young to preach, yet reverence Him Who knew you before you were made. […]

I think, too, we cannot leave out of sight that fire when we read that the Lord Jesus baptizes with the Holy Spirit and with fire, as John said in his Gospel. Rightly was the sacrifice consumed, for it was for sin. But that fire was a type of the Holy Spirit Who was to come down after the Lord's ascension, and forgive the sins of all, and Who like fire inflames the mind and faithful heart. Wherefore Jeremiah, after receiving the Spirit, says: "It became in my heart as a burning fire flaming in my bones, and I am vile and cannot bear it." In the Acts of the Apostles, also, when the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles and those others who were waiting for the Promise of the Father, we read that tongues as of fire were distributed among them. The soul of each one was so uplifted by His influence that they were supposed to be full of new wine, who instead had received the gift of a diversity of tongues.
20:9.s: On the Duties of the Clergy 3.18.102

20:9.t: Indeed, Christ, loving Moses, appeared to him in fire. And Jeremiah, having in himself the gift of divine love, said: "And there was a fire inflaming in my bones: and I was dissolved on every side, and I cannot bear it." Therefore, good charity having the wings of a burning fire, which flies through the chests and hearts of the saints, and consumes whatever is material and earthly: it tests whatever is sincere, and improves whatever it touches with its fire. This fire the Lord Jesus sent upon the earth, and faith shone forth, devotion was kindled, charity was illuminated, justice shone brightly. With this fire, he inflamed the hearts of his apostles, as Cleophas testifies, saying: Was not our heart burning within us, while he opened the Scriptures? Therefore, the flames of the Scriptures are divine. Indeed, the Scriptures were opening up, and the fire was coming forth, and it was penetrating the hearts of the listeners.

And thus with greater ardour she raises herself to the very bosom of the Father, wherein is the Only-Begotten Son of God Who declares the secrets of God, which in the time to come are to be revealed face to face. But even now He discloses them partly and in a figure to those whom He deems worthy, and at the same time sheds forth from the Spirit and from His own countenance floods of resplendent light, so that he who is illuminated thereby may say, "But it was as a fire blazing in my bones and I am melted on all sides, and cannot stay." And David says, "Let my sentence come forth from Thy presence!"

The interrogator. How is it that the service of hope is so delightful, and its labours so few and its work so easy to the soul?

The Father. This is because it excites the natural longing in the soul and gives them this cup to drink and makes them drunk. And from this moment they nevermore perceive fatigue but become apathetic against troubles. And during the whole of their course it is to them as if they were moving in the air without bodily motion, without seeing anything of the difficulty of the road or the streams and hills that are before them; but the crooked becomes to them straight and rough places plain, because they always see the bosom of their Father; and all those things which are far and invisible it makes to them clear in themselves, so that they gaze at them mysteriously with the hidden eye of faith. For all the parts of the soul become hot as by fire, on account of the expectation of those things which, though far, become as near; […]

20:10.t: "And it became in my heart as a burning fire, blazing in my bones, and I am utterly enfeebled and cannot bear it, because I heard the blame of many gathered round about." The blameless, the blessed Jeremiah (I speak with exception of this small sin and if he committed any other slight thing) was blamed by many. But the blame from the many was for him a commendation with God. For those who blamed him said, "Conspire, and let us all conspire against him, all the men his friends; watch his design, and he will be deceived." They wished to deceive him with another deception, a destructive one, opposite to the deception concerning which he said, "You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived." And these who conspire against him say, "And we shall prevail against him, and we shall take our vengeance upon him." Those convicted for their own sins think they have been wronged, and therefore, supposing they have been wronged, they say, "We shall take our vengeance upon him." […]
But many of the teachers in the Church even today endure similar things, hearing the reproach of many gathered round about against them and who say: Persecute, and let us persecute them!

All the men who were peaceable toward me and guarding my side: if somehow he may be deceived, and we may prevail against him and take our revenge on him! But the Lord is with me as a mighty warrior. When adversaries have risen up, and those who were once friends and peaceable have turned to war and have wished to lay snares for us, let us not be greatly concerned, but let us choose to say this, which the prophet too speaks: But the Lord is with me as a mighty warrior.

20:11.t: But Jeremiah says concerning these who conspire, "And the Lord is with me as a mighty warrior." If we become such as we ought to be, and receive that fire coming upon us for our sins, as upon Jeremiah and those like him, the Lord thereafter becomes with us "as a mighty warrior." And "therefore they persecuted and could not understand" [the Jews who persecuted him: "they were greatly ashamed and did not perceive their disgrace," being for so long a time disgraced they do not confess their own sins], because the Lord was with the persecuted one, and the persecuted one cannot come under their power. May it not then be, since many things of Jeremiah are referred to the Savior, that this too can be such? For "Conspire, and let us conspire against him" is said also concerning the Savior. And "the Lord" was with him "as a mighty warrior; therefore they persecuted and could not understand," the Jews who persecuted him; […]

Therefore those who persecute me shall fall and shall be weak — or therefore they persecuted and could not understand —, they shall be greatly confounded, because they did not understand the reproach or the everlasting ignominy, which will never be blotted out. Because they persecuted, therefore they could not understand the prophetic word, and vehement confusion followed upon their ignorance; nor did they understand the everlasting ignominy which will hold them fast and will be blotted out by no forgetting. Let them say, then, what they will, the men once peaceable and those who guarded my side, and let them desire to deceive, provided that so great a vindication and such great rewards attend the righteous man and teacher of the Church after persecution.

"They shall be greatly confounded, because they have not understood everlasting reproach." The second error concerns fatal necessity, as regarding the constellations: if a man is born under such a constellation, he will necessarily be a thief, or evil, or good. This empties free will and merit and reward of meaning: for if a man does of necessity what he does, what is the value of freedom of will? What will he merit? It also follows that God would be the origin of all evils. It is true that some disposition is left by the stars; but nevertheless God alone rules over the rational soul. Those who err thus shall have everlasting reproach.

20:12.t: For God does not hold out against his children when they beg his pity. And for you he will pray purely, held in high honor as an angel of God, and grieved not by you but for you. This is sincere repentance. "God is not mocked," nor does he give heed to vain words. For he alone searches the innermost recesses of the heart, and hears those that are in the fire, and listens to those who supplicate in the whale's belly and is near to all who believe, and far from the ungodly if they do not repent.
20:12.s: Who is the Rich Man that Shall Be Saved?

20:12.t: "The Lord," then, "of hosts" is with us, "who tests just things, understanding reins and hearts." The Lord tests just things and rejects unjust things, and he is, so to name it, a moneychanger of just and unjust things; and this Lord is also "one who understands reins and hearts." I inquire how "to understand reins and hearts" differs, and "to examine hearts and reins" is another thing. He does not examine the hearts and reins of all, but of those who have sinned; for I attend to the meaning of "examine," which is used in this life concerning those who are tortured. In the courts some examine, others are examined, and there are those also in the heaviest pains. But the Lord alone has a new manner of examinations, for he is one who examines hearts, and to the Lord alone belongs the examining of hearts and reins. […]

And you, Lord of hosts, tester of the righteous — or who test righteous things —, who see the reins and the heart, let me see, I pray, your vengeance on them! for to you I have revealed my cause. The Lord alone is the one who knows how to test righteousness, just as he alone is the one who beholds the inward parts of the heart; hence Jesus too, knowing the thoughts of men, is God not by advancement, as some think, but by nature. Something of the kind sounds in the Psalms as well: no one living shall be justified in your sight. If one who lives in virtues is not justified, how much more one who is dead in sins! And though the righteous man knows that he has God as his champion, yet through the impatience of human frailty he desires to see even now what he knows is to come. And he revealed his cause to him who says in another place: vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord. Happy, then, the conscience whose cause is revealed to the Lord, as the Apostle says: everything that is made manifest is light.

20:13.t: Sing to the Lord, praise the Lord, for he has delivered the soul of the poor man from the hand of the most wicked! He who is poor in spirit and has not the riches which have received their consolation in this world, and of which Paul speaks: only that we should be mindful of the poor, when he has obtained vengeance from the Lord, praises the Lord in spirit and glories that he has been rescued from the hand of the most wicked. Yet all this comes about not by our merit, but by the grace of him who delivered the poor man; and he has not the riches of a pride that falls to ruin, but the humility of a poor man set free.

20:14.t: For neither would so great and such a prophet — I mean Jeremiah, who was "sanctified in the womb" of his mother and "consecrated a prophet unto the nations" — have set down anything emptily in books that were to remain forever, unless it contained something secret and full of vast mysteries, when he says: "Cursed be the day in which I was born, and the night in which they said: Behold a male. Cursed be he that told my father, saying: A male is born to thee. Let that man be glad like the cities which the Lord overthrew in fury, and repented not." Does it seem to you that the prophet could have imprecated things so grave and so burdensome, unless he knew there was something in that bodily nativity which both seemed worthy of curses of this kind, and on account of which the lawgiver would arraign so many uncleannesses, upon which he would consequently impose fitting purifications?

How much dissatisfaction do we see that even the brief stages of our lives bring on us! The boy longs to be a young man. The young man counts the years when he will be older. The mature man, ungrateful for the blessing of being in the prime of life, eagerly desires the honor associated with old age. Thus, to all there comes naturally a desire for change, simply because we become dissatisfied with what we are now. Therefore, even the very things that we have wished for become wearisome to us on their enjoyment, and what we have desired to obtain we reject on its attainment. Consequently, holy people have not without reason lamented their prolonged sojourning here: David lamented it, Jeremiah lamented it, Elijah lamented it. If we can believe wise people, even those in whom the divine Spirit spoke were hastening to better things.

Cursed be the day on which I was born; the day on which my mother bore me, let it not be blessed! Cursed be the man — or the person —, who brought the news to my father, saying: A son, a male child, is born to you, and as it were made him glad with joy! Let that person be as the cities are which the Lord overthrew and did not repent! Let him hear a cry in the morning and wailing at the time of noon, who — or because he — did not kill me from the womb, so that my mother might become my grave, and her womb an everlasting conception! Why did I come forth from the womb, to see labor and sorrow, and that my days should be consumed in confusion? Those who think that souls were in the heavenly places and were cast down from a better state into a worse use this and testimonies of this kind, namely that it would have been better to dwell in the heavenly places than to dwell in the earthly ones and take on the body of humiliation, seeking certain new, nay rather already old, arguments for their heresy. […]

20:16.t: And as for his imprecating the likeness of the overthrown cities, I think it is said of Sodom and Gomorrah; and all time in mourning, so that in the morning there should be a cry and at noon wailing. And as for what he adds: who did not kill me in the womb, they think that God is meant. 'That there might be for me,' he says, 'an everlasting conception'; all of which is said hyperbolically. Finally he sets out the reasons why he prefers death to life, and not being at all to existing wretchedly, adding: why did I come forth from the womb, to see labor and sorrow, and that my days should be consumed in confusion?

21:1.t: The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur son of Malchiah, and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, the priest, saying: Inquire of the Lord for us, for Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is fighting against us; if perhaps the Lord will do for us according to all his wonders, and he will withdraw from us. Above, the high priest Phassur or Phaschor, who struck Jeremiah, had Immer as his father, but this Phassur is the son of Malchiah; this is said so that no one may think him the same man. Now King Zedekiah sends to the prophet without wishing either the people or the princes to know, so that by a secret message through envoys he may learn what sentence the Lord holds concerning the city of Jerusalem and the people of the Jews. And what he adds: for Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is fighting against us, shows that Zedekiah asks this of the prophet when Jerusalem was already besieged. […]

21:4.t: And Jeremiah said to them: Thus shall you say to Zedekiah: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I will turn back the vessels of war — or the weapons of war —, which are in your hands and with which you fight against the king of Babylon and the Chaldeans, who besiege you round about the walls, and I will gather those things — or those men — into the midst of this city, and I will vanquish you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm — or a lofty one — and in fury and in indignation and in great wrath, and I will strike the inhabitants of this city; men and beasts shall die of a great pestilence. 'In vain', he says, 'do you wish to resist the besieging Chaldeans and prepare weapons of war, of which you will have the use only in the midst of the city, so that you may seem to be armed. […]

21:7.t: And after this, says the Lord, I will give Zedekiah, king of Judah, and his servants and his people, and those who have been left in this city from the plague and the sword and the famine, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those who seek their life; and he shall strike them with the edge of the sword, and he shall not be moved, nor spare, nor have mercy. This, which we translated: into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies, is not found in the Seventy; and for what we said: he shall not be moved, nor spare, nor have mercy, the Seventy translated: I will not spare, nor have mercy. And it is better according to the Hebrew, so that the cruel and inflexible sentence may seem to belong to the Babylonian king rather than to the Lord. First, then, prophecy was made concerning the whole city; […]

21:8.t: There are two ways, one of life and one of death; but a great difference between the two ways. The way of life, then, is this: First, thou shalt love God who made thee; second, thy neighbour as thyself; and all things whatsoever thou wouldst should not occur to thee, thou also to another do not do. And of these sayings the teaching is this: Bless them that curse you, and pray for your enemies, and fast for them that persecute you. For what thank is there, if ye love them that love you? Do not also the Gentiles do the same? But do ye love them that hate you; and ye shall not have an enemy. Abstain thou from fleshly and worldly lusts. If one give thee a blow upon thy right cheek, turn to him the other also; and thou shalt be perfect. If one impress thee for one mile, go with him two. If one take away thy cloak, give him also thy coat. If one take from thee thine own, ask it not back for indeed thou art not able. Give to every one that asketh thee, and ask it not back; […]

And to this people you shall say: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death. He who dwells in this city shall die by the sword and by famine and by plague; but he who goes out and deserts to the Chaldeans, who besiege you, shall live, and his soul shall be to him as a spoil; for I have set my face against this city for evil and not for good, says the Lord; into the hand of the king of Babylon it shall be given, and he shall burn it with fire. To those who had been sent by the king and had come to beseech the prophet to inquire of the Lord for them, he had given the answer above, and what they should report to King Zedekiah; now he urges them to answer the people, and gives counsel that they desert to the Chaldeans against the royal will; and no one is unaware that this was dangerous for the prophet. Hence he even calls down death upon himself and says: cursed be the day on which I was born, and: why did I come forth from the womb, to see labor and sorrow?; […]

21:11.t: And to the house of the king of Judah: Hear the word of the Lord, house of David! Thus says the Lord: Judge judgment in the morning, and rescue the one oppressed by violence from the hand of the one falsely accusing, lest perhaps my indignation go forth — or so that my indignation may not go forth — like fire, and be kindled, and there be none to quench it; and what follows: because of the wickedness of your pursuits, is not found in the Seventy. Because he had said above: and to this people you shall say: thus says the Lord, he now accordingly adds: and to the house of the king of Judah, so that there is understood: 'you shall say: thus says the Lord'; for by apo koinou [in common, i.e. shared by both clauses] both what precedes and what follows are joined, so that the sense is: 'and to this people you shall say: thus says the Lord, and to the house of the king of Judah you shall say: thus says the Lord'.

21:12.t: Properly, however, the word is addressed to the royal house, chiefly on account of whose guilt the city is besieged, so that it may amend its error by repentance and obtain the mercy of the Lord. 'Judge', he says, 'judgment in the morning' — not in the darkness of iniquity, but in the light of righteousness — 'and rescue the one oppressed by violence from the hand of the false accuser, so that you do not respect persons in judgment, but, when the rich oppress the poor, the command of God may prevail more with you than the power of the persecutor! And if', he says, 'you do this, the fire of my fury will by no means be kindled among you, nor will it find material to consume.' And in this place an incredible mercy of God is shown: those of whom he had said above: for I have set my face against this city for evil and not for good; into the hand of the king of Babylon it shall be handed over, and fire shall burn it, he now, while the Lord's sentence is already bearing down upon them, calls to salvation; […]

21:13.t: Behold, I am against you, inhabitant of the solid and level valley, says the Lord, you who say: Who shall strike — or terrify — us, and who shall enter our houses? And I will visit upon you; and what follows: according to the fruit of your pursuits, says the Lord, is not found in the Seventy. And I will kindle, he says, a fire in its forest, and it shall devour everything round about it. For 'inhabitant of the solid and level valley' the Seventy translated: behold, I am against you who dwell in the level valley of Sor, for which Symmachus translated 'rock', Theodotion 'besieged', Aquila's first edition 'solid', the second 'Tyre'; for 'Sor' or 'Sur' in the Hebrew language means 'Tyre' and 'flint' and 'narrowed'. Now he speaks against Jerusalem, which was walled in by siege; or which, in the likeness of Tyre, is so surrounded by the Babylonian army, as by a great sea, that it cannot escape; […]

22:1.t: Thus says the Lord: Go down into the house of the king of Judah, and there you shall speak this word and say: Hear the word of the Lord, O king of Judah, who sit upon the royal seat of David, you and your servants and your people, who enter through these gates! Thus says the Lord: Do judgment and righteousness, and deliver him who is oppressed by force from the hand of the slanderer, and do not grieve the stranger and the orphan and the widow, nor oppress them unjustly — or impiously — and do not shed innocent blood in this place! For if you indeed do this word, there shall enter through the gates of this house kings of the race of David sitting upon his throne, and mounting chariots and horses, they and their servants and their people. But if you do not hear these words, by my own self I have sworn, says the Lord, that this house shall become a desolation. […]

22:3.t: Now it is the proper work of kings to do judgment and righteousness, and to deliver from the hand of slanderers those oppressed by force, and to give help to the stranger and the orphan and the widow, who are more easily oppressed by the powerful. And to instill in them a greater care for the precepts of God, he added: 'Do not grieve, so that you not only rescue them, but do not even allow them, through your connivance, to be grieved by others, and do not shed innocent blood in this place!' For to punish murderers and the sacrilegious and poisoners is not the shedding of blood, but the ministry of the laws.

Whatever was said to the royal house, let the bishops and their associates, the presbyters and deacons, and the whole ecclesiastical order understand: that if they do what has been commanded, and among other things do not shed innocent blood by causing even the least to stumble and by wounding the consciences of individuals, they will retain the dignity handed down to them by the Lord; but if they are unwilling to do it and despise it, they themselves will reduce the Church to desolation. Now those of the race of David enter through the gates of Jerusalem and sit upon the throne of him whose name means 'strong of hand', and they mount chariots and horses, when they rein in both their own disturbances and those of the people, and walk in the Church with composed step and with a choir of many virtues singing in harmony with them on every side. And that we may believe this to be true, he swears by himself, who, according to the Apostle, has no other greater by whom he could swear.

22:4.t: 'If', he says, 'you do these things, O kings of Judah, you will hold your former power and will enter the gates of Jerusalem with pomp; but if you are unwilling to do them, O royal house, it will be not so much the Lord's cruelty as your own will that the whole city is reduced to desolation.'

22:6.t: For thus says the Lord concerning the house — or to the house — of the king of Judah: You are Gilead to me, the head — or the beginning — of Lebanon; if I do not make you a desolation, cities uninhabitable. And I will sanctify against you a man who slays, and his weapons, and they shall cut down your choice cedars and hurl — or cast — into the fire. And many nations shall pass through this city, and each shall say to his neighbor: Why has the Lord done thus to this great city? And they shall answer: Because they forsook the covenant of the Lord their God and worshiped strange gods and served them. Scripture records that Gilead, which the half-tribe of Manasseh possessed, lies beyond the Jordan; on this mountain Laban overtook Jacob as he fled, and the mountain, according to Genesis, received the name sōros, that is, 'mound of witness', because Jacob and Laban swore there, after stones had been gathered into a heap. […]

He threatens, therefore, the royal house and the city of Jerusalem and the temple, which he calls the head of Lebanon, that it is to be reduced to desolation together with all its cities, not by the power of the Babylonian king but by the command of the Lord, who says: I will sanctify against you one who slays. And Nebuchadnezzar and all his army are called 'holy' because he carries out the sentence of God. 'And they shall cut down', he says, 'your choice cedars' — all the powerful men and princes of the city — 'and cast into the fire, so that the flame devouring all things may consume them.

22:7.t: Let the royal house of our city, too, hear this, and its princes and cedars, which lift their crown up to the clouds and say in their pride: 'Who will not see us?', that they will quickly be consumed by the flame of the Lord if they are unwilling to submit to his precepts. But the sanctification of the slayer and of his weapons is one thing, that of the priests and of those who minister to the Lord another.

22:8.t: And when everything has been destroyed, many nations will pass through the city and the temple, which before they were not permitted to enter, and each will say to his neighbor, why the Lord has wrought so sudden and so great an overthrow upon a city so renowned and great. And those who are asked', he says, 'will answer and set forth the causes of the ruins, saying: because they forsook the covenant of the Lord their God and venerated idols in place of God.'

22:10.t: Do not weep for the dead, nor mourn over him! Lament with weeping him who goes out, for he shall not return again, nor see the land of his birth! For thus says the Lord to Shallum son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned in place of Josiah his father, who went out from this place: He shall not return here any more, but in the place to which I have carried him away, there he shall die, and he shall not see this land any more. Josiah, a righteous king, had three sons, Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim and Zedekiah. The first of them Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, led captive into Egypt, and there he died; and he set up in his place as king his brother Eliakim, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. When he died, his son Jeconiah reigned, who was led into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, the Babylonian king, together with his mother and the princes; in his place his uncle Zedekiah reigned, who, when Jerusalem was taken, was led into Babylon. […]

22:13.t: But such a house as this sensual persons, they who dwell in cieled houses and delight in chased silver, do not build. For as they despise pure silver, so also they despise simple dwellings. They enlarge the site of their houses, they add more and more, joining house to house and farm to farm, they dig up the ground; so that the very earth itself gives way to their habitations, and like sons of the earth they are laid up within her womb, and hidden in her bowels. They surely are those of whom Jeremiah says, "Woe unto him that buildeth his house in unrighteousness." For he who builds in righteousness, builds not on earth but in heaven.

Woe to him who builds his house in unrighteousness and his upper rooms not in judgment, who oppresses his friend for nothing and does not pay him his wage; who says: I will build myself a broad house and spacious upper rooms, who opens windows for himself and makes ceilings of cedar and paints them with red ochre! Will you reign, since you compare yourself to the cedar? Did not your father eat and drink, and do judgment and righteousness then, when it was well with him? He judged the cause of the poor and needy to his own good; was it not therefore, because he knew me?, says the Lord. But your eyes and heart are for avarice, and for shedding innocent blood, and for slander, and for the course of evil work. LXX: O you who build your house not with righteousness and your upper rooms not in judgment! With him his neighbor works for nothing, and he will not pay him his wage. You have built yourself a little house, upper rooms open to the wind, set off with windows and raftered with cedar and daubed with red ochre. […]

We can, however, take this passage according to anagōgēn [the higher, spiritual sense] against the heretics, who build for themselves a house not great and most broad with the abundance of the Church, but a little one. And they build not with righteousness and judgment, desiring to plunder what belongs to others; whence it is said: You have built yourself a little house, upper rooms open to the wind, which are carried about by every wind of doctrine, and set off with windows; for they have no lasting building and no solid firmness. And raftered, he says, with cedar: they seem indeed to have the most beautiful rafters, but in the rains and the storm of persecutions they quickly rot and collapse. And daubed with red ochre: for they too promise the passion and the blood of the Lord, but they do not reign forever, because they contend with and provoke to anger 'araz', that is, 'cedar', their father. For every heretic is born in the Church, but is cast out of the Church, and contends and fights against his parent. […]

22:15.t: 'Will you', says the divine word, 'be able to reign forever, since you desire to compare yourself to the lofty cedar, that is, to your father Josiah, a righteous king? Your father', he says, 'both ate and drank and enjoyed royal wealth; and yet he did not offend God in this, that he had riches, but pleased him in this, that he did judgment and righteousness, and therefore it was well with him, and will be, both in the present age and in the one to come. He judged', he says, 'the cause of the poor and needy, and to the refreshment of those whom he heard, and properly to his own good. And all these things turned out prosperously for him because he knew me, says the Lord. But your eyes, O Jehoiakim, turn aside to avarice, and, so that you may shed innocent blood, to slander and to the course of evil work.' But what sense the words have according to the Seventy I cannot understand; […]

22:18.t: Therefore thus says the Lord to Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: They shall not lament for him: Woe, brother, and woe, sister! They shall not cry out together for him: Woe, lord, and woe, renowned one! But with the burial of an ass he shall be buried, rotted and cast out beyond the gates of Jerusalem. This, which we have set down from the Hebrew: They shall not lament for him: Woe, brother, and woe, sister, is not found in the Seventy. And it is said properly against Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and the riddle which before seemed hidden is opened, and the ambiguity among the three brothers is resolved, so that the word is not about Jehoahaz nor about Zedekiah, but properly about Jehoiakim, who, the Hebrew history relates, was killed by raiding bands of the Chaldeans, of Syria, of the Ammonites and of the Moabites; whence also in Malachim [Kings] it is written that he died, and his burial is passed over in silence. […]

22:20.t: Go up to Lebanon and cry out, and in Bashan give your voice, and cry to those passing by, for all your lovers are crushed! I spoke to you; in your abundance you said: I will not hear! This is your way from your youth, that you have not heard my voice. The wind shall feed all your shepherds — or lovers — and your lovers — or friends — shall go into captivity; and then you shall be confounded and shall blush for all your wickedness. You who sit in Lebanon and nest in the cedars, how you groaned when pains came upon you like the pains of a woman in labor! By metaphoran of Lebanon and Bashan, regions and mountains beyond the Jordan, the word is directed to Jerusalem, because she trusted in Egypt in vain; or to Jehoiakim himself, who at that time was reigning in Jerusalem and had been set up as king by the Egyptians, because he hopes in vain for the help of the Egyptians, and because they too are to be overcome by the Babylonian king and led into captivity.

And where we said: cry to those passing by, and in the Hebrew is written 'meabarim', the Seventy and Theodotion translated 'across the sea', Symmachus 'from opposite', to signify that the voice of the prophet must reach from Jerusalem as far as Mount Lebanon and Bashan.

22:21.t: And in saying: 'I spoke to you' — that is, God himself through the prophets — or: 'They spoke to you' — so that 'my prophets' is understood — 'and you in your abundance said: I will not hear', he convicts her of pride, and of having abused the greatness of her riches to despise God, and he relates that not only at this time but from the beginning, when she was led out of Egypt, she did not hear the voice of God; whence all her shepherds and princes too have been scattered hither and thither and have bowed their necks to the Babylonian captivity. And in adding: You who sit in Lebanon and nest in the cedars, he taunts her arrogance, which had grown out of the abundance of all things, and says that like a woman in childbirth sudden pain and an unexpected captivity will come upon her.

22:24.t: Wretched Grunnius, who opened his mouth to slander holy men and taught his tongue a lie, translated into Latin one book of Sextus the Pythagorean, a thoroughly pagan man, and divided it into two volumes, and dared to publish it under the name of the holy martyr Xystus, bishop of the city of Rome; in these volumes there is no mention of Christ, none of the Holy Spirit, none of God the Father, none of the patriarchs and prophets and apostles; and with his usual rashness and madness he named this book 'The Ring', and it is read through many provinces, and above all by those who preach apatheian [freedom from passion] and sinlessness. As, then, the Lord threatens that he will cast Jeconiah from his hand and finger like a ring, so I beseech the reader to throw away this wicked book, and, if he wishes, to read it as he reads the other books of the philosophers, not as a church volume.

In commentaries and expositions, whose custom it is to set down the differing opinions of interpreters, I am accustomed to insert language of this kind: 'Some say this, others assert that, certain ones think thus.' For this both wretched Grunnius himself and, many years later, the disciple of Jovinian and of him have slandered and still slander me, saying that I set down my own opinions under others' names, which I do for the sake of kindness, so as not to seem to tear anyone apart by name. Since, then, kindness has been turned into slander, I now say both to him who is dead and to this one who lives and tries to restore his heresy, that their master Origen refers this passage to Christ: that he was torn like a ring from the hand of God the Father and sent into the land of captivity, into the valley of tears, and handed over to the cross; and that his mother too — no doubt the synagogue — was taken and cast out. […]

As I live, says the Lord: though Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were a ring on my right hand, I will tear him — or you — from there, and I will give you into the hand of those who seek your life, and into the hand of those whose face you dread, and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, — which is not found in the Seventy — and into the hand of the Chaldeans. And I will send you — or I will cast you — and your mother who bore you into a strange land, in which you were not born, and there you shall die; but to the land to which they lift up their soul, to return, there they shall not return. He had said above: 'To the house of the king of Judah you shall speak these things', and then: Go down into the house of the king of Judah, and again: Thus says the Lord concerning the house of the king of Judah; and in reversed order, after he has spoken about Zedekiah, who was the last of the kings in Jerusalem, he returns to Jehoiakim his brother, who reigned before him. […]

22:28.t: As to Jeconias, whom the prophet Jeremiah declares in these words to have been rejected from the land of Judah, “Jeconias was dishonoured like a vessel for which there is no more use; and because he was cast out he and his seed; and none shall rise from his seed sitting upon the throne of David and ruling in Judah,” the matter is plain and clear. On the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, the kingdom had been destroyed, and there was no longer an hereditary succession of reigns as before. Nevertheless, at that time, the deposed descendants of David were living in captivity. On the return of Salathiel and Zerubbabel the supreme government rested to a greater degree with the people, and the sovereignty was afterwards transferred to the priesthood, on account of the intermingling of the priestly and royal tribes; whence the Lord, in things pertaining to God, is both King and High Priest. Moreover, the royal tribe did not fail until the coming of the Christ; […]

As for Ahab, it is clear enough, whose wife was Jezebel, and as for Jeconiah, Jeremiah is an amply sufficient witness that he was guilty of the greatest offence, and he even took from him the name that he had. And therefore he who in the books of Kings is called Joachim was named Jeconiah by Jeremiah, when he said: Jeconiah has been cast away like a vessel, there is no use in it, wherefore he has been cast out, he and his seed. Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord: write this man down as disowned, for there will not arise of his seed one sitting on the throne of David, a prince still in Judah. For while he was reigning the Babylonians laid Judaea waste, and never afterwards could anyone of his seed obtain the kingdom in Judaea; for afterwards the people, released from captivity, was under priests and tetrarchs. Hence tetrarchs remained right up to the generation of Christ, and not even they, as far as history teaches, kept the dignity of a royal line.

Is this man Coniah an earthen vessel, and broken? Is he a vessel without any pleasure — or usefulness —? Why are he and his seed cast away and cast forth into a land which they did not know? For what we said: Is he an earthen vessel, and broken, Symmachus translated: Is he refuse or worthless sweepings, and cast away?; in place of which there is nothing in the Seventy, but they translated only this: Jeconiah has been dishonored like a vessel in which there is no usefulness. And when this is said of Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, does anyone dare to refer it to the type of Christ, and, from the fact that the Apostle says that the Lord Savior is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, that is, wisdom, word, truth, life and righteousness, to say that he is called the ring which is cast off or torn away from the hand of the Lord and handed over to King Nebuchadnezzar? […]

22:29.t: Someone who is in a state of ignorance is sinful and considered "earth and ashes." Someone who is in a state of knowledge, being assimilated as far as possible to God, is already spiritual and thus is considered elect. Scripture calls the senseless and disobedient by the term "dirt," which is clear from what Jeremiah the prophet says in reference to Joachim and his brothers: "Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord. Inscribe this man as an outcast."

22:30.t: Land, land, land, hear the speech of the Lord! Thus says the Lord: Write this man barren, a man who shall not prosper in his days; for there shall not be of his seed a man who sits upon the royal seat of David and has power any longer in Judah. If I should wish to note, place by place, how much the Seventy have either passed over or changed, it would become long, especially since the diligent reader can consider from each edition what has been changed, what added, what taken away. For 'barren' in the Hebrew is written 'ariri', which Aquila's first edition translated 'barren', the second anauxēton, that is, 'not growing', Symmachus 'empty', the Seventy and Theodotion 'abominable' and 'disowned'. […]

23:1.t: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and tear the flock of my pasture — or O shepherds, who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture —, says the Lord. Therefore thus says the Lord, the God of Israel, to the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, you have driven them out and have not visited them; behold, I will visit upon you the wickedness of your pursuits, says the Lord. And I will gather the remnant of my flock from all the lands to which I shall have driven them out there, and I will bring them back to their fields — or I will restore them to their pastures — and they shall grow and be multiplied. And I will raise up shepherds over them and they shall feed them; they shall fear no more and shall not be dismayed, and none shall be sought from the number, says the Lord. The prophetic discourse is addressed to the shepherds, or concerns the shepherds; […]

23:5.t:
[Passages quoted, Jer. xxiii. 6-8, xxx. 8, 9.]

Jeremiah prophesies thus long after the death of David and even the time of Solomon concerning a king who is to arise from the seed of David, whom he first calls "the rising," not simply but with the adjective "just," as though he were to shine forth from the sun of righteousness, of whom I treated in my evidences about the Second Cause, where I shewed that the pre-existent Word of God besides many other names was called Sun of Righteousness, quoting the prophecy which said, "To them that fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise." Therefore the prophecy in the present passage is that God will raise up "a righteous rising" to David, in the sense of a sun of righteousness. And he calls the same Being an understanding king, and one who does judgment and justice on the earth. He gives him too the same name as David, who died very long before. […]
23:5.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 7, Chapter 3

23:5.t: Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch — or a righteous Rising — and a king shall reign and shall be wise — or shall understand — and shall do judgment and righteousness in the land. In those days Judah shall be saved and Israel shall dwell confidently, and this is the name by which they shall call him — or he shall call him — : the Lord our righteous one or our righteousness, which in Hebrew is said 'sadecenu'. This, which has been wrongly added in the Seventy: in the prophets, must be cut away entirely; for another chapter follows, which has been passed over by them, and when it is finished the title is: to the prophets or against the prophets, of which we shall speak in its own place. […]

23:6.t:
And Judah and Israel were to be saved in His days, that is to say all the Jews who through Him reached holiness, His apostles, disciples and evangelists, or perhaps all who represent the Jew mystically understood and the true Israel which sees God spiritually.

"For he is not a Jew," the apostle says, "that is one outwardly, nor circumcision the outward circumcision in the flesh, but he is a Jew which is one in secret, and circumcision is of the heart in the spirit not the letter, whose praise is not of men, but of God."

It is these, then, the secret Jew and the true Israel, that he says are through Christ's calling to be named by a new name, neither Jew nor Israel, but one quite different from these. For He says that the Lord will call them by the name of Josedekeim, which means, "The Lord's just ones."

And I ask you to consider whether this name Josedekeim, by which the disciples of Jesus are called by God, be not formed from Joshua; they would thus be named by men from the name of Christ which is Greek (i. e. […]
23:6.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 7, Chapter 3

23:7.t: Now I have shown a short time ago that the church is the seed of Abraham; and for this reason, that we may know that He who in the New Testament "raises up from the stones children unto Abraham," is He who will gather, according to the Old Testament, those that shall be saved from all the nations, Jeremiah says: "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that they shall no more say, The Lord liveth, who led the children of Israel from the north, and from every region whither they had been driven; He will restore them to their own land which He gave to their fathers."

Therefore, behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and they shall no longer say: The Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt, but: The Lord lives, who brought out and brought back the seed of the house of Israel from the land of the north and from all the lands to which I had driven them out there, and they shall dwell in their own land. This whole chapter is not found in the Seventy; and its sense is this: that the people of God is no longer to be freed from Egypt through Moses, but through Jesus Christ from the whole circle of the earth, into which it had been scattered. This is fulfilled in part even now in the world, and will be fulfilled wholly when from the east and the west, the north and the south they shall come and recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so that, after the fullness of the nations has come in, then all Israel may be saved.

23:9.t: To the prophets or in the prophets or against the prophets. This title, as we said above, has been placed in the edition of the Seventy as the end of the preceding chapter, where we read it written: and this is the name which the Lord shall call him, Iosedec, in the prophets. Not knowing this, very many invent various ravings of explanation; and it would have been much better simply to confess ignorance than to make others heirs of their own unskilfulness. The discourse, moreover, is against the prophets, nay rather the false prophets of Jerusalem and Samaria, whom he now calls by the common and popular name 'prophets', of whom it is written in what follows: and in the prophets of Samaria I saw iniquity and immediately: and in the prophets of Jerusalem I saw horrible things. But when he puts the conjunction 'and', he shows that the things above were said of the prophets of the Lord, who themselves too proved like the false prophets.

My heart is broken in the midst of me — or in me —, all my bones have trembled — or have been shaken —; I have become like a drunken man and like a man soaked — or overcome — with wine before the face of the Lord and before the face of his holy words or and before the face of the comeliness of his glory.
