Having considered the countenance of almighty God, that is, of the Father, and having considered the countenance of the Son, who according to the Apostle is called the 'radiance of his glory' and the 'form of the substance of God', the prophet shudders in both mind and body and understands that he is nothing, according to what is said in another place too: I have become like a beast of burden before you; or else he offers to God the victim of his conscience and humility, according to that which is written in the psalms: a sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise. […]

23:10.t: Because the land is filled with adulterers, because before the face of cursing — or of the oath — the land has mourned, the fields — or pastures — of the desert have dried up; their course has become evil and their strength unlike. This, which we have set down from the Hebrew: because the land is filled with adulterers, is not found in the Seventy, who said 'oath' for 'cursing'. And he gives the causes: that because of adulteries and curses, or superfluous swearing, nay rather perjuries, barrenness of the crops followed. Whatever you understand of the land of Judea according to the letter, refer to the congregation of believers, since because of adulteries and lies or perjuries there is in the churches a barrenness of the virtues and gifts of God.

23:11.t: For prophet and priest are polluted, and in my house I have found their evil, says the Lord. Therefore their way shall be like a slippery place in darkness; they shall be driven on and shall fall in it, for I will bring — or I will inflict — evils upon them, the year of their visitation, says the Lord. When evils are found in the Church of God, and especially in its princes, let us know that this has been fulfilled: prophet and priest are polluted; in my house I have found their evils, says the Lord. Now the house of Christ is the Church, of which Paul too writes to Timothy: that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. In the prophet understand the teacher, in the priest the dignity of the ministry; […]

23:12.t: Wherefore, as children of light and truth, avoid the dividing of your unity, and the wicked doctrine of the heretics, from whom "a defiling influence has gone forth into all the earth." But where the shepherd is, there do ye as sheep follow. For there are many wolves in sheep's clothing, who, by means of a pernicious pleasure, carry captive those that are running towards God; but in your unity they shall have no place.
23:12.s: Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians

23:13.t: And in the prophets of Samaria I saw folly — or iniquity —; they prophesied in Baal and deceived my people Israel. I think that by the prophets of Samaria, according to the mystical senses, the heretics are properly meant, and all who boast of a knowledge falsely so named. And as the prophets of Samaria, whatever they spoke, prophesied in Baal, namely an idol consecrated to demons, so the heretics, whatever they speak inside the Church or outside the Church, speak in demons, in order to trip up the people 'Israhel', which formerly 'saw God'; whence too he says significantly: and in the prophets of Samaria I saw folly; for they do not have him of whom it is said: 'Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God'.

23:14.t: And in the prophets of Jerusalem I saw a likeness — or horrible things —, adultery and the path of falsehood; and they strengthened the hands of the most wicked, so that no one turned back from his wickedness — or from his most wicked way —; they have all become to me as Sodom, and its inhabitants as Gomorrah. 'Not only', he says, 'have these things been found in the conventicles of the heretics, but in the prophets of Jerusalem too, that is, in the teachers of the Church, I have seen like things, or horrible things: men adulterating the word of God and walking along the way of falsehood, so that they acquiesced in the deceits of the heretics and strengthened the hands of the most wicked and joined their evils to their own crimes, and led to destruction those whom they ought to have corrected. Let those who have done this not think themselves unpunished! For both they themselves and those whom they favor will be as Sodom, and all who dwell with them and do not withdraw from such men, as Gomorrah'. […]

23:15.t: Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts to the prophets: Behold, I will feed them with wormwood — or with pains, and according to Symmachus with bitterness — and I will give them gall to drink — or bitter water —, for from the prophets of Jerusalem pollution has gone forth into all the land. Let us use this testimony against those who send out into the world letters full of lies and fraud and perjury, so as both to pollute the ears of the hearers and to injure the reputation of the simple: that what is written is fulfilled in them: from the prophets of Jerusalem pollution has gone forth into all the land; for it is not enough for them to devour their own iniquity and to injure their neighbors, but those whom they have once hated they try to defame throughout the whole world, and to sow blasphemies everywhere.

23:16.t: The Lord cries out and says, "Do not listen to the words of the prophets who invent a vain vision for themselves, which they speak as false prophets from their own heart and not from the mouth of the Lord. They say to them that reject the words of the Lord, "Peace shall be yours." They who themselves have neither peace nor the church are now offering peace; they who have withdrawn from the church are permitting the bringing back and recalling of the lapsed. God is one, and Christ, one, and the church, one, and the chair established on Peter by the voice of the Lord, one. Another altar cannot be set up or a new priesthood be made contrary to the one altar and the one priesthood.

Against such people as these the Lord cries out, from these he reins in and recalls his erring people, saying, "Do not listen to the words of the prophets who invent a vain vision for themselves, which they speak as false prophets from their own heart and not from the mouth of the Lord. They say to those who reject the words of the Lord, 'Peace shall be yours' and to all who walk according to their own desires, to everyone who walks in the error of his heart, they have said, 'No evil shall come on you.' "
23:16.s: Treatise I. On the Unity of the Church 11

23:16.t: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you and deceive you! They speak the vision of their own heart and not from the mouth of the Lord. They say to those who blaspheme me — or cast away my word — : The Lord has spoken: peace shall be to you; and to everyone who walks in the perversity of his heart they have said: Evils shall not come upon you. Lest the people should think itself free of guilt if it acquiesced in perverse teachers, 'Do not', he says, 'listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you a lie and deceive you', — for the punishment will be equal for master and disciple — 'they do not speak from the mouth of the Lord, but the things they have feigned in their own heart. They say to those who blaspheme me' — namely to heretics and perverse men — 'or who cast away my speech, what do they say?: The Lord has spoken: peace shall be to you; do not fear harsh punishments nor be terrified by empty threats; […]

23:18.t: What would you say of Isaiah or Ezekiel, who was an eyewitness of very great mysteries, and of the other Prophets; for one of these saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting on the Throne of glory, and encircled and praised and hidden by the sixwinged Seraphim, and was himself purged by the live coal, and equipped for his prophetic office. And the other describes the Cherubic Chariot of God, and the Throne upon them, and the Firmament over it, and Him that shewed Himself in the Firmament, and Voices, and Forces, and Deeds. And whether this was an appearance by day, only visible to Saints, or an unerring vision of the night, or an impression on the mind holding converse with the future as if it were the present; or some other ineffable form of prophecy, I cannot say; the God of the Prophets knoweth, and they know who are thus inspired. But neither these of whom I am speaking, nor any of their fellows ever stood before the Council and Essence of God, as it is written, or saw, or proclaimed the Nature of God.

For who has been present in the counsel of the Lord and seen and heard his speech? who has considered his word and heard? Where we translated 'in the counsel of the Lord' and in the Hebrew is written 'bassod', Aquila translated 'secret', Symmachus 'speech', the Seventy and Theodotion 'substance' or 'subsistence'. And the sense is: 'Do not believe, O untaught crowd, the prophets who announce false things to you, who say this: The Lord has spoken: peace shall be to you; evil shall not come upon you! For whence can they know the secrets of God, or at whose announcing have they learned the counsel of the Lord? How has the word of the divine dispensation reached them?' Some of our own think that in this place they have found where the substance of God is written of.

23:19.t: Behold, the whirlwind — or tempest and commotion — of the Lord's indignation goes forth, and a tempest bursting forth shall come upon the head of the ungodly, and the fury of the Lord shall not turn back until he does and until he fulfills the thought of his heart; in the last days you shall understand his counsel. He who had said above: 'It has been spoken to us by the Lord: peace shall be to you', and had rebuked them because they could not know the things to come nor know the sentence of God, now shows by contraries that they know nothing at all: for instead of peace and security a Babylonian tempest is coming, and coming not upon just anyone, but upon the heads of the ungodly, whether of the whole people or of those who announced false things to the people. Nor is the wrath and fury of God to be appeased as in times past, but what he foretold and very often threatened is to be fulfilled in deed, and his thought and sentence are to be proved by the punishments of the ungodly. […]

23:21.t: I did not send the prophets, and they ran; I did not speak to them, and they prophesied. If they had stood in my counsel and made my words known to my people, I would surely have turned them from their evil way and from their most wicked thoughts. This sense the Apostle too unfolds to the Romans: and as they did not see fit to have God in knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate sense, so that they do the things that are not fitting, filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication, wickedness, avarice and the rest. For when false teachers have once handed themselves over to lies and perjuries and to the deaths of those they have deceived, they run, not step by step nor with considered pace, but headlong, to the destruction both of themselves and of those whom they have deceived. […]

23:22.t: This enables us to see, brethren, that they of Nicaea breathe the spirit of Scripture, in that God says in Exodus, `I am that I am,' and through Jeremiah, `Who is in His substance and hath seen His word;' and just below, `if they had stood in My subsistence and heard My words:' now subsistence is essence, and means nothing else but very being, which Jeremiah calls existence, in the words, `and they heard not the voice of existence.' For subsistence, and essence, is existence: for it is, or in other words exists.
23:22.s: LETTER TO THE BISHOPS OF AFRICA 4

23:23.t: Jeremiah the prophet, gifted with consummate wisdom, or rather the Holy Spirit in Jeremiah, exhibits God. "Am I a God at hand," he says, "and not a God afar off? Shall a man do ought in secret, and I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth? Saith the Lord." For "the Lord who created the earth by His power," as Jeremiah says, "has raised up the world by His wisdom;" for wisdom, which is His word, raises us up to the truth, who have fallen prostrate before idols, and is itself the first resurrection from our fall.

so also our mind, the more loftily and highly it approaches Christ and presents itself nearer to the splendor of his light, so much the more magnificently and clearly will it be irradiated by his light, as he himself also says through the prophet: "Draw near to me, and I will draw near to you, says the Lord." And again he says: "I am a God drawing near, and not a God from afar."

He has been more obedient to human authority than to God. It matters not whether he has published what he has done with less either of disgrace or of guilt among people. Be that as it may, he will not be able to escape and avoid God his judge, seeing that the Holy Spirit says in the Psalms, "Your eyes did see my substance, that it was imperfect, and in your book shall all people be written." And again, "People see the outward appearance, but God sees the heart." The Lord also forewarns and prepares us, saying, "And all churches shall know that I am he who searches the reins and heart." He looks into the hidden and secret things and considers those things that are concealed; nor can anyone evade the eyes of the Lord, who says, "I am a God near at hand and not a God afar off. If a person shall be hidden in secret places, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?" He sees the heart and mind of every person, and he will not judge our deeds alone, but even our words and thoughts. […]

We ought therefore to fulfil every act as happening beneath the eyes of the Lord, and every thought as presided over by Him, remembering the voice of Him Who said: “Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the Lord”; and: “I am a God at hand, and not a God far off”; and: “Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” For thus fear will continue steadily, hating iniquity, as it is written, and insolence and arrogance and the ways of evil men, and love will be perfected, fulfilling the Lord’s words: “I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father that sent me,” since the soul is steadily convinced that good deeds are acceptable with the Judge and Umpire of our life, while their opposites receive condemnation from the same source.

For were He distant from us in place, thou mightest well doubt, but if He is present everywhere, to him that strives and is in earnest He is near. Wherefore also the prophet said, "I will fear no evil, for Thou art with me;" and God Himself again, "I am a God nigh at hand, and not a God afar off." Then as our sins separate us from Him, so do our righteousnesses draw us nigh unto Him. "For while thou art yet speaking," it is said, "I will say, Here I am." What father would ever be thus obedient to his offspring? What mother is there, so ready, and continually standing, if haply her children call her? There is not one, no father, no mother: but God stands continually waiting, if any of his servants should perchance call Him; and never, when we have called as we ought, hath He refused to hear. Therefore He saith, "While thou art yet speaking," I do not wait for thee to finish, and I straightway hearken.
23:23.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 54:8

23:23.t: He was fully conscious of his own wound and the power of him from whom nothing can be hidden, who says through the prophet, "I am a God near at hand and not a God afar off." For nobody can escape the notice of him who fills heaven and earth, and nobody can conceal from him the secrets of his heart.

Am I a God from near at hand, says the Lord, and not a God from afar? If a man is hidden in secret places, shall I not see him?, says the Lord; do I not fill heaven and earth?, says the Lord. LXX: I am a God drawing near, says the Lord, and not a God from afar. If a man shall hide in secret places, shall I not see him?, says the Lord; do I not fill heaven and earth?, says the Lord. Aquila and Symmachus translated similarly: Am I a God from near — or nearby — and not a God from afar? But the Seventy and Theodotion translated in a contrary sense, so as to say: I am a God drawing near, says the Lord, and not a God from afar: namely, the former assert that God knows not only things nearby but also those which are far off, and sees not only present things but future ones; while these think that God is present everywhere and that there is no place where God is not present. For God draws near to all, and especially to the saints, as a garment clings to the skin; but sinners, withdrawing far from him, will perish. […]

23:24.t: "I have known all that is hidden and all that is open to view. I was a pupil of Wisdom, who formed them all." There, in brief, you have the profession of our philosophy. The process of learning about these, if practiced under good supervision, leads upward via Wisdom, who formed the whole universe, to the ruler of the universe, a being hard to catch, hard to track down, who always distances himself in retreat from his pursuer. But this same ruler, distant as he is, has—truth be told!—drawn near. "I am God who is near at hand, declares the Lord." In his essential being he is distant—how could a creature subject to birth ever draw near to the unborn and the uncreated?—but very close by the exercise of that power that had enfolded all things in its embrace. It is written, "Can anyone act in secret without my seeing him?" Yes, the power of God is always present, touching us with a power that sees, is good and instructs.

But let our speech and petition when we pray be under discipline, observing quietness and modesty. Let us consider that we are standing in God's sight. We must please the divine eyes in our bodily manner and with appropriate restraint of voice. For as it is characteristic of a shameless person to be noisy with his cries, so it is fitting for the modest to pray with moderated petitions. Moreover, in his teaching the Lord has bidden us to pray in secret—in hidden and remote places, in our very bedchambers—which is best suited to faith, that we may know that God is everywhere present, hears and sees all and in the plenitude of his majesty penetrates even into hidden and secret places, as it is written, "I am a God at hand, and not a God afar off. If a person shall hide himself in secret places, shall I not then see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?"
23:24.s: Treatise IV. On the Lord's Prayer 4

23:24.t: And how shall we preserve the truth that God pervades all things and fills all, as it is written "Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the Lord," and "The Spirit of the Lord filleth the world," if God partly contains and partly is contained? For either He will occupy an empty Universe, and so all things will have vanished for us, with this result, that we shall have insulted God by making Him a body, and by robbing Him of all things which He has made; or else He will be a body contained in other bodies, which is impossible; or He will be enfolded in them, or contrasted with them, as liquids are mixed, and one divides and is divided by another;—a view which is more absurd and anile than even the atoms of Epicurus and so this argument concerning the body will fall through, and have no body and no solid basis at all.

But of what creature can it be said that it fills all things, as is written of the Holy Spirit: "I will pour My Spirit upon all flesh." This cannot be said of an Angel. Lastly, Gabriel himself, when sent to Mary, said: "Hail, full of grace," plainly declaring the grace of the Spirit which was in her, because the Holy Spirit had come upon her, and she was about to have her womb full of grace with the heavenly Word. For it is of the Lord to fill all things, Who says: "I fill heaven and earth." If, then, it is the Lord Who fills heaven and earth, Who can judge the Holy Spirit to be without a share in the dominion and divine power, seeing that He has filled the world, and what is beyond the whole world, filled Jesus the Redeemer of the whole world? For it is written: "But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, departed from Jordan," Who, then, except one who possessed the same fulness could fill Him Who fills all things?

Wherefore, if we sensibly hold to those things which be worthy of the Son of God, we ought to understand Him to have been sent in such a way that the Word of God, out of the incomprehensible and ineffable mystery of the depths of His majesty, gave Himself for comprehension to our minds, so far as we could lay hold of Him, not only when He "emptied" Himself, but also when He dwelt in us, as it is written: "I will dwell in them." Elsewhere also it stands that God said: "Go to, let us go down and confound their language." God, indeed, never descends from any place; for He says: "I fill heaven and earth." But He seems to descend when the Word of God enters our hearts, as the prophet has said: "Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make His paths straight." We are to do this, so that, as He Himself promised, He may come together with the Father and make His abode with us. It is clear, then, how He comes.

For, if we may presume to speak of ourselves after His image and likeness, as Scripture says, in the same way as He is established in the fulness of His Majesty, and sees all things, heaven, air, earth and sea, embracing the universe and penetrating each part, so that nothing escapes Him, and there is nothing which does not consist in Him and depend on Him, and which is not full of Him, as He Himself says, "I fill heaven and earth, saith the Lord," so likewise the mind of man sees all things and is not seen, but maintains its own essence invisible.

How shall I call on my God—my God and my lord? For when I call on him, I ask him to come into me. And what place is there in me into which my God can come—into which God can come, even he who made heaven and earth? Is there anything in me, O Lord my God, that can contain you? Do indeed the heaven and the earth that you have made and in which you have placed me, contain you? Or, since nothing could exist without you, does whatever exists contain you? Why, then, do I ask you to come into me, since I indeed exist and could not exist if you were not in me? Because I am not yet in hell, though you are even there. For "if I go down into hell, you are there." I could not exist, O my God, I could not exist at all, unless you were in me. Or should I not rather say that I could not exist unless I were in you, "from whom, through whom and in whom are all things?" It is even so, O Lord, even so. Where do I ask you to be, since I am in you? Or, from where can you come into me? […]

A person's conscience accuses itself if he doesn't love someone who loves him, or love in return someone who loves him, expecting nothing from that person but indications of his love. So he mourns if someone dies, experiences the gloom of sorrow, that saturating of the heart in tears. All sweetness turns into bitterness on the loss of the life of the dying, the death of the living. Blessed is the one who loves you and has his friend in you.… For he alone loses none dear to him. All are dear to him who cannot be lost. And who is this but our God, the God who created heaven and earth and fills them, because by filling them he created them? No one loses you but the one who leaves you.

It was by this same divine creative force, which knows not what it is to be made but only how to make, that roundness was given to the eye, to the apple and to other objects that are by nature round and that we see all about, taking on their form with no extrinsic cause but by the intrinsic power of the Creator, who said, "Do I not fill heaven and earth?" and whose wisdom "reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly."

The question still remains whether they will see God with their eyes open and by means of these bodily eyes. For, of course, if spiritual eyes in a spiritual body can see no better than our present eyes can see, then it will certainly be impossible for even spiritual eyes to behold God. If the spiritual realm, without material form, circumscribed by no place but everywhere wholly present, is to be visible to the eyes of a spiritual body, then those eyes will most certainly have to have a power altogether unlike the power of any eyes on earth. It is true that we say that God is in heaven and on earth, and he himself through a prophet says, "I fill heaven and earth." But this does not mean that in heaven we shall say that God has one part there and another part on earth. For he is entirely in heaven, and he is entirely on earth. He is in both simultaneously, not merely successively—which is utterly impossible in the case of any material substance.

Elsewhere also we read in the words of the prophet: "Do I not fill heaven and earth!" And he himself tells us why he fills all things: "Because I am with you to save you." Obviously then God shows us not merely his rule and the fulness of his power but also the might and benefits that result from its plenitude. For the fulness of divinity bears within it this fruit, that it saves all things that it fills.
23:24.s: On the Government of God, Book 2, Chapter 2

23:24.t:
It is plain, then, that there is a God. But what He is in His essence and nature is absolutely incomprehensible and unknowable. For it is evident that He is incorporeal. For how could that possess body which is infinite, and boundless, and formless, and intangible and invisible, in short, simple and not compound? How could that be immutable which is circumscribed and subject to passion? And how could that be passionless which is composed of elements and is resolved again into them? For combination is the beginning of conflict, and conflict of separation, and separation of dissolution, and dissolution is altogether foreign to God.

Again, how will it also be maintained that God permeates and fills the universe? as the Scriptures say, Do not I fill heaven and earth, saith the Lord? For it is an impossibility that one body should permeate other bodies without dividing and being divided, and without being enveloped and contrasted, in the same way as all fluids mix and commingle.
23:24.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 1, Chapter 4

23:25.t: I have heard what the prophets said who prophesy a lie in my name and say: I have dreamed, I have dreamed — or I have seen a dream —. How long is this in the heart of the prophets who prophesy a lie and prophesy the seductions — or the wishes — of their own heart? Who wish — or think — to make my people forget my name because of their dreams, which each one tells to his neighbor, as their fathers forgot my name because of Baal or in Baal. Since the preceding title is against the prophets or to the prophets, whom we clearly understand to be false prophets — and there are many kinds of prophesying, one of which is by dreams, such as was in Daniel —, therefore the prophetic discourse is directed also at those who believe in dreams and think that all they see is divine revelation, which is properly opened to the saints and servants of God. […]

23:28.t: Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream, and let him who has my word speak my word truly! what has chaff to do with wheat?, says the Lord; are not my words like fire, says the Lord, and like a hammer — or an axe — breaking the rock? It belongs to those to expound a dream who merit to have the word of God and to say: 'thus says the Lord', to whom the Lord has spoken, in whom there is truth and not fraudulent falsehood. What has the chaff of the heretics to do with the wheat of the Church? Of this John the Baptist speaks more fully: that Christ will purge his threshing floor and with the winnowing fan leave the chaff to be scattered by the blasts of the winds and burned with fire, but will store the wheat in the barns, that it may become heavenly bread and each of the believers may say: taste and see that the Lord is sweet! And beautifully is perverse doctrine compared to chaff, which has no marrow and cannot nourish the peoples of believers, but is threshed out of empty stalks.

23:29.t: And because the heretics are always wont to promise prosperity and to open the kingdoms of heaven to sinners, so as to say: 'The kingdoms of heaven are prepared for you; you can imitate the majesty of God, so as to be without sin; for you have received the power of free will and the knowledge of the law, through which you may attain what you will', and they deceive the wretched with blandishments, and especially silly women laden with sins, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine, always learning and never coming to the knowledge of the truth, and they deceive all their hearers with adulation, therefore the Lord, comparing his own words with the chaff of the heretics, says: 'are not my words like fire, says the Lord, and like a hammer breaking the rock? […]

23:30.t: Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, says the Lord, who steal my words each one from his neighbor; behold, I am against the prophets, says the Lord, who take up their tongues and say: He says — or they slumber a slumber — ; behold, I am against the prophets who dream a lie, says the Lord, who tell them and seduce my people in their lies and in their wonders — or astonishments and terrors — of their own, when I had not sent them nor commanded them, who have been of no profit to this people, says the Lord. Falsehood always imitates truth, and unless it has some likeness of what is right, it cannot deceive the innocent. […]

23:33.t: If therefore this people or a prophet or a priest asks you, saying: What is the burden of the Lord — or what is the taking up of the Lord — ?, you shall say to them: You are the burden — or the taking up — ; for I will cast you away — or I will dash you down, — says the Lord. And the prophet and the priest and the people who says: The burden — or the taking up — of the Lord, I will visit — or I will avenge — upon that man and upon his house. These things you shall say each one to his friend and to his brother: What has the Lord answered and what has the Lord spoken? and the burden — or the taking up — of the Lord shall be remembered no more, for the burden — or the taking up — shall be to each one his own word. The Hebrew word 'massa' Aquila translates arma, that is, 'burden' and 'weight'; Symmachus, the Seventy and Theodotion 'taking up'. Wherever, then, what the Lord threatens is heavy and full of weight and toil and unbearable, in the title too it is called arma, that is, 'weight'; […]

23:36.t: And you pervert the words of the living God, the Lord of hosts, our God. Thus shalt thou say — or shall you say — to the prophet: What has the Lord answered you and what has the Lord spoken? But if you say: The burden of the Lord — up to here it is not found in the Seventy; and there follows: because of this, thus says the Lord: Because you have said this word: The burden — or the taking up — of the Lord, and I sent to you saying: Do not say the burden — or the taking up — of the Lord, therefore, behold, I will lift — or I will take up — you, carrying you, and I will forsake you and the city which I gave to you and to your fathers, from before my face, and I will give you over to everlasting reproach and eternal ignominy, which shall never be blotted out by oblivion. The Lord commanded that the word of 'burden' and 'weight' and 'taking up' should by no means be spoken among the people, but that of 'answer' and 'word of God'. […]

24:1.t: The fifth book of the commentaries on Jeremiah, brother Eusebius, will take its beginning from two baskets, of which the one will show the sweetness of the right faith, the other the bitterness of the faithlessness of the heretics. Although Hananiah son of Azzur resists Jeremiah, and Shemaiah the Nehelamite desires that the prophet be sent into prison, and Zephaniah the priest swears himself to the words of the false prophets, yet truth can be shut up and bound, but it cannot be conquered; it is content with the fewness of its own and is not terrified by the multitude of its enemies. Therefore raise your hands to heaven with Moses and hang up the ancient serpent in the desert, and at once Amalek will be destroyed and the poisoned bites will not prevail, and the people of the Lord, secure, will cross the streams of the Jordan with Jesus [Joshua], and after the vast wilderness will eat the bread that was born in our little village of Bethlehem.

The Lord showed me, and behold, two baskets — or, according to Symmachus, hampers — full of figs, placed before the temple of the Lord, after Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had carried away Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and his princes and the smith and the setter from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon. One basket had very good figs, as figs of the first season usually are, and one basket had very bad figs, which could not be eaten because they were bad. And the Lord said to me: What do you see, Jeremiah? And I said: Figs, good ones, very good, and bad ones, very bad, which cannot be eaten because they are bad. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: As these figs are good, so will I know the exile of Judah, which I have sent out from this place into the land of the Chaldeans, for good. […]

It must also be noted that this vision came to the prophet in the times of Zedekiah, after Jeconiah had been led into 'exile'; for he did not say 'captivity', because Jeconiah had handed himself over of his own accord. And by the smiths and setters we ought to understand either interpreters and teachers of the law, or craftsmen and enclosers of gold and gems, an art that is most precious among the barbarian nations. For 'setters' the Seventy translated 'bound men', to signify the evil of captivity, and of their own they added 'rich men', which is not found in the Hebrew. And he compares the basket that had good figs, and very good ones, to the figs of the first season — which in Greek are called proima —, namely to Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and Moses and Aaron and Job and the other holy men, of whom one of the twelve prophets speaks: Like a grape in the desert I found Israel, and like figs on the fig tree I found their fathers; […]

24:2.t: "I gave you," he said, "directions in the first commandment to attend to faith, and fear, and self-restraint." "Even so, sir," said I. And he said, "Now I wish to show you the powers of these, that you may know what power each possesses. For their powers are double, and have relation alike to the righteous and the unrighteous. Trust you, therefore, the righteous, but put no trust in the unrighteous. For the path of righteousness is straight, but that of unrighteousness is crooked. But walk in the straight and even way, and mind not the crooked. For the crooked path has no roads, but has many pathless places and stumbling-blocks in it, and it is rough and thorny. It is injurious to those who walk therein. But they who walk in the straight road walk evenly without stumbling, because it is neither rough nor thorny. You see, then, that it is better to walk in this road." "I wish to go by this road," said I. "You will go by it," said he; "and whoever turns to the Lord with all his heart will walk in it."

24:5.t: Such, then, is the providence of the Lord that, wherever the fruit is of a softer quality, there the thickness of the leaf presents in defense of the fruit a stouter protective covering, as we see, for example, in the fruit of the fig tree. The more delicate fruits, therefore, need a stronger defense, as the Lord Himself teaches us, speaking through the mouth of Jeremias: ‘Like these good figs, so will I regard the captives of Juda, whom I have sent forth out of this place into the land of the Chaldeans for their good. And I will set my eyes upon them for their good.’ For He surrounded His precious ones, as it were, with a stouter covering of His mercy, lest the tender fruit should perish before its time. And so, too, He says of them in a later passage: ‘My delicate ones have walked rough ways.’ To these He speaks further on: ‘Be constant, my children, and cry to the Lord.’ Against all storms and injuries this is the sole and inviolable protection and impenetrable defense.

But let us follow the simple and true history: that he called Jeconiah the basket of good figs, who by the counsel of Jeremiah and the command of God had handed himself over to the Babylonian king, and to whom the Lord also promises prosperity; and the basket of bad figs Zedekiah, who, contradicting the sentence of God, was captured, and with his eyes blinded was led to Babylon and died there. And to such an extent did God set his eyes upon them for good, those who acquiesced in his command, and bring them back into their land, and build them and not destroy them, and plant them and not pluck them up, and give them a heart, that they might know him, that he himself was the Lord, and that they might become his people and he himself might be their God, that even in the captivity he set his eyes upon them and permitted them to work the land, to build houses and to plant orchards in the region of Babylonia; Daniel, through miracles of signs, was suddenly made a prince from a captive; […]

And lest we be thought to be setting down our own sense, Scripture itself lays itself open. As these figs, it says, are good, so will I know the exile of Judah, which I have sent out from this place into the land of the Chaldeans, for good, signifying Jeconiah and the princes who were captured with him. And on the contrary, of the basket that had bad figs: And as the very bad figs, he says, which cannot be eaten because they are bad, so will I give Zedekiah, king of Judah, and his princes and those who fled over into Egypt and who remained in this city, to vexation and affliction to all the kingdoms of the earth, when they were captured in Egypt too, and Nebuchadnezzar set his throne in Tahpanhes, and the Lord sent upon them the sword, famine and pestilence, until they were consumed from the land which he gave to their fathers. […]

24:7.t: Put away doubting from you and do not hesitate to ask of the Lord, saying to yourself, "How can I ask of the Lord and receive from Him, seeing I have sinned so much against Him?" Do not thus reason with yourself, but with all your heart turn to the Lord and ask of Him without doubting, and you will know the multitude of His tender mercies; that He will never leave you, but fulfil the request of your soul. For He is not like men, who remember evils done against them; but He Himself remembers not evils, and has compassion on His own creature.

25:1.t: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judea — or upon all the people of Judah — in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah. These things are earlier than the preceding vision; for that one took place under Zedekiah, after Jeconiah had been carried off to Babylon, but these under Jehoiakim, the son of Josiah and father of Jeconiah. For it was not their concern, as I have already said before, to preserve the chronological order of prophecy, which the laws of history require, but to write in whatever way they knew to be useful to those who would hear and read; hence also in the Psalter some wrongly look for the order of the psalms according to the sequence of history, which is not observed in lyric song.

This is the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, which is not found in the Seventy; and there follows: which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying. In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim son of Josiah, father of Jeconiah, Nebuchadnezzar took up the rule in Babylon, and so it came about that the year which was the first of Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon was the fourth of King Jehoiakim in Jerusalem. Then, in the eighth year of his reign, he led into captivity Jeconiah with his mother and the princes, who had reigned only three months after the slaying of his father Jehoiakim. Now Jehoiakim was slain in the eleventh year of his reign in Jerusalem.

25:3.t: From the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, up to this day, this is the twenty-third year, the word of the Lord has come to me, and I have spoken to you, rising by night and speaking; and you have not listened. In the thirteenth year of the reign of Josiah, who reigned in Jerusalem thirty-one years, Jeremiah began to prophesy, and he prophesied under him for nineteen years. His son Jehoahaz succeeded him in the kingdom; and when he was at once led into captivity by Neco, the Egyptian king, his brother Jehoiakim obtained the kingdom, in the fourth year of whose reign this word of the Lord comes to Jeremiah. And so it was the twenty-third year of Jeremiah the prophet since he began to speak to the people, and he never ceased to preach, but every day, rising at dawn and by night, he spoke to the people; and you have not, he says, listened. […]

25:4.t: And the Lord sent to you all his servants, the prophets, rising at dawn and sending; and you have not listened. Not through one prophet but through all of them God always admonished his people, and as though he himself were stationed on watch and on guard, he rose at dawn to warn his people. And you have not, he says, listened, so that the more frequent the admonition, the greater were the sins of those who despised it.

Nor did you incline your ears to hear, when I said: Return, each one, from his evil way and from your very wicked thoughts, and you will dwell in the land which the Lord gave to you and to your fathers from age and even unto age. So great was the hardness of the people that it would not even take on the bearing of one who listens and incline its ear, above all when the Lord was warning it that each one should turn back from his evil way and from his very wicked thoughts. And O infinite clemency: not to inflict punishment for the crime, but to call to repentance both for evil works, which the evil way signifies, and for very wicked thoughts, which even by themselves, without the deed, are reckoned as sin! And he promises a reward if they do what is commanded: that they should dwell in the land which was given to their fathers and taken away because of the vices of the sons. […]

25:6.t: And do not go after strange gods, to serve them and worship them, nor provoke me to anger in the works of your hands, and I will not afflict you; and you have not listened to me. 'And these things', he says, 'I was urging together with the earlier ones: that you should not serve strange gods and worship them, and that you should not, by doing these things, provoke me to anger because of the works of your hands, so that I should do what I did not wish and afflict you; and you have not listened to me'. And what follows: says the Lord, so that you provoked me to anger in the works of your hands, to your own harm, is not found in the Seventy.

25:8.t: Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: Because you have not listened to my words, behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, says the Lord, and Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant. 'Because you have provoked me to anger and done evil to your own destruction, and have trampled with a proud foot him who called you to repentance, I will send', he says, 'to all the families, or nations, of the north, and I will bring their prince Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant'. Now the Lord sends either angels to stir up the nations, or else he moves thoughts of such a kind that they do the will of the Lord. And as for his calling Nebuchadnezzar 'his servant', he is not called 'servant' in the way the prophets and all the saints are, who truly serve the Lord, but in that in the overthrow of Jerusalem he serves the will of the Lord, in accordance with what the Apostle too says: whom I have delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme. […]

25:9.t: And I will bring them upon this land and upon its inhabitants and upon all the nations that are round about it, and I will slay them and make them an astonishment and a hissing and everlasting desolations. These are the rewards of those who despise the words of God and refuse to hear them; whatever evil, therefore, is brought upon us, our sins have brought about. And just as all the nations were then brought against Jerusalem, so today they are brought against the negligent Church, that he may slay them and make them an astonishment and a hissing and everlasting desolations, so that they may be an example and a marvel to all. Now hissing is a sign of marvel and astonishment, and everlasting desolation is found in those who do not have God as their protector.

25:10.t: Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by the prophet; ‘I will take away from them the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the scent of myrrh, and the light of a lamp, and the whole land shall be destroyed.’ For the whole service of the law has been abolished from them, and henceforth and for ever they remain without a feast. And they observe not the Passover; for how can they? They have no abiding place, but they wander everywhere. And they eat unleavened bread contrary to the law, since they are unable first to sacrifice the lamb, as they were commanded to do when eating unleavened bread. But in every place they transgress the law, and as the judgments of God require, they keep days of grief instead of gladness. Now the cause of this to them was the slaying of the Lord, and that they did not reverence the Only-Begotten.

And I will destroy from them the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bride and the voice of the bridegroom, the voice of the mill and the light of the lamp. And all its land shall become a desolation and an astonishment. This is proved even today in the assembly of the malignant, in that their teachers do not teach the word of God but hiss like a serpent. And there perishes in them the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, so that they never hear that saying of the Apostle: rejoice, again I say, rejoice!; also the voice of the bride, that is, of the Church's faith, and the voice of the bridegroom, that is, of the Lord the Savior, for he who has the bride is the bridegroom; the voice of the mill, so that grain is not ground in it and given to the peoples to eat; and the light of the lamp, namely the teaching and knowledge of the prophets. […]

25:11.t: [Daniel 5:2] "Being now drunken, he therefore gave order that the golden and silver vessels be brought in which his father, Nebuchadnezzar, had taken away from the temple which was in Jerusalem, in order that the king might drink from them..." The Hebrews hand down some such story as this: that up until the seventieth year, on which Jeremiah had said (Jeremiah 25:11) that the captivity of the Jewish people would be released (a matter of which Zechariah also speaks [Zechariah 1:12] in the first part of his book), Belshazzar had esteemed God's promise to be of none effect; therefore he turned the failure of the promise into an occasion of joy and arranged a great banquet, scoffing somewhat at the expectation of the Jews and at the vessels of the Temple of God. Punishment, however, immediately ensued. […]
25:11.s: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER FIVE

25:11.t: And all these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years. And when the seventy years are fulfilled, I will visit upon the king of Babylon and upon that nation, says the Lord, their iniquities, and upon the land of the Chaldeans, and I will make it everlasting desolations. And I will bring upon that land all my words which I have spoken against it, all that is written in this book, whatever Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations. Just as Jerusalem after seventy years receives back its former inhabitants and, its punishments completed, because it obeyed the sentence of God, enjoys its former happiness, so the king of Babylon, because he was lifted up into pride and judged that his reigning over the nations was the work of his own strength and not of the Lord's will, will be destroyed when the Medes and Persians come. […]

We have seen the promises that God made to Abraham—to be the father, first, of the Jewish race according to the flesh, and second, of all nations who were to embrace the faith. The development in history of the City of God will show how these promises were kept. The end of the preceding book brought us up to the reign of King David. I shall now begin with his reign and treat of what ensued in as much detail as the theme of this book requires. There is a period that begins with the prophecies of Samuel and continues through the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity (which Jeremiah had foretold) and ends with the rebuilding of the temple, after the Israelites came home. This period is known as the age of the prophets, although, of course, the patriarch Noah, in whose lifetime the whole earth was destroyed by the flood, and others before and after him up to the time of the kings were prophets also. […]

25:14.t: Because they served them, though they were many nations and great kings; and I will repay them according to their works and according to the deeds of their hands. This is not found in the Seventy. And it signifies that Jeremiah prophesied not only against Babylon but also against the other nations which were in the Babylonian army and fought against the people of the Lord. Indeed, in what follows words are spoken against Egypt and the Philistines and Moab and Ammon and Idumea and Damascus and Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor and Elam, and at the last against Babylon and the land of Chaldea.

25:15.t: It is clear that Jesus wished to drink the cup of the passion. For by comparison it was better that it should pass because of his drinking of it than that it should not pass because he had not drunk it. For suppose the Lord had not drunk that cup and for this reason it had not passed from him: without doubt neither would the spirits working sins have passed from the human race, and fittingly neither would the penalties have passed which were owed for the sins. Therefore it was expedient for all that the cup should pass from him, because the Savior drank it, so that all of us who believe in him who drank it may not drink that cup "of unmixed wine", which gives to drink and is going to give to drink to "all the nations", so that those drinking it "may become drunk and vomit, and cease to rage". […]

Know that it was foretold that wars would continue frequently to prevail, death and famine accumulate anxiety, health would be shattered by raging diseases and the human race be wasted by the desolation of pestilence. It was predicted that evils should be multiplied in the last times and that misfortunes should be varied and that as the day of judgment is now drawing near, the censure of an indignant God should be more and more aroused for the scourging of the human race. For these things do not happen, as your false complaining and ignorant inexperience of the truth asserts and repeats, because your gods are not worshiped by us, but because God is not worshiped by you. […]
25:15.s: Treatise V. An Address to Demetrianus 5-6

25:15.t: 'In the ways', he says, 'of your sister Samaria you walked; therefore you must drink the cup of her whose sins you followed — and that a cup is often taken for punishments and torments, there are many examples, among which is this: A cup in the hand of the Lord, full of pure wine, mixed. And he has tilted it from this; yet its dregs are not emptied: all the sinners of the earth shall drink; and in Isaiah it is called 'the cup of ruin' and 'the draught of fury'; and God speaks to Jeremiah, saying: Take the cup of pure wine from my hand, and you shall give drink to all the nations to which I shall send you; and they shall drink and vomit, and go mad; for just as certain cathartics are given so that the noxious humor that is in bodies may be purged out, so the Lord too gives a most undiluted cup of torments, to take away from sinners whatever there is of gall and bitterness and restore them to their former health — ; […]

For thus says the Lord God of Israel to me: Take this cup of the wine of fury — or of pure wine — from my hand, and you shall give drink from it to all the nations to whom I shall send you; and they shall drink and be drunk — or vomit — and go mad before the sword which I shall send among them. And I took the cup from the hand of the Lord and gave drink to all the nations to whom the Lord sent me. The giving to drink of the cup, and of the cup 'of pure wine' or 'unmixed', which in Greek is called akratou, is a sign of the Lord's fury, so that all the nations which made war on the people of God drink of the cup of the Lord's fury, of which Isaiah too writes against Jerusalem: the bowl of fury, the cup of ruin you have drunk up and emptied; therefore arise! And this cup is drunk by all the nations for this reason: that they may vomit and go mad. […]

25:18.t: To Jerusalem and to the cities of Judah and to its kings and to its princes, to make them a desolation and an astonishment and a hissing and a curse, as it is this day. 'I thought', he says, 'that I was giving drink to the nations alone, and therefore I had gladly offered myself for this ministry; but among the other nations, nay rather before the other nations, I gave drink to Jerusalem and to the cities of Judah and to its kings and princes, to make them an astonishment and a desolation and a hissing and a curse, as is also proved by the present example'. Hence he also says above: You have deceived me, O Lord, and I was deceived; you were stronger, and you prevailed!

25:19.t: To Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and to his servants and to his princes and to all his people and to all in general. After Jerusalem, Pharaoh, king of Egypt, drinks, and his allies; the princes drank, and the whole people, and everyone who is indeed not an Egyptian but dwells in its regions, whom the Seventy translated symmiktous, that is, 'people of mixed stock', a populace not of the Egyptian region but foreign and immigrant.

25:20.t: To all the kings of the land of Ausitis. It is called 'Vs' in Hebrew, and the history relates that Job too was from it: there was a certain man in the region of Ausitis, named Job. And yet it should be known that this short verse is not found in the Seventy, and that Theodotion translated 'island' for 'Vs'.

And to all the kings of the land of the Philistines and of Ashkelon and of Gaza and of Ekron and to the remnants of Ashdod. In general he set down the Philistines, that is, the land of the Palestinians, and in particular their cities Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, Ashdod; Gath alone he passed over in silence, which is contained in the 'remnants'. For this is what is written: and to the remnants of Ashdod; for the region of the city of Gath is neighboring and bordering on Ashdod, which in Hebrew is called Esdod. And Isaiah too writes that the Palestinians were captured and laid waste by the Babylonians.

25:21.t: To Idumea and Moab and the sons of Ammon and to all the kings of Tyre and to all the kings of Sidon. Idumea is the land in which are the mountains of Seir, and which in Hebrew is called Edom; Moab and Ammon are themselves the sons of Lot, neighbors of the Dead Sea. Tyre and Sidon are the chief cities on the coast of Phoenicia, which themselves too were overcome when the Babylonian came; Carthage is their colony, whence also the Poeni are so called, by a corruption of the word, as though Phoeni, and their language is to a great extent akin to the Hebrew language.

25:22.t: And to the kings of the islands which are beyond the sea. He passes over to Cyprus and Rhodes and the islands which are called Kyklades [the Cyclades]; for these too were occupied by the Babylonians.

25:23.t: And Dedan and Teman and Buz and all who are shorn round the hair. These nations are in the wilderness, neighboring on and intermingled with the regions of the Ishmaelites, whom they now call Saracens, and of whom it is said: who are shorn round the hair.

25:24.t: And to all the kings of Arabia. This is not found in the Seventy. After Dedan, then, and Teman and Buz and the Ishmaelites, the order of the regions follows.
And to all the kings of the west, who dwell in the desert, and to all the kings of Zimri. This too is not found in the Seventy.

25:25.t: And to all the kings of Elam and to all the kings of the Medes. From the fact that Elam and the kings of the Medes follow Zimri, we judge that Zimri too is a region of Persia, unless perhaps, from the fact that Arabia came before, these too are to be understood as kings of the desert. Now Elam is a region of Persia beyond Babylon; hence also the Elamites, and the Medes too and the Persians, by whom Babylon was captured and destroyed; and they themselves also drank the undiluted cup when Alexander, king of the Macedonians, gave it them to drink.

25:26.t: And to all the kings of the north, near and far. Because he had enumerated the regions of Persia and Babylon, of Elam and of the Medes, he now sets down in general all the kings of the north, who are near and far. For 'north', which in Hebrew is called 'safun', the Seventy translated aphēliōtēn, which we can call 'the east wind'.

Each one against his brother, and to all the kingdoms of the earth which are upon its face. So that it should not become lengthy to enumerate one by one all the regions of the eastern province, he set down in general all the kingdoms of the earth which dwell on the earth. And as for his saying: against his brother, there is understood 'I gave the undiluted drink', so that all should rage, vomit, go mad and fight one another in mutual battles. And what he added:

King Sheshach shall drink after them, and is not found in the Seventy, has this sense: 'All the nations round about', he says, 'will be subject to the Babylonian empire, and he will subject all things to his power, so that all the nations which the preceding discourse has recounted serve him and drink of his cup'; hence also in the vision against Babylon it is written: Babylon is a golden cup that makes all the earth drunk. […]

25:27.t: And when he says that he gave it to drink to the other nations and to Jerusalem and the cities of Judea, he adds: Thus says the Lord Almighty, the God of Israel: Drink and be drunk, and vomit, and fall before the face of the sword which I shall send among you (Jer 25:27). And it is to be noted that this cup of the Lord's fury is his sword, which is sent into the midst of sinners. Here a question arises: how, after the drinking, the drunkenness and vomiting and the fall, it is said in Jeremiah that Jerusalem cannot arise, and now he speaks to her through Isaiah: Lift yourself up, lift yourself up, arise, Jerusalem. It is resolved thus: as long as someone drinks the cup, and is drunk, and raves, and vomits, and falls, he cannot arise; for he has not yet drained the cup of the Lord, nor come to the dregs, so as to have drunk it to the bottom. But now he speaks to Jerusalem in the past tense: who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury, and not, who are drinking.

And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Drink and be drunk and vomit and fall and do not rise, before the sword which I will send upon you! 'After', he says, 'you have given drink to all the nations and fulfilled the command of the Lord, you will again command these things with the words of the Lord and say: Drink and be drunk and vomit and fall and do not rise!' If 'to drink, to be drunk, to vomit and to fall' is a sign of salvation, so that, like a cathartic potion, everything harmful is expelled, how does there follow: and do not rise? And what the drink is that makes them fall forever he sets down more plainly, that is: before the sword which I will send among you.

25:28.t: And when they refuse to take the cup from the hand, to drink, you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Drinking you shall drink; for behold, in the city in which my name has been invoked, I am beginning to afflict; and will you, as though innocent, be exempt — or and will you be clean with cleanness — ? you shall not be exempt, or you shall not be clean. He covertly shows that those who have refused to do the command of God willingly will undergo it by necessity, and will hear: drinking you shall drink. 'Whether you will it', he says, 'or not, the sentence of God must be fulfilled. For if the city of Jerusalem, in which the name of God was known, as the prophet says: God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel, drank the undiluted cup, the cup of fury, how much more will you not be clean, who worship idols in place of the name of God!'

25:29.t: For I am calling a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth, says the Lord of hosts. This is the most undiluted drink, this the cup of the Lord's fury, which is called not upon Jerusalem alone but upon the whole earth and all the nations round about; of which he had said above: 'and I will send to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring them upon this land and upon its inhabitants and upon all the nations that are round about it.'

25:30.t: And you shall prophesy to them all these words and say to them: The Lord will roar from on high — or will give answer — and from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice; roaring he will roar over its beauty — or he will answer over his place —, a chant as of those who tread will be sung together against all the inhabitants of the earth. The sound — or destruction — has come to the ends — or upon a part — of the earth, for the Lord has judgment with the nations; he himself is judged with all flesh; the wicked he has given over to the sword, says the Lord. First let us say how the truth of the translation stands. 'To all the nations', he says, 'you shall prophesy and say that the Lord roars from on high, that is, gives a sign of his fury, according to what is written: the lion will roar, and who will not fear? the Lord has spoken, and who will not prophesy?' and from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice, so as to terrify all who hear. And he will roar over its beauty, that is, over the temple. […]

25:31.t: Again, it says that the Lord will enter into judgment with all flesh, that is, in the examination of the actions in the lives of each He subjected Himself to judgment and compared His own precepts with the actions of sinners, defending Himself with proofs that He has done all things depending upon Him for the salvation of those judged, in order that the sinners, being persuaded that they are liable to punishment for sins and acknowledging the divine justice, may willingly accept the penalty falling to their lot.

25:32.t: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, affliction — or evil — shall go forth from nation to nation, and a great whirlwind — or tempest — shall go forth from the heights — or the ends — of the earth. And the slain of the Lord — or those wounded by the Lord — shall be on that day from the height of the earth to its height; they shall not be lamented, and they shall not be gathered up nor buried; they shall lie as dung upon the face of the earth. Let them blush who try to do violence to holy Scripture by expounding in a good sense things that are full of threatening. Now of this passage I think the Lord too spoke: nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom, and the rest that is contained in that same saying of the Gospel. And let us understand that these things were done according to the history, when all the nations round about were subjugated by the Babylonian king and felt his cruel rule, or according to prophecy, as things that are to come long afterward at the consummation of the world. […]

25:34.t: Howl — or shout for joy —, you shepherds, and cry out, and sprinkle yourselves with ashes, you nobles of the flock — or lament, you rams of the sheep —, for your days are fulfilled, that you should be slain, and your scatterings, and you shall fall like precious vessels — or like choice rams —. And flight shall perish from the shepherds, and deliverance from the nobles — or rams — of the flock. It should be noted that only in this place have the Seventy put 'jubilation' in a bad sense, for which the other translators rendered 'howling', as it is written in the Hebrew. Between the shepherds and the rams, or nobles, of the flock there is this difference: the shepherds pertain to rational beings, while the rams and nobles refer to the rich, who themselves too are called part of the flock. […]

25:36.t: The voice of the cry of the shepherds and the howling of the nobles of the flock — or the jubilation of the rams —, for the Lord has laid waste their pastures. And the fields — or the beautiful things — of peace have fallen silent before the wrath of the fury of the Lord. Here too it should be noted that in the Seventy 'jubilation' is put for 'howling'. Now between the shepherds and the rams there is this difference: the shepherds are taken to be those in the Church who preside over the flock with wisdom and learning and teaching, but the rams those who seem indeed to be leaders among the people, but have in themselves nothing of teaching and wisdom, and through excessive simplicity are almost neighbors of folly. […]

25:38.t: He has forsaken, like a lion, the shade — or the lair — that is his — and, as is more correct, the tabernacle; for this is what the Hebrew 'soccho' means —, for their land has become a desolation — or trackless — before the wrath of the dove — or before the great sword — and before the wrath of the fury of the Lord. The Lord, of whom he had said above: from on high he will roar, and from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice; roaring he will roar over its beauty, will himself forsake his tabernacle, of which it is written: his place has been made in peace — or in Salem — and his dwelling in Zion; he himself will desert his seat and will fulfill what he spoke through this same prophet: I have left my house, I have forsaken my inheritance. And he has left, like a lion, his lair, so that all the beasts have power to lay waste his land. For while the lion is its guardian and protector, no one dares to approach it. […]

26:1.t: In the beginning of King Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord, saying: Thus says the Lord: Stand in the court of the house of the Lord, and you shall speak to all the cities of Judah, from which they come to worship in the house of the Lord, all the words that I have commanded you to speak to them; do not withhold a word! If perhaps they will hear and turn, each one from his evil way, and I may repent of the evil — or I may rest from the evil —, which I am thinking to do to them because of the wickedness of their pursuits. This prophecy is earlier than the former one, although it was made under the same king. For that one was made in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah king of Judah, but this one in the beginning of the same king, as Scripture says: in the beginning of King Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord, saying. […]

26:2.t: The Novatians bring up a question from the words of the apostle Peter. Because he said, "if perhaps," they think that he did not imply that forgiveness would be granted on repentance. But let them consider concerning to whom the words were spoken—of Simon, who did not believe through faith but was contemplating trickery. So, too, the Lord, to him who said, "Lord, I will follow you wherever you go," replied, "Foxes have holes." For he knew that the man was not being fully sincere. If, then, the Lord refused to him who was not baptized permission to follow him, because he saw that he was not sincere, do you wonder that the apostle did not absolve him who after baptism was guilty of deceit and whom he declared to be still in the bond of iniquity? But let this be my answer to them. As to myself, I say that Peter did not doubt, and I do not think that so great a question can be so easily disposed of by the questionable interpretation of a single word. […]

But he who is about to speak the word of the Lord ought to stand with Moses and to hear with the psalmist: you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. And he is commanded to speak to all the cities of Judah, although the Seventy did not translate 'cities', lest perhaps it should seem unfitting to speak, in the court of the house of the Lord, to cities which were not present; but when he speaks to the peoples and to the citizens, he speaks to the cities themselves. And he fittingly stands in the court and vestibule of the temple of the Lord, so that, on the occasion of prayer to the Lord and of worshiping him, they may be compelled to hear the words of the prophet. 'Do not', he says, 'withhold a word; although it be sad, although the rage of those who hear be stirred up against you, nevertheless say what has been commanded you, fearing not the persecutions of those who are to be stirred up against you, but the command of the Lord who orders it!'

26:3.t: And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God; if perhaps even they will hear, and if perhaps they will be quiet. Something similar is written in Jeremiah too: If perhaps they will hear and repent, and in the Gospel: Perhaps they will respect my son. Now God speaks these words with the disposition of one who is in doubt, so that they may show the free choice of man, lest the foreknowledge of future things make immutable, whether for evil or for good, what God knew would come to be: for it is not because he knows what is to come that we must necessarily do what he foreknew; rather, what we are going to do by our own will, he, as God, knows will come to be.

Perhaps, he says, they will hear and turn. The ambiguous word 'perhaps' cannot befit the majesty of the Lord, but he speaks according to our feeling, so that free will may be preserved for man, lest by his foreknowledge man be compelled, as if by necessity, either to do something or not to do it; for it is not because God knows that something is going to be that it is therefore going to be, but because it is going to be, God knows it, as one who foreknows things to come. And yet it must be known, according to this same Jeremiah, that if the Lord has foretold evils and the people has repented, he himself too will repent over the things which he threatened to do; and if he has promised prosperity and the people has acted negligently, God changes his sentence and brings evils instead of good things. Something of this kind is also that saying in the Gospel: I will send my son; perhaps they will reverence him; which is surely said in the person of almighty God. […]

26:4.t: And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: If you will not hear me, to walk in my law which I gave you, to hear the words of my servants, the prophets, whom I sent to you, rising up by night and sending, and you did not hear, I will make this house like Shiloh, and this city I will make a curse to all the nations of the earth. It is therefore placed in our power either to do something or not to do it, only in such a way that whatever good work we will, seek and accomplish, we refer to the grace of God, who, according to the Apostle, has given us both to will and to accomplish. But if it suffices to walk once in the law which was given to us through Moses, as the foolish heresy supposes, how is it that he added: to hear the words of my servants, the prophets? who surely were sent after the law, and not once but frequently, nor idly and as from one at ease, but always and as from one who is anxious.

26:6.t: 'I sent', he says, 'to you my servants daily and rising up by night; and if you will not hear them, I will make this house' — that is, the temple of God — 'like Shiloh', where the tabernacle was. And when the temple has been destroyed, consequently the city too will be a curse to all the nations of the earth. And just as, when the temple had been built on the threshing floor of Ornan and on Mount 'Moria', that is, 'of vision', on which Abraham is related to have offered his son Isaac, the worship of Shiloh ceased and no sacrifices were afterwards celebrated there, so, when the Church had been built and spiritual victims had been offered in it, the ceremonies of the law ceased, and the city of the Jews was made a curse to all the nations of the earth, from which the Lord has freed us, as the Apostle says: Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law, having been made a curse for us.

26:7.t: And the priests and the prophets — or false prophets — and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the Lord. And when Jeremiah had finished speaking all that the Lord had commanded him to speak to all the people, the priests and the prophets — or false prophets — and all the people seized him, saying: Let him die the death, because he has prophesied in the name of the Lord, saying: This house shall be like Shiloh, and this city shall be made desolate, so that there is no inhabitant. The priests and the prophets, whom the Seventy more plainly translated as 'false prophets', are angry with Jeremiah because he preaches true things, and because, with the temple overthrown and the city deserted, their religion would perish, and the profits coming from religion; therefore they seize him and, with the people consenting with them, destine him for death, because he had said in the name of the Lord: This house shall be like Shiloh, and the city shall be made desolate, so that there is no inhabitant. […]

26:9.t: And all the people was gathered against Jeremiah in the house of the Lord. And the princes of Judah heard these words, and they went up from the king's house to the house of the Lord and sat in the entrance of the new gate of the Lord. Jeremiah was prophesying the words of the Lord in the temple and had said: I will make this house like Shiloh, and this city a curse to all the nations of the earth, and at once, a riot having been stirred up by the priests and prophets and people, the whole crowd is gathered against the prophet into the temple, where the prophet was and was being held by the hands of the priests and prophets and crowd.

26:10.t: When the princes of the city, who were staying in the royal house, had heard this, they crossed over, or went up from the king's house to the house of the Lord. And it is to be noted that to go to the house of the Lord is always an ascent. And they sat in the entrance of the new gate of the Lord. For it was the duty of the princes to sit in the gate of the house of the Lord and there to learn the truth of the business and of the riot. But the gate is called 'new' because those who sat in it and presided over the judgment resisted the slanders of the priests and false prophets.

26:11.t: And the priests and the prophets spoke to the princes and to all the people, saying: There is a judgment of death for this man, because he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your ears. While the princes of the city, who had run from the king's palace to the temple so that the riot of the people might be calmed, were sitting in the gate of the temple and in the new gate, and an assembly of the people had been gathered, the priests and false prophets accuse him; and the prophet would have perished, as far as it lay with the priests and prophets, if the accusers themselves had had the power of judgment. From this we understand that those who seemed devoted to religion were crueler toward the prophet, through envy of his holiness, than those who presided over public needs.

26:12.t: And Jeremiah said to all the princes and to all the people, saying: The Lord sent me to prophesy to this house — or upon this house — and to this city — or upon this city — all the words which you have heard. Now therefore make good your ways and your pursuits, and hear the voice of the Lord your God, and the Lord will repent of the evil which he has spoken against you — or and the Lord will rest from the evils which he has spoken against you —. As for me, behold, I am in your hands; do to me as is good and right in your eyes — or as is expedient for you — ! Nevertheless, know and understand that, if you kill me, you will bring innocent blood against your very selves and against this city and its inhabitants; for in truth the Lord sent me to you, to speak in your ears all these words. […]

26:16.t: And the princes and all the people said to the priests and the prophets: There is no judgment of death for this man, because he has spoken to us in the name of the Lord our God. The people, which had earlier been tripped up by the priests and false prophets, joins the princes of the city and speaks for Jeremiah, saying that he is by no means guilty of death, but has prophesied in the name of the Lord and from his mouth; for the untaught crowd, once it has received a reason, quickly changes its opinion. But the resentment of the accusers, especially of the priests and false prophets, cannot be changed; and therefore, while they accuse and persevere in the accusation, the people is changed, because he had given them hope of the Lord's pardon, if they made their ways good and heard the voice of the Lord their God, so that the Lord too would bend his sentence.

26:17.t: And there rose up men of the elders of the land and said to the whole assembly of the people, speaking: Micah of Moresheth was a prophet in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah, and he spoke to all the people of Judah, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the house the heights of the forests. Did Hezekiah, king of Judah, and all Judah condemn him to death? Did they not fear the Lord and entreat the face of the Lord, and the Lord repented of the evil which he had spoken against them? So we are doing a great evil against our own souls. The princes of the city and the people understand the truth of the judgment; […]

26:20.t: There was also a man prophesying in the name of the Lord, Uriah, son of Shemaiah of Kiriath-jearim, and he prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah. And King Jehoiakim and all his mighty men and his princes heard these words, and the king sought to kill him; and Uriah heard and was afraid and fled and entered Egypt. And what follows: and King Jehoiakim sent men into Egypt, Elnathan, son of Achbor, and men with him into Egypt, is not found in the Seventy. Then is joined: and they brought Uriah out of Egypt and led him to King Jehoiakim; and he struck him with the sword and cast his corpse into the graves of the ignoble common people. Nevertheless the hand of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, was with Jeremiah, so that he should not be delivered into the hand of the people and they kill him. […]

26:22.t: It is also asked how Jehoiakim, king of Judah, a king of small dominion, weakened, and about to perish at any moment, had the power of sending into Egypt and of bringing Uriah out from there. This is easily solved if we consider that he had been appointed prince by Neco, king of Egypt, and that this prophecy was made in the beginning of his reign.

26:24.t: Jeremiah needed the help of Ahikam. How much more do we need that of God.
