But although Jeremiah was freed by the help of the Lord, yet it is reckoned as a reward to him also through whom the Lord freed his prophet, namely to Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as we shall read later, when Jeremiah is freed from the danger of death out of the cistern of mud by the counsel and protection of Ebed-melech the eunuch.

27:1.t: In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying. This is not found in the edition of the Seventy, and many think it is the beginning of the following chapter, which is by no means so; rather, it is to be joined to the preceding one, so that whatever is reported as said and done we should believe to have been done in the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim; whence too he had the power of sending into Egypt, as to a friendly king. But the Seventy seem to me to have passed over this title in silence for this reason, lest they should seem to say it a second time; for they had already set down at the beginning: in the beginning of King Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord, saying.

27:2.t: Thus says the Lord to me: Make for yourself bonds and chains — or kloious [collars], which in Hebrew are called 'mutoth', and in common speech they call them 'boias' [neck-shackles] — and you shall put them on your neck and you shall send to the king of Edom and to the king of Moab and to the king of the sons of Ammon and to the king of Tyre and to the king of Sidon by the hand of the messengers who have come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah, king of Judah. And you shall command them to speak to their masters: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Thus shall you say to your masters. The previous vision came to the prophet in the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, but this one under Zedekiah, who reigned last in Jerusalem and under whom the city was taken and overthrown. […]

27:5.t: I made the earth and man and the beasts that are upon the face of the earth, by my great strength and by my outstretched arm, and I gave it to him who pleased in my eyes. Although this scripture speaks anthrōpopathōs [in human terms], in the way that we men can speak and understand, yet the 'strength' of God and his 'arm' is he of whom the Apostle also speaks: 'Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God', and Isaiah: Lord, who has believed our hearing, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? John the evangelist also writes: all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. David too speaks in his song: by the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth. And as for his saying: I gave it to him who pleased in my eyes, this signifies that all things have been granted to the human race through the grace of God. I, he says, made the earth and man and the beasts. The order is reversed; […]

27:6.t: We have long felt that God is angry, yet we do not try to appease him. It is our sins that make the barbarians strong. It is our vices that vanquish Rome's soldiers. As if there were here too little material for carnage, civil wars have made almost greater havoc among us than the swords of foreign foes. Miserable must those Israelites have been compared with whom Nebuchadnezzar was called God's servant. Unhappy too are we who are so displeasing to God that he uses the fury of the barbarians to execute his wrath against us. Still, when Hezekiah repented, 185,000 Assyrians were destroyed in one night by a single angel. When Jehosaphat sang the praises of the Lord, the Lord gave his worshiper the victory. Again, when Moses fought against Amalek, it was not with the sword but with prayer that he prevailed. Therefore, if we wish to be lifted up, we must first prostrate ourselves.

Now therefore I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant; and moreover I have also given him the beasts of the field, that they may serve him. And all the nations shall serve him and his son and his son's son. Of what great unhappiness is Israel, when in comparison with it Nebuchadnezzar is called 'servant of God'! It is written in the Gospel: the world was made through him, and the world did not know him; he came to his own, and his own did not receive him. Rightly therefore does the Creator hand over his creation to whom he will. Finally the devil too, as whose type Nebuchadnezzar went before, confesses: all these things have been handed over to me. […]

27:7.t: And his 'son' and 'son's son' — according to the Hebrew — he calls Belshazzar and Evil-merodach, of whom Daniel writes.

Until the time of his land and of himself comes. Fittingly, lest the empire of Nebuchadnezzar be thought perpetual, he says that he himself too is to be taken by the Medes and Persians; for this is what it signifies: until the time of his land and of himself comes. But this too is not found in the Seventy.

And many nations and great kings shall serve him. He did not say 'all' — for this is properly due to the empire of Christ —, although according to Symmachus one does not read: many nations and great kings shall serve him, but: many nations and great kings shall subject him to servitude, so that he himself too, whom all the nations had served before, serves the Medes and Persians. This, which we have set down from the Hebrew: I have given him, that they may serve him, and all the nations shall serve him and his son and his son's son, until the time of his land and of himself comes and many nations and great kings subject him to servitude, is not read, as we have already said, in the edition of the Seventy.

27:8.t:
The great and honourable name of Godhead He withheld not from His righteous ones; even as, though He is the great King, without grudging He applied the great and honourable name of Kingship to men who are His creatures.

For by the mouth of His prophet God called the heathen King Nebuchadnezzar, King of Kings. For Jeremiah said:—Every people and kingdom that shall not put his neck into the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, King of Kings, My servant, with famine and with sword and with pestilence will I visit that people. Though He is the great King, He grudges not the name of Kingship to men. And (so), though He is the great God, yet He grudged not the name of Godhead to the sons of flesh.
27:8.s: Demonstration 17 (Of Christ the Son of God), Sections 5-6

27:8.t: But the nation and kingdom which will not serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and whoever will not bend his neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, with sword and famine and pestilence I will visit upon that nation, says the Lord, until I consume them by his hand. Not only does the Lord subject sinful nations to Nebuchadnezzar, but the Apostle too speaks of sinners: whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme; and in another place: I have handed over such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved. He also warns that the powers must be obeyed not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience, lest we be condemned by them.

27:9.t: You therefore, do not listen to your prophets and diviners and dreamers and augurs and sorcerers, who say to you: You shall not serve the king of Babylon; for they prophesy a lie to you, to remove you far from your land and to drive you out, and you perish. But the nation that puts its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serves him, I will leave it in its own land, says the Lord, and it shall till it and dwell in it. In this place too the allegorical interpreter raves, and exhorts those set in the heavenly Jerusalem not to hear their prophets and diviners, dreamers and augurs and sorcerers, but rather to serve Nebuchadnezzar and take on the body of humility, infancy, the wailing and the cradles of little ones; for if they do this, when their servitude and the condition of human mortality have been fulfilled, they will return to their land and dwell in it and work the works which they worked before. […]

27:12.t: And to Zedekiah, king of Judah, I spoke according to all these words, saying: Put your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him and his people, and you shall live. Why will you die, you and your people, by sword, famine and pestilence, as the Lord has spoken to the nation that will not serve the king of Babylon? Do not listen to the words of the prophets who say to you: Do not serve the king of Babylon; for they themselves speak a lie to you, for I did not send them, says the Lord, and they prophesy in my name falsely, so that I may drive you out and you perish, both you and the prophets who prophesy to you. After all the nations he passes to Zedekiah, king of Judah, and speaks with the same words with which he threatened the nations; for he who has sinned sins either like or greater than the other nations does not merit the privilege of the Israelite nation. Finally, because the rebellious people disdained to hear, it was consumed by sword, famine and pestilence. […]

27:16.t: And to the priests and to this people I spoke, saying: Thus says the Lord: Do not listen to the words of your prophets who prophesy to you, saying: Behold, the vessels of the Lord will return from Babylon now quickly; for they prophesy a lie to you. — This, which we have set down, 'now quickly', is not found in the Seventy, and likewise that which follows: — Do not listen to them, but serve the king of Babylon, that you may live! Why is this city given over to desolation? And after the nations and the king he speaks to the priests and to the people, because he had already announced destruction to the prophets above, saying: so that I may drive you out and you perish, both you and the prophets who prophesy to you. And he speaks the same things which he had spoken to the king and to the nations: that they should not hear the words of their prophets and say that the vessels which had been carried away with Jeconiah and the princes and his mother were to be brought back to the temple of the Lord right now; […]

27:18.t: And if they are prophets and the word of the Lord is in them, let them meet — and what follows, which we are about to subjoin up to the end of this chapter, is not found in the Seventy — the Lord of hosts, that the vessels which had been left in the house of the Lord and in the house of the king of Judah and in Jerusalem may not come into Babylon. For thus says the Lord of hosts to the pillars and to the sea and to the bases — for which in the Hebrew is written 'mechonoth' — and to the rest of the vessels which remained in this city, which Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, did not take when he carried Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, from Jerusalem into Babylon, and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem. […]

28:1.t: And it came to pass in that year, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, Hananiah son of Azzur, the prophet from Gibeon, said to me in the house of the Lord before the priests and all the people, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon; yet two years of days, and I will cause all the vessels of the Lord to be brought back to this place. Those whom the Hebrew calls 'prophets', that is 'nebeim', the Seventy translated 'false prophets', in order to make the understanding plainer. Indeed, in the present passage too he is called 'prophet', that is 'nebia', and not 'false prophet'. […]

28:3.t: Which Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, took from this place and carried over into Babylon. Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the exile of Judah, who went into Babylon, I will bring back to this place, says the Lord; for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon. For which the Seventy translated: Jeconiah and the exile of Judah, because I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon, briefly setting down the sense of the Hebrew truth rather than its words. Now Hananiah the 'prophet' — as he then seemed to the people — promises that not only the vessels but also King Jeconiah is to be brought back to Jerusalem, and that the yoke of the Babylonian king is to be broken, that is, his empire destroyed, and that this would come about before two years were yet completed, so that the nearness of the time of the promise might increase the greatness of the joy.

28:6.t: And Jeremiah the prophet said to Hananiah the prophet in the eyes of the priests and in the eyes of all the people who stood in the house of the Lord, and Jeremiah the prophet said: Amen, so may the Lord do; may the Lord raise up your words which you have prophesied, that the vessels may be brought back from the house of the Lord, and all the exile of Babylon, to this place! He wishes 'to be done' what the false prophet lyingly tells — for this is what 'amen' means, a word the Lord often uses in the Gospel: amen, amen I say to you —, and for the sake of the prosperity of affairs he desires that the other rather than himself be speaking the truth. Hence another prophet too testifies, saying: would that I were not a man having the spirit, and spoke a lie rather! Jonah, on the contrary, is grieved that he has lied, and is rebuked by the Lord, being shown that a lie on the prophet's part is more useful than the ruin of so great a multitude. […]

28:7.t: Nevertheless hear this word which I speak in your ears and in the ears of all the people: the prophets who were before me and you from the beginning, and prophesied over many lands and over great kingdoms of battle and of affliction and of famine; the prophet who prophesied peace, when his word comes, the prophet will be known whom the Lord has sent in truth. Jeremiah could have said to Hananiah: 'You speak falsely, you deceive the people, you are not a prophet but a false prophet.' But had he said that, the false prophet too could have turned the same words back upon Jeremiah; therefore he does him no insult and speaks as though to a 'prophet'. 'Not only,' he says, 'am I a prophet, and you, but before me and you there were many others, among whom were Isaiah, Hosea, Joel and Amos and the rest. They prophesied,' he says, 'against many lands and kingdoms not small but great, announcing to them war and adversity and want of all things; and on the contrary there were others who promised peace and prosperity. […]

28:10.t: And Hananiah the prophet took the chain — or the fork, which in Hebrew is called 'muthoth', — from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke it. And Hananiah spoke in the sight of all the people, saying: Thus says the Lord: so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, in two years of days, from the neck of all the nations. And Jeremiah went on his way. The Seventy did not translate 'two years'; nor did they call Hananiah 'prophet', lest, that is, they should seem to call a prophet one who was not a prophet — as if many things in the holy Scriptures were not said according to the opinion of the time to which the events reported belong, and not according to what the truth of the matter held; thus Joseph too is called in the Gospel the 'father' of the Lord, and Mary herself, who knew that she had conceived of the Holy Spirit and had answered the angel: how will this be, since I have not known a man?, says to her son: son, why have you done so to us? […]

About four hundred years have passed since the preaching of Christ burst on the world, and during that time in which his robe has been torn by countless heresies, almost the whole body of error has been derived from the Chaldaean, Syriac and Greek languages. Basilides, the master of licentiousness and the grossest sensuality, after the lapse of so many years and like a second Euphorbus, was changed by transmigration into Jovinian, so that the Latin tongue might have a heresy of its own. Was there no other province in the whole world to receive the gospel of pleasure and into which the serpent might insinuate itself, except that which was founded by the teaching of Peter, on the rock Christ? Idol temples had fallen before the standard of the cross and the severity of the gospel. Now, on the contrary, lust and gluttony endeavor to overthrow the solid structure of the cross. And so God says by Isaiah, "O my people, they which bless you cause you to err, and trouble the paths of your feet." […]

28:12.t: And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, after Hananiah the prophet had broken the chain — or fork — from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet, saying: Go, and you shall say to Hananiah: Thus says the Lord: the chain — or fork — of wood you have broken, and you will make — or I will make — in their place forks — or chains — of iron. For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: I have put a yoke of iron upon the neck of all these nations, that they may serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. And what follows: and they will serve him; moreover I have also given him the beasts of the earth, is not found in the Seventy. And in the present passage, according to the Seventy, Hananiah is not written 'prophet', nor in what follows, lest, that is, as I said before, they should seem to call a 'false prophet' a 'prophet'; but what is that to the Hebrew truth? […]

28:14.t: Now as to the first beast, he said concerning it, that it was like a lion, and it had the wings of an eagle. For the first beast was the kingdom of Babylon, which was like a lion. For thus Jeremiah wrote saying:—Israel is a wandering sheep. The lions caused them to wander. First the king of Assyria devoured him. And this last was stronger than he, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. So Jeremiah called him a lion. And he said:—He has the wings of an eagle. For thus it is written that, when Nebuchadnezzar went out to the wilderness with the beasts, he grew hair like (the plumage) of an eagle. And he said:—I saw that its wings were plucked away and it stood upright upon its feet as a man, and a man’s heart was given to it. For first, in the vision of the image, he was compared to gold which is more precious than anything which is used in the world. So in the vision of the beasts he is compared to a lion which excels in its might all the beasts. And again he was compared to an eagle which surpasses every bird. […]

28:15.t: And Jeremiah the prophet said to Hananiah the prophet: Hear, Hananiah: the Lord has not sent you, and you have made this people trust in a lie. Therefore thus says the Lord: behold, I will send away — or cast out — you from the face of the earth; this year you will die. And what follows: because you have spoken against the Lord. And Hananiah the prophet died in that year, in the seventh month, is not found in the Seventy, in place of which they put only: and he died in the seventh month. Here too in the Seventy Hananiah is not called 'prophet', though — according to the Hebrew — holy Scripture calls him 'prophet', even if, where Jeremiah rebukes him, saying: hear, Hananiah, the Lord has not sent you, he left out 'prophet'; for how could he call him 'prophet' whom he denied had been sent by the Lord? But the truth and order of the history are kept, as we said above, not according to what was, but according to what was thought at that time. […]

29:1.t: And these are the words of the book which Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the remnant of the elders of the exile, and to the priests, and to the prophets, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried over from Jerusalem into Babylon, after Jeconiah the king went out, and the lady — or the queen — and the eunuchs and the princes of Judah and Jerusalem — or from Jerusalem or the nobles — and the craftsmen from Jerusalem, by the hand of Elasah son of Shaphan and of Gemariah son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, into Babylon, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exile which I carried over from Jerusalem into Babylon: Build houses and dwell, and plant gardens — or orchards — and eat their fruit! Take wives and beget sons and daughters; give wives to your sons and give your daughters to husbands, and let them bear sons and daughters; and multiply, and do not be few in number! […]

29:5.t: But he admonishes them not with his own words but with the Lord's, that they should build houses and dwell in them, and plant gardens or orchards and eat their fruit, take wives and beget sons and daughters, and multiply in the place of exile and not be few in number, and seek the peace of the city or land to which the Lord had carried them over, and pray for it to the Lord. And giving the reasons he says: 'for in the peace of that land there will be peace for you'. To Jeremiah, because captivity was to overtake Jerusalem after a short time, it is commanded that he not take a wife, that he not beget sons. Hence to us also it is said through the Apostle: the time has been shortened; it remains that those who have wives be as though they had none. But if, because of the narrowness of the time, the use of wives is taken away from those who have them, how much more is it commanded to those who do not have them that they not take them! […]

29:7.t: Because the life of the flesh is the soul, so the blessed life of humankind is God, of whom the sacred writings of the Hebrews say, "Blessed are people whose God is the Lord." Miserable, therefore, are people who are alienated from God. Yet even this people has a peace of its own that is not to be lightly esteemed, though, indeed, it shall not in the end enjoy it, because it makes no good use of it before the end. But it is our interest that it enjoys this peace meanwhile in this life. As long as the two cities are combined, we enjoy the peace of Babylon. For from Babylon the people of God is so freed that it meanwhile travels in its company. Therefore the apostle also admonished the church to pray for kings and those in authority, assigning as the reason "that we may live a quiet and tranquil life in all godliness and love." […]

29:8.t: For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Let not your prophets who are in your midst, and your diviners, lead you astray, and do not attend to your dreams which you dream, for these prophesy falsehoods to you in my name, and I did not send them, says the Lord. That there were prophets, nay rather false prophets, and diviners and dreamers in Babylon among those whom Nebuchadnezzar had led away with Jeconiah and his mother, the prophet Ezekiel testifies, writing against those whom Jeremiah too commands are not to be believed. But at the time when this letter was being sent, Ezekiel had not yet begun to prophesy in Babylon; for this word is sent at the beginning of King Zedekiah, while Ezekiel began to prophesy in the fifth year of the exile of Jeconiah, which was the same year of Zedekiah's reign. […]

29:10.t: Only pray, I beseech you, that the Lord may not deliver us for aye to the enemies of the Cross of Christ, but that He will keep His Churches, until the time of that peace which the just Judge Himself knows when He will bestow. For He will bestow it. He will not always abandon us. As He limited seventy years for the period of captivity for the Israelites in punishment for their sins, so peradventure the Mighty One, after giving us up for some appointed time, will recall us once again, and will restore us to the peace of the beginning—unless indeed the apostasy is now nigh at hand, and the events that have lately happened are the beginnings of the approach of Antichrist. If this be so, pray that the good Lord will either take away our afflictions, or preserve us through our afflictions unvanquished.

[Daniel 9:2] "I, Daniel, understood by the books the number of the years concerning which the word of the Lord had come to the prophet Jeremiah, that seventy years would be accomplished for the desolation of Jerusalem." Jeremiah had predicted seventy years for the desolation of the Temple (Jeremiah 29:1-10), at the end of which the people would again return to Judaea and build the Temple and the city of Jerusalem. But this fact did not render Daniel careless, but rather encouraged him to pray that God might through his supplications fulfil that which He had graciously promised. Thus he avoided the danger that carelessness might result in pride, and pride cause offense to the Lord. Accordingly we read in Genesis that prior to the Deluge one hundred and twenty years were appointed for men to come to repentance (Genesis 6:3); […]
29:10.s: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER NINE

29:10.t: For thus says the Lord: When seventy years begin to be fulfilled in Babylon, I will visit you, and I will raise up over you my good word, to bring you back to this place. For I know the thoughts which I think over you, says the Lord, thoughts of peace and not of affliction, to give you an end and patience — or hope —. And you will call upon me and you will go — or, according to Symmachus, you will find — and you will pray to me, and I will hear you. You will seek me and you will find, when you seek me with your whole heart, and I will be found by you or I will appear to you. 'Do not,' he says, 'believe your false prophets, diviners and dreamers, who promise you a near return to Jerusalem! For unless the seventy years have been completed — Cyrus, king of the Persians, releasing the captives —, you will by no means return to your fatherland; and then I will fulfill my promises, to bring you back to this place; for I know the thoughts which I think over you, says the Lord'. […]

According to anagōgēn [the higher, spiritual sense], we dwell in the 'confusion' of this world for as long as it takes until we deserve to receive the 'rest' of the number seven, and, repentance having been received, God fulfills what he promised, and we are brought back to our place, the Church; for this is why the Lord seemed to strike, that he might heal, and he will give us an end of our labor and of our patience. And we shall call upon him and shall return to the Church and shall pray, and we shall be heard. We shall seek and shall find him, when we have sought him with our whole heart, and then he will appear to us. A certain one interprets the 'seventy years' according to that which is written: the days of our years, in them seventy years; and when these have been completed, then we may return to the Lord with our whole heart and be heard, and there may be an end of our labor and patience; for now we possess all things in shadow and image.

29:13.t: You will seek and you will find me, when you seek with your whole heart, in accordance with that saying of the Gospel: ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

29:14.t: ※ And I will be found by you, says the Lord, and I will bring back your captivity and gather you from all the nations and from all the places to which I drove you out, says the Lord, and I will make you return from the place to which I made you go into exile, because you have said: The Lord has raised up prophets for us in Babylon. For thus says the Lord to the king who sits upon the throne of David, and to all the people, the inhabitant of this city, and to your brothers who did not go out with you into exile; thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will send upon them the sword, famine and plague, and I will make them like bad figs, which cannot be eaten because they are very bad. […]

And in this place a delirious interpreter dreams of the ruin of the heavenly Jerusalem and supposes that the prophecy is directed to those who dwell in the Babylonian region of this world, that they did well to descend of their own accord into these bodies and in the land of the Chaldeans to build houses, plant orchards, take wives, beget sons, and by good works to be restored after seventy years to their former place and to the heavenly Jerusalem; but that those who were unwilling by their own will to descend to earthly things would suffer these things which the Lord threatens against Zedekiah and his people, who were unwilling to imitate their brothers or to come into Babylon: that he sends upon them the sword and famine and plague, that is, the want of all things, and makes them like very bad figs, which utterly cannot be eaten, and pursues them with an everlasting sword and gives them over to vexation to all the kingdoms of the earth, so that, namely, they become not men at all but demons, aerial powers, and […]

29:15.t: 'And since I,' he says, 'am going to do these things of my own accord and to restore you at a fixed time, you are deceived in vain and think that you have prophets in Babylon who promise you false things; so know, then, that you ought by no means to hope for a return now, but to build houses, plant orchards, take wives and beget sons and multiply in number and await the promised time. Hear what the Lord says to Zedekiah, who now reigns in Jerusalem, and to all the inhabitants of his city, that is, to your brothers, who were unwilling to obey my sentence and to migrate to Babylon with you: that they can by no means escape captivity, but will die by sword and famine and plague, and that he will make them like bad figs', which Theodotion and Aquila's first edition translated 'sudrinas', the second 'very bad', Symmachus 'last'; […]

29:18.t: 'And I will pursue,' he says, 'them, who now dwell in the city of Jerusalem, with sword, famine and pestilence, so that, first by the siege, and then at once, those who have been able to remain and escape may be scattered into all lands and be an example of curse, astonishment and hissing and reproach to all among whom I shall cast them out, because they did not hear my words, says the Lord, which I spoke to them through my servants, rising up by night and sending, and I never ceased admonishing them to imitate you, who now in exile enjoy a secure leisure until the Lord's promise is fulfilled. But you, who obeyed my sentence and handed yourselves over to the Babylonian king, hear what I am about to say'.

29:21.t: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to Ahab son of Kolaiah and to Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who prophesy to you in my name falsely: Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he will strike them before your eyes. And from them a curse will be taken up by all the exile of Judah that is in Babylon, saying: May the Lord make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon fried in the fire, because they did folly — or iniquity — in Israel and committed adultery with the wives of their friends — or fellow citizens — and spoke a word in my name falsely, which I did not command them; I am judge and witness, says the Lord. The Hebrews say that these are the elders who did folly in Israel and committed adultery with the wives of their fellow citizens, to one of whom Daniel says: you who have grown old in evil days and to the other: seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you and lust has perverted your heart! […]

29:22.t: [Daniel 13:60] "And the whole congregration (Vulgate: assembly) cried out with a great voice and blessed God, who saveth those who trust in Him..." If the whole congregation put them to death, the view which we mentioned earlier is apparently refuted, namely that these were the elders Ahab and Zedekiah, in conformity with Jeremiah's statement (Jeremiah 29:22). The only other possibility is that instead of taking the statement, "They killed them," literally, we interpret it as meaning that they gave them over to the king of Babylon to be put to death. That would be just like when we say that the Jews put the Savior to death; not that they smote Him themselves, but they gave Him over to be slain and cried out, "Crucify Him! Crucify Him!" (John 19:15).
29:22.s: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER THIRTEEN

29:22.t:
[Daniel 13:5] "And there were two of the elders of the people (the Vulgate omits: of the people) who were appointed judges that year." There was a Jew who used to allege that these men were Ahab and Zedekiah (variant: Alchias and Zedekiah), of whom Jeremiah wrote: "The Lord do to thee as Ahab and Zedekiah, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire because of the iniquity they had wrought in Israel and because they had committed adultery (variant: were committing adultery) with the wives of their citizens" (Jeremiah 29:22-23).

"It was concerning them that the Lord said that iniquity came forth from Babylon on the part of the ancient judges who appeared to govern the people. They used to frequent the house of Joakim..." Very appropriately it is not said of these sinful elders, "They governed the people," but rather, "They appeared to govern." […]
29:22.s: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER THIRTEEN

29:24.t: And to Shemaiah the Nehelamite you shall say; and what follows: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you have sent books in your own name to all the people that is in Jerusalem, is not found in the Seventy; and again they added of their own: I did not send you in my name, and consequently, in order: and to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, the priest, and again from the Hebrew: and to all the priests; and then the story is woven on: The Lord has made you priest in place of Jehoiada the priest, that you may be leader — or instructor and overseer — in the house of the Lord over every man who is possessed and prophesies, that you may put him in the stocks and in prison — or in custody and in the cataract, for which Symmachus put mochlon [a bar], and Aquila put the Hebrew word itself, 'sinac' —. And now why have you not rebuked Jeremiah the Anathothite, who prophesies to you? For on this account he sent to us in Babylon, saying: It is long; build houses and dwell, and plant gardens and eat their fruit! […]

29:28.t: He sent, he says, to us in Babylon, saying: It is far off. This is all that grieves him: that against his lie Jeremiah wrote the truth, that the return was far off and that they would return to Jerusalem after seventy years; and that therefore they ought to build houses, plant orchards and eat their fruit, take wives and beget sons, as the preceding discourse related.

29:29.t: When Zephaniah the priest had received this letter, which was written specifically in his name, he read it to Jeremiah, in a way insulting him and rebuking him by the very reading, as to why he dared to write such things to Babylon.

29:31.t: And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying: Send to all the exile, saying: Thus says the Lord to Shemaiah the Nehelamite: Because Shemaiah has prophesied to you and I did not send him, and he has made you trust in a lie, therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will visit upon Shemaiah the Nehelamite and upon his seed; there shall not be a man sitting in the midst of this people, and he shall not see the good which I will do to my people, says the Lord, because he has spoken transgression against the Lord. The false prophet Shemaiah, truly a 'Nehellamites', who had taken up foreign and troubled waters from the 'torrent', is angry that Jeremiah has written true things against his lie, and he sends letters to Zephaniah the priest, asking why the prophet dared to write the truth, and he desires that he be shut up in prison so that he may not speak. Zephaniah too secretly accuses the prophet, while he reads the letter of the liar and boasts that he holds his accusation. […]

29:32.t: Let the false prophet therefore hear, let the priest understand what he himself also deserves to hear through him: thus says the Lord: Behold, I will visit upon Shemaiah. This the Lord speaks, not the prophet: that he will visit upon Shemaiah the Nehelamite, not for remedy but for the punishment of the liar, according to that which is written: I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with scourges. Nor does he visit upon the false prophet alone, but also upon his seed, all the disciples whom he deceived by his error. There shall not be, he says, a man sitting in the midst of this people. Let the worst stock be blotted out of the assembly of the saints, and let him not sit in the midst of those at rest, who could not stand with those who stand, nor heard that saying: if he had stood in my substance. And whereas the Lord promises the perfection of all virtues when the sevenfold time is ended, he will not see the good which he claimed for himself in the present time. […]

30:2.t: This word, which came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Thus says the Lord God of Israel, saying: Write for yourself in a book all the words which I have spoken to you! For behold, days will come, says the Lord, and I will turn back the turning of my people Israel and Judah, says the Lord, and I will turn them back — or I will make them settle — into the land which I gave to their fathers, and they shall possess it. While the false prophets in Babylon were promising that the people who had been taken captive with Jeconiah would soon return, and while Hananiah son of Azzur was preaching the same things in Jerusalem, Jeremiah the prophet both asserted that this would indeed come to pass, not within two years, as they lied, but when the seventy years were finished, and now he is ordered to write in a book and to hand down to remembrance the things which the Lord foretells are to come. […]

30:3.t: The length of the book of Jeremiah the prophet overcomes our purpose, so that, however briefly, we nonetheless say much. Hence the present sixth book of the commentaries on Jeremiah will also contain the mystical promises which the Jews, and our Judaizers, think are to be fulfilled at the consummation of the world; for they cannot prove that they were already fulfilled under Zerubbabel. We, however, following the authority of the apostles and evangelists, and above all of the Apostle Paul, show that whatever is promised carnally to the people of Israel has been fulfilled spiritually in us and is being fulfilled today, and that there is no other contest between Jews and Christians but this: that, while they and we both believe that Christ the Son of God has been promised, the things that are to be under Christ are said by us to have been fulfilled, by them to be yet fulfilled. […]

30:5.t: And these are the words which the Lord spoke to Israel and to Judah, for thus says the Lord: We have heard a voice of terror — or of fear —; dread, and there is no peace. Ask and see whether a male gives birth! Why then have I seen the hand of every man upon his loins, as of a woman giving birth, and all faces have been turned into jaundice? First sad things are announced, so that after the greatness of the evils glad things may follow; for health is more welcome when sickness has been driven off, and the greatness of pain is turned into a greatness of joys. What he says, then, is this: so great will be the fear and so great the dread that, peace having been put to flight, all things will be filled with wars and blood, and that a womanish terror will take hold even of the men, whose proper task is to fight against adversaries, and they will put their hands by no means to arms but to holding their kidneys, as if a woman giving birth were clutching her flanks and loins. […]

30:7.t: Woe, for great is that day, nor is there any like it, and it is the time of the tribulation of Jacob! and from it he shall be saved. He foretells the time of misery in order to bring in the time of joy. 'Although,' he says, 'such great evils have gone before that the pain of all the men is compared to the pain of a woman giving birth, yet the time of the tribulation of Jacob, that is, of the people of God, will be changed into prosperity, and from it too he shall be saved' — 'time' is understood —, 'of which the discourse had spoken'. But by 'Jacob' understand the twelve tribes, which were saved by no means under Zerubbabel, as some falsely suppose, but by the calling of the Gospel.

30:8.t:
And God promises that He will break from those who are thus to be saved the old heavy yoke of bitter daemons and shatter the bonds of the sins by which they were held of old, so that they will no more serve strange gods, but bear fruit and please Him only. Compare with this the oracle in the Second Psalm concerning the Coming of Christ and the calling of the Gentiles, which says: "Let us break their bonds asunder, and cast off their yoke from us." To which, I think, this we are considering is akin when it says:

"In that day, saith the Lord, I will break the yoke from off their necks, and shatter their bonds, and they shall not serve other gods, but shall serve the Lord their God."
30:8.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 7, Chapter 3

30:8.t: And it shall be in that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will break his yoke from off your neck and I will burst his bonds, and strangers shall no longer rule over him, but they shall serve — or work for — the Lord their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them. This is the David whom the Gospel also mentions: that he would grant us that, without fear, delivered from the hand of our enemies, we might serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. For just as a first Adam and a second Adam are written of according to the truth of the body, so also the Lord and Savior is David, because according to the flesh he is from David, holy Mary contributing to him wholly whatever was of the stock of David, while she had the origin and conception from the Holy Spirit. And as for his saying: I will break his yoke from off your neck and I will burst his bonds, there is no doubt that under the type of Nebuchadnezzar it must be understood of the devil.

30:10.t: You therefore, do not fear, my servant Jacob, says the Lord, nor be afraid, Israel, for behold, I will save you from a far-off land, and your seed from the land of their captivity, and Jacob shall return and be at rest and abound in all things, and there shall be none whom he fears, since I am with you, says the Lord, to save you. For I will make a full end among all the nations among which I have scattered you; but you I will not bring to a full end, but I will chastise — or instruct — you in judgment, so that you may not seem to yourself guiltless or and cleansing, I will not cleanse you. This perikopē [passage] is not found in the Seventy, and in very many manuscripts of the common edition it has been added under asterisks from Theodotion. […]

30:11.t: And this will come about because they will enjoy the presence of the Lord, when the hostile nations which had captured them will perish and these will be set free from among the nations. And he teaches that they were handed over by no means to punishment but to instruction, so that they might be judged as his own, not destroyed as strangers; for he who does not believe has already been judged, that is, judged beforehand unto destruction. And what he added: so that you may not seem to yourself guiltless, or according to Symmachus: and cleansing, I will not cleanse you, or according to Aquila: when I have instructed you through judgment, I will by no means make you innocent, signifies that the whole world stands in need of the mercy of God, and that no one, however holy he may be, goes to the judge secure; […]

30:12.t: But that "contrition" and "a sore of pain through chastisement" are imposed on the soul for the sake of cure, Jeremiah teaches, saying: "Thus said the Lord: I have raised up contrition, thy sore is with pain, there is none that judges thy judgment, thou art cured with pain, there is no profit in thee. All thy friends have forgotten thee, nor will they now inquire concerning thee; because I have smitten thee with the wound of an enemy, with strong chastisement, for all thy iniquity, since thy sins are multiplied. Why criest thou out over thy contrition? Thy pain is violent, because of the multitude of thy iniquities thy sins have prevailed and have done these things to thee. Therefore all who devour thee shall be devoured, and all thine enemies shall devour their own flesh; and those who afflicted thee shall be in affliction, and all who devastated thee I will give over to plunder; for I will recall thy health, and from the pain of thy wound I will recall thee, said the Lord."

For thus says the Lord: Incurable is your fracture, most grievous your wound. There is none who judges your judgment for binding up; there is no benefit of healings for you. All your lovers have forgotten you, they will not seek you; for I have struck you with the blow of an enemy, with cruel chastisement — or strong —. Because of the multitude of your iniquity have become hard — or have been multiplied — your sins. Why do you cry out over your crushing? Incurable is your pain; because of the multitude of your iniquity and because of your hard sins I have done these things to you. He speaks as to a beautiful woman, to whom he had said above: I will chastise you in judgment, so that you may not seem to yourself guiltless or innoxia [guiltless, in the feminine]; […]

30:16.t: Therefore all who devour you shall be devoured, and all your enemies shall be led into captivity, and those who lay you waste shall be laid waste, and all your plunderers I will give up as plunder. For I will draw a scar over you and from your wounds I will heal you, says the Lord, because they have called you cast out — or scattered —, Zion: this is she who had no one seeking her. And we know that these things were done under Zerubbabel too. When the Babylonians and Chaldeans laid waste the Assyrians, that is, Nineveh, and the Medes and Persians in turn captured the Babylonians and Chaldeans and Babylon was destroyed, then Zion began to have the Lord seeking her, and a scar was drawn over her wound and she was healed of her blows; which is fulfilled more fully and more perfectly in Christ.

30:18.t: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will turn back the turning of the tents of Jacob, and on the dwellings — or captivity — of them I will have mercy, and the city shall be built on its height, and the temple shall be founded according to its order. And from them shall go forth praise and the voice of those playing, and I will multiply them and they shall not be diminished; and what follows: and I will glorify them and I will not make them few, is not found in the Seventy. And his sons, he says, shall be as from the beginning, and his assembly shall abide before me, and I will visit against all who afflict him. And his leader shall be from himself, and a prince shall be brought forth from his midst, and I will draw him close and he shall approach me; for who is this who draws his heart close so as to come near to me?, says the Lord; and again, what follows in the Hebrew is not found in the Greek: and you shall be, he says, my people, and I will be your God. […]

30:19.t: Then there went forth praise or thanksgiving — for this is what 'thoda' signifies —, so that all the apostles said: grace to you and peace, and the voice of those playing, not with that play with which the people ate and drank and rose up to play, but with that with which David played before the ark of the Lord. And they were multiplied and not diminished, so that the whole world believed in God the Savior, and they were glorified, so that what is written was fulfilled: Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God!

30:20.t: And his sons, that is, the apostles, were as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the princes of the race of Israel, were from the beginning. Then the Lord visited against all who afflicted the people of God, namely the adverse powers.

30:21.t: And there was his leader from himself — no doubt the Lord and Savior, according to the flesh from the race of Israel — and a prince from his midst was brought forth. The Father drew him close to himself, and he approached him, so that the Son might say: I in the Father and the Father in me, because no one can so draw his heart close to the Lord, nor be joined to him as the Son is to the Father.

30:22.t: And what he says according to the Hebrew only, but not according to the Seventy: and you shall be my people, and I will be your God, we see fulfilled in deed, in part in Israel and wholly in the multitude of the nations.

30:23.t: Behold, the whirlwind of the Lord, fury going forth, a storm rushing down, shall come to rest upon the head of the wicked. The Lord will not turn back the anger of his indignation until he does and fulfills the purpose of his heart; in the last of days you will understand these things. The whirlwind of the Lord's fury and the rushing storm and tempest will rest upon the head of the wicked, whether of the demons or of those who blasphemed the Son of God; and he will not turn back the anger of his indignation until he does and fulfills the purpose of his heart, and until Jerusalem is surrounded by an army and utterly destroyed. Now just as a craftsman cannot be understood except when the work is completed, nor the diligence of medicine except after health has been attained, so, when the overthrow of Jerusalem and the casting off of the former people have come about, then believers will understand that the rejection of the Jews is the occasion of our salvation.

31:1.t: At that time, says the Lord, I will be God to all the families of Israel — or to the race of Israel — and they shall be to me for a people. Unless the thought of the Lord has been fulfilled and his fury has come to rest upon the head of the ungodly, the Lord of the universe cannot be God to the families of Israel; but this he says to the remnant, which has been saved. But if what is said is set against us: I will be God to the race of Israel or to all the families of Israel, let us take up an example: 'if you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of your father'; and the Apostle writes: behold Israel according to the flesh. From this he teaches that there is another Israel according to the spirit. That one, then, is Israel who discerns God with the mind, or is the most upright one of the Lord, and an Israel of this kind will be the people of God.

31:2.t: With this sense the words of Jeremiah also agree, spoken in the person of the Lord: As something warm in the desert, I found Israel with those slain by the sword (Jer 38:2 LXX; Vulg. 31:2). For when, he says, the whole world lay lifeless, wounded by the swords of idolatry, I found Israel in Abraham to have the warmth of faith, like a physician who after a battle, among the corpses of the dead, where he perceives that someone still has something of life in his beating veins, applies care to his wounds to restore him to health. For what is written ὡς θερμὸν, that is, as something warm, the Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, rendered lupine, and in this most of the Greeks also err. And yet it should be known that in the Hebrew, for warmth, THODA (תודה) is written, which means grace: namely, that Israel was saved by the grace of God, and not by the merit of its own works.

Thus says the Lord: the people that had remained from the sword found grace in the desert; Israel shall go to its rest. LXX: thus said the Lord: I found warm in the desert with those who had perished by the sword; go, and do not kill Israel! Ridiculously, in this place the Latin codices, through the ambiguity of the Greek word, translated 'lupines' for 'warm'; for the Greek THERMON signifies both, and it is not itself found in the Hebrew. For there is written 'hen', which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion translated as charin, that is, 'grace'; the Seventy alone put 'warm', thinking that the last letter was 'm'. For if we read 'hen' with the letter 'n', it means 'grace'; if with 'm', it is interpreted 'heat'. Now the sense according to the Hebrew is this: the people of the Jews, which had remained from the Roman sword, or at any rate had been able to escape the wrath of the Lord's fury, found grace in the desert of the nations, so that amid the crowd of the nations it might be saved in the Church; […]

31:3.t: From afar the Lord appeared to me — or to him — : and with an everlasting love I have loved you; therefore I have drawn you, having pity. And again I will build you and you shall be built, virgin Israel. Again you shall be adorned with your timbrels — or you shall take up your timbrels — and you shall go forth in the dance of those who make merry. Again you shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria; plant plantings and gather the vintage! for there shall be a day on which the watchmen on Mount Ephraim shall cry: arise, and let us go up into Zion to the Lord our God! Because Israel had offended the Lord and had said: we have no king but Caesar, and: come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours, and had withdrawn far from God, therefore the Lord after a long time appeared to him — not in the time of Zerubbabel and Ezra, after they were taken captive again —, but with an everlasting love, which will be blotted out by no end, he loved him, and drew him, having pity; […]

31:4.t: And again, he says, I will build you and you shall be built, virgin Israel. Let us understand this properly of the Church; for they rave who sigh for a golden and jeweled Jerusalem, consecrating their own avarice in the mystery of the Lord's city. 'Again you shall be adorned with your timbrels, so that you may sing to the Lord in the churches, all the flesh of evil works in you having been consumed, and you shall go forth in the dance of those who make merry with the crowds of the nations, you shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria', not at all in the valleys and low places, but on the mountains of Samaria, which after the captivity of the people of Israel were possessed by foreigners, to whom it is said: plant plantings and gather the vintage!

31:6.t: Then was the day of the Lord, on which the watchmen — namely the apostles and apostolic men — cried on mount 'Samaria' and on mount 'Ephraim', of which the one sounds 'guard', the other 'fruitfulness'; but what do the watchmen of Samaria say, nay rather, what do they cry on Mount Ephraim? 'Arise, you who lie down, leave lowly things, spurn the offerings of victims' — a sacrifice to the Lord is a troubled spirit —, 'let us go up into Zion, that is, into the Church, where there is 'contemplation' and the beholding of God; and when we are in Zion, nay rather have gone up to it, we shall go up likewise to the Lord our God'.

31:7.t: For thus says the Lord: exult with gladness, Jacob, and neigh against the head of the nations; sound aloud, sing and say: save, O Lord, your people, the remnant of Israel! Significantly, not the whole of Israel is saved, but the remnant of Israel, the Lord commanding and saying: 'exult with gladness, you who are of Jacob, and neigh toward the head of the nations, referring all things to it, because the tail was once turned into the head; sound aloud and sing and say!' What is it that they are bidden to say? Save, O Lord, your people. Which people? Surely the remnant of Israel, which has been saved according to election, of whom Paul too speaks, taking up the testimony of Isaiah: unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us seed, we should have become as Sodom and we should have been made like Gomorrah.

31:8.t: When Jeremiah says, "And I will gather them together from the extremities of the land in the feast day," he signifies the day of the Passover and of Pentecost, which is properly a "feast day." However, every day is the Lord's. Every hour, every time, is apt for baptism. If there is a difference in the solemnity, there is no distinction in the grace.

Behold, I will bring them from the land of the north and will gather them from the ends of the earth; and what follows: at the solemnity of the Passover; and it shall beget many sons, is not found in the Hebrew, but is read only in the Seventy, in place of which among the Hebrews is written: among whom shall be the blind and the lame and the woman with child and the woman giving birth together, a great church of those returning hither. The remnant of the people of Israel is gathered through the apostles and apostolic men, of whom we read above: the watchmen shall cry on the mount, and to whom it is commanded: sound aloud and sing and say, so that the remnant of Israel may be saved. […]

31:9.t: With weeping they shall come — or they shall go out — and in mercy I will lead them back, and I will bring them through torrents of waters in a straight way, and they shall not stumble — or they shall not go astray — in it, for I have become a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn. If we read according to the Hebrew: with weeping they shall come — for this is what 'iabu' indicates —, we shall say that sometimes weeping is also a sign of excessive joy, according to that saying: I weep for joy. But if according to the Seventy, who said: with weeping they shall go out and in mercy — or in consolation — I will lead them back, we shall set down that sense which is also spoken in the Psalms: going they went and wept, carrying their seeds; but coming they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves. For they wept when they were led away captive, and they received the greatest consolation when they were led back by the mercy of the Lord. […]

31:10.t: Hear the word of the Lord, O nations, and declare it to the islands that are far off, and say: he who scattered Israel will gather him and will keep him as a shepherd his flock, for the Lord has redeemed Jacob and has delivered him from the hand of one more powerful — or stronger —. And they shall come and shall praise on Mount Zion and shall flow together to the good things of the Lord, over grain and wine and oil and the young of flocks and of herds. Their soul shall be like a watered garden — or like a fruit-bearing tree — and they shall hunger no more. Then the virgin shall rejoice in the dance — or virgins — and young men and old together, and I will turn their mourning into joy and will console them and make them glad from their sorrow, and I will inebriate the soul of the priests with fatness — or of the sons of Levi — and my people shall be filled with my good things, says the Lord. […]

31:12.t: And they shall come, he says, — no doubt delivered from the hand of the powerful — and shall praise their deliverer on Mount Zion, that is, in the Church, and shall flow together to the good things of the Lord, the abundance of all things, which is perceived not in the fruits and foods of this flesh, but in the variety of the virtues. Over grain, he says, and wine and oil — from which the bread of the Lord is made, and the type of his blood is fulfilled, and the blessing of sanctification is shown, Scripture saying: God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows — and the young of flocks, who are the simple in the Church, and of herds, which are horned and toss the adversaries. But that we may know that these blessings do not pertain at all to the body but to the soul, there follows: and their soul shall be like a watered garden or like a fruit-bearing tree, which is planted beside the streams of waters, and the paradise of the Lord in delights. And no more, he says, shall they hunger; […]

31:13.t: Then the virgin shall rejoice in the dance — of whom the Apostle writes: for I have betrothed you to one husband, to present a chaste virgin to Christ — and the young men — to whom John speaks: I write to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one — and the old, to whom the same testifies in mystical speech: I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. And I will turn, he says, their mourning into joy — so that the resurrection may gladden those whom the cross had terrified — and I will console them and make them glad from their sorrow — according to what the Lord says: blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be consoled — and I will inebriate the soul of the priests, who have the knowledge of God, from whose mouth they ask the law of the Lord, who believe in him to whom the prophet sings: you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. […]

31:15.t: Why then need I watch the rising and setting of the stars, at whose rising the fallows should be ploughed up and pierced by the hard plough-shares, and at whose setting the fruitful crop should be cut down by the sickle? One star suffices for me in the place of all others, the bright and morning Star, at Whose rising was sown the seed not of corn but of martyrs; when Rachel wept for her children, and offered in the stead of Christ her children washed in her own tears. The setting of this Star raised from the tomb not the senseless relics of the funeral pile, but the triumphant bands of the re-animated dead.

Then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah, saying: A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and great wailing, Rachel weeping for her sons, and she would not be consoled, because they are not. Of Rachel was born Benjamin, in whose tribe Bethlehem does not lie. It is asked, therefore, how Rachel weeps for the sons of Judah, that is, of Bethlehem, as if they were her own. We shall answer briefly: because she was buried near Bethlehem in Ephrathah (from the inner lodging of her little body she received the name of mother); or else because Judah and Benjamin were two joined tribes, and Herod had commanded that the boys be killed not only in Bethlehem but in all its borders round about; by occasion of Bethlehem we understand that many of Benjamin also were slain. And she weeps for her sons and does not receive consolation according to a twofold understanding: either because she thought them dead for ever, or because she would not be consoled for those whom she knew would live. […]

Thus says the Lord: a voice of lamentation was heard on high, of weeping and mourning, of Rachel bewailing her sons, and she would not be consoled over her sons, because they are not. LXX: thus said the Lord: a voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation and weeping and mourning, of Rachel bewailing her sons, and she would not be quieted, because they are not. Matthew took the testimony neither according to the Hebrew nor according to the Seventy; for we read in him, after the description of the slaughter of the infants: then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: a voice was heard in Ramah, wailing and much howling, of Rachel weeping for her sons, and she would not be consoled, because they are not. From this it is clear that the evangelists and apostles did not at all follow anyone's translation from the Hebrew, but, as Hebrews from Hebrews, expressed in their own words what they read in Hebrew. […]

According to the oracle of Jeremiah, "A voice was heard in Ramah," that is, "on high," "of lamentation and great wailing." This clearly denotes that holy church's mourning, by which it grieves for the violent death of its members, does not, as our enemies foolishly claim, pass away into a void, but it ascends right to the throne of the heavenly judge.

31:16.t: Thus says the Lord: let your voice cease from wailing and your eyes from tears, for there is a reward for your work, says the Lord, and they shall return from the land of the enemy — or of the enemies — and there shall be hope for your last end, says the Lord, and the sons shall return to their borders. This has not yet happened according to the letter — for we do not read that the ten tribes, which are in exile in the cities of the Medes and of the Persians, have returned to the land of Judea —, but according to the spirit it was fulfilled in the passion of the Lord and is being fulfilled up to now, when Israel is saved from the whole world and it is said to Rachel: let your voice cease from wailing and your eyes from tears!, and the sense is: 'cease to wail — for the Lord has looked upon your former works — and your sons shall return from the land of the enemy, and do not be held by present sorrow! […]

31:18.t: Let us purify ourselves by tears, that the Lord our God may hear us when we lament, as he heard Ephraim when weeping, as it is written: "I have surely heard Ephraim weeping." He expressly repeats the words of Ephraim: "You have chastised me, and I was chastised; like a calf I was not trained." For a calf shows itself off and leaves its stall, and so Ephraim was untrained like a calf far away from the stall, because he had forsaken the stall of the Lord, followed Jeroboam and worshiped the calves, which future event was prophetically indicated through Aaron, namely, that the people of the Jews would fall after this manner. And so repenting, Ephraim says, "Turn me, and I shall be turned, for you are the Lord my God. Surely in the end of my captivity I repented, and after I learned I mourned over the days of confusion and subjected myself to you because I received reproach and made you known."

Hearing I heard Ephraim going into exile — or lamenting — : you have chastised me and I was instructed like an untamed bullock — or like a calf, and I did not learn — ; convert me, and I shall be converted, for you are the Lord my God. For after you converted me — or I was taken captive —, I repented, and after I knew — or you showed me —, I struck my thigh — or I groaned — ; I was confounded and blushed — or from the day of confusion and I showed you —, because I bore the reproach of my youth. God says what he heard Ephraim saying and lamenting. Now no one doubts that it signifies the ten tribes, over which Jeroboam son of Nebat first ruled, who also made the golden calves in Dan and Bethel, so that the people, seduced by this error, might cease to worship and adore the God of Israel. You have chastised me, he says, and I was chastised. Every correction, which for the present seems to be of sadness, profits for salvation and afterwards brings peaceable fruits. […]

31:19.t: See how great is the help of God and how frail the human condition, that this very thing, that we repent, we are not at all able to accomplish unless the Lord has first converted us. 'And after', he says, 'you showed me either repentance itself or the knowledge of you, or I knew you, I struck my thigh.' This is the sign of one grieving and lamenting and bewailing his former error: that he strikes his thigh with his hand and confesses that he was foolish before. I was confounded, he says, and blushed or from the day of confusion. For what time is not one of our confusion, if we recall our ancient sins and call to memory all the things we have done ill? And what the Seventy said: and I showed you, signifies that, after he groaned and knew his own offenses, he then came to such progress that he even showed God to others who did not know him, according to what David too says in repentance: I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly shall be converted to you. Because I bore, he says, the reproach of my youth. […]

31:20.t: For we reckon the ages of soul and of body alike, not by the reckoning of time but by the quality of virtue, so that he is called a perfect man who is free from the error of childhood and through maturity of mind does not feel the slipperiness of youth, but he is called little who seems to have made as yet no progress in virtue. Hence that saying in Jeremiah, when the Lord had pity on Ephraim weeping and begging pardon for his own sins: From my youth he says Ephraim is a beloved son to me, a child in delights. For had he not been a child in delights, he would never have sinned. And well did he say both, that he was in delights and that he was a child; for he is a child who does not sin. Behold my child, whom I have chosen. Through delights, then, he sinned who had been so formed by the Lord as to be ignorant of error. […]

Is Ephraim an honorable son — or beloved — to me, is he a delicate child? for, since I spoke of him — or my words in him —, I will still remember him; therefore my bowels are troubled over him; pitying I will have pity on him, says the Lord. Since Ephraim repents and says at the beginning: you have instructed me and I was instructed like an untamed bullock, and at the end: because I bore the reproach of my youth, the Lord answers, and sustains him, turned to him with his whole mind, with such an oracle: 'Ephraim is a beloved son to me, whom I loved so much from the beginning that I preferred him to his brother Manasseh.' An honorable son, who against the order of nature received the honor of the firstborn by the condescension of the Lord; a delicate child, of whom he writes: the sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle, against whom and to whom the whole book of the prophet Hosea is addressed, whom Jacob blesses. […]

31:21.t: Set up for yourself watchtowers, put for yourself bitternesses, direct your heart into the straight way in which you walked; return, virgin Israel, return to these your cities! How long will you be dissolved in delights, wandering daughter? for the Lord has created a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man. LXX: set up for yourself lookouts, make punishment, give your heart to your shoulders; the way in which you walked, return, virgin Israel, return to your cities mourning! How long will you turn away, despised daughter? for the Lord has created you as salvation for a new planting; in your salvation men shall go about. Where we said: how long will you be dissolved in delights?, Symmachus put: how long will you sink into the deep? Now I have set out each edition in full, in order to show that a most obscure passage, one containing the mysteries of the Church, was either unknown to or omitted by the Seventy — or whoever else translated this prophet. […]

31:22.t:
A figure preceded in the woman and the man, because Jeremiah says: "A woman shall encompass a man." All of this was fulfilled in the glorious Virgin. Whence Bernard says: "What was shown to Moses in the bush and fire, to Aaron in the rod and flower, to Gideon in the fleece and dew: this Solomon clearly foresaw in the strong woman and her price; more clearly Jeremiah foretold concerning the woman and the man; most clearly Isaiah declared concerning the Virgin and her son; and at last Gabriel made it manifest by greeting the Virgin."

The word of Jeremiah concerns the woman and the man: "A new thing," he says, "the Lord will make upon the earth; a woman shall encompass a man." Who brought it about that the Virgin conceived? Certainly the Holy Spirit, who is a love fervent, fruitful, undefiled, virile, incorrupt, and deifying. That he is a virile love is signified to us in the woman and the man, because the "woman encompassed the man," that is, enclosed him on every side.

31:23.t: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: they shall still say this word in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I turn back their captivity: the Lord bless you, beauty of righteousness, holy mountain! And Judah shall dwell in it, and all its cities together, husbandmen and those who drive flocks. LXX: thus said the Lord of powers, the God of Israel: they shall still say this speech in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I bring back its exile: blessed be the Lord upon his righteous holy mountain, and those who dwell in the land of Judea and in every city of it with the husbandman; and he shall be lifted up in the flock. According to the Hebrew it is plain that at the return of Israel, its captivity having been turned back into its own land, the cities of Judah dwell, and it is said to them one by one: the Lord bless you, who is truly the beauty of righteousness and the holy mountain, in which whoever dwells will fear no snares; […]

31:25.t: For I have inebriated the weary soul — or for I have inebriated every thirsting soul — and every hungering soul I have satisfied — or I have filled —, therefore I awoke and saw, and my sleep was sweet to me. The change of persons makes the understanding of the prophets obscure. The Lord had said: they shall still say this word in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I turn back their captivity. And what shall they say? No doubt this, which follows: the Lord bless you, beauty of righteousness, holy mountain, and the rest. And again, while they say these things, the Lord answers: for I have inebriated the weary soul — or thirsting — and every hungering soul I have satisfied. And while he says these things, the people that had come from captivity answers: therefore I awoke and saw, and my sleep was sweet to me. […]

31:26.t: Let us, then, submit ourselves to God, and not be subject to sin, and when we ponder the remembrance of our offences, let us blush as though at some disgrace, and not speak of them as a glory to us, as some boast of overcoming modesty, or putting down the feeling of justice. Let our conversion be such, that we who did not know God may now ourselves declare Him to others, that the Lord, moved by such a conversion on our part, may answer to us: "Ephraim is from youth a dear son, a pleasant child, for since My words are concerning him, I will verily remember him, therefore have I hastened to be over him; I will surely have mercy on him, saith the Lord." And what mercy He promises us, the Lord also shows, when He says further on: "I have satiated every thirsty soul, and have satisfied every hungry soul. Therefore, I awaked and beheld, and My sleep was sweet unto Me." We observe that the Lord promises His sacraments to those who sin. Let us, then, all be converted to the Lord.

For you should not be surprised if the Prophet says that his soul is disturbed, since the Lord Jesus himself said: "Now my soul is troubled." For he who took on our weaknesses also took on our emotions, in which he was sad even unto death, not because of death; for voluntary death could not have sorrow, in which the joy and refreshment of all was to come. Of this he also said elsewhere: "And I arose, and saw, and a sweet sleep came to me." Blessed sleep that made the hungry not hunger, the thirsty not thirst, for whom he prepared the sweetness of the sacraments. So how then was his soul troubled by fear, who made the souls of others not fear? Sorrowful even unto death, until grace was perfected: which is proven by his own testimony saying of his death: "With the baptism I am to be baptized, and how am I distressed until it is accomplished?"

And those who had been weary and had hungered, inebriated and satisfied, give thanks, answering: 'I awoke and saw the Lord', namely raising them up and saying: arise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you. 'And my sleep', he says, 'was sweet to me, so that I might imitate the words of my Lord, who says: I slept and was put to rest; and I rose up, because the Lord sustained me'.

31:27.t: Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of men and the seed of beasts. And as I watched over them to pluck up and to demolish and to scatter and to destroy and to afflict, so I will watch over them to build and to plant, says the Lord. In those days they shall no longer say: the fathers have eaten a sour grape and the teeth of the sons are set on edge; but each one shall die in his own iniquity; every man who eats the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge. 'House' and 'house', that is, the house of Israel and the house of Judah, is not in the Seventy, but only: Israel and Judah, so that it reads: and I will sow Israel and Judah. And what he added: with the seed of men and the seed of beasts, we ought to refer to the rational and the simple.

31:28.t: And as at the beginning of Jeremiah it was said to him: 'behold, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to pluck up and pull down and destroy and scatter and build and plant, — and I watched over them, to do what I threatened, — so', he says, 'now I will watch over them to build and to plant; God's indeed husbandry, God's building you are.' All promises of this kind are thought, according to the Jews and our Judaizers, to be fulfilled in a kingdom of a thousand years. But we, since the Apostle says: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase, and the prophet Isaiah records that the Savior is the builder of hedges and of houses, maintain that they were fulfilled spiritually at the first coming of Christ — and fulfilled in part, not in whole, because now we see in a mirror and in an enigma, and we do not know as we ought to know; […]

31:29.t: In the mean time, whom will you be able to persuade that by receiving the lapsed the whole Church hath perished? That by the admission of penitents, the people of those who admit them has been made a denier of the Faith? But even if the people here or there have been too lax, have the other peoples also who approved not of their deed, but followed custom and peace, lost the Christian name? Hear the voice of Jeremiah, In those days shall they not say, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children's teeth are set on edge. But every one shall die for his own iniquity.

And what is brought in: in those days they shall no longer say: the fathers have eaten a sour grape and the teeth of the sons are set on edge, and the rest, we discussed more fully in the explanations of Ezekiel, when we interpreted that place: son of man, what is this parable to you among the sons of Israel, who say: the fathers have eaten a sour grape and the teeth of the sons are set on edge? As I live, says the Lord, if this parable shall be any longer in Israel! for all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son; the soul that sins, it shall die. By this we learn that it is not the Lord who makes death, but sin; for the soul that sins, it shall die. And this is said in the present place: that Israel will not at all stumble forever because of the sins of the fathers, but will be saved by its own merits and by faith in Christ after many ages. […]

31:31.t: All things therefore are of one and the same substance, that is, from one and the same God; as also the Lord says to the disciples "Therefore every scribe, which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven, is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old." He did not teach that he who brought forth the old was one, and he that brought forth the new, another; but that they were one and the same. For the Lord is the good man of the house, who rules the entire house of His Father; and who delivers a law suited both for slaves and those who are as yet undisciplined; and gives fitting precepts to those that are free, and have been justified by faith, as well as throws His own inheritance open to those that are sons. And He called His disciples "scribes" and "teachers of the kingdom of heaven;" of whom also He elsewhere says to the Jews: "Behold, I send unto you wise men, and scribes, and teachers; and some of them ye shall kill, and persecute from city to city." […]

For we find in the Scriptures, as the Lord says, "Behold, I make with you a new covenant, not as I made with your ancestors in Mount Horeb." He made a new covenant with us. For what belonged to the Greeks and Jews is old. But we, who worship him in a new way, in the third form, are Christians. For clearly, as I think, he showed that the one and only God was known by the Greeks in a Gentile way, by the Jews Judaically and in a new and spiritual way by us.
